problems.title: Estimating the Avogadro constant
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (36 points, 9% of the total). Estimating the Avogadro constant

Many different methods have been used to determine the Avogadro constant. Three different methods are given below.

Method A – from X-ray diffraction data (modern)

The unit cell is the smallest repeating unit in a crystal structure. The unit cell of a gold crystal is found by X-ray diffraction to have the face-centred cubic unit structure (i.e. where the centre of an atom is located at each corner of a cube and in the middle of each face). The side of the unit cell is found to be $0.408\,\mathrm{nm}$.

a) (4 pt) Sketch the unit cell and calculate how many Au atoms the cell contains.

b) (4 pt) The density of Au is $1.93\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Calculate the volume and mass of the cubic unit cell.

c) (4 pt) Hence calculate the mass of a gold atom and the Avogadro constant, given that the relative atomic mass of Au is 196.97.

Method B – from radioactive decay (Rutherford, 1911)

The radioactive decay series of $\ce{^{226}Ra}$ is as follows:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2009-1-fig1.png

The times indicated are half-lives, the units are y = years, d = days, m = minutes. The first decay, marked $t$ above, has a much longer half-life than the others.

d) (2 pt) In the table below, identify which transformations are α-decays and which are β-decays.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} & \alpha\text{-decay} & \beta\text{-decay} \\ \hline \ce{^{226}Ra -> ^{222}Rn} & & \\ \ce{^{222}Rn -> ^{218}Po} & & \\ \ce{^{218}Po -> ^{214}Pb} & & \\ \ce{^{214}Pb -> ^{214}Bi} & & \\ \ce{^{214}Bi -> ^{214}Po} & & \\ \ce{^{214}Po -> ^{210}Pb} & & \\ \ce{^{210}Pb -> ^{210}Bi} & & \\ \ce{^{210}Bi -> ^{210}Po} & & \\ \ce{^{210}Po -> ^{206}Pb} & & \end{array}$$

e) (1 pt) A sample containing $192\,\mathrm{mg}$ of $\ce{^{226}Ra}$ was purified and allowed to stand for 40 days. Identify the first isotope in the series (excluding Ra) that has not reached a steady state.

f) (2 pt) The total rate of α-decay from the sample was then determined by scintillation to be $27.7\,\mathrm{GBq}$ (where $1\,\mathrm{Bq} = 1\,\mathrm{count\,s^{-1}}$). The sample was then sealed for 163 days. Calculate the number of α particles produced.

g) (3 pt) At the end of the 163 days the sample was found to contain $10.4\,\mathrm{mm^{3}}$ of He, measured at $101325\,\mathrm{Pa}$ and $273\,\mathrm{K}$. Calculate the Avogadro constant from these data.

h) (6 pt) Given that the relative isotopic mass of $\ce{^{226}Ra}$ measured by mass spectrometry is 226.25, use the textbook value of the Avogadro constant ($6.022\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$) to calculate the number of $\ce{^{226}Ra}$ atoms in the original sample, $n_\mathrm{Ra}$, the decay rate constant, $\lambda$, and the half-life, $t$, of $\ce{^{226}Ra}$ (in years). You need only consider the decays up to but not including the isotope identified in (e).

Method C – dispersion of particles (Perrin, 1909)

One of the first accurate determinations of the Avogadro constant was carried out by studying the vertical distribution under gravity of colloidal particles suspended in water. In one such experiment, particles with radius $2.12\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}$ and density $1.206\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ were suspended in a tube of water at $15\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. After allowing sufficient time to equilibrate, the mean numbers of particles per unit volume observed at four heights from the bottom of the tube were:

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c} \text{height}\ /\ 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m} & 5 & 35 & 65 & 95 \\ \hline \text{mean number per unit volume} & 4.00 & 1.88 & 0.90 & 0.48 \end{array}$$

i) (4 pt) Assuming the particles to be spherical, calculate: the mass, $m$, of a particle; the mass of the water it displaces, $m_\mathrm{H_2O}$; and the effective mass, $m^*$, of the particle in water accounting for buoyancy (i.e. taking account of the upthrust due to the displaced volume of water). Take the density of water to be $999\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

At equilibrium, the number of particles per unit volume at different heights may be modelled according to a Boltzmann distribution:

$$\frac{n_h}{n_{h_0}} = \exp\left[-\frac{E_h - E_{h_0}}{RT}\right]$$

where $n_h$ is the number of particles per unit volume at height $h$,

$n_{h_0}$ is the number of particles per unit volume at the reference height $h_0$,

$E_h$ is the gravitational potential energy per mole of particles at height $h$ relative to the particles at the bottom of the tube,

$R$ is the gas constant, $8.3145\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$.

A graph of $\ln(n_h/n_{h_0})$ against $(h - h_0)$, based on the data in the table above, is shown below. The reference height is taken to be $5\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ from the bottom of the tube.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2009-1-fig2.png

j) (3 pt) Derive an expression for the gradient (slope) of the graph.

k) (3 pt) Determine the Avogadro constant from these data.

problems.title: Interstellar production of H2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (33 points, 9% of the total). Interstellar production of H₂

If two atoms collide in interstellar space the energy of the resulting molecule is so great that it rapidly dissociates. Hydrogen atoms only react to give stable $\ce{H2}$ molecules on the surface of dust particles. The dust particles absorb most of the excess energy and the newly formed $\ce{H2}$ rapidly desorbs. This question examines two kinetic models for $\ce{H2}$ formation on the surface of a dust particle.

In both models, the rate constant for adsorption of H atoms onto the surface of dust particles is $k_a = 1.4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{cm^{3}\,s^{-1}}$. The typical number density of H atoms (number of H atoms per unit volume) in interstellar space is $[\mathrm{H}] = 10\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$.

[Note: in the following, you may treat numbers of surface-adsorbed atoms and number densities of gas-phase atoms in the same way as you would normally use concentrations in the rate equations. As a result, the units of the rate constants may be unfamiliar to you. Reaction rates have units of numbers of atoms or molecules per unit time.]

a) (2 pt) Calculate the rate at which H atoms adsorb onto a dust particle. You may assume that this rate is constant throughout.

Desorption of H atoms is first order with respect to the number of adsorbed atoms. The rate constant for the desorption step is $k_d = 1.9\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

b) (2 pt) Assuming that only adsorption and desorption take place, calculate the steady-state number, $N$, of H atoms on the surface of a dust particle.

The H atoms are mobile on the surface. When they meet they react to form $\ce{H2}$, which then desorbs. The two kinetic models under consideration differ in the way the reaction is modelled, but share the same rate constants $k_a$, $k_d$, and $k_r$, for adsorption, desorption, and bimolecular reaction, as given below.

$k_a = 1.4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{cm^{3}\,s^{-1}}$

$k_d = 1.9\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$

$k_r = 5.1\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$

Model A

Reaction to form $\ce{H2}$ is assumed to be second order. On a dust particle the rate of removal of H atoms by reaction is $k_r N^2$.

c) (4 pt) Write down an equation for the rate of change of $N$, including adsorption, desorption and reaction. Assuming steady state conditions, determine the value of $N$.

d) (2 pt) Calculate the rate of production of $\ce{H2}$ per dust particle in this model

Model B

Model B attempts to analyse the probability that the dust particles carry 0, 1 or 2 H atoms. The three states are linked by the following reaction scheme. The assumption is made that no more than 2 atoms may be adsorbed simultaneously.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2009-2-fig1.png

$x_0$, $x_1$ and $x_2$ are the fractions of dust particles existing in state 0, 1 or 2, respectively. These fractions may be treated in the same way as concentrations in the following kinetic analysis. For a system in state $m$ with fraction $x_m$, the rates of the three possible processes are

Adsorption ($m \rightarrow m+1$): rate $= k_a[\mathrm{H}]x_m$

Desorption ($m \rightarrow m-1$): rate $= k_d m x_m$

Reaction ($m \rightarrow m-2$): rate $= \tfrac{1}{2} k_r m(m-1) x_m$

e) (6 pt) Write down equations for the rates of change, $\mathrm{d}x_m/\mathrm{d}t$, of the fractions $x_0$, $x_1$ and $x_2$.

f) (6 pt) Assuming steady-state conditions, use the above rate equations to find expressions for the ratios $x_2/x_1$ and $x_1/x_0$, and evaluate these ratios.

g) (3 pt) Evaluate the steady state fractions $x_0$, $x_1$ and $x_2$

[If you were unable to determine the ratios in (f), use $x_2/x_1 = a$ and $x_1/x_0 = b$ and give the result algebraically].

h) (2 pt) Evaluate the rate of production of $\ce{H2}$ per dust particle in this model

i) (6 pt) It is currently not possible to measure the rate of this reaction experimentally ., but the most recent computer simulations of the rate give a value of $9.4\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Which of the following statements apply to each model under these conditions? Mark any box you consider to be appropriate.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} \textbf{Statement} & \textbf{Model A} & \textbf{Model B} & \textbf{Neither model} \\ \hline \text{The rate determining step is adsorption of H atoms.} & & & \\ \hline \text{The rate-determining step is desorption of } \ce{H2} \text{ molecules.} & & & \\ \hline \text{The rate determining step is the bimolecular reaction of H atoms on the surface.} & & & \\ \hline \text{The rate determining step is adsorption of the second H atom.} & & & \\ \hline \text{The implicit assumption that reaction can take place regardless of the number of atoms} & & & \\ \text{adsorbed leads to substantial error (at least a factor of two).} & & & \\ \hline \text{Limiting the number of atoms adsorbed on the particle to 2 leads to substantial error} & & & \\ \text{(at least a factor of two).} & & & \end{array}$$

problems.title: Protein Folding
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (23 points, 11% of the total). Protein Folding

The unfolding reaction for many small proteins can be represented by the equilibrium:

$$\text{Folded} \rightleftharpoons \text{Unfolded}$$

You may assume that the protein folding reaction takes place in a single step. The position of this equilibrium changes with temperature; the melting temperature $T_m$ is defined as the temperature at which half of the molecules are unfolded and half are folded.

The intensity of the fluorescence signal at a wavelength of $356\,\mathrm{nm}$ of a $1.0\,\mathrm{\mu M}$ sample of the protein Chymotrypsin Inhibitor 2 (CI2) was measured as a function of temperature over the range 58 to $66\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Temp}\ /\,^\circ\mathrm{C} & 58 & 60 & 62 & 64 & 66 \\ \hline \text{Fluorescence intensity (arbitrary units)} & 27 & 30 & 34 & 37 & 40 \end{array}$$

A $1.0\,\mathrm{\mu M}$ sample in which all of the protein molecules are folded gives a fluorescence signal of 21 units at $356\,\mathrm{nm}$. A $1.0\,\mathrm{\mu M}$ sample in which all of the protein molecules are unfolded gives a fluorescence signal of 43 units.

a) (2.5 pt) Assuming that the fluorescence intensity from each species is directly proportional to its concentration, calculate the fraction, $x$, of unfolded molecules present at each temperature.

b) (3.5 pt) Give an expression for the equilibrium constant, $K$, in terms of $x$, and hence calculate the value of $K$ at each temperature.

c) (1 pt) Estimate the value of $T_m$ for this protein (to the nearest $1\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$).

Assuming that the values of $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ for the protein unfolding reaction are constant with temperature then:

$$\ln K = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{RT} + C$$

where $C$ is a constant.

d) (6 pt) Plot a suitable graph and hence determine the values of $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ for the protein unfolding reaction.

If you have been unable to calculate values for $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$, you should use the following incorrect values for the subsequent parts of the question:

$\Delta H^\circ = 130\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ $\qquad$ $\Delta S^\circ = 250\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$

e) (2 pt) Calculate the equilibrium constant for the unfolding reaction at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

If you have been unable to calculate a value for $K$, you should use the following incorrect values for the subsequent parts of the question: $K = 3.6\times10^{-6}$

The first order rate constant for the CI2 protein folding reaction can be determined by following the fluorescence intensity when a sample of unfolded protein is allowed to refold (typically the pH of the solution is changed). The concentration of unfolded protein when a $1.0\,\mathrm{\mu M}$ sample of unfolded CI2 was allowed to refold was measured at a temperature of $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{time}\ /\ \mathrm{ms} & 0 & 10 & 20 & 30 & 40 \\ \hline \text{concentration}\ /\ \mathrm{\mu M} & 1 & 0.64 & 0.36 & 0.23 & 0.14 \end{array}$$

f) (4 pt) Plot a suitable graph and hence determine the value of the rate constant for the protein folding reaction, $k_f$, at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

If you have been unable to calculate the values for $k_f$, you should use the following incorrect value for the subsequent parts of the question: $k_f = 60\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

g) (2 pt) Determine the value of the rate constant for the protein unfolding reaction, $k_u$, at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

h) (2 pt) At $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ the rate constant for the protein folding reaction is $33\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Calculate the activation energy for the protein folding reaction.

problems.title: Synthesis of Amprenavir
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (23 points, 9% of the total). Synthesis of Amprenavir

One class of anti-HIV drugs, known as protease inhibitors, works by blocking the active site of one of the enzymes used in assembly of the viruses within the host cell. Two successful drugs, saquinavir and amprenavir, contain the structural unit shown below which mimics the transition state within the enzyme. In the structure, $\mathrm{R^1}$, $\mathrm{R^2}$ and $\mathrm{R^3}$ may represent any atom or group other than hydrogen.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2009-4-fig1.png

Amprenavir may be synthesised as shown in the convergent scheme below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2009-4-fig2.png

The reagent $\ce{R2B-H}$ used in the first step is chiral. Product $\mathbf{A}$ is formed as the ($S$)-enantiomer.

3 of the signals in the $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectrum of Amprenavir disappear on shaking with $\ce{D2O}$: $\delta$ 4.2 (2H), $\delta$ 4.9 (1H) and $\delta$ 5.1 (1H).

Suggest structures for a) the intermediates $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{W}$, $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$, and b) for Amprenavir. Your answers should clearly show the stereochemistry at each centre.

[Points: a) $\mathbf{A}$ 4, $\mathbf{B}$ 3, $\mathbf{C}$ 2, $\mathbf{W}$ 3, $\mathbf{X}$ 3, $\mathbf{Y}$ 2, $\mathbf{Z}$ 3; b) Amprenavir 3.]

problems.title: Epoxy resins
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (35 points, 10% of the total). Epoxy resins

The synthesis of epoxy resins is a multi-billion dollar industry worldwide. Epoxy resins are high performance adhesives synthesised from the reaction of a bis-epoxide with a diamine. The bis-epoxide is made from $\mathbf{H}$ and epichlorohydrin, $\mathbf{C}$. $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ can be synthesised according to the schemes below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2009-5-fig1.png

The synthesis of epichlorohydrin $\mathbf{C}$ begins with the reaction of propene with chlorine in the presence of light.

a) (4 pt: $\mathbf{A}$ 2, $\mathbf{B}$ 2) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

b) (1 pt) Give the formula of a suitable reagent for the conversion of $\mathbf{B}$ into epichlorohydrin $\mathbf{C}$.

The synthesis of $\mathbf{H}$ commences with the reaction of benzene with propene in the presence of an acid catalyst which gives $\mathbf{D}$ as the major product and $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$ as minor products.

c) (6 pt: $\mathbf{D}$ 2, $\mathbf{E}$ 2, $\mathbf{F}$ 2) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$, and $\mathbf{F}$ from the following data:

$\mathbf{D}$: Elemental composition: C 89.94%, H 10.06%; 6 signals in the $\ce{^{13}C}$ NMR spectrum

$\mathbf{E}$: Elemental composition: C 88.82%, H 11.18%; 4 signals in the $\ce{^{13}C}$ NMR spectrum

$\mathbf{F}$: Elemental composition: C 88.82%, H 11.18%; 5 signals in the $\ce{^{13}C}$ NMR spectrum

Bubbling oxygen through a hot solution of $\mathbf{D}$ gives $\mathbf{G}$ which on exposure to acid gives phenol (hydroxybenzene) and acetone (propanone).

$\mathbf{G}$ turns starch iodide paper from white to dark blue. $\mathbf{G}$ has 6 signals in the $\ce{^{13}C}$ NMR spectrum and the following signals in the $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectrum: $\delta$ 7.78 (1H, s), 7.45–7.22 (5H, m), 1.56 (6H, s); addition of $\ce{D2O}$ results in the disappearance of the signal at $\delta = 7.78$.

d) (3 pt) Draw the structure of $\mathbf{G}$.

Exposure of phenol and acetone to hydrochloric acid gives compound $\mathbf{H}$. The $\ce{^{13}C}$ NMR spectrum for $\mathbf{H}$ is shown in Fig. 1. The $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectrum is shown in Fig. 2 together with a four-fold expansion of the region 6.5 – 7.1 ppm. The $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectrum after the addition of a drop of $\ce{D2O}$, is shown in Fig. 3. Peaks due to the solvent are marked with an asterisk (*).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2009-5-fig2.png

e) (3 pt) Draw the structure of $\mathbf{H}$.

f) (1 pt) Draw one resonance structure of phenol which explains the regioselective formation of $\mathbf{H}$.

A second compound, $\mathbf{I}$, is also formed in the reaction of phenol with acetone. The $\ce{^{13}C}$ NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{I}$ has 12 signals. The $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectrum has the following signals: $\delta$ 7.50–6.51 (8H, m), 5.19 (1H, s), 4.45 (1H, s), 1.67 (6H, s); addition of $\ce{D2O}$ results in the disappearance of the signals at $\delta = 5.19$ and 4.45

g) (2 pt) Draw a structure for $\mathbf{I}$.

Excess phenol reacts with epichlorohydrin $\mathbf{C}$ in the presence of base to give compound $\mathbf{L}$ which has 6 signals in its $\ce{^{13}C}$ NMR spectrum. If the reaction is stopped before completion compounds $\mathbf{J}$ and $\mathbf{K}$ can also be isolated. Compound $\mathbf{L}$ is formed from compound $\mathbf{K}$ and compound $\mathbf{K}$ is formed from compound $\mathbf{J}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2009-5-fig3.png

h) (6 pt: $\mathbf{J}$ 2, $\mathbf{K}$ 2, $\mathbf{L}$ 2) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{J}$, $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{L}$.

Treatment of $\mathbf{H}$ with a large excess of epichlorohydrin $\mathbf{C}$ and base gives a monomeric bis-epoxide $\mathbf{M}$. $\mathbf{M}$ contains no chlorine atoms or OH groups.

i) (2 pt) Draw the structure of $\mathbf{M}$.

Treatment of $\mathbf{H}$ with a small excess of epichlorohydrin and base gives $\mathbf{N}$. $\mathbf{N}$ has the form: endgroup1-[repeat unit]$_n$-endgroup2 where $n$ is approximately 10 – 15. $\mathbf{N}$ does not contain chlorine atoms and contains one OH group per repeat unit.

j) (4 pt) Draw the structure of $\mathbf{N}$ in the form indicated above (endgroup1-[repeat unit]$_n$-endgroup2).

k) (3 pt) Draw the repeat unit of the polymeric epoxy resin $\mathbf{O}$ formed from the reaction of the bis-epoxide $\mathbf{M}$ with ethane-1,2-diamine.

problems.title: Transition metal complexes
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (61 points, 12% of the total). Transition metal complexes

Alfred Werner used the technique of ‘isomer counting’ to deduce the structure of metal complexes with coordination number six. Three of the shapes he considered are shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2009-6-fig1.png

In each structure, the empty circle shows the location of the central metal atom and the filled circles show the location of the ligands. Structure $\mathbf{X}$ is hexagonal planar, structure $\mathbf{Y}$ is trigonal prismatic and structure $\mathbf{Z}$ is octahedral.

For each of the three shapes, there is just one structure when all of the ligands are the same, i.e. when the complex has the general formula $\ce{MA6}$ where A is the ligand. However, when achiral ligands A are substituted by one or more achiral ligands, it may be possible for each structure to form geometrical isomers. It might also be possible for one or more of the geometrical isomers to be optically active and exist as pairs of enantiomers.

a) (18 pt) Fill in the table below to indicate how many geometrical isomers may be formed for each structure $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$, and $\mathbf{Z}$ as the monodentate ligands A are substituted by monodentate ligands B or by symmetrical bidentate ligands, denoted C—C. Bidentate ligand C—C can only link between two atoms on adjacent positions, i.e. those positions connected by a line in the structures $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$, and $\mathbf{Z}$.

In each case write the number of geometrical isomers in the space provided. If one of the isomers exists as a pair of enantiomers, include an asterisk, *, in the box. If two exist as two pairs of enantiomers, include two asterisks and so on. For example, if you think there are five geometrical isomers of a particular structure, three of which exist as pairs of enantiomers, write 5***.

[Table heading of the three columns: Number of predicted geometrical isomers.]

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} & \text{Hexagonal planar } \mathbf{X} & \text{Trigonal Prismatic } \mathbf{Y} & \text{Octahedral } \mathbf{Z} \\ \hline \ce{MA6} & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ \hline \ce{MA5B} & & & \\ \hline \ce{MA4B2} & & & \\ \hline \ce{MA3B3} & & & \\ \hline \ce{MA4(C-C)} & & & \\ \hline \ce{MA2(C-C)2} & & & \\ \hline \ce{M(C-C)3} & & & \end{array}$$

There are no known complexes that adopt the hexagonal planar geometry $\mathbf{X}$, but structures are known for both the trigonal prismatic geometry $\mathbf{Y}$ and the octahedral geometry $\mathbf{Z}$. In these complexes, the orbitals derived from the metal d orbitals have different energies depending on the geometry of the complex. The splitting patterns for the trigonal prismatic geometry and for the octahedral geometry are shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2009-6-fig2.png

The separations in energy, $\Delta E$, $\Delta E'$ and $\Delta E''$ depend on the particular complex.

b) (5 pt) For each of the splitting patterns shown below label which d orbitals are which.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2009-6-fig3.png

The two complexes $\ce{[Mn(H2O)6]^{2+}}$ and $\ce{[Mn(CN)6]^{2-}}$ are both octahedral. One has a magnetic moment of 5.9 BM, the other has a magnetic moment of 3.8 BM but you must decide which is which.

c) (4 pt) On the diagram below, draw the electronic arrangements for each of the complexes.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2009-6-fig4.png

The magnetic moments of complexes $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ shown below have been measured and found to be 1.9 and 2.7 BM but you must decide which is which.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2009-6-fig5.png

d) (6 pt) Draw the orbital splitting diagrams for the two complexes, including the arrangements of the electrons.

Octahedral complexes are far more common than trigonal prismatic. Werner isolated five compounds $\mathbf{C}$ – $\mathbf{G}$ containing Co(III), Cl, and $\ce{NH3}$ only, each of which contained one octahedral complex. (There is actually a sixth compound but Werner could not isolate it). Werner’s five compounds had the molar conductivities shown below. The conductivities are extrapolated to infinite dilution and are expressed in arbitrary units. Compound $\mathbf{G}$ does not react with aqueous $\ce{AgNO3}$; compounds $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, and $\mathbf{E}$ react with different stoichiometric ratios of aqueous $\ce{AgNO3}$; $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$ react with the same stoichiometric ratio of aqueous $\ce{AgNO3}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} & \mathbf{C} & \mathbf{D} & \mathbf{E} & \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{G} \\ \hline \text{molar conductivity} & 510 & 372 & 249 & 249 & \sim 0 \end{array}$$

e) (5 pt) As far as you are able, suggest a structure for each of the compounds $\mathbf{C}$ – $\mathbf{G}$.

Werner was also the first person to separate the enantiomers of an octahedral compound, $\mathbf{H}$, which contained no carbon atoms. The compound, $\mathbf{H}$, is composed of only cobalt, ammonia, chloride and an oxygen species which could be either $\ce{H2O}$, or $\ce{HO^-}$ or $\ce{O^{2-}}$. The compound contains octahedrally coordinated cobalt ions. All of the chloride is easily removed from the compound by titration with aqueous silver nitrate. A $0.2872\,\mathrm{g}$ sample of $\mathbf{H}$ (containing no water of crystallization) required $22.8\,\mathrm{cm^{3}}$ of $0.100\,\mathrm{M}$ silver nitrate to exchange all of the chloride.

f) (2 pt) Calculate the percentage, by mass, of chloride in $\mathbf{H}$.

$\mathbf{H}$ is stable to acids, but is hydrolysed in alkali. A $0.7934\,\mathrm{g}$ sample of $\mathbf{H}$ (containing no water of crystallization) was heated with excess aqueous sodium hydroxide. Cobalt(III) oxide was formed and ammonia gas given off. The ammonia produced was distilled off and absorbed into $50.0\,\mathrm{cm^{3}}$ of $0.500\,\mathrm{M}$ aqueous HCl. The residual HCl required $24.8\,\mathrm{cm^{3}}$ of $0.500\,\mathrm{M}$ aqueous KOH to be neutralized.

The remaining suspension of cobalt(III) oxide was allowed to cool, approximately $1\,\mathrm{g}$ of potassium iodide was added, and then the mixture was acidified with aqueous HCl. The liberated iodine was then titrated with $0.200\,\mathrm{M}$ aqueous sodium thiosulfate and required $21.0\,\mathrm{cm^{3}}$ for complete reaction.

g) (3 pt) Calculate the percentage, by mass, of ammonia in $\mathbf{H}$.

h) (2 pt) Give the equation for the reaction of cobalt(III) oxide with potassium iodide in aqueous acid.

i) (4 pt) Calculate the percentage, by mass, of cobalt in $\mathbf{H}$.

j) (4 pt) Calculate the identity of the oxygen species contained in $\mathbf{H}$. Show your working.

k) (2 pt) Give the empirical formula of $\mathbf{H}$.

l) (6 pt) Suggest a structure for the chiral compound $\mathbf{H}$.

problems.title: Discovery of argon and helium
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (17 points, 8% of the total). [Discovery of argon and helium]

In 1894, Lord Rayleigh reported that the mass of chemically prepared nitrogen was different from that of nitrogen extracted from the atmosphere, as shown in Tables 1 and 2. Later, this difference was attributed to the presence of argon in $\textit{atmospheric nitrogen}$. The masses of gases were measured by using a glass vessel with a known volume under atmospheric pressure ($1.013\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{Pa}$).

Table 1. Mass of $\textit{Chemical Nitrogen}$ in the Vessel

problems.title: Sodium chloride: crystal structure, Born–Haber cycle and the Solvay process
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (20 points, 6% of the total). [Sodium chloride: crystal structure, Born–Haber cycle and the Solvay process]

Crystal structure of alkali metal halide

In crystals of ionic compounds, cations are generally arranged in the interstices of the closest packed lattice of anions. The structure of an ionic crystal such as sodium chloride becomes stable when the cations are in contact with the nearest anions.

a) (4 pt) In the crystal of sodium chloride, both $\ce{Na+}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$ ions form a face-centered cubic lattice. Give the numbers of $\ce{Na+}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$ ions in a unit cell and the coordination numbers of $\ce{Na+}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$ ions in sodium chloride crystal.

b) (4 pt) The ionic radii of $\ce{Na+}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$ ions in the crystal of sodium chloride are $0.102\,\mathrm{nm}$ and $0.181\,\mathrm{nm}$, respectively. Calculate the density [$\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$] of the sodium chloride crystal.

Born-Haber cycle and lattice enthalpy

In ionic inorganic compounds such as sodium chloride, the heat of lattice formation from gaseous ions is very high, and the contribution of the change in entropy is small. Therefore, the lattice formation enthalpy is estimated from enthalpy data by using a Born-Haber cycle.

c) (4 pt) The figure below shows the Born-Haber cycle of NaCl. The labels "g" and "s" represent "gas" and "solid" states respectively. Show chemical equations in the A and F steps.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2010-2-fig1.png

d) (3 pt) Calculate the enthalpy of the lattice formation of NaCl [$\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$] by using the following enthalpy data of the respective steps in the above Born-Haber cycle.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \text{Formation of NaCl (s)} & \text{Sublimation of Na (s)} & \text{Ionization of Na (g)} & \text{Dissociation of }\ce{Cl2} & \text{Electron gain by Cl (g)} \\ \hline -411\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & 109\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & 496\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & 242\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & -349\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \end{array}$$

Synthesis of sodium carbonate by the ammonia-soda process (Solvay process)

Sodium carbonate (anhydrous soda ash) is a raw material in the manufacture of glass, medicaments, alkaline detergents, etc.

e) (5 pt) The total chemical reaction in the ammonia-soda process is represented as follows:

$$\ce{2NaCl + CaCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CaCl2}$$

This reaction between sodium chloride and calcium carbonate does not proceed directly. The process comprises the following five reactions involving ammonia:

$$\begin{array}{l} \ce{CaCO3} \xrightarrow{\Delta} [\ \mathrm{A}\ ] + [\ \mathrm{B}\ ] \\ \ce{NaCl + NH3} + [\ \mathrm{B}\ ] + \ce{H2O} \rightarrow [\ \mathrm{C}\ ] + [\ \mathrm{D}\ ] \\ 2\,[\ \mathrm{C}\ ] \xrightarrow{\Delta} \ce{Na2CO3 + H2O} + [\ \mathrm{B}\ ] \\ [\ \mathrm{A}\ ] + \ce{H2O} \rightarrow [\ \mathrm{E}\ ] \\ [\ \mathrm{E}\ ] + 2\,[\ \mathrm{D}\ ] \rightarrow \ce{CaCl2 + 2H2O + 2NH3} \end{array}$$

where $\Delta$ represents applying heat treatment. Insert the chemical formulas of the appropriate compounds in the blank spaces [ A ]–[ E ] in the above reactions.

problems.title: Chemical oxygen demand
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (9 points, 7% of the total). [Chemical oxygen demand]

The chemical oxygen demand (COD) refers to the amount of oxidizable substance, such as organic compounds, in a sample solution, and it is used as an indication of water quality in seas, lakes, and marshes. For example, the COD of service water is kept below $1\,\mathrm{mg\,L^{-1}}$. The COD ($\mathrm{mg\,L^{-1}}$) is represented by mass of $\ce{O2}$ (mg) which accepts the same amount of electrons which would be accepted by the strong oxidizing agent when 1 L of a sample solution is treated with it. An example of the operation is presented below.

Analytical Operation

A 1.00-L sample solution was acidified with a sufficient amount of sulfuric acid, and chloride ions were removed by the addition of silver nitrate solution. To the sample solution, $1.00\times10^{-1}\,\mathrm{L}$ of $5.00\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ potassium permanganate solution was added, and the mixture was heated for 30 min. Further, $1.00\times10^{-1}\,\mathrm{L}$ of $1.25\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ disodium oxalate ($\ce{Na2C2O4}$ or $\ce{NaOOC-COONa}$) standard solution was added, and the mixture was stirred well. Oxalate ions that remained unreacted were titrated with $5.00\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ potassium permanganate solution; $3.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{L}$ of the solution was used for the titration.

a) (2 pt) Give the equation of the redox reaction of potassium permanganate and disodium oxalate.

b) (3 pt) Calculate the amount of $\ce{O2}$ (mg) that will oxidize the same number of moles of oxidizable substance as $1.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $5.00\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ potassium permanganate does.

c) (1 pt) From the following choices, select the most appropriate reason for the removal of chloride ions:

• [A] Some of the chloride ions react with potassium permanganate, resulting in an error in COD.
• [B] Some of the chloride ions react with disodium oxalate, resulting in an error in COD.
• [C] Some of the chloride ions react with organic compounds in the sample solution, resulting in an error in COD.
• [D] A color is developed during titration, resulting in an error in COD.

d) (3 pt) Calculate the COD ($\mathrm{mg\,L^{-1}}$) of the sample solution described in the analytical operation above.

problems.title: Photoelectron spectroscopy of the hydrogen molecule
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (18 points, 7% of the total). [Photoelectron spectroscopy of the hydrogen molecule]

When an atom X absorbs radiation with a photon energy greater than the ionization energy of the atom, the atom is ionized to generate an ion $\mathrm{X^+}$ and the electron (called a photoelectron) is ejected at the same time. In this event, the energy is conserved as shown in Figure 1, that is,

Photon energy ($h\nu$) = ionization energy (IE) of X + kinetic energy of photoelectron.

When a molecule, for example, $\ce{H2}$, absorbs short-wavelength light, the photoelectron is ejected and an $\ce{H2+}$ ion with a variety of vibrational states is produced. A photoelectron spectrum is a plot of the number of photoelectrons as a function of the kinetic energy of the photoelectrons. Figure 2 shows a typical photoelectron spectrum when $\ce{H2}$ in the lowest vibrational level is irradiated by monochromatic light of 21.2 eV. No photoelectrons are detected above 6.0 eV. eV is a unit of energy and 1.0 eV is equal to $1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2010-5-fig1.png

Figure 1. Schematic diagram of photoelectron spectroscopy.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2010-5-fig2.png

Figure 2. Photoelectron spectrum of $\ce{H2}$. The energy of the incident light is 21.2 eV.

a-1) (1 pt) Determine the energy difference $\Delta E_\mathrm{A1}$ (eV) between $\ce{H2}$ ($v = 0$) and $\ce{H2+}$ ($v_\mathrm{ion} = 0$) to the first decimal place. $v$ and $v_\mathrm{ion}$ denote the vibrational quantum numbers of $\ce{H2}$ and $\ce{H2+}$, respectively.

a-2) (1 pt) Determine the energy difference $\Delta E_\mathrm{A2}$ (eV) between $\ce{H2+}$ ($v_\mathrm{ion} = 0$) and $\ce{H2+}$ ($v_\mathrm{ion} = 3$) to the first decimal place.

b) (2 pt) The electronic energy levels $E_n^\mathrm{H}$ of a hydrogen atom are given by the equation

$$E_n^\mathrm{H} = -\frac{Ry}{n^2} \qquad (n = 1, 2, 3 \cdots).$$

Here $n$ is a principal quantum number, and $Ry$ is a constant with dimensions of energy. The energy from $n = 1$ to $n = 2$ of the hydrogen atom is 10.2 eV. Calculate the ionization energy $E_\mathrm{B}$ (eV) of the hydrogen atom to the first decimal place.

c) (2 pt) The energy threshold for the generation of two electronically excited hydrogen atoms $\mathrm{H^*}$ ($n = 2$) from $\ce{H2}$ ($v = 0$) has been derived to be 24.9 eV by an experiment. Determine the bond energy $E_\mathrm{C}$ (eV) of $\ce{H2}$ to the first decimal place.

d) (3 pt) Considering an energy cycle, determine the bond energy $E_\mathrm{D}$ (eV) of $\ce{H2+}$ to the first decimal place. If you don't have the values for $E_\mathrm{B}$ and $E_\mathrm{C}$, then use 15.0 eV and 5.0 eV for $E_\mathrm{B}$ and $E_\mathrm{C}$, respectively.

e) (4 pt) Calculate the threshold energy $E_\mathrm{E}$ (eV) of the following dissociative ionization reaction to the first decimal place:

$$\ce{H2 -> H^{*}}\,(n = 2) + \ce{H+ + e-}.$$

If you don't have the values for $E_\mathrm{B}$ and $E_\mathrm{C}$, then use 15.0 eV and 5.0 eV for $E_\mathrm{B}$ and $E_\mathrm{C}$, respectively.

f) (5 pt) When $\ce{H2}$ absorbs monochromatic light of 21.2 eV, the following dissociation process occurs at the same time.

$$\ce{H2} \xrightarrow{21.2\ \mathrm{eV}} \mathrm{H}\,(n = 1) + \mathrm{H}\,(n = 1)$$

Two hydrogen atoms move in opposite directions with the same speed. Calculate the speed $u$ ($\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$) of the hydrogen atoms generated in the above reaction. $\ce{H2}$ is assumed to be at rest. If you don't have the value for $E_\mathrm{C}$, then use 5.0 eV for $E_\mathrm{C}$.

problems.title: Polycondensation and the average degree of polymerization
problems.problem:
Problem 8 (20 points, 6% of the total). [Polycondensation and the average degree of polymerization]

The esterification reaction between bi-functional molecules gives one of the typical linear chain polymers as shown in eq.(1) by polycondensation (often called "condensation polymerization"). The control of polymerization conditions and procedures determines the length of polymer strands, i.e., $\textit{the average degree of polymerization}$, $\boldsymbol{X}$ (note that $\boldsymbol{X} = 2\boldsymbol{n}$ in the present instance). $\underline{\text{Because }\boldsymbol{X}\text{ (and also }\boldsymbol{n}\text{) is an averaged number, it is not always an integer but a value with decimal figures}}$.

$$n\,\ce{HOOC-R^1-COOH} + n\,\ce{HO-R^2-OH} \rightarrow \ce{HO-[COR^1CO-OR^2O]}_{n}\ce{-H} + (2n-1)\ce{H2O} \qquad (1)$$

$\boldsymbol{X}$ can be estimated from the consumption of functional groups (here, $\ce{-COOH}$ and $\ce{-OH}$). Let us define the degree of reaction, $\boldsymbol{p}$, as $\boldsymbol{p} = (N_0 - N)/N_0\ (\le 1)$, where $N_0$ and $N$ denote the total numbers of functional groups before and after the polymerization, respectively. For each functional group of the dicarboxylic acid molecules ($\mathbf{A}$) and diol molecules ($\mathbf{B}$), we add the suffixes of "$_\mathrm{A}$" or "$_\mathrm{B}$" such as $N_\mathrm{A0}$, $N_\mathrm{B0}$, $N_\mathrm{A}$ or $N_\mathrm{B}$, respectively, i.e., $N_0 = N_\mathrm{A0} + N_\mathrm{B0}$ and $N = N_\mathrm{A} + N_\mathrm{B}$. When the initial feed is unbalanced such as $N_\mathrm{A0} \le N_\mathrm{B0}$, $\boldsymbol{X}$ is expressed by $\boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{A}$ and $\boldsymbol{r}$ as shown in eq.(2), where $\boldsymbol{r} = N_\mathrm{A0}/N_\mathrm{B0}\ (\le 1)$. If $\boldsymbol{r} = 1$, $\boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{A}$ is identical to $\boldsymbol{p}$ and eq.(2) becomes the same to the Carothers equation.

$$\boldsymbol{X} = (1 + \boldsymbol{r})\,/\,(1 + \boldsymbol{r} - 2\boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{A}\boldsymbol{r}) \qquad (2)$$

[The answer box states: Calculation procedures must be shown by suitable equation(s) (otherwise, no score will be provided).]

a-3) (3 pt) Give the $\boldsymbol{p}$ value necessary to prepare this nylon-6,6 sample of $\boldsymbol{M} = 5507.25$ ($\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$) to $\textit{the fifth decimal place}$. If you get no numerical answer in a-2), use 52.50 instead.

b) The low-molecular-weight polyester (oligoester) is prepared from the mixture of 36.54 (g) of adipic acid (hexanedioic acid) and an unknown amount [$\boldsymbol{W}$ (g)] of butane-1,4-diol (Bdiol). Under the condition of $\boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{A} \rightarrow 1$, the oligoester with $\boldsymbol{X} = 11.00$ carrying $\underline{\text{Bdiol units in both chain ends}}$ is obtained.

b-1) (4 pt) Show the $\textit{precise}$ chemical structure of this oligoester of $\boldsymbol{X} = 11.00$.

problems.title: Kinetics of the reaction of NO with H2
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (22 points, 7.0% of the total). [Kinetics of the reaction of NO with H2]

Nitrogen oxides, common pollutants in the ambient air, are primarily nitric oxide, $\ce{NO}$, and nitrogen dioxide, $\ce{NO2}$. Atmospheric nitric oxide is produced mainly during thunderstorms and in the internal combustion engines. At high temperatures $\ce{NO}$ reacts with $\ce{H2}$ to produce nitrous oxide, $\ce{N2O}$, a greenhouse gas.

$$\ce{2 NO(g) + H2(g) -> N2O(g) + H2O(g)}$$

To study the kinetics of this reaction at $820\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, initial rates for the formation of $\ce{N2O}$ were measured using various initial partial pressures of $\ce{NO}$ and $\ce{H2}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Exp.} & P_\mathrm{NO}\ (\text{initial pressure, torr}) & P_\mathrm{H_2}\ (\text{initial pressure, torr}) & \text{Initial rate of production of } \ce{N2O},\ \mathrm{torr\cdot s^{-1}} \\ \hline 1 & 120.0 & 60.0 & 8.66\times10^{-2} \\ 2 & 60.0 & 60.0 & 2.17\times10^{-2} \\ 3 & 60.0 & 180.0 & 6.62\times10^{-2} \end{array}$$

$\textbf{Throughout this problem do not use concentrations. Use units of pressure in torr and time in seconds.}$

a. (3 pt) Determine the experimental rate law and calculate the rate constant.

b. (2 pt) Calculate the initial rate of disappearance of $\ce{NO}$, if $2.00\times10^{2}$ torr $\ce{NO}$ and $1.00\times10^{2}$ torr $\ce{H2}$ are mixed at $820\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. (If you do not have the value for the rate constant then use $2\times10^{-7}$ in appropriate unit.)

c. (6 pt) Calculate the time elapsed to reduce the partial pressure of $\ce{H2}$ to the half of its initial value, if $8.00\times10^{2}$ torr $\ce{NO}$ and $1.0$ torr of $\ce{H2}$ are mixed at $820\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. (If you do not have the value for the rate constant then use $2\times10^{-7}$ in appropriate unit.)

d. A proposed mechanism for the reaction between $\ce{NO}$ and $\ce{H2}$ is given below:

$$\ce{2 NO(g) <=>[k_1][k_{-1}] N2O2(g)}$$

$$\ce{N2O2(g) + H2(g) ->[k_2] N2O(g) + H2O(g)}$$

d.i (6 pt) Derive the rate law for the formation of $\ce{N2O}$ from the proposed mechanism using the steady-state approximation for the intermediate.

d.ii (1.5 pt) Under what condition does this rate law reduce to the experimentally determined rate law found in Part a?

• If $k_{-1} \ll k_2 P_\mathrm{H_2}$
• If $k_{-1} \gg k_2 P_\mathrm{H_2}$
• If $k_{-1} > k_2$
• If $k_1 > k_{-1}$

d.iii (1 pt) Express the experimentally determined rate constant $k$ in terms of $k_1$, $k_{-1}$ and $k_2$.

e. (2.5 pt) Select the schematic energy diagram that is consistent with the proposed reaction mechanism and experimental rate law.

problems.title: Combustion of ammonia
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (23 points, 7.0% of the total). [Combustion of ammonia]

Anhydrous ammonia is an ultra-clean, energy-dense alternative liquid fuel. It produces no greenhouse gases on combustion.

In an experiment, gaseous $\ce{NH3}$ is burned with $\ce{O2}$ in a container of fixed volume according to the equation given below.

$$\ce{4 NH3(g) + 3 O2(g) -> 2 N2(g) + 6 H2O(l)}$$

The initial and final states are at $298\ \mathrm{K}$. After combustion with $14.40\ \mathrm{g}$ of $\ce{O2}$, some of $\ce{NH3}$ remains unreacted.

a. (6 pt) Calculate the heat given out during the process.

Given: $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\ce{NH3(g)}) = -46.11\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\ce{H2O(l)}) = -285.83\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

b. To determine the amount of $\ce{NH3}$ gas dissolved in water, produced during the combustion process, a $10.00\ \mathrm{mL}$ sample of the aqueous solution was withdrawn from the reaction vessel and added to $15.0\ \mathrm{mL}$ of $0.0100\ \mathrm{M}$ $\ce{H2SO4}$ solution. The resulting solution was titrated with $0.0200\ \mathrm{M}$ standard $\ce{NaOH}$ solution and the equivalence point was reached at $10.64\ \mathrm{mL}$. ($K_\mathrm{b}(\ce{NH3}) = 1.8\times10^{-5}$; $K_\mathrm{a}(\ce{HSO4-}) = 1.1\times10^{-2}$)

b.i (9 pt) Calculate pH of the solution in the container after combustion.

b.ii (6 pt) At the end point of titration, $\ce{NH4+}$ and $\ce{SO4^{2-}}$ ions are present in the solution. Write the equations for the relevant equilibria to show how the presence of these two ions affect the pH and calculate their equilibrium constant(s).

b.iii (2 pt) Circle the correct statement for the pH of solution at the equivalence point.

• pH > 7.0
• pH = 7.0
• pH < 7.0

problems.title: Isotope effects and the energy levels of H2
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (23 points, 8.0% of the total). [Isotope effects and the energy levels of H2]

At 0 K, the total energy of a gaseous diatomic molecule AB is approximately given by:

$$E = E_\mathrm{o} + E_\mathrm{vib}$$

where $E_\mathrm{o}$ is the electronic energy of the ground state, and $E_\mathrm{vib}$ is the vibrational energy.

Allowed values of the vibrational energies are given by the expression:

$$E_\mathrm{vib} = \left(v + \frac{1}{2}\right)\varepsilon \qquad v = 0, 1, 2, \ldots \qquad \varepsilon = \frac{h}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}} \qquad \mu(\mathrm{AB}) = \frac{m_\mathrm{A} m_\mathrm{B}}{m_\mathrm{A} + m_\mathrm{B}}$$

where $h$ is the Planck's constant, $v$ is the vibrational quantum number, $k$ is the force constant, and $\mu$ is the reduced mass of the molecule. At 0 K, it may be safely assumed that $v$ is zero, and $E_\mathrm{o}$ and $k$ are independent of isotopic substitution in the molecule.

a. (7 pt) Calculate the enthalpy change, $\Delta H$, in $\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$ for the following reaction at 0 K.

$$\ce{H2(g) + D2(g) -> 2 HD(g)}$$

Deuterium, D, is an isotope of hydrogen atom with mass number 2. For the $\ce{H2}$ molecule, $k$ is $575.11\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^{-1}}$, and the isotopic molar masses of H and D are $1.0078$ and $2.0141\ \mathrm{g\cdot mol^{-1}}$, respectively. Given: $\varepsilon_\mathrm{H_2} = 1.1546\,\varepsilon_\mathrm{HD}$ and $\varepsilon_\mathrm{D_2} = 0.8167\,\varepsilon_\mathrm{HD}$ at 0 K.

b. (4 pt) Calculate the frequency in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ of infrared photons that can be absorbed by HD molecule. (If you do not have the value for $\varepsilon_\mathrm{HD}$ then use $8.000\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{J}$ for the calculation.)

c. The allowed electronic energies of H atom are given by the expression

$$E = -\frac{R_H}{n^2}, \quad n = 1, 2, \ldots \qquad \text{where } R_H = 13.5984\ \mathrm{eV}, \quad 1\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$$

c.i (2 pt) The total energy of $\ce{H2}$ molecule in its ground state is $-31.675\ \mathrm{eV}$, relative to the same reference as that of hydrogen atom. Calculate the dissociation energy in eV of a hydrogen molecule in its ground state such that both H atoms are produced in their ground states.

c.ii (5 pt) A $\ce{H2}$ molecule in the ground state dissociates into its atoms after absorbing a photon of wavelength $77.0\ \mathrm{nm}$. Determine all possibilities for the electronic states of H atoms produced. In each case, what is the total kinetic energy in eV of the dissociated hydrogen atoms?

d. (5 pt) Calculate the electron affinity of $\ce{H2+}$ ion in eV if its dissociation energy is $2.650\ \mathrm{eV}$. (If you do not have the value for the dissociation energy for $\ce{H2}$ then use $4.500\ \mathrm{eV}$ for the calculation.)

problems.title: Hydrogen from sodium borohydride and the fuel cell
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (30 points, 9.0% of the total). [Hydrogen from sodium borohydride and the fuel cell]

For sustainable energy, hydrogen appears to be the best energy carrier. The most efficient way of using hydrogen is generation of electrical energy in a fuel cell. However, storing hydrogen in large quantities is a challenge in fuel cell applications. Among the chemical hydrides considered as solid hydrogen storage materials, sodium borohydride ($\ce{NaBH4}$), being nontoxic, stable and environmentally benign, appears to be the most promising one. The hydrolysis of sodium borohydride that releases $\ce{H2}$ gas is a slow reaction at ambient temperature and, therefore, needs to be catalyzed.

$$\ce{NaBH4(aq) + 2 H2O(l) ->[catalyst] Na+(aq) + BO2^{-}(aq) + 4 H2(g)}$$

Colloidal ruthenium(0) nanoclusters are the most active catalysts in this hydrolysis even at room temperature and lead to a complete $\ce{H2}$ release from sodium borohydride. Kinetic studies show that the catalytic hydrolysis of $\ce{NaBH4}$ is first order with respect to the catalyst, but zero order with respect to the substrate. The rate of hydrogen production per mole of ruthenium is $92\ \mathrm{mol\ H_2\cdot(mol\ Ru)^{-1}\cdot min^{-1}}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

a. (4 pt) Calculate the amount of ruthenium catalyst (in mg) which must be added to $0.100\ \mathrm{L}$ solution of $1.0\ \mathrm{mol\cdot L^{-1}}$ $\ce{NaBH4}$ to supply the hydrogen gas at a rate of $0.100\ \mathrm{L\cdot min^{-1}}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $1.0\ \mathrm{atm}$, that is required for a portable fuel cell.

b. (3 pt) For how many minutes will this system supply hydrogen gas at this rate?

c. (6 pt) The Arrhenius activation energy for this catalytic hydrolysis of sodium borohydride is $E_\mathrm{a} = 42.0\ \mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$. Calculate the temperature required to achieve the same rate of hydrogen evolution by using half the amount of ruthenium catalyst used at $25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

d. (3 pt) A fuel cell is made up of three segments sandwiched together: the anode, the electrolyte, and the cathode. Hydrogen is used as fuel and oxygen as oxidant. Two chemical reactions occur at the interfaces of the three different segments.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2011-4-fig1.png

$$\ce{O2(g) + 2H2O(l) + 4e- -> 4OH-(aq)}$$

$$\ce{H2(g) + 2OH-(aq) -> 2H2O(l) + 2e-}$$

The net result of the two reactions is

$$\ce{2 H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2 H2O(l)}$$

The hydrogen for the fuel cell is supplied from the hydrolysis of sodium borohydride.

Calculate the standard potential for the cathode half reaction if the standard reduction potential for the anode half reaction is $-0.83\ \mathrm{V}$ and $\Delta_\mathrm{f}G^\circ(\ce{H2O(l)})$ is $-237\ \mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

e. (4 pt) Calculate the volume of air at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $1.0\ \mathrm{atm}$ needed to generate a constant current of $2.5\ \mathrm{A}$ for $3.0\ \mathrm{h}$ in this fuel cell. Assume that air contains 20% by volume $\ce{O2(g)}$.

f. (6 pt) The efficiency of a fuel cell is given by the ratio of the work produced to the heat dissipated by the cell reaction. Thus, the maximum efficiency for a fuel cell is given by:

$$\eta_\text{fuel cell} = \frac{\text{work}}{\text{heat}}$$

Calculate the maximum efficiency for the fuel cell using the data given below at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and standard pressure.

$$\begin{array}{l|c} & S^\circ\ (\mathrm{J\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot K^{-1}}) \\ \hline \ce{H2(g)} & 130.7 \\ \ce{O2(g)} & 205.2 \\ \ce{H2O(l)} & 70.0 \end{array}$$

g. (4 pt) The second law of thermodynamics states that it is impossible to convert all of the heat, $q_\mathrm{H}$, from a high-temperature reservoir at $T_\mathrm{H}$ into work. At least, some of the energy, $q_\mathrm{C}$, must be transferred to a low-temperature reservoir at $T_\mathrm{C}$. Thus, a heat engine with 100% efficiency is thermodynamically impossible. When the heat engine is working reversibly, as in a Carnot cycle, the efficiency will be maximum.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2011-4-fig2.png

For a heat engine working reversibly between two reservoirs the following relations applies:

$$q_H = w + q_C$$

and

$$\frac{q_\mathrm{H}}{T_\mathrm{H}} = \frac{q_\mathrm{C}}{T_\mathrm{C}}$$

What should be the temperature of the hot reservoir, $T_\mathrm{H}$, of a Carnot heat engine to maintain the efficiency of the fuel cell calculated in part (f), if the temperature of cold reservoir $T_\mathrm{C}$ is $40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$? (If you do not have the value for the efficiency then use 0.80)

problems.title: Polynitrogen compounds
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (30 points, 7.0% of the total). [Polynitrogen compounds]

Polynitrogen compounds have great potential for being used as high energy density materials. They are thermodynamically unstable. Huge amount of energy is released from their decomposition or reactions leading to more stable products. The only known polynitrogen species are $\ce{N2}$, $\ce{N3-}$ and $\ce{N5+}$, isolated in 1772, 1890 and 1999, respectively, and the recently reported cyclic anion, $\ce{N5-}$.

a.i (5 pt) Write the Lewis structure for $\ce{N5+}$ with three energetically favorable resonance forms. Indicate the lone pairs and formal charges. Draw the molecular geometry of $\ce{N5+}$.

a.ii (3 pt) Write the Lewis structures for cyclic $\ce{N5-}$ with five energetically favorable resonance forms. Indicate the lone pairs and formal charges. Draw the molecular geometry of cyclic $\ce{N5-}$.

b. (1 pt) The synthesis of $\ce{[N5+][AsF6-]}$, a white ionic solid, was achieved by reacting $\ce{[N2F+][AsF6-]}$ with hydrazoic acid, $\ce{HN3}$, in liquid $\ce{HF}$ at $-78\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Write the balanced chemical equation for this reaction.

The preparation of $\ce{[N2F+][AsF6-]}$ requires the reaction of $\ce{N2F2}$ with strong Lewis acid, $\ce{AsF5}$, as follows:

$$x\ \mathrm{C(graphite)} + \ce{AsF5} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_x\cdot\ce{AsF5} \qquad \text{(graphite intercalate with } x = 10\text{–}12)$$

$$2\,\mathrm{C}_x\cdot\ce{AsF5} + \ce{N2F4} \rightarrow 2\,[\mathrm{C}_x^{+}][\ce{AsF6-}] + \textit{trans}\text{-}\ce{N2F2}$$

$$\textit{trans}\text{-}\ce{N2F2 + AsF5 -> [N2F+][AsF6-]}$$

In the synthesis of $\ce{N2F2}$, the $\textit{trans}$ isomer is formed, which is thermodynamically less stable than $\textit{cis}$-$\ce{N2F2}$. However, conversion of $\textit{trans}$-$\ce{N2F2}$ to $\textit{cis}$-$\ce{N2F2}$ requires surmounting a high energy barrier of $251\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}$, so that equilibration between the $\textit{cis}$ and the $\textit{trans}$ isomers does not significantly take place without a suitable catalyst.

When $\textit{trans}$-$\ce{N2F2}$ is maintained in a closed container for 6 days at room temperature, in the presence of a small amount of $\ce{SbF5}$ as a catalyst, $\textit{cis}$–$\textit{trans}$ thermal equilibrium is established.

$$\textit{trans}\text{-}\ce{N2F2} \ce{<=>[{25 °C}]} \textit{cis}\text{-}\ce{N2F2}$$

The standard enthalpies of formation of $\textit{trans}$- and $\textit{cis}$-$\ce{N2F2}$ are $67.31$ and $62.03\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}$, respectively, and their standard entropies at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ are $262.10$ and $266.50\ \mathrm{J\cdot K^{-1}\cdot mol^{-1}}$, respectively.

c. (6 pt) Find the ratio of the number of $\textit{cis}$-$\ce{N2F2}$ molecules over that of the $\textit{trans}$-$\ce{N2F2}$ molecules in an equilibrium mixture at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

d. (5 pt) Write the Lewis structures showing the geometry of the $\ce{N2F+}$ ion and of the $\textit{trans}$- and $\textit{cis}$-isomers of $\ce{N2F2}$. Include all lone pairs and formal charges. Suggest an appropriate hybridization for each nitrogen atom in $\ce{N2F2}$ and $\ce{N2F+}$.

Solid $\ce{[N5+][AsF6-]}$ is marginally stable at room temperature but reacts explosively with water to produce arsenic pentafluoride, hydrogen fluoride, molecular nitrogen and oxygen.

e. (2 pt) Write a balanced equation for the reaction between $\ce{[N5+][AsF6-]}$ and water.

Conversion of $\ce{[N5+][SbF6-]}$ into other $\ce{N5+}$ salts can be achieved by a metathesis reaction:

$$\ce{[N5+][SbF6-] + [M+][X-] -> [N5+][X-] + [M+][SbF6-]}$$

$\ce{M+} = \ce{Na+}, \ce{K+}, \ce{Cs+}$; $\ce{X-}$ = large anion such as $\ce{SnF6^{2-}}$ and $\ce{B(CF3)4-}$.

Since $\ce{[Cs+][SbF6-]}$ has a low solubility in anhydrous $\ce{HF}$, and $\ce{[K+][SbF6-]}$ has a low solubility in $\ce{SO2}$, these two solvents were used extensively to carry out metathesis reactions at $-78\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $-64\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, respectively.

f. (2 pt) Write the balanced equation for the preparation of $\ce{[N5+]2[SnF6^{2-}]}$ and $\ce{[N5+][B(CF3)4-]}$ in solution starting with $\ce{[Cs+]2[SnF6^{2-}]}$ and $\ce{[K+][B(CF3)4-]}$, respectively. Indicate the appropriate solvent.

When $\ce{[N5+]2[SnF6^{2-}]}$ decomposes under carefully controlled conditions at $25$–$30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $\ce{[N5+][SnF5-]}$ and $\ce{N5F}$ are formed. The $\ce{[N5+][SnF5-]}$ salt is a white solid and has a thermal stability comparable to that of $\ce{[N5+][SbF6-]}$ ($50$–$60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$). The solution $\ce{^{119}Sn}$ NMR spectrum has shown that the $\ce{SnF5-}$ anion in this compound is, in fact, a mixture of dimeric and tetrameric polyanions. In both of these polyanions the coordination number of Sn atom is 6 and there are bridging fluorine atoms.

g. (6 pt) Draw the structures of dimeric and tetrameric polyanions.

problems.title: Thiosulfate leaching of gold
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (23 points, 7.0% of the total). [Thiosulfate leaching of gold]

Extraction of gold using sodium cyanide, a very poisonous chemical, causes environmental problems and gives rise to serious public concern about the use of this so called "cyanide process". Thiosulfate leaching of gold has been considered as an alternative. In this process, the main reagent is ammonium thiosulfate, $\ce{(NH4)2S2O3}$, which is relatively nontoxic. Although this process appears to be environmentally benign, the chemistry involved is very complex and needs to be studied thoroughly. The solution used for leaching gold contains $\ce{S2O3^{2-}}$, $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$, $\ce{NH3}$, and dissolved $\ce{O2}$. The solution must have a pH greater than 8.5 to allow free ammonia to be present.

According to the proposed mechanism, a local voltaic micro-cell forms on the surface of gold particles during the leaching process and operates as follows:

Anode:

$$\ce{Au(s) + 2 NH3(aq) -> [Au(NH3)2]+(aq) + e-}$$

$$\ce{[Au(NH3)2]+(aq) + 2 S2O3^{2-}(aq) -> [Au(S2O3)2]^{3-}(aq) + 2 NH3(aq)}$$

Cathode:

$$\ce{[Cu(NH3)4]^{2+}(aq) + e- -> [Cu(NH3)2]+(aq) + 2 NH3(aq)}$$

$$\ce{[Cu(NH3)2]+(aq) + 3 S2O3^{2-}(aq) -> [Cu(S2O3)3]^{5-}(aq) + 2 NH3(aq)}$$

a. (5 pt) Write the overall cell reaction for this voltaic cell.

b. (3 pt) In the presence of ammonia, $\ce{O2}$ oxidizes $\ce{[Cu(S2O3)3]^{5-}}$ back to $\ce{[Cu(NH3)4]^{2+}}$. Write a balanced equation for this oxidation-reduction reaction in basic solution.

c. (4 pt) In this leaching process, the $\ce{[Cu(NH3)4]^{2+}}$ complex ion functions as catalyst and speeds up the dissolution of gold. Write the net overall oxidation-reduction reaction for dissolution of the gold metal, which is catalyzed by $\ce{[Cu(NH3)4]^{2+}}$ complex ion.

d. (2 pt) Draw the coordination geometries of the metal in $\ce{[Au(NH3)2]+}$ and $\ce{[Au(S2O3)2]^{3-}}$ complex ions, indicating the coordinating atoms.

e. (5 pt) The formation constants, $K_\mathrm{f}$, of $\ce{[Au(NH3)2]+}$ and $\ce{[Au(S2O3)2]^{3-}}$ complexes are $1.00\times10^{26}$ and $1.00\times10^{28}$, respectively. Consider a leaching solution, in which the equilibrium concentrations of the species are as follows:

$[\ce{S2O3^{2-}}] = 0.100\ \mathrm{M}$; $[\ce{NH3}] = 0.100\ \mathrm{M}$; total concentration of gold(I) species $= 5.50\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{M}$.

Calculate the percentage of gold(I) ion, which exists in the form of thiosulfate complex.

f. (3 pt) When the concentration of $\ce{O2}$ is not high enough and pH > 10, $\ce{S2O3^{2-}}$ reduces $\ce{[Cu(NH3)4]^{2+}}$ to $\ce{[Cu(S2O3)3]^{5-}}$ with the formation of tetrathionate ion, $\ce{S4O6^{2-}}$:

$$\ce{2 [Cu(NH3)4]^{2+}(aq) + 8 S2O3^{2-}(aq) -> 2 [Cu(S2O3)3]^{5-}(aq) + S4O6^{2-}(aq) + 8 NH3(aq)}$$

In basic solution tetrathionate disproportionates to trithionate, $\ce{S3O6^{2-}}$, and thiosulfate. Write a balanced equation for this disproportionation reaction.

g. (1 pt) When the $\ce{O2}$ concentration is too high it oxidizes $\ce{S2O3^{2-}}$ to yield trithionate and sulfate ions. Write a balanced equation for this reaction.

problems.title: Synthesis of a carbasugar
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (26 points, 8.5% of the total). Synthesis of a carbasugar

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2011-7-fig1.png

Carbohydrates are essential components of living cells and a source of energy for animals. They include simple sugars with small molecules as well as macromolecular substances. When the ring oxygen (endocyclic oxygen) in sugars is replaced by a methylene group, the compounds formed are called as $\textbf{pseudosugars}$ or $\textbf{carbasugars}$. Since carbasugars are hydrolytically stable towards acids and enzymes, several carbasugars have found application in the field of glycosidase inhibition.

The total syntheses of two isomeric carbasugars having skeleton $\mathbf{1}$ are described below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2011-7-fig2.png

The total synthesis of $\mathbf{1}$ starts with a reduction of benzene by sodium in liquid ammonia to give $\mathbf{A}$. The C-13 NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{A}$ consists of two signals at 124.0 and 26.0 ppm.

Trichloroacetyl chloride in the presence of Zn gives a reactive species $\mathbf{S}$. One equivalent of $\mathbf{S}$ undergoes [2+2] cycloaddition with $\mathbf{A}$ to form a racemic product $\mathbf{B}$. The reaction of $\mathbf{B}$ with Zn in acetic acid gives $\mathbf{C}$. Compound $\mathbf{C}$ contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen: The C-13 NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{C}$ exhibits three $\mathrm{sp^2}$ carbon signals at 210.0, 126.5 and 125.3 ppm.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2011-7-fig3.png

The reaction of $\mathbf{C}$ with one equivalent $m$-chloroperbenzoic acid ($m$-CPBA) in methylene chloride gives $\mathbf{D}$ as a major product. The C-13 NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{D}$ exhibits also three signals in the $\mathrm{sp^2}$ region at 177.0, 125.8, 124.0 ppm.

Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, and the intermediate $\mathbf{S}$. [Points: $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{S}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$ 2 pt each.]

Reduction of $\mathbf{D}$ with $\ce{LiAlH4}$ yields $\mathbf{E}$, which reacts with excess acetyl chloride in pyridine to give $\mathbf{F}$. Draw the structures (use one enantiomer) of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$ using dashed-wedged line notation. Assign the configurations ($R$ or $S$) at the asymmetric carbon atoms in $\mathbf{E}$. [Points: $\mathbf{E}$ 2 pt, $\mathbf{F}$ 1 pt.]

The compound $\mathbf{F}$ (use the drawn enantiomer) is reacted with bromine to give the stereoisomers $\mathbf{G_1}$ and $\mathbf{G_2}$. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{G_1}$ and $\mathbf{G_2}$ using dashed-wedged line notation. [Points: $\mathbf{G_1}$ 1 pt, $\mathbf{G_2}$ 1 pt.]

A mixture of $\mathbf{G_1}$ and $\mathbf{G_2}$ is reacted with two equivalents of 1,8-diazabicyclo[5.4.0]undec-7-ene (DBU), which is a strong amine base, to afford $\mathbf{H}$. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{H}$ using dashed-wedged line notation. [Points: $\mathbf{H}$ 2 pt.]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2011-7-fig4.png

Reaction of $\mathbf{H}$ with singlet oxygen (in situ generated) affords $\mathbf{I}$. Although two isomers are theoretically possible, $\mathbf{I}$ is formed as the single isomer due to steric hindrance and electronic repulsion.

The reaction of $\mathbf{I}$ with excess $\ce{LiAlH4}$ results in the formation of $\mathbf{J}$. The C-13 NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{J}$ shows 8 signals, two in the $\mathrm{sp^2}$ region.

Reaction of $\mathbf{J}$ with excess acetyl chloride in the presence of pyridine yields $\mathbf{K}$. Subsequent reaction of $\mathbf{K}$ with $\ce{OsO4}$ in the presence of 4-methylmorpholine 4-oxide (NMO) gives stereoisomers $\mathbf{L}$ and $\mathbf{M}$.

Click chemistry is a chemical concept introduced by K. B. Sharpless in 2001 and describes a set of chemical reactions that generate substances quickly, reliably and quantitatively by joining molecules through small units under mild conditions. This methodology has recently been applied as a key step in the following synthesis of bicyclic compounds.

Mandelic acid is a versatile natural compound and widely used as a "chiral pool" in synthesis. The reduction of ($R$)-mandelic acid with $\ce{LiBH4}$ affords $\mathbf{A}$.

Problem 1 (20 points, 7.5% of the total). [Boron chemistry]

a. Boron Hydrides and Other Boron Compounds

Boron hydride chemistry was first developed by Alfred Stock (1876-1946). More than 20 neutral molecular boron hydrides with the general formula $\ce{B_{x}H_{y}}$ have been characterized. The simplest boron hydride is $\ce{B2H6}$, diborane.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2012-1-fig1.png

a.i (4 pt) Using the data below derive the $\textbf{molecular}$ formulae for two other members of this series of boron hydrides, $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$).

$$\begin{array}{c|l|l|l} \textbf{Substance} & \textbf{State (25 °C, 1 bar)} & \textbf{Mass Percent Boron} & \textbf{Molar mass (g/mol)} \\ \hline \mathbf{A} & \text{Liquid} & 83.1 & 65.1 \\ \mathbf{B} & \text{Solid} & 88.5 & 122.2 \end{array}$$

a.ii (2 pt) William Lipscomb received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1976 for "studies on the structures of boron hydrides illuminating the problems of chemical bonding." Lipscomb recognized that, $\textit{in all boron hydrides, each B atom has a normal 2-electron bond to at least one H atom}$ (B–H). However, additional bonds of several types occur, and he developed a scheme for describing the structure of a borane by giving it a $\textit{styx}$ number where:

• s = number of B–H–B bridges in the molecule
• t = the number of 3-center BBB bonds in the molecule

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2012-1-fig2.png

• y = the number of two-center B–B bonds in the molecule
• x = the number of $\ce{BH2}$ groups in the molecule

The $\textit{styx}$ number for $\ce{B2H6}$ is 2002. Propose a structure for tetraborane, $\ce{B4H10}$, with a $\textit{styx}$ number of 4012.

Spectral measurements indicate the molecule has two types of B atoms, with tetrahedral and trigonal planar geometry, in a 1:3 ratio, respectively. These spectra are also consistent with a CO triple bond. Given that the molecular formula of the compound is $\ce{B4CCl6O}$, suggest a structure for the molecule.

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \textbf{Compound} & \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ\ \textbf{(kJ/mol)} \\ \hline \ce{BCl3(g)} & -403 \\ \ce{B2Cl4(g)} & -489 \end{array}$$

problems.title: Platinum(II) Compounds, Isomers, and the Trans Effect
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (20 points, 7.8% of the total). Platinum(II) Compounds, Isomers, and the Trans Effect

Platinum and other Group 10 metals form square planar complexes and the mechanisms of their reactions have been studied extensively. For example, it is known that substitution reactions of these complexes proceed with retention of stereochemistry.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2012-2-fig1.png

It is also known that the rate of substitution of ligand X by Y depends on the nature of the ligand $\textit{trans}$ to X, that is, on ligand T. This is known as the $\textbf{\textit{trans}}$ $\textbf{effect.}$ When T is one of the molecules or ions in the following list, the rate of substitution at the trans position decreases from left to right.

$$\ce{CN- > H- > NO2-, I- > Br-, Cl- > pyridine, NH3, OH-, H2O}$$

The preparations of $\textit{cis}$- and $\textit{trans}$-$\ce{Pt(NH3)2Cl2}$ depend on the $\textit{trans}$ affect. The preparation of the $\textit{cis}$ isomer, a cancer chemotherapy agent commonly called cisplatin, involves the reaction of $\ce{K2PtCl4}$ with ammonia.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2012-2-fig2.png

a.i (4 pt) Draw all possible stereoisomers for square planar platinum(II) compounds with the formula $\ce{Pt(py)(NH3)BrCl}$ (where py = pyridine, $\ce{C5H5N}$).

a.ii (4 pt) Write reaction schemes including intermediate(s), if any, to show the preparation in aqueous solution for each of the stereoisomers of $\ce{[Pt(NH3)(NO2)Cl2]^-}$ using, as reagents, $\ce{PtCl4^{2-}}$, $\ce{NH3}$, and $\ce{NO2-}$. The reactions are controlled kinetically by the $\textit{trans}$ effect.

[In the answer boxes for the $\textit{cis}$-isomer and for the $\textit{trans}$-isomer the starting complex $\ce{[PtCl4]^{2-}}$ is printed as a square-planar structure.]

b. Kinetic Studies of Substitution Reactions of Square Planar Complexes

Substitutions of the ligand X by Y in square planar complexes

$$\ce{ML3X + Y -> ML3Y + X}$$

can occur in either or both of two ways:

• $\textit{Direct substitution:}$ The incoming ligand Y attaches to the central metal, forming a five-coordinate complex, which then rapidly eliminates a ligand, X, to give the product, $\ce{ML3Y}$.

$$\mathrm{ML_3X} \xrightarrow[\ast\ast]{+\,\mathrm{Y}} [\mathrm{ML_3XY}] \xrightarrow{-\,\mathrm{X}} \mathrm{ML_3Y}$$

** = rate determining step, Rate constant = $k_\mathrm{Y}$

• $\textit{Solvent-assisted substitution:}$ A solvent molecule S attaches to the central metal to give $\ce{ML3XS}$, which eliminates the X to give $\ce{ML3S}$. Y rapidly displaces S to give $\ce{ML3Y}$.

$$\mathrm{ML_3X} \xrightarrow[\ast\ast]{+\,\mathrm{S}} [\mathrm{ML_3XS}] \xrightarrow{-\,\mathrm{X}} [\mathrm{ML_3S}] \xrightarrow[-\,\mathrm{S}]{+\,\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{ML_3Y}$$

** = rate determining step, Rate constant = $k_\mathrm{S}$

The overall rate law for such substitutions is

$$\text{Rate} = k_\mathrm{s}[\ce{ML3X}] + k_\mathrm{Y}[\mathrm{Y}][\ce{ML3X}]$$

When $[\mathrm{Y}] \gg [\ce{ML3X}]$, then $\text{Rate} = k_\mathrm{obs}[\ce{ML3X}]$.

The values of $k_\mathrm{s}$ and $k_\mathrm{Y}$ depend on the reactants and solvent involved. One example is the displacement of the $\ce{Cl-}$ ligand in a square planar platinum(II) complex, $\ce{ML2X2}$, by pyridine ($\ce{C5H5N}$). (The $\ce{ML3X}$ scheme above applies to $\ce{ML2X2}$.)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2012-2-fig3.png

Data for reaction at 25 °C in methanol where [pyridine] >> the concentration of the platinum complex are given in the table below.

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \text{Concentration of pyridine (mol/L)} & k_\mathrm{obs}\ (\mathrm{s^{-1}}) \\ \hline 0.122 & 7.20\times10^{-4} \\ 0.061 & 3.45\times10^{-4} \\ 0.030 & 1.75\times10^{-4} \end{array}$$

b.i (6 pt) Calculate the values of $k_\mathrm{s}$ and $k_\mathrm{Y}$. Give the proper unit for each constant. A grid is given if you wish to use it.

b.ii (1 pt) When [pyridine] = 0.10 mol/L, which of the following is true? (Tick the box next to the correct answer.)

• ☐ Most pyridine product is formed by the solvent-assisted ($k_\mathrm{s}$) substitution pathway.
• ☐ Most pyridine product is formed by the direct substitution ($k_\mathrm{Y}$) pathway
• ☐ Comparable amounts of product are formed by the two pathways.
• ☐ No conclusions may be drawn regarding the relative amounts of product produced by the two pathways.

c. A chemotherapy agent

c (5 pt) In an effort to better target cisplatin to cancer cells, Professor Lippard's group at MIT attached a platinum(IV) complex to oligonucleotides bound to gold nanoparticles.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2012-2-fig4.png

The experiments use gold nanoparticles with a diameter of 13 nm. Attached to each nanoparticle are 90 oligonucleotide groups, with 98% of them being bound to a Pt(IV) complex. Suppose that the reaction vessel used for treating cells with the Pt(IV) nanoparticle reagent has a volume of 1.0 mL and that the solution is $1.0\times10^{-6}$ M in Pt. $\textbf{Calculate the mass of gold and of platinum used in this experiment}$. (The density of gold is $19.3\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$)

problems.title: Thiomolybdate ions
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (34 points, 7.5% of the total). [Thiomolybdate ions]

Thiomolybdate ions are derived from molybdate ions, $\ce{MoO4^{2-}}$, by replacing oxygen atoms with sulfur atoms. In nature, thiomolybdate ions are found in such places as the deep waters of the Black Sea, where biological sulfate reduction generates $\ce{H2S}$. The molybdate to thiomolybdate transformation leads to rapid loss of dissolved Mo from seawater to underlying sediments, depleting the ocean in Mo, a trace element essential for life.

The following equilibria control the relative concentrations of molybdate and thiomolybdate ions in dilute aqueous solution.

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{MoS4^{2-} + H2O(l) <=> MoOS3^{2-} + H2S(aq)} & K_1 = 1.3\times10^{-5} \\ \ce{MoOS3^{2-} + H2O(l) <=> MoO2S2^{2-} + H2S(aq)} & K_2 = 1.0\times10^{-5} \\ \ce{MoO2S2^{2-} + H2O(l) <=> MoO3S^{2-} + H2S(aq)} & K_3 = 1.6\times10^{-5} \\ \ce{MoO3S^{2-} + H2O(l) <=> MoO4^{2-} + H2S(aq)} & K_4 = 6.5\times10^{-6} \end{array}$$

a (4 pt) If at equilibrium a solution contains $1\times10^{-7}$ M $\ce{MoO4^{2-}}$ and $1\times10^{-6}$ M $\ce{H2S(aq)}$, what would be the concentration of $\ce{MoS4^{2-}}$?

Solutions containing $\ce{MoO2S2^{2-}}$, $\ce{MoOS3^{2-}}$ and $\ce{MoS4^{2-}}$ display absorption peaks in the visible wavelength range at 395 and 468 nm. The other ions, as well as $\ce{H2S}$, absorb negligibly in the visible wavelength range. The molar absorptivities ($\varepsilon$) at these two wavelengths are given in the following table:

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} & \varepsilon\ \text{at 468 nm}\ (\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}) & \varepsilon\ \text{at 395 nm}\ (\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}) \\ \hline \ce{MoS4^{2-}} & 11870 & 120 \\ \ce{MoOS3^{2-}} & 0 & 9030 \\ \ce{MoO2S2^{2-}} & 0 & 3230 \end{array}$$

b (12 pt) A solution $\underline{\textit{not}}$ at equilibrium contains a mixture of $\ce{MoS4^{2-}}$, $\ce{MoOS3^{2-}}$ and $\ce{MoO2S2^{2-}}$ and no other Mo-containing species. The total concentration of all species containing Mo is $6.0\times10^{-6}$ M. In a 10.0 cm absorption cell, the absorbance of the solution at 468 nm is 0.365 and at 395 nm is 0.213. Calculate the concentrations of all three Mo-containing anions in this mixture.

c. A solution initially containing $2.0\times10^{-7}$ M $\ce{MoS4^{2-}}$ hydrolyzes in a closed system. The $\ce{H2S}$ product accumulates until equilibrium is reached. Calculate the final equilibrium concentrations of $\ce{H2S(aq)}$, and all five Mo-containing anions (that is, $\ce{MoO4^{2-}}$, $\ce{MoO3S^{2-}}$, $\ce{MoO2S2^{2-}}$, $\ce{MoOS3^{2-}}$ and $\ce{MoS4^{2-}}$). Ignore the possibility that $\ce{H2S}$ might ionize to $\ce{HS-}$ under certain pH conditions. $\textit{(One-third credit is given is given for writing the six independent equations that constrain the problem, and two-thirds credit is given for the correct concentrations.)}$

c.i (6 pt) Write the six independent equations that determine the system.

c.ii (12 pt) Calculate the six concentrations making reasonable approximations, giving your answers to two significant figures.

problems.title: The YBCO superconductor
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (60 points, 7.8% of the total). [The YBCO superconductor]

In the 1980's a class of ceramic materials was discovered that exhibits superconductivity at the unusually high temperature of 90 K. One such material contains yttrium, barium, copper and oxygen and is called "YBCO". It has a nominal composition of $\ce{YBa2Cu3O7}$, but its actual composition is variable according to the formula $\mathrm{YBa_2Cu_3O_{7-\delta}}$ $(0 < \delta < 0.5)$.

a (12 pt) One unit cell of the idealized crystal structure of YBCO is shown below. Identify which circles correspond to which elements in the structure.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2012-4-fig1.png

The true structure is actually orthorhombic ($a \ne b \ne c$), but it is approximately tetragonal, with $a \approx b \approx (c/3)$.

b (14 pt) A sample of YBCO with $\delta = 0.25$ was subjected to X-ray diffraction using Cu K$\alpha$ radiation ($\lambda = 154.2\ \mathrm{pm}$). The lowest-angle diffraction peak was observed at $2\theta = 7.450^\circ$. Assuming that $a = b = (c/3)$, calculate the values of $a$ and $c$.

c (10 pt) Estimate the density of this sample of YBCO (with $\delta = 0.25$) in $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. If you do not have the values for $a$ and $c$ from part (b), then use $a = 500.\ \mathrm{pm}$, $c = 1500.\ \mathrm{pm}$.

d. When YBCO is dissolved in 1.0 M aqueous HCl, bubbles of gas are observed (identified as $\ce{O2}$ by gas chromatography). After boiling for 10 min to expel the dissolved gases, the solution reacts with excess KI solution, turning yellow-brown. This solution can be titrated with thiosulfate solution to a starch endpoint. If YBCO is added directly to a solution that 1.0 M in both KI and HCl under Ar, the solution turns yellow-brown but no gas evolution is observed.

d.i (4 pt) Write a balanced net ionic equation for the reaction when solid $\mathrm{YBa_2Cu_3O_{7-\delta}}$ dissolves in aqueous HCl with evolution of $\ce{O2}$.

d.ii (2 pt) Write a balanced net ionic equation for the reaction when the solution from (i) reacts with excess KI in acidic solution after the dissolved oxygen is expelled.

d.iii (2 pt) Write a balanced net ionic equation for the reaction when the solution from (ii) is titrated with thiosulfate ($\ce{S2O3^{2-}}$).

d.iv (4 pt) Write a balanced net ionic equation for the reaction when solid $\mathrm{YBa_2Cu_3O_{7-\delta}}$ dissolves in aqueous HCl containing excess KI in an Ar atmosphere.

e. Two identical samples of YBCO with an unknown value of $\delta$ were prepared. The first sample was dissolved in 5 mL of 1.0 M aqueous HCl, evolving $\ce{O2}$. After boiling to expel gases, cooling, and addition of 10 mL of 0.7 M KI solution under Ar, titration with thiosulfate to the starch endpoint required $1.542\times10^{-4}$ mol thiosulfate. The second sample of YBCO was added directly to 7 mL of a solution that was 1.0 M in KI and 0.7 M in HCl under Ar; titration of this solution required $1.696\times10^{-4}$ mol thiosulfate to reach the endpoint.

e.i (4 pt) Calculate the number of moles of Cu in each of these samples of YBCO.

e.ii (8 pt) Calculate the value of $\delta$ for these samples of YBCO.

problems.problem:
Problem 7 (52 points, 7.5% of the total). [An artificial Diels–Alder enzyme]
