problems.title: New and well-forgotten old refrigerants
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (8 points; 33 marks). New and well-forgotten old refrigerants

The problem of choosing a refrigerant for refrigeration and air conditioning systems attracted the attention of scientists and technologists throughout the last century. It has been suggested that during this time refrigerants progressed through four generations. Ammonia, which was ascribed to the first generation, had been used in most of the oldest refrigeration units. It was later replaced by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) – derivatives of methane and ethane with the hydrogen atoms replaced by fluorine and chlorine.

In Baku, at "Bakkonditsioner" factory, production of the first Soviet serial household air conditioners BK-1500 had been launched. A second-generation refrigerant chlorodifluoromethane $\ce{CHF2Cl}$ was used in them. In this problem, we compare various refrigerants in terms of thermodynamics.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-1-fig1.png

First air conditioner of Baku factory in a souvenir shop in the Old City ("Icheri Sheher")

Thermodynamic properties of various refrigerants

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Refrigerant} & \text{"Generation"} & \Delta H_\mathrm{vap}\ /\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\ (\text{at } 280\,\mathrm{K}) & C_{V(\mathrm{gas})}\ /\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}} \\ \hline \ce{NH3} & 1 & 21.3 & 26.7 \\ \ce{CHF2Cl} & 2 & 20.0 & 48.8 \\ \ce{CF3CH2F} & 3 & 22.1 & 79 \\ \ce{CF3CF=CH2} & 4 & 19.1 & 120 \end{array}$$

Consider a model refrigeration cycle consisting of 4 steps schematically shown below in the pressure ($p$) – internal energy ($U$) coordinates.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-1-fig2.png

Diagram 1 (dashed line indicates the phase boundaries)

During the first step of the cycle (line 0-1 in diagram 1), a liquid refrigerant is boiling at constant pressure $p_1$ and temperature $T_1$ (boiling temperature) until it completely evaporates. At this step, the refrigeration unit absorbs heat from surrounding objects. At the second step, the refrigerant undergoes reversible adiabatic compression and heats up to temperature $T_2$ (line 1-2). After that the compressed refrigerant is cooled in a condenser at constant pressure $p_2$ (line 2-3) and then returns to the initial state (line 3-0).

Let the cycle involve 1 mole of refrigerant, which is initially (point 0) completely liquid, $T_1 = 280\,\mathrm{K}$, $T_2 = 380\,\mathrm{K}$, assume that the vapor of any refrigerant behaves like an ideal gas. The thermodynamic characteristics of refrigerants are listed in the table above.

1.1 (4 marks) For each of refrigerants, ammonia and chlorodifluoromethane, calculate the amount of heat $Q$ absorbed by refrigeration unit during heat exchange (line 0-1) and the work $W$ required to compress its vapor adiabatically (line 1-2).

1.2 (2 marks) Which quantity(ies) remain(s) constant during the adiabatic compression step? Indicate by the circle(s).

$U \qquad H \qquad S \qquad G \qquad V$

To compare the energy efficiency of refrigeration cycles with different parameters and refrigerants, the coefficient of performance ($COP$) is used, which is defined as a ratio of heat removed from a cooled system to the work of compressor: $COP = Q/W$.

1.3 (2 marks) Calculate the values of $COP$ in a considered cycle for ammonia and chlorodifluoromethane.

2.1 (1 mark) Why was ammonia replaced by CFCs in household refrigeration units? (Choose only one option)

a) to increase the energy efficiency of refrigeration cycles
b) because the density of ammonia is less than that of air under the same conditions
c) for user safety reasons

A search for replacement of CFCs as refrigerants started when it was shown that their use can cause irreparable damage to the protective ozone layer of the atmosphere. The third, ozone-friendly generation of refrigerants came on the scene. Its typical representatives are fluoroalkanes.

2.2 (1 mark) What is the cause of the damage made by CFCs to the ozone layer? (Choose only one option)

a) ozone molecule easily adds to C–F bond
b) C–F bond is easily broken by radiation, which leads to the formation of free radicals
c) ozone molecule easily adds to C–Cl bond
d) C–Cl bond is easily broken by radiation, which leads to the formation of free radicals

However, under the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, fluoroalkanes also had to be replaced because they accumulate in the atmosphere and rapidly absorb infrared radiation, causing a rise in temperature of the atmosphere (the greenhouse effect). The refrigerants of the fourth generation such as 2,3,3,3-tetrafluoropropene $\ce{CF3CF=CH2}$ have been suggested and are coming into use.

2.3 (1 mark) Why does this compound enhance the greenhouse effect less than fluoroalkanes? (Choose only one option)

a) it is more reactive and easier to decompose
b) it easily reacts with ozone
c) it is better soluble in water

3 (3 marks) Calculate the values of the $COP$ in the refrigeration cycle considered above for two refrigerants of the third and fourth generations – $\ce{CF3CH2F}$ and $\ce{CF3CF=CH2}$. Did the energy efficiency improve in comparison with $\ce{CHF2Cl}$? Choose "Yes" or "No".

Unlike household appliances, industrial refrigeration systems are often still using ammonia. It does not contribute to the greenhouse effect nor does it destroy the ozone layer. Industrial units can have a huge size and a large cost. Prior to their construction, they should be carefully modeled taking into account many different factors. In real systems, some part of the refrigerant at the start of the heat exchange with the environment is in the vapor phase (point 0 in the diagram below), and at the end (point 1) it is always overheated above the boiling point.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-1-fig3.png

Diagram 2 (dashed line indicates the phase boundaries)

Consider a cycle with 1 mole of ammonia. Its thermodynamic properties are the following: enthalpy of vaporization $\Delta H_\mathrm{vap} = 23.35\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ at $T_\mathrm{vap} = 239.8\,\mathrm{K}$ (boiling temperature at 1 bar pressure). Heat capacity of the liquid phase $C_{V(\mathrm{liq})} = 77\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$, of the gas phase $C_{V(\mathrm{gas})} = 26.7\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$. Assume that the heat capacities are temperature-independent and the vapor behaves like an ideal gas. The temperature dependence of the saturated vapor pressure of ammonia can be described by the empirical equation:

$$\log\,(p/\mathrm{bar}) = 4.87 - 1114\,/\,(T/\mathrm{K} - 10.4).$$

During the first step of the cycle (line 0-1 in diagram 2), the equilibrium mixture of liquid refrigerant and its vapor receives heat from the environment at constant pressure $p_1 = 3.0\,\mathrm{bar}$. The refrigerant completely evaporates and overheats up to the temperature $T_1 = 275\,\mathrm{K}$. In the beginning of the process (point 0), the molar fraction of gaseous ammonia is $x = 0.13$.

4.1 (10 marks) Calculate the initial temperature of refrigerant $T_0$, its volume change $\Delta V$ and the amount of heat $Q$ absorbed by refrigeration unit during this step. Take into account that the dependence of $\Delta H_\mathrm{vap}$ from the temperature cannot be neglected.

Then the refrigerant is reversibly and adiabatically compressed. It heats up to the temperature $T_2 = 393\,\mathrm{K}$ (line 1-2).

4.2 (2 marks) Find the work $W$ required for compression and the $COP$ of the system. If you were not able to find $Q$ in 4.1, use $Q = 20.15\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

At the next step corresponding to the line 2-3 in diagram, the compressed refrigerant is cooled in a condenser at constant pressure. Then it returns to the initial state through adiabatic expansion with zero work (line 3-0).

4.3 (6 marks) Determine the temperature $T_3$ at point 3 to which the refrigerant is cooled in a condenser.

In the production of refrigeration units it is necessary to consider climatic factors. If a condenser is cooled by atmospheric air, the temperature $T_3$ increases as the air temperature increases.

4.4 (1 mark) How will the $COP$ change if $T_3$ increases while $T_0$, $T_1$, $T_2$ remain the same?

a) Increase
b) Remain the same
c) Decrease

problems.title: Coupling of chemical reactions
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (7 points; 25 marks). Coupling of chemical reactions

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-2-fig1.png

I. Prigogine (left) · N. Shilov · W. Ostwald

When in the system one reaction allows another one to proceed they say that these two reactions are coupled. Ilya Prigogine, Nobel prize winner in chemistry (1977) in his books widely used the concept of "coupled reactions". Coupling of reactions is an essential feature of living systems, including human body.

How one reaction makes another one to occur? In this problem we are going to discuss several possible mechanisms of coupling.

(I) "Chemical coupling"

"On Chemical coupling" was the title of the dissertation defended by Russian chemist N. Shilov in 1905. N. Shilov was the graduate student of famous professor W. Ostwald. Dr. Shilov described the following set of reactions.

The substance $\mathbf{A}$ does not react with $\mathbf{Ac}$. In the presence of the third reagent (called inductor), $\mathbf{In}$, however, the reaction of $\mathbf{A}$ with $\mathbf{Ac}$ takes place:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{Ac} \xrightarrow{\text{In the absence of In}} \text{no reaction!} & \quad (1) \\ \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{Ac} \xrightarrow{\text{In the presence of In}} \mathbf{P}_1 & \quad (2) \end{array}$$

$\mathbf{In}$ is not a catalyst! Its concentration decreases in the course of the reactions.

According to the scheme proposed by Shilov, $\mathbf{Ac}$ reacts not with $\mathbf{A}$ itself, but with the intermediate product $\mathbf{R}$ of the reaction of $\mathbf{A}$ with $\mathbf{In}$. There is another, competing reaction of $\mathbf{R}$ that forms $\mathbf{P}_2$.

$$\left.\begin{array}{ll} (a) & \alpha\mathbf{A} + \beta\mathbf{In} \xrightarrow{k(3a)} \mathbf{R} \\ (b) & \mathbf{R} \xrightarrow{k(3b)} \mathbf{P}_2 \\ (c) & \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{Ac} \xrightarrow{k(3c)} \mathbf{P}_1 \end{array}\right\} \quad (3)$$

$\alpha$ and $\beta$ are stoichiometric coefficients. Other stoichiometric coefficients and reaction order with respect to all reactants in all three reactions are unity.

In the Shilov's experiments the ratio of the consumed amounts of $\mathbf{Ac}$ and $\mathbf{In}$, $I = \dfrac{\Delta n_{\mathbf{Ac}}}{\Delta n_{\mathbf{In}}}$ increased up to the constant value with the increasing initial concentration $[\mathbf{Ac}]_0$ at $[\mathbf{In}]_0 = \text{const}$.

1.1 (4 marks) What was this limiting constant value of $I$ at $[\mathbf{Ac}]_0 \to \infty$, $[\mathbf{In}]_0 = \text{const}$?

1.2 (6 marks) Derive an expression for $I$ using the steady-state approximation if necessary. Plot the graph of $I$ vs $[\mathbf{In}]_0$ at $[\mathbf{Ac}]_0 = \text{const}$. Assume that $\mathbf{In}$ was completely consumed and $\mathbf{Ac}$ was in excess.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-2-fig2.png

[Axes printed on the answer sheet for the graph]

What if Shilov's mechanism is not valid and $\mathbf{In}$ is a conventional catalyst of the reaction (2)? Simultaneously $\mathbf{In}$ reacts with $\mathbf{A}$ and its concentration decreases. The reaction scheme in this case is

$$\left.\begin{array}{ll} (a) & \alpha\mathbf{A} + \beta\mathbf{In} \longrightarrow \mathbf{P}_2 \\ (b) & \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{Ac} \xrightarrow{\mathbf{In},\ \text{catalysis}} \mathbf{P}_1 \end{array}\right\} \quad (4)$$

1.3 (4 marks) What is the limiting value of $I$ for the reaction scheme (4) at $[\mathbf{Ac}]_0 \to \infty$, $[\mathbf{In}]_0 = \text{const}$?

(II) «Kinetic coupling»

The standard Gibbs energy of the gas-phase reaction

$$\ce{Br + H2} \underset{k_{-5}}{\overset{k_5}{\rightleftharpoons}} \ce{HBr + H} \qquad (5)$$

is positive, $\Delta G^\circ(5) = 66\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ at $T = 600\,\mathrm{K}$.

2.1 (3 marks) What is the ratio of the rates of forward and reverse reactions, $\dfrac{r_5}{r_{-5}}$, at this temperature, standard pressures of $\ce{H2}$ and $\ce{HBr}$ and equal pressures of $\ce{H}$ and $\ce{Br}$?

If you could not answer this question, for further calculations use the reference value $r_5/r_{-5} = 3.14\cdot10^{-7}$.

Reaction (5) proceeds in the forward direction due to the reaction (6) which simultaneously occurs in the system:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{Br + H2} \underset{k_{-5}}{\overset{k_5}{\rightleftharpoons}} \ce{HBr + H} & \qquad (5) \\ \ce{H + Br2} \xrightarrow{k_6} \ce{HBr + Br} & \qquad (6) \end{array}$$

$k_5$, $k_{-5}$, $k_6$ are rate constants of forward and reverse reaction (5) and forward reaction (6), respectively.

This is the kinetic coupling of two reactions.

Let pressures of neutral molecules keep standard values $p(\ce{H2}) = p(\ce{Br2}) = p(\ce{HBr}) = 1\,\mathrm{bar}$, and pressures of radicals $p(\ce{H})$, $p(\ce{Br})$ reach steady-state values. Rate constant $k_6$ is 10 times larger than $k_{-5}$.

2.2 (6 marks) Calculate $\Delta G(5)$ and $\dfrac{r_5}{r_{-5}}$ under such conditions.

(III) "Second law of thermodynamics restricts coupling"

According to the Second Law of thermodynamics, two simultaneously occurring chemical reactions should decrease the system's Gibbs energy $G_\mathrm{syst}$, $\dfrac{\Delta G_\mathrm{Syst}}{\Delta t} < 0$.

One of these reactions may have positive Gibbs energy and still proceed in the forward direction due to the coupling with the second reaction. This second reaction must have negative Gibbs energy and the requirements of the Second law must be fulfilled! Consider the example.

The synthesis of urea under specific conditions

$$\ce{2NH3 + CO2 -> (NH2)2CO + H2O} \qquad (7)$$

$\Delta G(7) = 46.0\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

is supposed to be coupled with the complete oxidation of glucose (under the same conditions)

$$\ce{1/6 C6H12O6 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O} \qquad (8)$$

$\Delta G(8) = -481.2\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, $r(8) = 6.0\cdot10^{-8}\,\mathrm{M\,min^{-1}}$.

Both reactions are presented schematically. No other reactions are considered.

3 (2 marks) What is the maximum rate of the reaction (7) permitted by the Second Law if this reaction is coupled to reaction (8)?

problems.title: Two binding centers – competition or cooperation?
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (7 points; 28 marks). Two binding centers – competition or cooperation?

Many chemical reactions in living organisms include the formation of "host-guest" complexes where the host molecule reversibly binds one or several guest molecules. Consider a host molecule $\mathbf{H}$ with two binding centers – say, $a$ and $b$ which have different affinities for the guest molecules $\mathbf{G}$:

$$\begin{array}{lll} \mathbf{H} + \mathbf{G} \rightleftharpoons \mathbf{HG}_a & \qquad K_a = \dfrac{[\mathbf{HG}_a]}{[\mathbf{H}][\mathbf{G}]} & \\ \mathbf{H} + \mathbf{G} \rightleftharpoons \mathbf{HG}_b & \qquad K_b = \dfrac{[\mathbf{HG}_b]}{[\mathbf{H}][\mathbf{G}]} & \qquad K_b \neq K_a. \end{array}$$

where $\mathbf{HG}_a$ and $\mathbf{HG}_b$ denote a complex where guest is bound to $a$ center and $b$ center, respectively. $K_a$ and $K_b$ are the binding constants for the centers $a$ and $b$, brackets denote molar concentrations.

Attachment of one $\mathbf{G}$ molecule to $\mathbf{H}$ can change the binding ability of the second centre. This change is described by the "interaction factor" $\beta$ which reflects the influence of one binding center on another and is defined as follows:

$$\mathbf{HG}_a + \mathbf{G} \rightleftharpoons \mathbf{HG}_2 \qquad \frac{[\mathbf{HG}_2]}{[\mathbf{HG}_a][\mathbf{G}]} = \beta K_b$$

where $\mathbf{HG}_2$ is the completely bound complex.

1.1 (3 marks) Determine the range of values (or one value, if necessary) of $\beta$ which correspond to three possible ways of interaction between binding centers: a) cooperation (binding by one center facilitates subsequent binding); b) competition (first binding complicates the second); c) independence (no interaction).

1.2 (2 marks) Find the equilibrium constant for the process: $\mathbf{HG}_b + \mathbf{G} \rightleftharpoons \mathbf{HG}_2$ in terms of binding constant(s) and interaction factor.

2.1 (8 marks) The solution was prepared with the initial concentrations $[\mathbf{H}]_0 = 1\,\mathrm{M}$ and $[\mathbf{G}]_0 = 2\,\mathrm{M}$. After the reactions were completed, the concentration of $\mathbf{H}$ decreased by 10 times and that of $\mathbf{G}$ by 4 times. For these host and guest, $K_b = 2K_a$. Determine the concentrations of all other species in the solution and find the binding constant $K_a$ and the factor $\beta$.

If you could not answer this question, for further calculations use reference values $K_a = 3.14$ and $\beta = 2.72$.

2.2 (3 marks) Find the correct order of standard molar Gibbs energies of formation of host $\mathbf{H}$ and all host-guest complexes from $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{G}$. In the scheme below, write the corresponding chemical formula near every line.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-3-fig1.png

2.3 (6 marks) Some amount of $\mathbf{G}$ was added to 1 mole of $\mathbf{H}$ and the mixture was dissolved in water to obtain 1 liter of the solution. The number of the totally bound molecules $\mathbf{HG}_2$ in the solution is equal to the total number of single-bound molecules $\mathbf{HG}$. Find the initial amount of $\mathbf{G}$ (in mol). The constants $K_a$ and $K_b$ and the factor $\beta$ are the same as in question 2.1.

2.4 (6 marks) What would be the equilibrium composition of the solution if: a) $\beta = 0$; b) $\beta$ is very large ($\beta \to \infty$). The constants $K_a$ and $K_b$ as well as the initial concentrations of $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{G}$ are the same as in question 2.1.

problems.title: From one yellow powder to another: A simple inorganic riddle
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (6 points; 24 marks). From one yellow powder to another: A simple inorganic riddle

The yellow binary compound $\mathbf{X}_1$ was completely dissolved in concentrated nitric acid by heating, the gas evolved is 1.586 times denser than air. Upon adding an excess of barium chloride to the solution formed a white solid $\mathbf{X}_2$ precipitates. It was filtered. The filtrate reacts with an excess of silver sulfate solution forming a precipitate of two solids $\mathbf{X}_2$ and $\mathbf{X}_3$, also separated from solution by filtration. To the new filtrate the solution of sodium hydroxide was being added drop-wise until the solution became nearly neutral (about pH 7). At this time a yellow powder $\mathbf{X}_4$ (77.31 wt.% of Ag) crystallized from the solution. The mass of $\mathbf{X}_4$ is nearly 2.4 times larger than that the mass of the first portion of $\mathbf{X}_2$.

1 (8 marks) Determine the chemical formulae of $\mathbf{X}_1$ – $\mathbf{X}_4$.

2 (8 marks) Determine the chemical formula of the gas and provide equations for all reactions in ionic or non-ionic form.

[Headings printed in the answer box: Chemical formula of the gas; Dissolution of $\mathbf{X}_1$; Formation of $\mathbf{X}_2$; Formation of $\mathbf{X}_2$ and $\mathbf{X}_3$; Addition of NaOH and formation of $\mathbf{X}_4$.]

3 (3 marks) In the structural unit of $\mathbf{X}_1$ all atoms of only one element are in equivalent positions. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{X}_1$.

4 (5 marks) Predict the products of $\mathbf{X}_1$ interaction with:

a) excess oxygen;
b) excess of hot concentrated sulfuric acid;
c) solid $\ce{KClO3}$ with grinding.

Write down the reaction equations.

problems.title: Indispensable glucose
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (8 points; 34 marks). Indispensable glucose

Carbohydrates are the most important providers of energy for living cells. Monosaccharide glucose is a source of energy for the living cell, but for persons who suffer from diabetes glucose may be dangerous. High level of glucose may lead to cardiovascular diseases and even death. That is why people avoid consuming too much carbohydrates and glucose particularly.

1. Determination of reducing sugars in fruit juice

One of the technique for determination of reducing sugars in different samples includes the use of Fehling's reagent. A 10.00-mL aliquot of fruit juice (assuming the initial sample contained only glucose and fructose) was transferred into a titration flask and Fehling's reagent was added. This reagent was prepared by mixing 50.00 mL of 0.04000 M copper sulfate (solution A) and potassium-sodium tartrate and sodium hydroxide (solution B). Solution C thus obtained, was then heated and red precipitate was formed.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-5-fig1.png

Glucose

1.1 (2 marks) Write the balanced ionic equation of chemical reaction occurring upon heating of the solution C. Use $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ for initial copper solution.

After that 10 mL of 10% solution of potassium iodide and 1 M sulfuric acid were added to the flask. The mixture was covered with watch glass and was then placed in a dark place. An excess of iodine was then titrated with 0.05078 M sodium thiosulphate solution. 11.87 mL of the titrant was required to reach the endpoint.

1.2 (3 marks) Write the balanced equation(s) in molecular or ionic form for all the reactions taking place in the flask.

1.3 (6 marks) Consider all fructose was transformed into glucose under the experimental conditions; calculate the total mass content of sugars (in g/L) in a fruit juice. $M_\mathrm{w} = 180.16\,\mathrm{g/mol}$.

A new 10.00-mL aliquot of the same juice was treated with a 10.00-mL portion of acidified potassium iodate(V) solution (0.01502 M) and 10 mL of 10 % solution of potassium iodide. After the mixture turned brown, an excess of sodium hydroxide solution was added. The flask was then covered with a watch glass and put into a dark place. The obtained solution was acidified and titrated with 0.01089 M solution of sodium thiosulphate. The average titrant volume used for titration was 23.43 mL. Note that fructose is not converted into glucose under these conditions.

1.4 (4 marks) Write all the balanced equations for the described reactions in molecular or ionic form.

1.5 (6 marks) Calculate the mass content of each sugar (in g/L) in the juice.

1.6 (1 mark) One bread exchange unit (1 BEU) corresponds to the content of 12 g of digestible carbohydrates in product. How many BEU are in one glass (200 mL) of juice?

2. Diagnosis of diseases

The derivative of glucose, 2-deoxy-2-($\ce{^{18}F}$)fluoro-D-glucose (FDG), is the most common radiopharmaceuticals for diagnosis of cancer using positron emission tomography. The first step of FDG preparation is to produce a radionuclide fluoro-18 by nuclear reaction in a cyclotron. The next step is the radiochemical synthesis. Fluorine-18 is introduced into D-glucose molecule by nucleophilic substitution. 2-deoxy-2-($\ce{^{18}F}$)fluoro-D-glucose once injected into the patient actively accumulates in cells of malignant tumors; this process is accompanied by decomposition of fluorine-18. This radionuclide is a $\beta^+$ emitter – nucleus emits a positron (anti-electron). Positron interacts with an electron and after that annihilation occurs, which can be detected. This allows determining precisely the tumor sizes and type.

2.1 (2 marks) Complete the nuclear reactions leading to various fluorine isotopes.

$$\begin{array}{ll} \text{a)} & \ce{^{18}O} + \ce{^{1}_{1}H} \rightarrow \ldots + \ce{^{18}F} \\ \text{b)} & \ldots + \ce{^{2}_{1}D} \rightarrow \ce{^{18}F} + \alpha \\ \text{c)} & \ce{^{19}F} + \ce{^{2}_{1}D} \rightarrow \ce{^{20}F} + \ldots \\ \text{d)} & \ce{^{16}O} + \ldots \rightarrow \ce{^{18}F} + \ce{^{1}_{1}H} + n \end{array}$$

2.2 (2 marks) The decay mode of unstable light nuclei depends on the ratio between the number of neutrons and protons in them. If this ratio is greater than that for a stable isotope then the nucleus decays in a $\beta^-$-mode, if it is smaller – in a $\beta^+$-mode.

Determine the type of decay for the nuclei in the table:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \text{Nucleus} & \ce{^{11}C} & \ce{^{20}F} & \ce{^{17}F} & \ce{^{14}C} \\ \hline \text{Decay mode} & & & & \end{array}$$

When nuclear reaction (a) is used for fluorine-18 preparation, the target material is presented as water enriched with $\ce{H2^{18}O}$. The presence of usual water $\ce{H2^{16}O}$ leads to a side nuclear reaction with $\ce{^{16}O}$, leading to the formation of isotope $\ce{^{17}F}$.

2.3 (4 marks) It is known that within five minutes after completion of irradiation of the target the ratio of radioactivities of $\ce{^{18}F}$ and $\ce{^{17}F}$ is $10^5$. Assuming that irradiation time is short and the radioactivity of each isotope is proportional to the nuclear reaction yield and the mole fraction of a component in the irradiated target, calculate the mass fraction of $\ce{H2^{18}O}$ in the target. $t_{1/2}(\ce{^{18}F}) = 109.7$ minutes, $t_{1/2}(\ce{^{17}F}) = 65$ seconds. The ratio between nuclear reactions yields is $\eta_{^{18}\mathrm{O}-^{18}\mathrm{F}} / \eta_{^{16}\mathrm{O}-^{17}\mathrm{F}} = 144.7$.

2.4 (2 marks) Calculate the yield of labeling D-glucose with fluorine-18, if initial radioactivity of a fluorine-18 sample was 600.0 MBq and radioactivity of the obtained 2-deoxy-2-($\ce{^{18}F}$)fluoro-D-glucose is 528.2 MBq. Synthesis time is 3.5 minutes.

2.5 (2 marks) Biological half-life (through the excretory organs) of 2-deoxy-2-($\ce{^{18}F}$)fluoro-D-glucose is 120.0 minutes. How much radioactivity (in MBq) will remain in the patient ten hours after injection of FDG with the initial radioactivity of 450.0 MBq.

problems.title: Bread is the stuff of life
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (8 points; 40 marks). Bread is the stuff of life

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-6-fig1.png

When you pass by the bakery, you are stopped by the smell of freshly baked bread. The hero of one of the novels said on a similar occasion: "If you tell me that this is not perfect, you are my enemy forever." The principle bread flavour component was identified in 1969 as compound $\mathbf{X}$ which occurs in equilibrium with its tautomer $\mathbf{Y}$ in a 2:1 ratio. Unfortunately, both forms are labile, and after some hours bread has no the same nice smell.

This tautomeric mixture of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ was synthesized in 1993 from piperidine by the reaction sequence given in Scheme 1. It is noteworthy that the initial ratio of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ was 1:4; on standing this ratio gradually changed to an equilibrium one.

Scheme 1.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-6-fig2.png

Compound $\mathbf{B}$ which is characterized by 3-fold axis of symmetry (i.e., rotation by 120° results in a molecule indistinguishable from the original) occurs in equilibrium with its diastereomer $\mathbf{C}$. The interconversion of these two forms proceeds via intermediate $\mathbf{A}$ which is also intermediate in $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ formation as well as their transformation to $\mathbf{D}$. Compounds $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$ have the same elemental composition: $\omega_\mathrm{C} = 72.24\%$, $\omega_\mathrm{H} = 10.91\%$, $\omega_\mathrm{N} = 16.85\%$.

1 (28 marks) Write down the structural formulae of compounds $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$.

Treatment of compound $\mathbf{E}$ with $\ce{CH3Li*LiBr}$ complex in $\ce{(C2H5)2O}$ at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ failed to produce the target products $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$. Instead, a yellow precipitate $\mathbf{F}$ was initially formed. Aqueous workup of this precipitate led to the mixture of compound $\mathbf{E}$ and its tautomer $\mathbf{G}$.

2 (4 marks) Write down the structural formulae of compounds $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$.

Another approach to compound $\mathbf{X}$ is based on the use of pipecolinic acid derivative $\mathbf{H}$. It was shown that $\mathbf{X}$ can be synthesized by reaction sequence presented in Scheme 2.

Scheme 2.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-6-fig3.png

3 (8 marks) Write down the structural formulae of compounds $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{J}$.

problems.title: Not by bread alone
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (8 points; 50 marks). Not by bread alone

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-7-fig1.png

Pomegranate is called in Azerbaijan, which is famous for its vegetables, as the "king of all fruits". Pomegranate is honored in various religions as a "fruit of Paradise", symbol of righteousness, wealth, hope for eternal life.

In 1878 alkaloid pelletierine was isolated from the bark of pomegranate tree (Punica granatum L., Lythraceae). This alkaloid is traditionally used as an anti-helminthic drug. Initially $\mathbf{X}_\mathbf{W}$ (3-(piperidin-2-yl)propanal) was incorrectly proposed for pelletierine. But now it is accepted that natural pelletierine is ($S$)-1-(piperidin-2-yl)propan-2-one ($\mathbf{X}_\mathbf{S}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-7-fig2.png

1 (8 marks) Write down the structural formulae of $\mathbf{X}_\mathbf{W}$ and $\mathbf{X}_\mathbf{S}$ (the latter – with the stereochemical information).

The synthesis of natural pelletierine ($\mathbf{X}_\mathbf{S}$) based on the transformation of nortropanol $\mathbf{A}$ was recently described.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-7-fig3.png

2 (24 marks) Write down the structural formulae of compounds $\mathbf{B}$–$\mathbf{G}$ with the stereochemical information.

3 (2 marks) Nortropanol $\mathbf{A}$ was used in this reaction as a single stereoisomer. How many stereoisomers can exist for compound $\mathbf{A}$ (including $\mathbf{A}$)? Ignore nitrogen chirality.

Enantiomer of $\mathbf{X}_\mathbf{S}$ was synthesized using chiral tert-butanesulfinamide ($\mathbf{H}$):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-7-fig4.png

4 (16 marks) Write down the structural formulae of compounds $\mathbf{I}$–$\mathbf{L}$ with the stereochemical information.

problems.title: Oil for Life and Life after Oil
problems.problem:
Problem 8 (8 points; 55 marks). Oil for Life and Life after Oil

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-8-fig1.png

Azerbaijan is known for its vast oil and gas fields. The first drilling for oil was done in Bibi-Heybat in 1846, 13 years before establishment of the first commercial oil well in Pennsylvania (USA). This remarkable date in the history of Azerbaijan is regarded as a starting point of contemporary oil industry, the leading sector of today's world economy. Currently, on-land and shelf sea oil production is being developed in Azerbaijan. Though serious precautions are taken, there is always a risk of hydrocarbon pollution of the environment during production, transportation, and processing of oil. In this task we will consider diverse technologies of oil spills clean up and specific features of metabolic pathways involved.

Application of complex solvents (dispersants) leading to capture of marine oil spills is among most promising clean up approaches. Organic substance $\mathbf{X}$ (11.94% of H by mass) is a typical component of such dispersants. Safety of $\mathbf{X}$ to human is fiercely debated. $\mathbf{X1}$ (54.53% of carbon by mass) composed of three elements and excreted with urine is the major metabolite of $\mathbf{X}$ in humans. The numbers of atoms of different elements in $\mathbf{X1}$ are three consecutive terms of a geometric progression ($n$, $nq$, $nq^2$), whereas the sum of these numbers does not exceed 25.

1a (1 mark) Decide on the relationship (tick the correct variant) between the numbers of carbon and oxygen atoms in $\mathbf{X1}$.

$n(\mathrm{C}) > n(\mathrm{O}) \qquad n(\mathrm{C}) < n(\mathrm{O}) \qquad n(\mathrm{C}) = n(\mathrm{O}) \qquad \text{Data insufficient}$

1b (4 marks) Derive the empirical formula of $\mathbf{X1}$ (hereafter always show your work where required). Be sure you prove the answer by calculations.

The biotransformation of $\mathbf{X}$ into $\mathbf{X1}$ occurs in two enzymatically catalyzed steps according to the hereunder reaction balanced equations ($\ce{NAD+}$ and NADH are the oxidized and reduced forms of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, respectively):

$$\begin{array}{ll} \mathbf{X} + \ce{NAD+} \rightarrow \mathbf{X0} + \ce{NADH + H+} & \qquad (1) \\ \mathbf{X0} + \ce{NAD+ + H2O} \rightarrow \mathbf{X1} + \ce{NADH + H+} & \qquad (2) \end{array}$$

1c (4 marks) Derive the molecular formula of $\mathbf{X}$.

A minor metabolic transformation of $\mathbf{X}$ is catalyzed by cytochrome P450-dependent monooxygenase. This reaction leads to two compounds $\mathbf{X2}$ (51.56% of oxygen and 9.74% of hydrogen by mass) and $\mathbf{X3}$.

1d (3 marks) Derive the molecular formula of $\mathbf{X2}$ and draw its structure.

$\mathbf{X}$ contains only primary and secondary carbon atoms. $\mathbf{X0}$ and $\mathbf{X3}$ contain common functional group.

1e (12 marks) Draw the structural formulae of $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{X1}$, and $\mathbf{X3}$.

In a medical study, personnel permanently exposed to $\mathbf{X}$-based solvents without proper protection was found to have a stationary concentration of $\mathbf{X}$ in blood.

2 (5 marks) $\mathbf{X1}$ is excreted with urine. Choose the graph of $\mathbf{X1}$ daily mass content in the body of a volunteer participated in this experiment. Write down the number of the correct graph.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-8-fig2.png

The use of different bacteria is also considered as a promising way for the removal of hydrocarbon (even aromatic) contaminants from sea water and soil. Under aerobic conditions, benzene undergoes biodegradation as follows (first three steps are balanced):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-8-fig3.png

Under the same conditions, a monocyclic aromatic hydrocarbon $\mathbf{P}$ (91.25% of carbon by mass) undergoes the following transformation (first three steps are balanced):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-8-fig4.png

$\mathbf{P3}$ gives a positive iodoform test. A 100 mg sample of $\mathbf{P3}$ requires 6.41 mL of 0.100 M KOH solution for complete neutralization.

3 (13 marks) Derive the structures of $\mathbf{P}$–$\mathbf{P3}$. Give the most stable tautomer of $\mathbf{P3}$.

Microorganisms Alicycliphilus are capable of biodegradation of aromatic hydrocarbons even in soil. The process requires a suitable electron acceptor such as inorganic anion $\mathbf{Y1}$ (first three steps are balanced).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-8-fig5.png

The intermediate anion $\mathbf{Y2}$ is enzymatically decomposed according to the balanced reaction equation:

$$\mathbf{Y2}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathbf{Y3}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathbf{Y4}(\mathrm{g}),$$

wherein each of $\mathbf{Y3}$ and $\mathbf{Y4}$ is composed of atoms of only one element. $\mathbf{T2}$ does not contain two identical oxygen-containing functional groups. $\mathbf{T2}$ gives a precipitate when treated with the ammonia solution of $\ce{Ag2O}$, whereas $\mathbf{Y3}$ does not.

4 (13 marks) Deduce and give formulas of $\mathbf{Y1}$–$\mathbf{Y4}$. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{T1}$–$\mathbf{T2}$. Give the most stable tautomer of $\mathbf{T2}$.

problems.title: Nitrogen fluorides
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (17 points, 5% of the total). [Nitrogen fluorides]

Nitrogen trifluoride is a surprisingly stable compound that was first prepared in the melt electrolysis of a mixture of ammonium fluoride and hydrogen fluoride.

1.1 (3 pt) On which electrode does nitrogen trifluoride form? Write a balanced chemical equation for the electrode half reaction for the formation of $\ce{NF3}$.

[Options printed on the answer sheet: Cathode / Anode.]

Interestingly the related fluoroamine ($\ce{NH2F}$) and difluoroamine ($\ce{NHF2}$) are very unstable materials; decomposition of either pure substance can even be explosive. This is dangerous as they are formed in the electrolysis as side products.

1.2 (1 pt) Which of $\ce{NF3}$, $\ce{NHF2}$ or $\ce{NH2F}$ compound is expected to condense at the lowest temperature?

The N-F bond lengths in these molecules were determined to be 136, 140 and 142 pm. The change in the bond lengths can be explained with a simple electrostatic model taking into account the partial charges on the atoms.

1.3 (2 pt) Assign the N-F bond lengths (136, 140, 142 pm) to the molecules.

[Template printed on the answer sheet:]

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} \text{Molecule} & \ce{NH2F} & \ce{NHF2} & \ce{NF3} \\ \hline \text{N-F bond length, pm} & & & \end{array}$$

When $\ce{NHF2}$ is bubbled through a solution of $\ce{KF}$ in $\ce{HF}$, a binary nitrogen – fluorine compound can be obtained as a mixture of two geometric isomers.

1.4 (2 pt) Write a balanced chemical equation for the formation of the binary nitrogen-fluorine compound.

Tetrafluoroammonium ion ($\ce{NF4+}$) and its corresponding salt can form from $\ce{NF3}$ with elementary fluorine in the presence of an appropriate reagent.

1.5 (2 pt) Propose a suitable reagent and write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction.

$\ce{NF4+}$ ions form stable salts with a number of anions. These are very sensitive to humidity, because $\ce{NF4+}$ ion hydrolyzes forming $\ce{NF3}$ and $\ce{O2}$. Interestingly nitrogen trifluoride always forms quantitatively, while the quantity of oxygen is often less than expected due to side reactions.

1.6 (4 pt) Write a balanced chemical equation for the hydrolysis of $\ce{NF4+}$. Write a balanced chemical equation for a possible side reaction that can decrease the theoretically expected $\ce{O2}:\ce{NF3}$ mole ratio.

Tetrafluoroammonium salts were investigated for use as solid rocket fuels, because $\ce{NF3}$ and $\ce{F2}$ are released from them on heating. One of them has a fluorine content of 65.6 m/m%, all of which is converted into $\ce{NF3}$ and $\ce{F2}$ upon decomposition. During the decomposition 2.5 times as many moles of $\ce{F2}$ are formed as of $\ce{NF3}$.

1.7 (3 pt) Determine the formula of the salt in question.

problems.title: Copper(I) oxide
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (33 points, 8% of the total). [Copper(I) oxide]

One of the first materials used in solid state electronics was red copper(I) oxide. Interest is renewed nowadays because it could be a non-toxic and cheap component of solar cells.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2016-2-fig1.png

The two figures above depict the cubic unit cell of the $\ce{Cu2O}$ crystal. The lattice constant of the structure is 427.0 pm.

2.1.1 (5 pt) Which of the atoms (A or B) is copper? Which basic structure (primitive cubic, face centered cubic, body centered cubic, diamond) is formed by the A atoms and which structure is formed by the B atoms? What are the coordination numbers of the atoms?

[Template printed on the answer sheet:]

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} & \text{pr. cubic} & \text{fcc} & \text{bcc} & \text{diamond} \\ \hline \text{A} & & & & \\ \text{B} & & & & \end{array}$$

2.1.2 (3 pt) Calculate the smallest O-O, Cu-O and Cu-Cu distances in the structure.

2.1.3 (2 pt) What is the density of pure copper(I) oxide?

A common defect in this crystal is some copper atoms missing with the oxygen lattice unchanged. The composition of one such crystal sample was studied, and 0.2% of all copper atoms were found to be in oxidation state +2.

2.2 (2 pt) What percentage of normal copper sites are empty in the crystal sample? What is $x$ in the empirical formula $\mathrm{Cu}_{2-x}\mathrm{O}$ of the crystal?

Copper(I) oxide is insoluble in water. It is stable in dry air, but humidity in the air catalyzes a transformation (Reaction 1).

When copper(I) oxide is dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid, a blue solution containing a precipitate is formed without evolution of a gas (Reaction 2). When hot, concentrated sulfuric acid is used, no precipitate remains, but an odorous gas forms (Reaction 3). The same gas forms when the precipitate from reaction 2 is dissolved in hot concentrated sulfuric acid.

2.3 (3 pt) Write balanced chemical equations for reactions (1-3).

Copper(I) oxide can be produced in a number of ways. Heating copper in air is a common method in the synthesis of semiconductor $\ce{Cu2O}$. In a pure oxygen atmosphere, the three species containing copper ($\ce{Cu(s)}$, $\ce{Cu2O(s)}$ or $\ce{CuO(s)}$) can potentially interconvert.

Suppose that the $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ$ and $S^\circ$ data given for $10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$ are independent of temperature:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} & \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ\ /\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & S^\circ\ /\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \\ \hline \ce{Cu(s)} & 0 & 65 \\ \ce{O2(g)} & 0 & 244 \\ \ce{CuO(s)} & -156 & 103 \\ \ce{Cu2O(s)} & -170 & 180 \end{array}$$

2.4 (6 pt) Determine the temperature ranges, if any, of thermodynamic stability of copper and its oxides between 500 and 1500 K in a $10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$ oxygen atmosphere.

[Template printed on the answer sheet:]

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Temperature range between 500-1500 K} & \text{The most stable form } (\ce{Cu}, \ce{Cu2O} \text{ or } \ce{CuO}) \\ \hline & \\ & \\ & \end{array}$$

Important data are given for 298 K. Use this temperature in the following calculations:

$$\begin{array}{ll} K_\mathrm{sp}(\ce{Cu(OH)2}) = 2\cdot10^{-19} & \\ \ce{Cu2O(s) + H2O(l) + 2e- -> 2Cu(s) + 2OH^{-}(aq)} & E^\circ = -0.360\,\mathrm{V} \\ \ce{Cu^{2+}(aq) + e- -> Cu^{+}(aq)} & E^\circ = +0.159\,\mathrm{V} \\ \ce{Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2e- -> Cu(s)} & E^\circ = +0.337\,\mathrm{V} \end{array}$$

One possibility for producing $\ce{Cu2O}$ is the anodic oxidation of copper. Electrolysis of an aqueous basic solution (e.g. $\ce{NaOH}$) with a copper anode and platinum cathode can lead to formation of copper(I) oxide on the anode.

2.5 (2 pt) Write the half reaction equations for the electrode processes during the anodic production of $\ce{Cu2O}$ in $\ce{NaOH}$ solution with a platinum cathode and copper anode.

Electrolytic reduction of copper(II) ions in solution is another possibility.

2.6.1 (1 pt) Write the half reaction equation of the cathode process giving $\ce{Cu2O}$ in acidic medium.

Let us use $0.100\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ solution and carry out electrolysis with platinum electrodes.

2.6.2 (3 pt) What is the maximum pH at which the concentration of copper(II) can be maintained at $0.100\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$?

If the pH is too low, reduction to metallic copper is preferred to the formation of copper(I) oxide.

2.6.3 (6 pt) What is the minimum pH at which the cathodic production of $\ce{Cu2O}$ in a $0.100\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ solution is still possible?

problems.title: Iodine content of iodized salt
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (48 points, 9% of the total). [Iodine content of iodized salt]

Iodine deficiency is of special concern in Georgia because it occupies a region where iodine is scarce in soil and water. Iodine deficiency can be effectively and inexpensively prevented if salt for human consumption is fortified with small amounts of iodine. Methods for analyzing salt for iodine content are thus important. Current regulations in Georgia are that iodized salt must contain between 25-55 ppm iodine (1 ppm = 1 mg iodine/kg salt).

Most salt is iodized by fortification with potassium iodate ($\ce{KIO3}$). Iodate content can be determined in salt samples using iodometric titration. In a typical procedure, 10.000 g of an iodized salt sample is dissolved in $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $1.0\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ aqueous $\ce{HCl}$ to which 1.0 g $\ce{KI}$ has been added. The solution is then titrated with $0.00235\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ aqueous sodium thiosulfate solution to a starch endpoint; this requires $7.50\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of titrant.

3.1.1 (2 pt) Write a balanced net ionic equation for the reaction when iodate reacts with excess iodide in acidic solution.

3.1.2 (2 pt) Write a balanced net ionic equation for the reaction taking place during the titration with thiosulfate.

3.1.3 (6 pt) Calculate the iodization level, in ppm, of this salt sample.

A less common agent for iodizing salt is potassium iodide, which cannot be easily measured by iodometric titration.

One possible method for analyzing iodide in the presence of chloride is potentiometric titration. However, this method is not very precise in the presence of large amounts of chloride.

In this method, a silver wire is immersed in the solution (containing iodide and chloride) to be analyzed and silver ion is gradually added to the solution. The potential of the silver wire is measured relative to a reference electrode consisting of a silver wire in a $1.000\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ solution of $\ce{AgNO3}$. The measured potentials are negative and the absolute values of these potentials are reported. The solution to be analyzed has a volume of $1.000\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ (which you may assume does not change as silver ion is added), and $T = 25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

The results of this experiment are governed by three equilibria: the solubility of $\ce{AgI(s)}$ [$K_\mathrm{spI}$] and $\ce{AgCl(s)}$ [$K_\mathrm{spCl}$] and the formation of $\ce{AgCl2^{-}(aq)}$ [$K_\mathrm{f}$]. (Iodide also forms complex ions with silver but this may be neglected at the very low concentrations of iodide present in this experiment).

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{AgI(s) <=> Ag^{+}(aq) + I^{-}(aq)} & K_\mathrm{spI} \\ \ce{AgCl(s) <=> Ag^{+}(aq) + Cl^{-}(aq)} & K_\mathrm{spCl} \\ \ce{Ag^{+}(aq) + 2Cl^{-}(aq) <=> AgCl2^{-}(aq)} & K_\mathrm{f} \end{array}$$

Below are shown the results of two experiments measuring the observed potential as a function of added number of moles of silver ion. Experiment $\mathbf{A}$ (solid circles) was carried out with $1.000\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ of solution containing $1.00\cdot10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ iodide and no chloride ion. Experiment $\mathbf{B}$ (open circles) was done using $1.000\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ of solution containing $1.00\cdot10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ iodide and $1.00\cdot10^{-1}\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ chloride.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2016-3-fig1.png

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \mathrm{\mu mol}\ \ce{Ag+}\ \text{added} & |E|,\ \mathrm{V}\ \text{exp. }\mathbf{A} & |E|,\ \mathrm{V}\ \text{exp. }\mathbf{B} \\ \hline 1.00 & 0.637 & 0.637 \\ 3.00 & 0.631 & 0.631 \\ 5.00 & 0.622 & 0.622 \\ 7.00 & 0.609 & 0.610 \\ 9.00 & 0.581 & 0.584 \\ 10.0 & 0.468 & 0.558 \\ 11.0 & 0.355 & 0.531 \\ 12.0 & 0.337 & 0.517 \\ 13.0 & 0.327 & 0.517 \\ 15.0 & 0.313 & 0.517 \end{array}$$

3.2.1 (5 pt) Select an appropriate data point from the experiments and use it to calculate the solubility product of $\ce{AgI}$ ($K_\mathrm{spI}$).

3.2.2 (4 pt) Select an appropriate data point from the experiments and use it to calculate the solubility product of $\ce{AgCl}$ ($K_\mathrm{spCl}$).

3.2.3 (7 pt) Select an appropriate data point from the experiments and use it to calculate $K_\mathrm{f}$. You may need to use values of $K_\mathrm{spI}$ or $K_\mathrm{spCl}$ to do this calculation. If you were unable to carry out the calculations in 3.2.1. or 3.2.2., you may use the arbitrary values of $K_\mathrm{spI} = 1.00\cdot10^{-15}$ and $K_\mathrm{spCl} = 1.00\cdot10^{-9}$ without penalty.

An analytical method that is more practical, because it is not sensitive to the presence of chloride, uses the Sandell-Kolthoff reaction. This is the reaction of $\ce{H3AsO3}$ with Ce(IV) to give Ce(III) in acidic solution, which is strongly catalyzed by iodide ion.

3.3.1 (6 pt) Write balanced net ionic equations for the reaction of cerium(IV) with $\ce{H3AsO3}$ in acidic solution, as well as reactions of cerium(IV) with a species containing the element iodine and $\ce{H3AsO3}$ with a species containing the element iodine, that could reasonably account for the catalysis of the net reaction by iodide.

The reaction of Ce(IV) with $\ce{H3AsO3}$ can be monitored by measuring the absorbance at 405 nm, as Ce(IV) is orange and absorbs significantly at 405 nm, while the other reactants and products are colorless and do not absorb appreciably. Three runs were carried out, all in $0.50\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ $\ce{H2SO4}$ at $25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ using the following initial concentrations:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Run} & [\ce{H3AsO3}]_0,\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}} & [\text{Ce(IV)}]_0,\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}} & [\ce{I-}]_0,\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}} \\ \hline 1 & 0.01250 & 0.00120 & 1.43\cdot10^{-6} \\ 2 & 0.00625 & 0.00060 & 1.43\cdot10^{-6} \\ 3 & 0.01250 & 0.00120 & 7.16\cdot10^{-7} \end{array}$$

An analyst initiated the reactions by mixing the reagents in a cuvette. After a short variable delay absorbance measurements were started, with the first measurement recorded at $t = 0\,\mathrm{s}$. The data obtained are shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2016-3-fig2.png

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} t,\ \mathrm{s} & A_{405}\ \text{Run }\mathbf{1} & A_{405}\ \text{Run }\mathbf{2} & A_{405}\ \text{Run }\mathbf{3} \\ \hline 0 & 0.621 & 0.287 & 0.818 \\ 20 & 0.348 & 0.149 & 0.608 \\ 40 & 0.198 & 0.083 & 0.455 \\ 60 & 0.113 & 0.046 & 0.340 \\ 80 & 0.064 & 0.025 & 0.254 \\ 100 & 0.037 & 0.014 & 0.191 \end{array}$$

Under these conditions ($0.5\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ $\ce{H2SO4}$, $25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$), the rate law for the reaction can be written as

$$\text{Rate} = k[\ce{H3AsO3}]^m[\text{Ce(IV)}]^n[\ce{I-}]^p \qquad \text{where } m, n, \text{ and } p \text{ are integers.}$$

3.3.2 (11 pt) Determine the values of $m$, $n$, and $p$ and calculate the value of $k$ (be sure to specify its units).

A 1.000 g sample of iodized salt is dissolved in water to give $10.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of solution. A $0.0500\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquot of this solution is added to a mixture of $1.000\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ $0.025\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ $\ce{H3AsO3}$ in $0.5\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ $\ce{H2SO4}$ and $0.800\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ $0.5\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ $\ce{H2SO4}$. To this mixture is added $0.200\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ $0.0120\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ $\ce{Ce(NH4)2(NO3)6}$ in $0.5\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ $\ce{H2SO4}$ and the absorbance at 405 nm is measured as a function of time at $25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2016-3-fig3.png

$$\begin{array}{c|c} t,\ \mathrm{s} & A_{405} \\ \hline 0 & 0.756 \\ 20 & 0.531 \\ 40 & 0.373 \\ 60 & 0.262 \\ 80 & 0.185 \\ 100 & 0.129 \end{array}$$

3.3.3 (5 pt) Calculate the iodization level, in ppm, of this salt sample.

problems.title: Kinetics in water treatment and drug degradation
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (25 points, 8% of the total). [Kinetics in water treatment and drug degradation]

Application of kinetic studies in water treatment

Industrial waste is a major cause of water pollution and kinetic studies are carried out in a laboratory to design effluent treatment. 1,4-dioxane, more commonly known as dioxane ($\ce{C4H8O2}$), an industrial solvent and by-product, is a significant water contaminant. It can be oxidised to hazard free chemicals using oxidants such as peroxodisulfate, ozone or hydrogen peroxide.

The data obtained in the kinetic study of oxidation of dioxane with potassium peroxodisulfate ($\ce{K2S2O8}$) as oxidant and $\ce{AgNO3}$ as catalyst at $T = 303.15\,\mathrm{K}$ are given below. The reaction was monitored by the estimation of unreacted peroxodisulfate. The concentration of $\ce{AgNO3}$ used in this study was $1.00\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mmol\cdot dm^{-3}}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Trial} & \text{Dioxane},\ \mathrm{mmol\cdot dm^{-3}} & \ce{K2S2O8},\ \mathrm{mmol\cdot dm^{-3}} & \text{Initial rate},\ \mathrm{mmol\cdot dm^{-3}\cdot min^{-1}} \\ \hline 1 & 0.0100 & 2.50 & 1.661\cdot10^{-2} \\ 2 & 0.0100 & 5.10 & 3.380\cdot10^{-2} \\ 3 & 0.00500 & 13.8 & 9.200\cdot10^{-2} \\ 4 & 0.0110 & 13.8 & 9.201\cdot10^{-2} \end{array}$$

In many countries the accepted maximum level of dioxane in drinking water is specified as $0.35\,\mathrm{\mu g\,dm^{-3}}$.

A water sample contains an initial dioxane concentration of $40.00\,\mathrm{\mu g\,dm^{-3}}$. Assume that 1 mol dioxane requires 1 mol of peroxodisulfate for oxidation. The concentration of $\ce{AgNO3}$ used in this study was $1.00\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mmol\cdot dm^{-3}}$.

4.1.1 (5 pt) Calculate the time in minutes the oxidation process has to continue in order to reach the accepted level of dioxane at 303.15 K if the initial concentration of $\ce{K2S2O8}$ is $5.0\cdot10^{-6}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$. Assume that the rate law obtained from the data above is valid under these conditions.

Various mechanisms have been proposed for the peroxodisulfate oxidation of dioxane. Misra and Ghosh (1963) proposed the following mechanism:

$$\ce{S2O8^{2-} + Ag+} \underset{k_2}{\overset{k_1}{\rightleftarrows}} \ce{Ag^{3+} + 2SO4^{2-}}$$

$$\ce{Ag^{3+}} + \mathrm{D}\ (\text{dioxane}) \xrightarrow{k_3} \mathrm{D'}\ (\text{dioxane oxidised}) + \ce{2H+ + Ag+}$$

4.1.2 (3 pt) Assuming Ag(III) to be in steady state, deduce the rate equation for the oxidation of dioxane.

4.1.3 (2 pt) Which of the following is/are correct?

A) The rate equation based on the mechanism given in 4.1.2, at very high concentrations of dioxane, is consistent with the experimental data in 4.1.1.
B) The rate equation based on the mechanism given in 4.1.2, at very low concentrations of dioxane, is consistent with the experimental data in 4.1.1.
C) The units of the observed rate constant are $\mathrm{dm^3\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot s^{-1}}$ at very high concentrations of dioxane.
D) The units of the observed rate constant are $\mathrm{dm^3\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot s^{-1}}$ at very low concentrations of dioxane.

Degradation of pharmaceutical products – a kinetic overview

Kinetic studies are important in deciding the shelf life of a pharmaceutical product. Several chemical reactions can affect the shelf life of pharmaceutical products and the rates of these reactions depend on conditions such as pH, temperature, humidity.

Lysine acetylsalicylate (LAS) is prescribed as a pain killer and anti-inflammatory drug under the brand name Aspegic. LAS on hydrolysis forms lysine salicylate and acetic acid.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2016-4-fig1.png

Hydrolysis of LAS can proceed via three different pathways (a) acid catalysed, (b) uncatalysed and (c) base catalysed.

If [LAS] denotes the concentration of LAS at time '$t$', the overall rate of the hydrolysis reaction can be written as

$$-\frac{d[\mathrm{LAS}]}{dt} = k_\mathrm{H}[\mathrm{LAS}][\ce{H+}] + k_0[\mathrm{LAS}] + k_\mathrm{OH}[\mathrm{LAS}][\ce{OH-}]$$

where $k_\mathrm{H}$, $k_0$ and $k_\mathrm{OH}$ are the rate constants of the acid catalysed, uncatalysed and base catalysed pathways of hydrolysis, respectively. The observed rate constant is defined by:

$$-\frac{d[\mathrm{LAS}]}{dt} = k_\mathrm{obs}[\mathrm{LAS}]$$

4.2.1 (1 pt) Write an expression for $k_\mathrm{obs}$ in terms of $k_\mathrm{H}$, $k_0$, $k_\mathrm{OH}$ and $[\ce{H+}]$.

Hydrolysis of LAS was carried out at 298.15 K at various pH values (0.50 to 13.0). A very low initial concentration of LAS ensured that the pH did not change during the course of the reaction.

The following graph shows the pH dependence of the hydrolysis of LAS.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2016-4-fig2.png

4.2.2 (2 pt) Which of the following is/are correct?

A) $k_\mathrm{obs} \cong k_0$ at pH = 12
B) $k_\mathrm{obs} \cong k_0$ at pH = 5.0
C) The rate of the reaction increases when the pH is changed from 0.50 to 1.0.
D) The rate of the reaction increases when the pH is changed from 10 to 12.

4.2.3 (6 pt) Using the diagram and the data given below, calculate $k_\mathrm{H}$, $k_0$ and $k_\mathrm{OH}$. Make sure to specify the units.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{pH} & 1.300 & 5.300 & 12.180 \\ \hline \log(k_\mathrm{obs}/\mathrm{min^{-1}}) & -3.886 & -4.000 & -1.726 \end{array}$$

Acetylsalicylic acid, more commonly known as aspirin, is a medicine often used for reducing fever, pain and inflammation. Like LAS, the hydrolysis of aspirin can also take different pathways depending on the pH. The pH rate profile of aspirin hydrolysis at 333.15 K is given below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2016-4-fig3.png

The following are possible reactions for the hydrolysis of aspirin. Depending on the pH, one or more of these reactions will predominate.

$$\begin{array}{ll} \text{I.} & \ce{CH3COOC6H4COOH + H3O+ -> HOC6H4COOH + CH3COOH + H+} \\ \text{II.} & \ce{CH3COOC6H4COOH + H2O -> HOC6H4COOH + CH3COOH} \\ \text{III.} & \ce{CH3COOC6H4COOH + OH- -> HOC6H4COO- + CH3COOH} \\ \text{IV.} & \ce{CH3COOC6H4COO- + H3O+ -> HOC6H4COOH + CH3COOH} \\ \text{V.} & \ce{CH3COOC6H4COO- + H2O -> HOC6H4COO- + CH3COOH} \\ \text{VI.} & \ce{CH3COOC6H4COO- + OH- -> HOC6H4COO- + CH3COO-} \end{array}$$

4.3.1 (2 pt) Using the pH-rate profile diagram and the reactions given above, state which of the following statements is/are correct. ($\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ of aspirin = 3.57 at 333.15 K)

a) In the region C-D, reaction IV is predominant
b) In the region C-D, reaction V is predominant
c) In the region D-E reaction VI is predominant
d) In the region A-B, reaction II is predominant

A separate plot of $k_\mathrm{obs}$ vs pH for the hydrolysis of aspirin has been confirmed to show a minimum at a particular pH. At 290.15 K the following rate constants for reactions I, II and III were determined:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} k_\mathrm{H}\ (\text{reaction I}) & k_0\ (\text{reaction II}) & k_\mathrm{OH}\ (\text{reaction III}) \\ \hline 1.99\,\mathrm{dm^3\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot day^{-1}} & 2.29\cdot10^{-4}\,\mathrm{day^{-1}} & 3.18\cdot10^{9}\,\mathrm{dm^3\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot day^{-1}} \end{array}$$

The ionic product of water at 290.15 K can be taken as $1.0\cdot10^{-14}$.

4.3.2 (4 pt) Assuming that only reactions I, II and III occur, calculate the value of the pH at the minimum of $k_\mathrm{obs}$.

problems.title: Egyptian blue and Chinese blue
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (19 points, 8% of the total). [Egyptian blue and Chinese blue]

5500 years ago in ancient Egypt people learned for the first time how to synthesize a blue pigment. Now we know this pigment as Egyptian blue. About 2000 years later in ancient China another pigment was widely used, which is now referred to as Chinese blue. The two pigments are similar in structure, but have different elemental compositions.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2016-5-fig1.png

Ushabti figurines from Egyptian pharaoh tomb covered with Egyptian blue and a Chinese blue soap dispenser sold at Alibaba

The ancient method of preparation for these pigments can be easily reproduced in a modern laboratory.

When considering the amounts, assume that all of the compounds in this task are pure, and the yields are quantitative.

To make Egyptian blue, one should heat 10.0 g of mineral $\mathbf{A}$ with 21.7 g of $\ce{SiO2}$ and 9.05 g of mineral $\mathbf{B}$ at 800–900 °C for a prolonged time. $16.7\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ of a mixture of two gaseous products are released (the volume is measured at 850 °C and $1.013\cdot10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$ (1.013 bar) pressure). In result, 34.0 g of the pigment was obtained. No other products are formed. As the gaseous mixture is cooled, one component of the mixture condenses. As the remaining gas is further cooled to 0 °C, the gaseous volume reduces to $3.04\,\mathrm{dm^3}$.

5.1.1 (1 pt) Find the mass of the gaseous mixture formed upon heating of $\mathbf{A}$ with $\mathbf{B}$ and $\ce{SiO2}$.

5.1.2 (3 pt) Determine the quantitative composition of this gas mixture.

[Template printed on the answer sheet: "The gaseous mixture formed at 850 °C contains ……… mol of ……… and ……… mol of ………"]

When 10.0 g of mineral $\mathbf{A}$ is heated with 21.7 g of $\ce{SiO2}$ in the absence of $\mathbf{B}$, it forms $8.34\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ of gaseous products (measured at 850 °C and $1.013\cdot10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$ = 1.013 bar pressure). Mineral $\mathbf{A}$ contains only one metal.

5.1.3 (2 pt) Calculate the molar mass and determine the formula of mineral $\mathbf{B}$. Hint: it is an ionic solid insoluble in water and containing no water of crystallization.

In order to obtain Chinese blue, one should take 17.8 g of mineral $\mathbf{C}$ instead of mineral $\mathbf{B}$ (keeping the amounts of mineral $\mathbf{A}$ and $\ce{SiO2}$ same as for Egyptian blue), and run the reaction at higher temperatures. Besides the pigment, the same gaseous products in the same quantities are formed as in the preparation of Egyptian blue.

5.1.4 (2 pt) Determine the formula of mineral $\mathbf{C}$.

5.1.5 (5 pt) Determine the formulae of Egyptian blue and Chinese blue.

5.1.6 (2 pt) Determine the formula of mineral $\mathbf{A}$.

Elemental analysis of some samples of Chinese blue shows traces of sulfur. This led to a conclusion that those were synthesized using another common mineral instead of $\mathbf{C}$.

5.2.1 (1 pt) Suggest a formula for the mineral used in place of $\mathbf{C}$.

5.2.2 (1 pt) Could the temperature of synthesis of Chinese blue be decreased if this mineral is used instead of $\mathbf{C}$?

[Options printed on the answer sheet: Yes / No.]

If during the synthesis of Chinese blue we take a smaller amount of silica than in the process above, we will obtain a purple pigment: Chinese violet. It was used, in particular, for coloring the famous Terracotta army soldiers.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2016-5-fig2.png

Terracotta army from Xian, China and reconstruction of its original coloring

Although there is currently no known cure for Alzheimer's disease, there are medications available to manage the neurodegenerative disorder. Among these are acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, of which galantamine $\mathbf{1}$ is an example. This molecule can be isolated from the Caucasian snowdrop, a plant native to Georgia; however, the large amounts needed for therapy require a synthetic route. Shown below is the route used to prepare galantamine industrially.

Notes about the synthesis:

One way of describing optical purity is enantiomeric excess ($ee$). It is defined as the difference in the percentages of the enantiomers in a mixture. For example in a mixture of 70% $R$ and 30% $S$, the $ee$ is 40%.

problems.title: Production of propene using heterogeneous catalysts
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (20 points, 6% of the total). Production of propene using heterogeneous catalysts

Propene or propylene is one of the most valuable chemicals for the petrochemical industry in Thailand and around the world. One good example of the commercial use of propene is for the production of polypropylene (PP).

Part A.

Propene can be synthesized via a direct dehydrogenation of propane in the presence of a heterogeneous catalyst. However, such a reaction is not economically feasible due to the nature of the reaction itself. Provide a concise explanation to each of the questions below. Additional information: $H_\mathrm{bond}(\ce{C=C}) = 1.77\,H_\mathrm{bond}(\ce{C-C})$, $H_\mathrm{bond}(\ce{H-H}) = 1.05\,H_\mathrm{bond}(\ce{C-H})$, and $H_\mathrm{bond}(\ce{C-H}) = 1.19\,H_\mathrm{bond}(\ce{C-C})$, where $H_\mathrm{bond}$ refers to average bond enthalpy of the indicated chemical bond.

1-A1) (4 pt) What is the enthalpy change of the direct dehydrogenation of propane? Show your calculation and express your answer in terms of $H_\mathrm{bond}(\ce{C-C})$.

1-A2) (1 pt) It is difficult to increase the amount of propene by increasing pressure at constant temperature. Which law or principle can best explain this phenomenon? Select your answer by marking "✓" in one of the open circles.

• ◯ Boyle's law
• ◯ Charles' law
• ◯ Dalton's law
• ◯ Raoult's law
• ◯ Le Chatelier's principle

1-A3) (2 pt) Initially, the system is in equilibrium. Consistent with question 1-A1), what is/are correct set(s) of signs for the following thermodynamic variables of the system for the direct dehydrogenation of propane? Select your answer(s) by marking "✓" in any of the open circle(s).

$$\begin{array}{c|cccc} & \Delta H & \Delta S & \Delta G & T^{*} \\ \hline \bigcirc & - & + & + & \text{lower} \\ \bigcirc & - & + & - & \text{higher} \\ \bigcirc & - & - & + & \text{lower} \\ \bigcirc & - & - & - & \text{higher} \\ \bigcirc & + & + & + & \text{lower} \\ \bigcirc & + & + & - & \text{higher} \\ \bigcirc & + & - & + & \text{lower} \\ \bigcirc & + & - & - & \text{higher} \\ \bigcirc & \text{None of the above is correct} & & & \end{array}$$

$^{*}$ Relative to the initial temperature at the same partial pressure.

Part B.

A better reaction to produce large quantity of propene is the oxidative dehydrogenation (ODH) using solid catalysts, such as vanadium oxides, under molecular oxygen gas. Although this type of reaction is still under intense research development, its promise toward the production of propene at an industrial scale eclipses that of the direct dehydrogenation.

1-B) (7 pt) The overall rate of propane consumption in the reaction is

$$r_{\ce{C3H8}} = \frac{1}{\left(\dfrac{p^\circ}{k_\mathrm{red}\, p_{\ce{C3H8}}} + \dfrac{p^\circ}{k_\mathrm{ox}\, p_{\ce{O2}}}\right)},$$

where $k_\mathrm{red}$ and $k_\mathrm{ox}$ are the rate constants for the reduction of metal oxide catalyst by propane and for the oxidation of the catalyst by molecular oxygen, respectively, and $p^\circ$ is the standard pressure of 1 bar. Some experiments found that the rate of oxidation of the catalyst is 100,000 times faster than that of the propane oxidation. The experimental $r_{\ce{C3H8}} = k_\mathrm{obs}\,\dfrac{p_{\ce{C3H8}}}{p^\circ}$ at $600\,\mathrm{K}$, where $k_\mathrm{obs}$ is the observed rate constant ($0.062\,\mathrm{mol\,s^{-1}}$). If the reactor containing the catalyst is continuously passed through with propane and oxygen at a total pressure of $1\,\mathrm{bar}$, determine the value of $k_\mathrm{red}$ and $k_\mathrm{ox}$ when the partial pressure of propane is $0.10\,\mathrm{bar}$. Assume that the partial pressure of propene is negligible.

Part C.

The metal oxide catalyst contains oxygen atoms on its surface that serve as active sites for the ODH. Denoting red* as a reduced site and O($s$) as an oxygen atom on the surface of the catalyst, one of the proposed mechanisms for the ODH in the presence of the catalyst can be written as follows:

$$\ce{C3H8(g) + O(s) ->[$k_1$] C3H6(g) + H2O(g) + red^{*}}\qquad(1)$$

$$\ce{C3H6(g) + 9O(s) ->[$k_2$] 3CO2(g) + 3H2O(g) + 9red^{*}}\qquad(2)$$

$$\ce{O2(g) + 2red^{*} ->[$k_3$] 2O(s)}\qquad(3)$$

Given $\beta = \dfrac{\text{number of reduced sites}}{\text{total number of active sites}}$, the rate laws for the above 3 steps are:

$$r_1 = k_1\, p_{\ce{C3H8}}\,(1-\beta),$$

$$r_2 = k_2\, p_{\ce{C3H6}}\,(1-\beta),$$

and $r_3 = k_3\, p_{\ce{O2}}\,\beta$.

1-C) (6 pt) Assuming that the amount of oxygen atoms on the surface stays constant at any time of reaction, calculate $\beta$ as a function of $k_1$, $k_2$, $k_3$, $p_{\ce{C3H8}}$, $p_{\ce{C3H6}}$, and $p_{\ce{O2}}$.

problems.title: Kinetic isotope effect (KIE) and zero-point vibrational energy (ZPE)
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (24 points, 6% of the total). Kinetic isotope effect (KIE) and zero-point vibrational energy (ZPE)

Calculation of ZPE and KIE

Kinetic isotope effect (KIE) is a phenomenon associated with a change in rate constant of the reaction when one of the atoms is replaced by its isotope. KIE can be used to confirm whether a particular bond to hydrogen is broken in the reaction. Harmonic oscillator model is used to estimate the difference in the rate between C-H and C-D bond activation (D = $\ce{^{2}_{1}H}$).

The vibrational frequency ($\nu$) represented by harmonic oscillator model is

$$\nu = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}},$$

where $k$ is the force constant and $\mu$ is the reduced mass.

The vibrational energies of the molecule are given by

$$E_n = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)h\nu,$$

where $n$ is vibrational quantum number with possible values of 0, 1, 2, ... The energy of the lowest vibrational energy level ($E_n$ at $n = 0$) is called zero-point vibrational energy (ZPE).

2-A1) (2 pt) Calculate the reduced mass of C-H ($\mu_\mathrm{CH}$) and C-D ($\mu_\mathrm{CD}$) in atomic mass unit. Assume that the mass of deuterium is twice that of hydrogen.

[If students are unable to calculate the values for $\mu_\mathrm{CH}$ and $\mu_\mathrm{CD}$ in 2-A1), use $\mu_\mathrm{CH} = 1.008$ and $\mu_\mathrm{CD} = 2.016$ for the subsequent parts of the question. Note that the given values are not necessarily close to the correct values.]

2-A2) (2 pt) Given that the force constant ($k$) for C-H stretching is the same as that for the C-D stretching and the C-H stretching frequency is $2900\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, find the corresponding C-D stretching frequency (in $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$).

2-A3) (7 pt) According to the C-H and C-D stretching frequencies in question 2-A2), calculate the zero-point vibrational energies (ZPE) of C-H and C-D stretching in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

[If students are unable to calculate the values for $ZPE$ in 2-A3), use $ZPE_\mathrm{CH} = 7.23\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ and $ZPE_\mathrm{CD} = 2.15\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ for the subsequent parts of the question. Note that the given values are not necessarily close to the correct values.]

Kinetic isotope effect (KIE)

Due to the difference in zero-point vibrational energies, a protonated compound and its corresponding deuterated compounds are expected to react at different rates.

For the C-H and C-D bond dissociation reactions, the energies of both transition states and both products are identical. Then, the isotope effect is controlled by the difference in the ZPE's of the C-H and C-D bonds.

2-A4) (3 pt) Calculate the difference in the bond dissociation energy (BDE) between C-D bond and C-H bond ($BDE_\mathrm{CD} - BDE_\mathrm{CH}$) in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

2-A5) (3 pt) Assume that the activation energy ($E_\mathrm{a}$) for the C-H/C-D bond cleavage is approximately equal to the bond dissociation energy and the Arrhenius factor is the same for both C-H and C-D bond cleavage. Find the relative rate constant for the C-H/C-D bond cleavage ($k_\mathrm{CH}/k_\mathrm{CD}$) at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Using KIE to study reaction mechanism

The oxidation of nondeuterated and deuterated diphenylmethanol using an excess of chromic acid was studied.

problems.problem:
Problem 3 (24 points, 6% of the total). Thermodynamics of chemical reactions

Part A.

Methanol is produced commercially by using a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen over zinc oxide/copper oxide catalyst:

$$\ce{CO(g) + 2H2(g) -> CH3OH(g)}.$$

The standard enthalpy of formation ($\Delta H_\mathrm{f}^\circ$) and the absolute entropy ($S^\circ$) for each of the three gases at room temperature ($298\,\mathrm{K}$) and at a standard pressure of $1\,\mathrm{bar}$ are given as follows.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Gas} & \Delta H_\mathrm{f}^\circ\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) & S^\circ\ (\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}) \\ \hline \ce{CO}(g) & -111 & 198 \\ \ce{H2}(g) & 0 & 131 \\ \ce{CH3OH}(g) & -201 & 240 \end{array}$$

3-A1) (7 pt) Calculate $\Delta H^\circ$, $\Delta S^\circ$, $\Delta G^\circ$, and $K_p$ for the reaction at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

If you are unable to calculate $K_p$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$ in problem 3-A1), use $K_p = 9 \times 10^{5}$ later on.

3-A2) (3 pt) A commercial reactor is operated at a temperature of $600\,\mathrm{K}$. Calculate the value of $K_p$ at this temperature, assuming that $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are independent of temperature.

If you are unable to calculate $K_p$ at $600\,\mathrm{K}$ in problem 3-A2), use $K_p = 1.0\times10^{-2}$ later on.

3-A3) (8 pt) Production of methanol in industry is based on flowing of the gas comprising 2.00 moles of $\ce{H2}$ for each mole of CO into the reactor. The mole fraction of methanol in the exhaust gas from the reactor was found to be 0.18. Assuming that equilibrium is established, what is the total pressure in the reactor at a high temperature of $600\,\mathrm{K}$?

Part B.

3-B) (6 pt) Consider the following closed system at $300\,\mathrm{K}$. The system comprises 2 compartments, separated by a closed valve, which has negligible volume. At the same pressure $P$, compartment A and compartment B contain $0.100\,\mathrm{mol}$ argon gas and $0.200\,\mathrm{mol}$ nitrogen gas, respectively. The volumes of the two compartments, $V_\mathrm{A}$ and $V_\mathrm{B}$, are selected so that the gases behave as ideal gases.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2017-3-fig1.png
