problems.title: Phosphate and silicate in soil
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (10 points, 5% of the total). Phosphate and silicate in soil

Distribution and mobility of phosphorus in soil are usually studied by sequential extraction. Sequential extraction is performed by the use of acid or alkaline reagents to fractionate inorganic phosphorus in soil. Soil sample was extracted and analyzed as follows:

Part A. Determination of total phosphate ($\ce{PO4^{3-}}$) and silicate ($\ce{SiO4^{4-}}$)

A 5.00 gram of soil sample is digested to give a final volume of $50.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ digesting solution which dissolves total phosphorus and silicon. The extract is analyzed for the total concentrations of phosphorus and silicon. The concentrations of phosphorus and silicon are found to be $5.16\,\mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}$ and $5.35\,\mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}$, respectively.

5-A1) (1 pt) Determine the mass of $\ce{PO4^{3-}}$ in mg per 1.00 g of soil. [Printed in the answer box: answer with 3 digits after decimal point.]

5-A2) (1 pt) Determine the mass of $\ce{SiO4^{4-}}$ in mg per 1.00 g of soil. [Printed in the answer box: answer with 3 digits after decimal point.]

Part B. Determination of available $\ce{PO4^{3-}}$ in acid extract

Phosphate can be analyzed by using molybdenum blue method. One mole of phosphate is converted into one mole of molybdenum blue compound. This method is used for determination of phosphate in the acid extract. Absorbance (A) and transmittance (T) are recorded at $800\,\mathrm{nm}$. The molar absorptivity of the molybdenum blue compound is $6720\,\mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$ and all measurement is carried out in a 1.00-cm cuvette.

Transmittance and absorbance are given by the following equations:

$$T = I / I_\mathrm{o}$$

$$A = \log\,(I_\mathrm{o} / I)$$

where $I$ is the intensity of the transmitted light and $I_\mathrm{o}$ is the intensity of the incident light.

5-B1) (3 pt) When the sample containing high concentration of phosphate is analyzed, a reference solution of $7.5 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ of molybdenum blue compound is used for adjusting zero absorbance. The transmittance of the sample solution is then measured to be 0.55. Calculate the concentration of phosphate ($\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$) in the sample solution.

Part C. Determination of $\ce{PO4^{3-}}$ and $\ce{SiO4^{4-}}$ in alkaline extract

Both phosphate and silicate ions can react with molybdate in alkaline solution, producing the yellow molybdophosphate and molybdatosilicate. Further reduction with ascorbic acid produces intense color molybdenum blue compounds. Both complexes exhibit maximum absorption at $800\,\mathrm{nm}$. Addition of tartaric acid helps preventing interference from silicate in the determination of phosphate.

Two series of phosphate standard are treated with and without tartaric acid whereas a series of silicate standard is not treated with tartaric acid. Linear equations obtained from those calibration curves are as follows:

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \text{Conditions} & \text{Linear equations} \\ \hline \text{Phosphate with and without tartaric acid} & y = 6720\,x_1 \\ \text{Silicate without tartaric acid} & y = 868\,x_2 \end{array}$$

$y$ is absorbance at $800\,\mathrm{nm}$,
$x_1$ is concentration of phosphate as $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$,
$x_2$ is concentration of silicate as $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$

Absorbance at $800\,\mathrm{nm}$ of the alkaline fraction of the soil extract after treated with and without tartaric acid are 0.267 and 0.510, respectively.

5-C1) (1 pt) Calculate the phosphate concentration in the alkaline soil extract in $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ and calculate the corresponding phosphorous in $\mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}$. [Printed in the answer box: concentration of P with 2 digits after decimal point.]

5-C2) (2 pt) Calculate the silicate concentration from the soil sample in t the alkaline fraction in $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ and calculate the corresponding silicon in $\mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}$. [Printed in the answer box: both answers with 2 digits after decimal point.]

Part D. Preconcentration of ammonium phosphomolybdate

A $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of aqueous sample of ammonium phosphomolybdate ($\ce{(NH4)3PMo12O40}$) compound is extracted with $5.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of an organic solvent. The organic-water partition coefficient ($K_\mathrm{ow}$) is defined as the ratio of the concentration of the compound in the organic phase ($c_\mathrm{o}$) to that in the water phase ($c_\mathrm{w}$). $K_\mathrm{ow}$ of the ammonium phosphomolybdate is 5.0. The molar absorptivity of ammonium phosphomolybdate in the organic phase is $5000\,\mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$.

5-D) (2 pt) If the absorbance in the organic phase is 0.200, calculate the total mass of phosphorus (in mg unit) in the original aqueous sample solution. The optical pathlength of the cuvette is $1.00\,\mathrm{cm}$.

problems.title: Iron
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (29.5 points, 6% of the total). Iron

Iron (Fe) is the fourth most abundant element in the Earth's crust and has been used for more than 5,000 years.

Part A.

Pure iron is easily oxidized, which limits its utilization. Element $\mathbf{X}$ is one of the alloying elements that is added to improve the oxidation resistance property of iron.

6-A1) (3 pt) Below is some information about the element $\mathbf{X}$:

• (1) In first ionization, an electron with quantum numbers $n_1 = 4 - l_1$ is removed.
• (2) In second ionization, an electron with quantum numbers $n_2 = 5 - l_2$ is removed.
• (3) The atomic mass of $\mathbf{X}$ is lower than that of Fe.

What is the element $\mathbf{X}$? (Answer by writing the proper symbol according to the periodic table.)

6-A2) (8 pt) Both Fe and $\mathbf{X}$ crystallize in the body centered cubic structure. Approximating the Fe atoms as hard-spheres, the volume taken up by the Fe atoms inside the unit cell is $1.59\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. The volume of the unit cell of $\mathbf{X}$ is $0.0252\,\mathrm{nm^3}$. A complete substitutional solid solution usually occurs when $\Delta R = \left(\dfrac{|R_\mathrm{X} - R_\mathrm{Fe}|}{R_\mathrm{Fe}}\right) \times 100$ is less than or equal to 15, where $R_\mathrm{X}$ and $R_\mathrm{Fe}$ are the atomic radii of $\mathbf{X}$ and Fe, respectively. Can $\mathbf{X}$ and Fe form a complete substitutional solid solution? Show your calculation. No credit is given without calculation presented. The volume of sphere is $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$.

[Printed in the answer box: mark ✓ in an appropriate box: ☐ Yes ($\Delta R \le 15$) ☐ No ($\Delta R > 15$); and give $R_\mathrm{Fe}$ (nm), $R_\mathrm{X}$ (nm) and $\Delta R$.]

Part B.

Iron in natural water is in the form of $\ce{Fe(HCO3)2}$, which ionizes to $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\ce{HCO3^-}$. To remove iron from water, $\ce{Fe(HCO3)2}$ is oxidized to an insoluble complex $\ce{Fe(OH)3}$, which can be filtered out of the water.

6-B1) (4 pt) $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ can be oxidized by $\ce{KMnO4}$ in a basic solution to yield $\ce{Fe(OH)3}$ and $\ce{MnO2}$ precipitates. Write the balanced ionic equation for this reaction in a basic solution.

Under this condition, $\ce{HCO3^-}$ ions are converted to $\ce{CO3^{2-}}$. Write the balanced ionic equation for this reaction in a basic solution.

6-B2) (3.5 pt) A covalent compound $\mathbf{A}$ which contains more than 2 atoms and, a potential oxidizing agent, can be prepared by the reaction between diatomic halogen molecule ($\mathbf{Q}_2$) and $\mathrm{Na}\mathbf{Q}\mathrm{O}_2$.

$$1\,\mathbf{Q}_2 + x\,\mathrm{Na}\mathbf{Q}\mathrm{O}_2 \rightarrow y\,\mathbf{A} + z\,\mathrm{Na}\mathbf{Q}\qquad \text{where } x+y+z \le 7$$

where $x$, $y$ and $z$ are the coefficients for the balanced equation. Among the binary compounds between hydrogen and halogen, $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{Q}$ has the lowest boiling point. Identify $\mathbf{Q}$ and if $\mathbf{A}$ has an unpaired electron, draw a Lewis structure of compound $\mathbf{A}$ with zero formal charge on all atoms. (Answer by writing the proper symbol according to the periodic table.)

What is the molecular geometry of compound $\mathbf{A}$? (Mark ✓ in an appropriate box.)

☐ linear ☐ bent ☐ cyclic ☐ tetrahedral ☐ trigonal planar ☐ other

6-B3) (5 pt) Compound $\mathbf{D}$ is an unstable oxidizing agent that can be used to remove $\ce{Fe(HCO3)2}$ from natural water. It consists of elements $\mathbf{G}$, $\mathbf{Z}$ and hydrogen and the oxidation number of $\mathbf{Z}$ is +1. In this compound, hydrogen is connected to the element having the higher electronegativity among them. Below is some information about the elements $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$:

• (1) $\mathbf{G}$ exists in its normal state as a diatomic molecule, $\mathbf{G}_2$.
• (2) $\mathbf{Z}$ has one proton fewer than that of element $\mathbf{E}$. $\mathbf{E}$ exists as a gas under standard conditions. $\mathbf{Z}_2$ is a volatile solid.
• (3) The compound $\mathbf{E}\mathbf{G}_3$ has a pyramidal shape.

Identify the elements $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ and draw a molecular structure of compound $\mathbf{D}$. (Answer by writing the proper symbol according to the periodic table.)

Part C.

$\ce{^{59}Fe}$ is a radiopharmaceutical isotope which is used in the study of iron metabolism in the spleen. This isotope decays to $\ce{^{59}Co}$ as follows:

$$\ce{^{59}_{26}Fe -> ^{59}_{27}Co} + \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}\qquad(1)$$

6-C1) (2 pt) What are $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ in equation (1)? (Mark ✓ in the appropriate boxes.)

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{proton} & \text{neutron} & \text{beta} & \text{positron} & \text{alpha} & \text{gamma} \\ \hline \phantom{00} & \phantom{00} & \phantom{00} & \phantom{00} & \phantom{00} & \phantom{00} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

6-C2) (4 pt) Consider equation (1), if the $\ce{^{59}Fe}$ isotope is left for 178 days which is $n$ times of its half-life ($t_{1/2}$), the mole ratio of $\ce{^{59}Co}$ to $\ce{^{59}Fe}$ is 15:1. If $n$ is an integer, what is the half-life of $\ce{^{59}Fe}$ in day(s)? Show your calculation. [Printed in the answer box: half-life of $\ce{^{59}Fe}$ in days, 1 decimal place.]

problems.title: DNA
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (62 points, 7% of the total). DNA

Palindromic sequences are an interesting class of DNA. In a palindromic double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) species, the sequence of one strand read in the 5′→3′ direction matches the 5′→3′ reading on the complementary strand. Hence, a palindromic dsDNA consists of two identical strands that are complementary to each other. An example is the so-called Drew–Dickerson dodecanucleotide ($\mathbf{1}$):

$$\begin{array}{c} \text{5'-CGCGAATTCGCG-3'} \\ \text{| | | | | | | | | | | |} \\ \text{3'-GCGCTTAAGCGC-5'} \\ (\mathbf{1}) \end{array}$$

1.1 (5 pt) How many different palindromic double-stranded DNA dodecanucleotides (i.e., dsDNA species with twelve base pairs) exist?

1.2 (5 pt) How many different palindromic double-stranded DNA undecanucleotides (i.e., dsDNA species with eleven base pairs) exist?

The melting temperature of dsDNA, $T_\mathrm{m}$ is defined as the temperature at which 50% of the original amount of DNA double strands are dissociated into separate strands.

1.3 (4 pt) Consider the Drew–Dickerson dodecanucleotide ($\mathbf{1}$). Assume that a G–C nucleobase pair contributes to the DNA duplex stability more than an A–T pair does. What is the probability that its $T_\mathrm{m}$ increases when a single randomly selected base pair is replaced by a G–C pair?

Let us analyze the thermodynamics of formation of double-helical DNA from single strands, and its dependence on the length of the DNA and on the temperature. The equilibrium constant of association of single strands to form dsDNA differs for palindromic and non-palindromic dsDNA. A solution of dsDNA with the initial concentration of $c_\mathrm{init} = 1.00 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ was heated to $T_\mathrm{m}$ and equilibrium was reached.

1.4 (12 pt) Calculate the equilibrium constant of association of single strands at $T_\mathrm{m}$ for both non-palindromic and palindromic DNA.

The mean contributions to the Gibbs energy of association of two single strands to form dsDNA were estimate over a certain range of experimental conditions, and they amount to $-6.07\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ per one G–C pair, and $-1.30\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ per one A–T pair present in a dsDNA.

1.5 (12 pt) How many base pairs are there in the shortest dsDNA oligonucleotide that has $T_\mathrm{m}$ above $330\,\mathrm{K}$? At this $T_\mathrm{m}$, consider the following values of the equilibrium constant of association of single strands to form a dsDNA: $K_\mathrm{np} = 1.00 \times 10^{6}$ for a non-palindromic dsDNA, $K_\mathrm{p} = 1.00 \times 10^{5}$ for a palindromic dsDNA. Is the shortest oligonucleotide palindromic or non-palindromic?

The shortest oligonucleotide is:

• palindromic (P)
• non-palindromic (NP).

Finally, let us leave the simplified idea of base pairs contributing individually to the association of DNA strands. The Gibbs energy of this process may be considered explicitly dependent on temperature. The dependence of the inverse $T_\mathrm{m}$ of the Drew–Dickerson dodecanucleotide ($\mathbf{1}$) on the logarithm of the initial duplex concentration $c_\mathrm{init}$ is shown below. (Note: a standard concentration $c_0 = 1\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ is introduced.)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-1-fig1.png

$$\begin{array}{l|cccccc} c_\mathrm{init}\ /\ 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}} & 0.25 & 0.50 & 1.00 & 2.0 & 4.0 & 8.0 \\ \hline T_\mathrm{m}\ /\ \mathrm{K} & 319.0 & 320.4 & 321.8 & 323.3 & 324.7 & 326.2 \end{array}$$

1.6 (24 pt) Calculate the standard enthalpy $\Delta H^\circ$ and the standard entropy $\Delta S^\circ$ of the association of DNA single strands to form the palindromic double-stranded Drew–Dickerson dodecanucleotide ($\mathbf{1}$). Assume that $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ do not vary with temperature.

problems.title: Repatriation of remains in the middle ages
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (58 points, 8% of the total). Repatriation of remains in the middle ages

At ambient temperatures, racemization is a slow reaction. As such, it can be used for dating biological objects and, moreover, for studying their thermal history. Let us take L-isoleucine (L-Ile) ((2$S$,3$S$)-2-amino-3-methylpentanoic acid) as an example. It isomerizes on the $\alpha$-carbon and forms (2$R$,3$S$)-2-amino-3-methylpentanoic acid, also known as D-allo-isoleucine. As the configuration changes on only one of the two stereogenic centres, this process is called epimerization rather than racemization.

2.1 (1 pt) Choose all true statements.

• D-allo-isoleucine and L-isoleucine have the same values of specific optical rotation but they have different melting points.
• D-allo-isoleucine has an identical absolute value of specific optical rotation as L-isoleucine but the sign is opposite. The melting point is the same for both isomers.
• D-allo-isoleucine and L-isoleucine have different values of specific optical rotation but they have the same melting points.
• D-allo-isoleucine and L-isoleucine have different values of specific optical rotation and different melting points.
• D-allo-isoleucine is not optically active.

2.2 (4 pt) Assign the absolute configurations for each stereoisomer of isoleucine.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-2-fig1.png

• 2$S$,3$R$ (L-allo-isoleucine)
• 2$R$,3$S$ (D-allo-isoleucine)
• 2$S$,3$S$ (L-isoleucine)
• 2$R$,3$R$ (D-isoleucine)

2.3 (4 pt) The equilibrium constant $K_\mathrm{ep}$ for L-isoleucine epimerization has the value of 1.38 (at $374\,\mathrm{K}$). If we set molar Gibbs free energy of L-isoleucine $G^\circ_\mathrm{m} = 0\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, determine the Gibbs free energies for all structures $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{D}$ from question 2.2 at $374\,\mathrm{K}$.

2.4 (2 pt) If we take into account stereoisomerism at all stereocentres, what is the maximum possible number of the stereoisomers of the tripeptide Ile-Ile-Ile?

At the start of the epimerization, we can neglect the reverse reaction. The epimerization then follows the first-order kinetics:

$$\text{L-isoleucine} \xrightarrow{\ k_1\ } \text{D-allo-isoleucine}$$

The value of the rate constant at $374\,\mathrm{K}$ is $k_1(374\,\mathrm{K}) = 9.02 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{h^{-1}}$ and at $421\,\mathrm{K}$ it is $k_1(421\,\mathrm{K}) = 1.18 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{h^{-1}}$.

In the following calculation, shorten the concentration of L-isoleucine to [L] and of D-allo-isoleucine to [D].

We can define a quantity $de$ (diastereomeric excess):

$$de = \frac{[\mathrm{L}] - [\mathrm{D}]}{[\mathrm{L}] + [\mathrm{D}]} \times 100(\%).$$

2.5 (6 pt) Let us boil L-isoleucine for 1 943 hours at $374\,\mathrm{K}$. What is the value of $de$ (with three significant figures) for L-isoleucine a) before boiling and b) after boiling?

2.6 (10 pt) How long does it take to convert 10% of L-isoleucine to D-allo-isoleucine at $298\,\mathrm{K}$?

In fact, the reverse reaction cannot be neglected. The correct kinetic scheme is expressed as

$$\text{L-isoleucine} \underset{k_2}{\overset{k_1}{\rightleftharpoons}} \text{D-allo-isoleucine}$$

Let us define the deviation of concentration from its equilibrium value $[\mathrm{L}]_\mathrm{eq}$

$$x = [\mathrm{L}] - [\mathrm{L}]_\mathrm{eq}$$

It is possible to derive that $x$ evolves with time according to the following equation:

$$x = x(0) \times \mathrm{e}^{-(k_1 + k_2)t},$$

where $x(0)$ is the deviation from equilibrium at $t = 0\,\mathrm{h}$.

2.7 (17 pt) Let us boil $1.00\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ L-isoleucine solution for 1 943 hours at $374\,\mathrm{K}$. The rate constant for the forward reaction is $k_1(374\,\mathrm{K}) = 9.02 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{h^{-1}}$, $K_\mathrm{ep}$ for L-isoleucine epimerization has the value of 1.38 (at $374\,\mathrm{K}$). In the following calculation, shorten the concentration of L-isoleucine to [L] and of D-allo-isoleucine to [D]. Evaluate (with three significant figures) a) $[\mathrm{L}]_\mathrm{eq}$, b) diastereomeric excess ($de$) after boiling.

Amino acids with a single chiral centre undergo racemization, e.g. L-arginine racemizes:

$$\text{L-arginine} \underset{k_1}{\overset{k_1}{\rightleftharpoons}} \text{D-arginine}$$

The time evolution of concentrations is governed by

$$\ln \frac{1 + \dfrac{[\mathrm{D}]}{[\mathrm{L}]}}{1 - \dfrac{[\mathrm{D}]}{[\mathrm{L}]}} = 2k_1 t + C$$

Here [D] and [L] are concentrations of D- and L-arginine at time $t$, $k_1$ is the rate constant, and the term $C$ is set according to the initial concentrations.

Holy Roman Emperor Lothar III passed away during his journey to Sicily in 1137. To facilitate the repatriation of the remains, his body was immediately after his death boiled in water ($373\,\mathrm{K}$) for a certain time. Let us try to estimate the boiling time with the help of chemical kinetics. We know that the rate constant $k_1$ of arginine racemization within the protein at $373\,\mathrm{K}$ and pH = 7 has the value of $5.10 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{h^{-1}}$.

In order to analyse the isomeric composition of arginine in Lothar’s bones, we need to start with transferring arginine into solution. Lothar’s bones were hydrolyzed in a highly acidic environment for 4 hours at $383\,\mathrm{K}$. The ratio of the optical isomers was $\frac{[\mathrm{D}]}{[\mathrm{L}]} = 0.090$. Lothar’s wife Richenza was not boiled after her death. Her bones were hydrolyzed using the same procedure and in this case the ratio was $\frac{[\mathrm{D}]}{[\mathrm{L}]} = 0.059$. (Note that the racemization also takes place during the hydrolysis, with the rate constant $k_1'$, different from $k_1$).

2.8 (14 pt) How long was the Holy Roman Emperor Lothar III boiled in water in 1137?

Note: The racemization of arginine is an extremely slow process at temperatures typically encountered in graves. As both bodies are only some 880 years old, we can neglect the natural racemization during this time.

problems.title: Emerging electro-mobility
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (62 points, 8% of the total). Emerging electro-mobility

Contemporary means of transportation rely on burning fossil fuels, although the efficiency of real combustion engines is inherently limited and typically ranges between 20 and 40%.

3.1 (2 pt) Mark the factors that can make the efficiency of a heat engine higher:

• Increasing the friction in the mechanical parts of the engine
• Increasing the burning temperature of the fuel in the engine
• Narrowing the working temperature interval of the engine
• Increasing the working pressure of the gas

Fuel cells represent a way to improve the engine efficiency for future vehicles. The engine efficiency can be improved by using hydrogen-based fuel cells.

3.2 (6 pt) The standard enthalpy of formation of liquid water is $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\ce{H2O},\mathrm{l}) = -285.84\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, and the standard combustion enthalpy of isooctane is $\Delta_\mathrm{c}H^\circ(\ce{C8H18},\mathrm{l}) = -5\,065.08\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ (both at $323.15\,\mathrm{K}$). Calculate the values of specific (per unit of mass) combustion enthalpy of pure liquid isooctane and pure gaseous hydrogen.

3.3 (7 pt) Calculate the standard electromotive force (EMF) of a fuel cell using gaseous oxygen and hydrogen, both ideal gases at $100\,\mathrm{kPa}$ and $323.15\,\mathrm{K}$, to produce liquid water. Use the following entropy data for $323.15\,\mathrm{K}$: $S^\circ(\ce{H2O},\mathrm{l}) = 70\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$, $S^\circ(\ce{H2},\mathrm{g}) = 131\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$, $S^\circ(\ce{O2},\mathrm{g}) = 205\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$.

3.4 (3 pt) Determine the ideal thermodynamic efficiency ($\eta$) of a fuel cell producing liquid water at $353.15\,\mathrm{K}$. At this temperature, the enthalpy of formation of water is $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\ce{H2O},\mathrm{l}) = -281.64\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and the corresponding reaction Gibbs energy change is $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G^\circ = -225.85\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

3.5 (7 pt) A polymer membrane electrolyzer facility operates at the voltage of $2.00\,\mathrm{V}$ and is powered by a $10.0\,\mathrm{MW}$ wind turbine plant which was running at full power from 10 pm to 6 am. The electrolysis yielded $1\,090\,\mathrm{kg}$ of pure hydrogen. Calculate the electrolysis yield defined as the mass of produced hydrogen divided by its theoretical produced mass.

3.6 (8 pt) Calculate the mass of hydrogen required to drive the distance between Prague and Bratislava ($330\,\mathrm{km}$) at the average speed of $100\,\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$ with a car fitted with a $310\,\mathrm{kW}$ electric engine running on average at a 15% rate of its maximum power. Assume that the efficiency of the hydrogen cell producing electrical energy is 75%, the efficiency of the electric engine is 95%, and the Gibbs energy change for combustion of hydrogen fuel is $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G = -226\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

The low efficiency of hydrogen production and the safety issues connected with its storage impede spreading the hydrogen-based transportation technology. Hydrazine ($\ce{N2H4}$) fuel cells might be a suitable alternative.

The following standard reduction potentials for aqueous hydrazine systems are available:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{N2(g) + 5 H+(aq) + 4 e- -> N2H5+(aq)} & E^\circ = -0.23\,\mathrm{V} \\ \ce{N2H5+(aq) + 3 H+(aq) + 2 e- -> 2 NH4+(aq)} & E^\circ = +1.28\,\mathrm{V} \\ \ce{N2(g) + 4 H2O(l) + 4 e- -> N2H4(aq) + 4 OH- (aq)} & E^\circ = -1.16\,\mathrm{V} \\ \ce{N2H4(aq) + 2 H2O(l) + 2 e- -> 2 NH3(aq) + 2 OH- (aq)} & E^\circ = +0.10\,\mathrm{V} \\ \ce{2 H2O(l) + 2 e- -> H2(g) + 2 OH- (aq)} & E^\circ = -0.83\,\mathrm{V}. \end{array}$$

3.7 (6 pt) Fill in the following Latimer diagrams with the forms of hydrazine and ammonia prevailing at the given conditions and write the redox potential value for each arrow representing the electrochemical half-reaction. Record all the necessary calculations.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-3-fig1.png

Due to the toxicity, odour and its environmental impact, it is extremely unfavourable to produce ammonia in fuel cells.

3.8 (10 pt) Write down the net reaction for the decomposition of hydrazine under basic conditions to (i) ammonia and nitrogen and (ii) nitrogen and hydrogen and calculate the corresponding equilibrium constants at $T = 298.15\,\mathrm{K}$.

Rechargeable lithium-based batteries are an alternative to fuel cells. Lithium-ion batteries commonly use graphite for one of the electrodes, in which lithium clusters intercalate in between the graphite sheets. The other electrode is made of lithium cobalt oxide, which can reversibly absorb lithium ions moving from one electrode to the other during the charge and discharge processes. The half-reactions relevant for the system can be formally written as:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{(C)_{n} + Li+ + e- -> Li(C)_{n}} & E^\circ = -3.05\,\mathrm{V}, \\ \ce{CoO2 + Li+ + e- -> LiCoO2} & E^\circ = +0.19\,\mathrm{V}. \end{array}$$

3.9 (5 pt) Using the formalism given above, write down the overall chemical reaction occurring in the battery during the discharge process. Give the oxidation states of the cobalt atom.

3.10 (2 pt) Tick the boxes to get the correct statements which are valid for the discharge of the lithium-based battery described in 3.9:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-3-fig2.png

3.11 (6 pt) Assume that a $\ce{C6}$ unit, a $\ce{CoO2}$ unit and Li atom form the active battery mass required to transfer one electron between the electrodes. Using the corresponding standard EMF, calculate the theoretical specific reversible charge capacity (in $\mathrm{mAh\,g^{-1}}$) and the energy density (in $\mathrm{kWh\,kg^{-1}}$) of such a model lithium ion battery related to the whole active battery mass.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-4-fig1.png

The activated target is dissolved in concentrated hydrochloric acid (HCl (aq)) to give a mixture containing $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$ ions and their respective chlorido complexes.
