Before you start the calculation, write down the charges in the upper right boxes:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-4-fig2.png

Table 1. Overall complexation constants $\beta$ of Cu and Zn species (charges were omitted in the formulas). $\beta_i = \dfrac{[\ce{MCl}_i]}{[\ce{M}]\cdot[\ce{Cl}]^i}$, M = Cu or Zn

$$\begin{array}{l|cccc} i & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline \beta_i \text{ for } i \text{ in } [\ce{CuCl}_i] & 2.36 & 1.49 & 0.690 & 0.550 \\ \beta_i \text{ for } i \text{ in } [\ce{ZnCl}_i] & 1.60 & 6.30 & 12.6 & 7.90 \end{array}$$

(Mole fraction: answer with 2 digits after decimal point.)

The mixture containing $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$ ions and their respective chlorido complexes was separated with an anion exchange resin. Dry resin in $\ce{OH-}$ form was dispersed in water and the suspension was transferred into a column. To occupy all sites with $\ce{Cl-}$ ions (i.e. to obtain resin in a $\ce{Cl-}$ form), the resin was washed with hydrochloric acid and then with deionized water to wash out all the unbound $\ce{Cl-}$ ions.

4.3 (4 pt) Everything was initially at laboratory temperature before washing with hydrochloric acid. Does the column temperature change during the washing with hydrochloric acid?

• No.
• Yes, the temperature decreases.
• Yes, the temperature increases.

The mixture containing $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$ ions and their respective chlorido complexes was transferred onto the resin-filled column. Hydrochloric acid solution was used as an eluent.

Using the simple experimental formula, you can calculate quantities that determine average elution properties of both copper species and zinc species on the column.

The retention volume $V_\mathrm{R}$ (the mobile phase volume at which 50% of the compound has been eluted from the column) can be calculated as follows:

$$V_\mathrm{R} = D_\mathrm{g} \times m_\mathrm{resin,dry,OH\ form} + V_0$$

4.4 (2 pt) Using average mass distribution coefficients $D_\mathrm{g}$ ($D_\mathrm{g}$(Cu species) $= 17.4\,\mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}}$, $D_\mathrm{g}$(Zn species) $= 78.5\,\mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}}$), calculate the retention volumes $V_\mathrm{R}$ in $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of both copper species and zinc species if the mass of dry resin in $\ce{OH-}$ form $m_\mathrm{resin,dry,OH\ form} = 3.72\,\mathrm{g}$ and the void volume of a column $V_0 = 4.93\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. (Answer $V_\mathrm{R}$(Cu species) with 1 digit after the decimal point and $V_\mathrm{R}$(Zn species) with 0 digit after the decimal point.)

If you cannot find the answer, use $V_\mathrm{R}$(Cu species) $= 49.9\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ and $V_\mathrm{R}$(Zn species) $= 324\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ for further calculations.

Using the simple experimental formula, separation of two sets of species, $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, can be considered complete if

$$V_{0.001}(\mathbf{A}) - V_{0.999}(\mathbf{B}) > 10 V_\mathrm{c}$$

where $V_{0.001}$ is the mobile phase volume at which 0.1% of $\mathbf{A}$ has been eluted from the column, and $V_{0.999}$ is the mobile phase volume at which 99.9% of $\mathbf{B}$ has been eluted from the column.

$$V_{0.001}(\mathbf{A}) = V_\mathrm{R}(\mathbf{A}) \times \left(1 - 6.91\sqrt{d_\mathrm{p}/L_\mathrm{c}}\right)$$

$$V_{0.001}(\mathbf{B}) = V_\mathrm{R}(\mathbf{B}) \times \left(1 - 6.91\sqrt{d_\mathrm{p}/L_\mathrm{c}}\right)$$

$$V_{0.999}(\mathbf{B}) = 2V_\mathrm{R}(\mathbf{B}) - V_{0.001}(\mathbf{B})$$

4.5 (7 pt) Based on a calculation, decide whether copper species were separated completely from zinc species. The volume of the column filled with the swollen resin $V_\mathrm{c} = 10.21\,\mathrm{cm^3}$, the resin particle diameter $d_\mathrm{p} = 0.125\,\mathrm{mm}$, and the height of the wet resin in a swollen state in the column $L_\mathrm{c} = 13.0\,\mathrm{cm}$.

Answer template: $V_{0.001}(\mathbf{A}) = \ldots\,\mathrm{cm^3}$; $V_{0.999}(\mathbf{B}) = \ldots\,\mathrm{cm^3}$; “It is possible to separate copper species from zinc species.”

• True
• False

4.6 (2 pt) Calculate the theoretical value of the total ion exchange mass capacity of the dry resin used in this problem, $Q_\mathrm{m,theor}$, in $\mathrm{mmol\,g^{-1}}$. Consider tetralkylammonium groups were the only ones responsible for ion exchange of the resin. No other nitrogen containing groups were present. The mass fraction of nitrogen in the dry resin was 4.83%. (Answer with 2 digits after decimal point.)

If you cannot find the answer, use $Q_\mathrm{m,theor} = 4.83\,\mathrm{mmol\,g^{-1}}$ for further calculations.

In reality, not all tetraalkylammonium groups are involved in the ion exchange. To determine the total ion exchange volume capacity, $Q_\mathrm{v}$, the column filled with $3.72\,\mathrm{g}$ dry resin converted to the $\ce{Cl-}$ form was washed with the excess of sodium sulfate solution. The effluent was collected in a $500\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask, which was then filled with water to the mark. An aliquot of $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ was potentiometrically titrated with $0.1027\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ silver nitrate. The silver nitrate solution volume at the equivalence point was $22.20\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. The volume of the column filled with the swollen resin, $V_\mathrm{c}$, was $10.21\,\mathrm{cm^3}$.

4.7 (3 pt) Calculate the $Q_\mathrm{v}$ of the swollen resin in mmol of active tetraalkylammonium groups per $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the swollen resin. (Answer in $\mathrm{mmol\,cm^{-3}}$ with 2 digits after decimal point.)

If you cannot find the answer, use $Q_\mathrm{v} = 1.00\,\mathrm{mmol\,cm^{-3}}$ for further calculations.

4.8 (2 pt) Calculate the mole fraction ($x$) of the tetraalkylammonium groups actively involved in the ion exchange. (Answer with 3 digits after decimal point.)

problems.title: Bohemian garnet
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (50 points, 8% of the total). Bohemian garnet

Bohemian garnet (pyrope) is a famous Czech blood coloured semi-precious stone. The chemical composition of natural garnets is expressed by the general stoichiometric formula of $\ce{A3B2(SiO4)3}$, where $\ce{A^{II}}$ is a divalent cation and $\ce{B^{III}}$ is a trivalent cation. Garnets have a cubic unit cell that contains 8 formula units. The structure comprises 3 types of polyhedra: the $\ce{A^{II}}$ cation occupies a dodecahedral position (it is surrounded with eight O atoms), the $\ce{B^{III}}$ cation occupies an octahedral position (it is surrounded with six O atoms) and $\ce{Si^{IV}}$ is surrounded with four O atoms arranged into a tetrahedron.

The most common garnet mineral is almandine with the formula of $\ce{Fe3Al2(SiO4)3}$. Its unit cell parameter is $a = 11.50\,\text{Å}$.

5.1 (3 pt) Calculate the theoretical density of almandine.

The Bohemian garnet has the composition of $\ce{Mg3Al2(SiO4)3}$. Pure compound is colourless and the colour of natural garnets comes from chromophores – transition metal cations that substitute the host material cations. The red colour of the Bohemian garnet comes from trace amounts of $\ce{Cr^{III}}$ ions in the octahedral sites and $\ce{Fe^{II}}$ ions in the dodecahedral sites.

5.2 (3 pt) Draw the splitting diagram for the $[\ce{Cr^{III}O6}]^\mathrm{oct}$ d-orbitals and fill it with electrons.

5.3 (1 pt) Identify the 1st transition row element(s) whose trivalent cation(s) $\ce{M^{III}}$ placed in an octahedral position is/are diamagnetic in the low-spin arrangement and paramagnetic in the high-spin arrangement.

5.4 (5 pt) The figure below shows d-orbitals splitting in the dodecahedral crystal field. Fill in the electrons for the $[\ce{Fe^{II}O8}]^\mathrm{dod}$ chromophore for both existing arrangements.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-5-fig1.png

5.5 (3 pt) Derive the inequalities (e.g. $P < E_1 + E_2 + E_3$) for the pairing energy ($P$) magnitude in relation to energies $E_1$, $E_2$ and $E_3$ for both arrangements (a) high-spin arrangement; b) low-spin arrangement).

5.6 (2 pt) Assuming that $P > E_3$, identify the 1st transition row element(s) whose divalent cation $\ce{M^{II}}$ placed in dodecahedral position is diamagnetic in the low-spin arrangement and paramagnetic in the high-spin arrangement.

The figures below show simplified absorption spectra of four coloured minerals – blood-coloured Bohemian garnet, green uvarovite, blue sapphire and yellow-orange citrine.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-5-fig2.png

5.7 (4 pt) Match the spectra with the minerals (Bohemian garnet, uvarovite, sapphire, citrine).

5.8 (1 pt) If illuminated with monochromatic blue-green (blue-green) light, how will the Bohemian garnet look?

• Red
• Yellow
• Blue
• Blue-green
• Yellow-orange
• Violet
• Black
• White

Andradite is another garnet mineral; its chemical composition is $\ce{Ca3Fe2(SiO4)3}$. A double cation substitution – $\ce{Ti^{IV}}$ for $\ce{Fe^{III}}$ in the octahedral position and $\ce{Fe^{III}}$ for $\ce{Si^{IV}}$ in the tetrahedral position – gives rise to black schorlomite. Its chemical composition can be expressed as $\ce{Ca3}[\ce{Fe,Ti}]^\mathrm{oct}_2([\ce{Si,Fe}]^\mathrm{tet}\ce{O4})_3$.

5.9 (2 pt) Calculate the percentage of $\ce{Si^{IV}}$ ions in a sample of schorlomite that must be substituted with $\ce{Fe^{III}}$, if we know that 5% of $\ce{Fe^{III}}$ ions in octahedral position are substituted with $\ce{Ti^{IV}}$.

The colour of the mineral is caused by two chromophores: $[\ce{Fe^{III}O6}]^\mathrm{oct}$ and $[\ce{Fe^{III}O4}]^\mathrm{tet}$. The central ions of both chromophores have equal number of unpaired electrons.

5.10 (5 pt) Draw the d-orbitals splitting diagrams for both chromophores and fill in the electrons.

Tetrahedral field causes a smaller splitting than the octahedral field ($\Delta_\mathrm{tet} = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_\mathrm{oct}$). Surprisingly for the $\ce{Fe^{III}}$ ion, the energy of the first d–d transition (although very weak) for the octahedral chromophore is smaller ($11\,000\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$) than for the tetrahedral one ($22\,000\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$).

5.11 (7 pt) Calculate the size of pairing energy ($P$) and the sizes of $\Delta_\mathrm{oct}$ and $\Delta_\mathrm{tet}$ splitting. Assume that the pairing energy is equal in both chromophores.

Synthetic garnet YAG (YttriumAluminiumGarnet), used in optoelectronics, has the composition of $\ce{Y3Al5O12}$. Its structure is derived from the general garnet structure $\ce{A3B2(SiO4)3}$ by placing the ions $\ce{Y^{III}}$ and $\ce{Al^{III}}$ to the A, B and Si positions.

5.12 (3 pt) Based on your knowledge of the relative ion radii, determine which cation occupies which position (A, B, Si).

5.13 (2 pt) For the use in LED technology, YAG is doped with $\ce{Ce^{III}}$. Determine the values of $x$ and $y$ in the formula of YAG ($\ce{Y}_x\ce{Ce}_y\ce{Al5O12}$) in which 5% of yttrium atoms are substituted with cerium.

If you don’t get result, use $x = 2{,}25$.

5.14 (6 pt) The $\ce{Ce^{III}}$-doped YAG is prepared by annealing the mixture of $\ce{Y2O3}$, $\ce{Al2O3}$ and $\ce{CeO2}$ in $\ce{H2}$ atmosphere. Use the formula from 5.13, write down a balanced equation for this reaction with the smallest whole-number stoichiometric coefficients.

Doping the YAG structure with rare-earths ions enables the production of lasers with emission wavelengths ranging from the UV to the mid-IR region. In the scheme below, simplified f–f energy transitions of selected rare-earths ions are shown.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-5-fig3.png

5.15 (1 pt) Which cation has a transition which corresponds to blue light emission.

• $\ce{Er^{3+}}$
• $\ce{Sm^{3+}}$
• $\ce{Tm^{3+}}$
• $\ce{Pr^{3+}}$
• $\ce{Yb^{3+}}$
• $\ce{Nd^{3+}}$
• $\ce{Tb^{3+}}$

5.16 (1 pt) Calculate the emission wavelength of this light.

5.17 (1 pt) According to a legend, Noah used a stick with a garnet stone for illumination during his voyage. Assuming only the photoluminescence effect, determine the colour of the laser light emitted from his stick if the stone were the blood-coloured Bohemian garnet.

• Red
• Yellow
• Blue
• Blue-green
• Yellow-orange
• Violet
• Black
• White

problems.title: Let’s go mushrooming
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (68 points, 7% of the total). Let’s go mushrooming

Mushrooming belongs to Czech and Slovak traditional pastimes. While some of our mushroom species are edible, some are inedible or even poisonous.

Inky cap (Coprinopsis atramentaria) is considered edible and delicious. It contains a natural compound called coprine ($\mathbf{E}$), which can be easily synthesized from ethyl 3-chloropropanoate ($\mathbf{1}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-6-fig1.png

6.1 (18 pt) Draw the formulae of compounds $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{E}$ including stereochemistry when necessary. Hint: The first reaction affording compound $\mathbf{A}$ proceeds via an organometallic compound which then cyclizes.

In the human body, coprine undergoes hydrolysis to L-glutamic acid ($\mathbf{3}$) and compounds $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{4}$, which are responsible for the coprine adverse side-effects. They inhibit the enzyme acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, which is involved in the metabolism of alcohol. When the enzyme is inhibited, acetaldehyde formed by alcohol dehydrogenase accumulates in the body, causing strong symptoms of hangover (so called antabuse effect). The active site of the enzyme contains a cysteine SH group, which is blocked either by compound $\mathbf{C}$ or $\mathbf{4}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-6-fig2.png

Enzyme = acetaldehyde dehydrogenase

6.2 (4 pt) Using the pictogram for acetaldehyde dehydrogenase above, draw the structure $\mathbf{F}$ of the enzyme inhibited by compound $\mathbf{4}$.

The antabuse effect got its name after antabuse ($\mathbf{5}$), the most known drug used in alcohol-addiction treatment. This drug can be synthesized according to the following scheme.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-6-fig3.png

6.3 (8 pt) Draw the formulae of compounds $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{H}$. Hint: Compound $\mathbf{H}$ contains five carbon atoms.

6.4 (3 pt) Mark all possible reagents which could be used for $\mathbf{I}$ from the following list.

• m-chloroperbenzoic acid (mCPBA)
• diluted $\ce{H2O2}$
• $\ce{Zn/CH3COOH}$
• $\ce{NaBH4}$
• $\ce{I2}$
• hot concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$
• $\ce{K2CO3}$, $\ce{H2O}$
• $\ce{AlCl3}$

The way antabuse inhibits acetaldehyde dehydrogenase is similar to the effect of compounds $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{4}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-6-fig4.png

Enzyme = acetaldehyde dehydrogenase

6.5 (4 pt) Using the pictogram for acetaldehyde dehydrogenase above, draw the structure $\mathbf{J}$ of the enzyme inhibited by antabuse ($\mathbf{5}$). Hint: Three sulfur atoms should be in the structure.

False morel (Gyromitra esculenta) is another interesting mushroom. Although it was considered edible in the past (esculentus means edible in Latin), there is clear evidence that this mushroom is poisonous due to the content of gyromitrin ($\mathbf{M}$). This natural compound can be prepared from $N$-methylhydrazine ($\mathbf{6}$):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-6-fig5.png

6.6 (12 pt) Draw the formulae of compounds $\mathbf{K}$–$\mathbf{M}$.

In human body, gyromitrin ($\mathbf{M}$) hydrolyzes and provides $N$-methylhydrazine ($\mathbf{6}$), which is strongly hepatotoxic. Gyromitrin ($\mathbf{M}$) hydrolysis occurs as soon as it enters the acidic environment in human stomach where both its amide and imine groups are hydrolyzed.

Let us focus on the hydrolysis of the amide moiety within the gyromitrin molecule. The vibrational wavenumber of the stretching mode of the relevant C−N bond amounts to $1\,293.0\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and the potential energy surface does not significantly alter its shape with isotope substitution effect.

6.7 (16 pt) Calculate the highest possible hypothetical kinetic isotope effect at the temperature of human body, $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, for the given hydrolysis reaction assuming that both relevant nitrogen and carbon atoms were simultaneously substituted, $\ce{^{14}N}$ with the $\ce{^{15}N}$ isotope and $\ce{^{12}C}$ with the $\ce{^{13}C}$ isotope. Consider that only the zero point vibrational energy affects the rate constants. Assume that the molar masses of all isotopes are integers. In all steps consider five significant digits.

6.8 (3 pt) After making these isotopic changes, the rates of hydrolysis are not significantly different. Which of the following is the most likely the rate determining step?

• Nucleophilic attack of water on a protonated amidic moiety
• C−N bond cleavage
• Protonation of the gyromitrin molecule

problems.title: Cidofovir
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (57 points, 7% of the total). Cidofovir

Cidofovir ($\mathbf{1}$), originally designed and prepared by the group of Professor Holy in former Czechoslovakia, is a nucleotide analogue with antiviral activity. It is used to treat viral infections, mostly in patients with AIDS.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-7-fig1.png

The key intermediate in the synthesis of cidofovir is optically pure diol $\mathbf{2}$, which can be prepared from L-mannitol ($\mathbf{3}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-7-fig2.png

7.1 (10 pt) Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{D}$, including stereochemistry. One molecule of $\mathbf{A}$ produces two molecules of $\mathbf{B}$.

7.2 (6 pt) Draw the structural formulae of all alternative stereoisomers of compound $\mathbf{3}$ which could be used in the same reaction sequence to afford only the same product $\mathbf{2}$.

Diol $\mathbf{2}$ is further modified to provide compound $\mathbf{I}$. The synthesis of phosphonate $\mathbf{4}$ used to convert compound $\mathbf{F}$ to $\mathbf{G}$ will be discussed later.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-7-fig3.png

7.3 (15 pt) Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{E}$–$\mathbf{I}$, including stereochemistry. Use the abbreviation MMT for the (4-methoxyphenyl)diphenylmethyl group.

Phosphonate $\mathbf{4}$ can be prepared according to the following scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-7-fig4.png

7.4 (9 pt) Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{J}$–$\mathbf{L}$.

The reaction of $\mathbf{I}$ (from question 7.2) with cytosine ($\mathbf{5}$) leads to a 3:1 mixture of isomeric compounds $\mathbf{M}$ and $\mathbf{N}$. The formation of these two products may be understood by realizing that cytosine ($\mathbf{5}$) can also exist as an aromatic tautomer $\mathbf{P}$. The reaction of $\mathbf{M}$ with cyclohexa-1,4-diene and palladium hydroxide on carbon leads to compound $\mathbf{O}$. The phosphonic ester moiety in compound $\mathbf{O}$ reacts with bromotrimethylsilane to provide cidofovir ($\mathbf{1}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-7-fig5.png

7.5 (11 pt) Draw the structures of the two isomers $\mathbf{M}$, $\mathbf{N}$, and of compound $\mathbf{O}$, including stereochemistry and the structure of the aromatic tautomer $\mathbf{P}$ of cytosine ($\mathbf{5}$). Transformation of $\mathbf{M}$ to $\mathbf{O}$ is the removal of a protecting group.

7.6 (6 pt) Draw the structures of the two simple organic side products $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ formed during the conversion of $\mathbf{M}$ to $\mathbf{O}$ ($\mathbf{Q}$ from cyclohexadiene, $\mathbf{R}$ from the protecting group).

problems.title: Caryophyllene
problems.problem:
Problem 8 (75 points, 9% of the total). Caryophyllene

$\beta$-Caryophyllene ($\mathbf{3}$) is a naturally occurring sesquiterpene present in clove tree and in some traditional Czech and Slovak plants, such as the hop plant or small-leaved linden.

The synthesis of $\beta$-caryophyllene starts from a single enantiomer of dienone $\mathbf{A}$. The reaction of $\mathbf{A}$ with silyl ketene acetal $\mathbf{1}$ followed by immediate reduction and aqueous work-up affords ketone $\mathbf{2}$. This intermediate then undergoes reaction with tosyl chloride, providing $\mathbf{B}$. Basic cyclization of this compound affords $\mathbf{C}$. Finally, the reaction of $\mathbf{C}$ with ylide $\mathbf{D}$ provides $\beta$-caryophyllene.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-8-fig1.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-8-fig2.png

8.1 (14 pt) Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{D}$, including the appropriate stereochemistry. Hint: In transformation $\mathbf{A} \to \mathbf{2}$, the silyl ketene acetal acts as a nucleophile. ($\mathbf{A}$: $\ce{C10H14O}$.)

One of the double bonds in $\mathbf{2}$ as well as in $\mathbf{3}$ has trans configuration and the scaffold is stable enough due to the large ring size. trans-Cyclooctene ($\mathbf{4}$) is the smallest ring that can accommodate a trans double bond. It can be prepared according to the following scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-8-fig3.png

8.2 (14 pt) Draw the structure of reagent $\mathbf{E}$ and intermediates $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$, including the appropriate stereochemistry. For $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$, tick the box indicating the stereochemical outcome:

• achiral
• single enantiomer
• racemic mixture
• mixture of diastereoisomers

8.3 (2 pt) Draw the structure of the enantiomer of cycloalkene $\mathbf{4}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-8-fig4.png

The two double bonds in $\beta$-caryophyllene display different reactivity: the double bond in the ring (endocyclic) is more reactive than the other one (exocyclic) due to the ring strain.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-8-fig5.png

8.4 (16 pt) Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{Ha}$ + $\mathbf{Hb}$, $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{Ja}$ + $\mathbf{Jb}$, including the appropriate stereochemistry. Hint: $\mathbf{Ha}$ + $\mathbf{Hb}$ and $\mathbf{Ja}$ + $\mathbf{Jb}$ are pairs of diastereomers.

Interestingly, the reactivity of the double bonds is reversed when isocaryophyllene ($\mathbf{5}$) is used instead of $\beta$-caryophyllene ($\mathbf{3}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-8-fig6.png

8.5 (6 pt) Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{Ka}$ and $\mathbf{Kb}$. Hint: $\mathbf{Ka}$ + $\mathbf{Kb}$ are a pair of diastereomers.

Isotope-labelled compounds are invaluable tools for reaction mechanism investigation, structure determination, and mass or NMR spectroscopy studies. Let us have a look at the synthesis of some labelled analogues of $\beta$-caryophyllene.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-8-fig7.png

8.6 (8 pt) Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{L}$ and $\mathbf{M}$.

$\beta$-Caryophyllene ($\mathbf{3}$) undergoes acid-catalyzed cyclization, which leads to a complex mixture of products. Among them, the pair of diastereomers $\mathbf{Na}$ + $\mathbf{Nb}$ and the pair of diastereomers $\mathbf{7a}$ + $\mathbf{7b}$ are the most abundant. The reaction starts with protonation of the more reactive internal double bond affording cation $\mathbf{O}$. This cyclizes without the cleavage of a carbon-carbon single bond to yield diastereomeric tricyclic cations $\mathbf{Pa}$ and $\mathbf{Pb}$, which undergo hydration to give the target alcohols $\mathbf{Na}$ and $\mathbf{Nb}$. Alternatively, the cations $\mathbf{Pa}$ and $\mathbf{Pb}$ rearrange with the cleavage of a carbon-carbon single bond to cations $\mathbf{Qa}$ and $\mathbf{Qb}$, which deprotonate to compounds $\mathbf{7a}$ and $\mathbf{7b}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2018-8-fig8.png

8.7 (9 pt) Draw the structures of the three intermediates $\mathbf{O}$, $\mathbf{Pa}$, $\mathbf{Qa}$ leading to the diastereomer $\mathbf{7a}$.

8.8 (6 pt) Draw the structures of diastereomers $\mathbf{Na}$ + $\mathbf{Nb}$ ($\ce{C15H26O}$).

problems.title: Infinite well and butadiene
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (33 points, 6% of the total). Infinite well and butadiene

The buta-1,3-diene molecule is often written $\ce{CH2=CH-CH=CH2}$, with alternating single and double bonds. Nevertheless, its chemical reactivity is not consistent with this description and the $\pi$ electrons are better described by a distribution along the three bonds:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-1-fig1.png

This system can be modeled as a 1D box (i.e. infinite well) where the electrons are free. The energy of an electron in an infinite well of length $L$ is: $E_n = \dfrac{n^2h^2}{8m_\mathrm{e}L^2}$, where $n$ is a non-zero positive integer.

1. (3 pt) Two different models are studied. Sketch at least the three lowest-energy levels $E_n$ for each model in the respective diagrams, showing how the relative energy levels differ within and between models.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-1-fig2.png

Model 1 (« localized »): The $\pi$ electrons are localized on the extremal bonds and evolve in two separate infinite potential wells of length $d$. Model 2 (« delocalized »): The $\pi$ electrons are delocalized on the whole molecule and evolve in a single infinite potential well of length $3d$.

2. (4 pt) Place the $\pi$ electrons for model 1 in the previous diagrams and express the total energy of the $\pi$ system in model 1, as a function of $h$, $m_\mathrm{e}$ and $d$.

3. (4 pt) Place the $\pi$ electrons for model 2 in the previous diagrams and express the total energy of the $\pi$ system in model 2, as a function of $h$, $m_\mathrm{e}$ and $d$.

The conjugation energy is the total energy of the actual $\pi$ system, minus the sum of the energies of ethylene molecules involving the same number of electrons.

4. (2 pt) Express the conjugation energy $\Delta E_\mathrm{c}$ of butadiene, as a function of $h$, $m_\mathrm{e}$ and $d$.

Models 1 and 2 are too simplistic. A new model will be detailed in the following.

5. (3 pt) Draw three other resonance structures of butadiene using Lewis notation.

To take into account the size of carbon atoms, model 2 is now modified into model 3, as follows:
• the new length of the well is $L$ and is located between the abscissa 0 and $L$;
• the carbon atoms are located at the abscissas $L/8$; $3L/8$; $5L/8$ and $7L/8$.
For each level $n$, the $\pi$ wavefunction is:

$$\psi_n(x) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{L}}\,\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)$$

and the $\pi$ electron density for a system with $N$ $\pi$ electrons is:

$$\rho(x) = 2\sum_{i=1}^{N/2}\left|\psi_i(x)\right|^2$$

The four $\pi$ wavefunctions, which correspond to the molecular orbitals of the $\pi$ system, are depicted below (arbitrary order).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-1-fig3.png

6. (2 pt) Sort the energies of the four $\pi$ wavefunctions ($E_\mathrm{A}$, $E_\mathrm{B}$, $E_\mathrm{C}$ and $E_\mathrm{D}$).

7. (2 pt) Give the labels (A, B, C or D) of the orbitals that are filled with electrons in butadiene.

8. (4.5 pt) Within model 3, give the values of the $\pi$ wavefunctions $\psi_n$ for occupied levels at positions 0, $L/4$ and $L/2$, for $n = 1$ and $n = 2$, as a function of $L$.

9. (2.5 pt) Within model 3, give the value of the $\pi$ electron density at positions 0, $L/4$ and $L/2$.

10. (3 pt) Draw the $\pi$ electron density between 0 and $L$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-1-fig4.png

11. (3 pt) Sort the following CC bonds (B1, B2, …, B5) by increasing length, using the symbols = or <:
• B1: C1C2 in the butadiene molecule
• B2: C2C3 in the butadiene molecule
• B3: C3C4 in the butadiene molecule
• B4: CC in the ethane molecule
• B5: CC in the ethene molecule

problems.title: Hydrogen production by water-splitting
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (34 points, 7% of the total). Hydrogen production by water-splitting

Data:

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c} \text{Compound} & \ce{H2(g)} & \ce{H2O(l)} & \ce{H2O(g)} & \ce{O2(g)} \\ \hline \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) & 0 & -285.8 & -241.8 & 0 \\ \hline S_\mathrm{m}^\circ\ (\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}) & 130.6 & 69.9 & 188.7 & 205.2 \end{array}$$

Molecular hydrogen ($\ce{H2}$) can be used as an alternative to carbon dioxide-emitting fuels. Hence, lowering the cost and the environmental impact of its production is a major challenge. In this field, water-splitting is a promising candidate technology.

1. (1 pt) Write down the balanced equation of liquid water splitting reaction using a stoichiometric coefficient of 1 for water.

2. (4 pt) Using only the provided thermodynamic data, justify numerically whether this reaction is thermodynamically favorable at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.
Reaction thermodynamically favorable? ☐ Yes ☐ No

Water splitting can be performed electrochemically using two electrodes in an acidic water bath, connected by a generator (Fig. 1). Gas bubbles are formed at both electrodes.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1 – Water-splitting electrochemical cell.

3. (2 pt) Write down the balanced net electrochemical half reactions occurring at each electrode (electrode (1) and electrode (2)).

4. (3 pt) Using only the provided thermodynamic data (or question 2), derive the condition on the applied voltage $\Delta E_\mathrm{applied}$ between electrodes, compared to value $\Delta E_\mathrm{th}$ (to determine), for the process to be thermodynamically favorable at $298\,\mathrm{K}$, when all reactants and products are in their standard state. Tick the right condition and give the numerical value with 3 decimal places.
☐ $\Delta E_\mathrm{applied} = \Delta E_\mathrm{th}$ ☐ $\Delta E_\mathrm{applied} > \Delta E_\mathrm{th}$ ☐ $\Delta E_\mathrm{applied} < \Delta E_\mathrm{th}$, where $\Delta E_\mathrm{th}$ ………… V (give the result with 3 decimal places)

If you could not calculate $\Delta E_\mathrm{th}$, the value $1.200\,\mathrm{V}$ can be used in the rest of the problem.

Experimentally, a higher voltage is needed to observe water splitting. For a given Pt cathode, the minimum voltage necessary to observe water splitting, $\Delta E_\mathrm{min}$, depends on the nature of the anode, as displayed in the table below:

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Anode} & \Delta E_\mathrm{min}\ (\mathrm{V}) \\ \hline \ce{IrO_{$x$}} & 1.6 \\ \ce{NiO_{$x$}} & 1.7 \\ \ce{CoO_{$x$}} & 1.7 \\ \ce{Fe2O3} & 1.9 \end{array}$$

The difference between $\Delta E_\mathrm{min}$ and $\Delta E_\mathrm{th}$ is responsible for losses in the device.

5. (3 pt) Give the expression of the device power efficiency $\eta_\mathrm{elec}$ (fraction of the power used for water splitting) as a function of $\Delta E_\mathrm{th}$ and $\Delta E_\mathrm{min}$. Assuming an identical current value $I$, calculate the water electrolysis power efficiency when a Pt cathode and a $\ce{Fe2O3}$ anode are used. Give the most efficient anode.

If you could not calculate $\eta_\mathrm{elec}$, the value $\eta_\mathrm{elec} = 75\%$ can be used in the rest of the problem.

An alternative to water electrolysis is direct photocatalytic water-splitting. It uses a semiconductor that can be activated by absorbing light.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2 – Activation condition and equivalent electrode potentials of different semiconductors. Dashed lines correspond to water oxidation and reduction potentials. SHE = Standard Hydrogen Electrode

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3 – Left axis: Spectral distribution of the solar photon flux $\phi$. The photon flux is the number of photons per unit area per unit time arriving on the semiconductor. Right axis and dashed line: cumulative photon flux (i.e. fraction of the photon flux with smaller wavelength).

6. (6 pt) Estimate the fraction of the solar photon flux that can activate the following semiconductors: $\ce{TiO2}$, $\ce{CdS}$, Si. State explicitly the equations and units used for the computation.

The activation of the semi-conductor results in a modification of the surface potentials, so that it can be seen as two electrodes of different potentials.

7. (4 pt) Using the data in Fig 2, choose the semiconductor(s) in the following list that, once activated, can play both roles of anode and cathode for water-splitting reaction.
☐ $\ce{ZrO2}$ ☐ $\ce{ZnO}$ ☐ $\ce{TiO2}$ ☐ $\ce{WO3}$ ☐ $\ce{CdS}$ ☐ $\ce{Fe2O3}$ ☐ $\ce{CdSe}$ ☐ Si

8. (1 pt) Give the semiconductor that, used as both cathode and anode, is expected to be the most efficient for water splitting upon a given solar shining.

The evolution of $\ce{H2}$ and $\ce{O2}$ when a semiconductor is irradiated by simulated solar light at $T = 25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at $p_\mathrm{atm}$ was recently studied. Using an incident power light of $P = 1.0\,\mathrm{kW\,m^{-2}}$ and a photoelectrode with a $S = 16\,\mathrm{mm^2}$ surface, the production of $V = 0.37\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $\ce{H2(g)}$ was measured after $\Delta t = 1$ hour of reaction.

9. (8 pt) Calculate the power efficiency $\eta_\mathrm{direct}$ of the conversion.

If you could not calculate $\eta_\mathrm{direct}$, the value $\eta_\mathrm{direct} = 10\%$ can be used in the rest of the problem.

Two modes of converting solar energy to hydrogen can thus be compared: direct photocatalysis, and indirect photo-electrolysis combining a photovoltaic panel with an electrolyzer. The efficiency of photovoltaic panels on the market is around $\eta_\mathrm{panels} = 20\%$.

10. (2 pt) Compare the power efficiencies of the two modes, $\eta_\mathrm{direct}$ and $\eta_\mathrm{indirect}$, using $\ce{Fe2O3}$ and Pt electrodes for the electrolysis.
☐ $\eta_\mathrm{direct} > \eta_\mathrm{indirect}$ ☐ $\eta_\mathrm{direct} \approx \eta_\mathrm{indirect}$ ☐ $\eta_\mathrm{direct} < \eta_\mathrm{indirect}$

problems.title: About silver chloride
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (40 points, 5% of the total). About silver chloride

Data at 298 K:
$\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{s1}(\ce{AgCl}) = 9.7$; $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{s2}(\ce{Ag2CrO4}) = 12$
Formation constant of the complex $\ce{[Ag(NH3)_{$n$}]+}$: $\beta_n = 10^{7.2}$
Potentials against the standard hydrogen electrode:
Standard potential of $\ce{Ag+}$/Ag(s): $E^\circ(\ce{Ag+}/\ce{Ag(s)}) = 0.80\,\mathrm{V}$
Apparent potential of $\ce{O2(aq)}$/$\ce{HO-(aq)}$ (in seawater): $E'(\ce{O2(aq)}/\ce{HO-(aq)}) = 0.75\,\mathrm{V}$

Part A: Quotes from a chemistry lesson by Louis Joseph Gay-Lussac

The following quotes from a chemistry lesson by Louis Joseph Gay-Lussac (French chemist and physicist, 1778–1850) deal with some properties of silver chloride.

Quote A: “I will now talk about silver chloride, a milk-white solid. It is easily obtained by pouring hydrochloric acid into an aqueous solution of silver nitrate.”
Quote B: “This salt has no taste since it is insoluble.”
Quote C: “This compound is completely insoluble in alcohol and even in acids, except in concentrated hydrochloric acid which dissolves it readily.”
Quote D: “On the other hand, silver chloride is highly soluble in aqueous solution of ammonia.”
Quote E: “Then, we can make silver chloride appear again by adding an acid which reacts with ammonia.”
Quote F: “If you take a bowl made of silver to evaporate salty seawater, you will get impure sodium chloride, mixed with a milk-white solid.”

1. (1 pt) Quote A: Write the balanced chemical equation of $\ce{AgCl(s)}$ synthesis.

2. (3 pt) Quote B: Calculate the solubility $s$ of $\ce{AgCl(s)}$ in water at $298\,\mathrm{K}$ in $\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$.

3. (3 pt) Quote C: In a highly concentrated solution of chloride ions, a well-defined complex of stoichiometry 1:2 is formed. On the following qualitative axis (with pCl increasing from left to right), place in each domain the silver-containing species that is predominant (or exists, for solids). pCl values at frontiers are not expected.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-3-fig1.png

Quote D: When ammonia is added to silver chloride, a well-defined complex of stoichiometry $n$ is formed.

4. (3 pt) Write the balanced equation corresponding to the synthesis of the complex $\ce{[Ag(NH3)_{$n$}]+}$ from silver chloride and calculate the corresponding equilibrium constant.

If you could not calculate $K$, the following value can be used in the rest of the problem: $K = 10^{-3}$

5. (4 pt) Ammonia is added to $0.1\,\mathrm{mol}$ of silver chloride in $1\,\mathrm{L}$ of water until the last grain of solid disappears. At this moment, $[\ce{NH3}] = 1.78\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$. Determine the stoichiometry of the complex neglecting dilution effects.

6. (2 pt) Write the balanced chemical equation corresponding to quote E.

7. (7 pt) Assuming that seawater is slightly basic and rich in dioxygen, and that silver metal can reduce dioxygen in such conditions, write a balanced chemical equation corresponding to the formation of the solid mentioned in quote F. A stoichiometric coefficient of 1 will be chosen for dioxygen. Calculate its equilibrium constant at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

Part B: The Mohr method

The Mohr method is based on the colorimetric titration of $\ce{Cl-}$ by $\ce{Ag+}$ in the presence of potassium chromate ($\ce{2K+}$, $\ce{CrO4^{2-}}$). Three drops ($\sim 0.5\,\mathrm{mL}$) of a $\ce{K2CrO4}$ solution at about $7.76\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ are added to $V_0 = 20.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of a sodium chloride solution of unknown concentration $C_\mathrm{Cl}$. This solution is then titrated by silver nitrate ($\ce{Ag+}$, $\ce{NO3-}$) at $C_\mathrm{Ag} = 0.050\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$, which immediately leads to the formation of solid $\mathbf{A}$. A red precipitate (solid $\mathbf{B}$) appears at $V_\mathrm{Ag} = 4.30\,\mathrm{mL}$.

8. (2 pt) Write the balanced equations of the two reactions occurring during the experiment. Calculate the corresponding equilibrium constants ($K^\circ_1$ and $K^\circ_2$).

9. (2 pt) Identify the solids ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$).

10. (3 pt) Calculate the unknown concentration $C_\mathrm{Cl}$ of chloride ions in the sodium chloride solution.

If you could not calculate $C_\mathrm{Cl}$, the value $C_\mathrm{Cl} = 0.010\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ can be used in the rest of the problem.

11. (4 pt) Calculate the minimal volume $V_\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{min})$ for which $\ce{AgCl(s)}$ precipitates.

12. (6 pt) Calculate the residual concentration $[\ce{Cl-}]_\mathrm{res}$ of chloride ions when silver chromate begins to precipitate. Justify why $\ce{CrO4^{2-}}$ is a good titration endpoint indicator by comparing two values.

problems.title: From gunpowder to the discovery of iodine
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (50 points, 7% of the total). From gunpowder to the discovery of iodine

In the 19th century, the French entrepreneur B. Courtois specialized in the production of nitrate $\mathbf{A}$ ($\mathbf{M_A}(\ce{NO3})_m$), used for gunpowder. Initially imported from Asia, $\mathbf{A}$ was later produced from nitrate $\mathbf{B}$ ($\mathbf{M_B}(\ce{NO3})_n$) using exchange reaction with compound $\mathbf{C}$, obtained from algae.

1. (6 pt) Find the formulas of nitrates $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ knowing that they are anhydrous salts of alkaline or alkaline-earth metal ($\mathbf{M_A}$ and $\mathbf{M_B}$). One of the nitrates contains no more than 1 w% of non-metallic impurities while the other contains $9 \pm 3$ w% of impurities. The content of metals $\mathbf{M_A}$ and $\mathbf{M_B}$ in the samples is 38.4 w% and 22.4 w% respectively. Support your answer with calculations.

To obtain $\mathbf{A}$, $262.2\,\mathrm{g}$ of solid compound $\mathbf{C}$ were added to the solution containing $442.8\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathbf{B}$. $\mathbf{B}$ is known to be in excess. As a result, $190.0\,\mathrm{g}$ of white precipitate $\mathbf{D}$ were formed and removed by filtration. The filtrate was evaporated, and the obtained solid mixture $\mathbf{E}$ was heated until the mass of the sample (containing only nitrites, $\ce{NO2-}$) was constant. The only gaseous product was dioxygen: $60.48\,\mathrm{L}$ at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at $1\,\mathrm{atm}$ (dioxygen can be considered as an ideal gas).

2. (9 pt) Calculate the composition (in w%) of mixture $\mathbf{E}$ considering that it contained only compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ and no other impurities, and that $\mathbf{C}$ was taken in pure anhydrous state.

3. (8 pt) Determine the formulas of compounds $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ and write the balanced reaction equation between $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$.

In 1811, when working with algae ashes, Courtois observed that copper vessels were worn out faster than usual. While he was studying this phenomenon, his cat entered the laboratory and spilled the solution of concentrated sulfuric acid on the dry algae ashes: violet vapors instantly came out of the vessel (1, sulfuric acid is the oxidizing agent): iodine ($\ce{I2}$) had just been discovered! Iodine was the cause of the copper corrosion (2). However, because of the medicinal applications of iodine, Courtois opened a new manufacture to produce it by reaction of algae with chlorine (3).
Nowadays, iodine is prepared from the set of reactants ($\ce{NO3-}$, $\ce{I-}$, $\ce{H+}$) (4) or ($\ce{IO3-}$, $\ce{I-}$, $\ce{H+}$) (5).

4. (5 pt) Write balanced equations for reactions 1–5.

The solubility of iodine is very low in water but significantly increases when iodide ions are added. Together they form ions such as triiodide, $\ce{I3-}$:

$$\ce{I^{-}(aq) + I2(aq) = I3^{-}(aq)} \tag{6}$$

Equilibrium (6) can be studied through the extraction of $\ce{I2}$ with dichloromethane. Indeed, $\ce{I-}$ and $\ce{I3-}$ do not dissolve in organic solvents but $\ce{I2}$ does and, when extracted, it is 15 times more concentrated in dichloromethane than in water.
The following experiment was performed. To prepare the initial solution, a few crystals of solid iodine were dissolved in $50.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ of an aqueous solution of potassium iodide ($0.1112\,\mathrm{g}$). Then, $50.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ of dichloromethane were added, and the mixture was vigorously shaken until equilibration. After phase separation, each phase was titrated by $16.20\,\mathrm{mL}$ (organic phase) and by $8.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ (aqueous phase) of the standard aqueous solution of sodium thiosulphate pentahydrate ($14.9080\,\mathrm{g}$ in $1.000\,\mathrm{L}$ of solution) in the presence of starch. The process is schematically represented below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-4-fig1.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-4-fig2.png

5. (6 pt) Find the correspondence between the stages on the scheme (1–9) and the schematic pictures representing them (a–i).

6. (2 pt) Write balanced equations for the two possible chemical reactions in the aqueous phase during the titration involving iodine species and sodium thiosulphate.

7. (2 pt) Calculate the mass of iodine used to prepare the initial solution.

8. (12 pt) Calculate the equilibrium constant $K^\circ$ for equilibrium of reaction (6).

problems.title: Azobenzene – β-cyclodextrin complexes for the formation of nanomachines
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (41 points, 8% of the total). Azobenzene – β-cyclodextrin complexes for the formation of nanomachines

Nanomachines are molecular assemblies that enable the transformation of an energy source into a nano-movement for applications such as drug delivery. Numerous nanomachines make use of the isomerization of azo compounds ($\ce{R-N=N-R'}$) upon irradiation.

1. (3 pt) Draw the stereoisomers of azobenzene ($\ce{H5C6-N=N-C6H5}$) and draw a line between the two carbon atoms that are the furthest apart. Compare these two distances ($d_\mathrm{trans}$ and $d_\mathrm{cis}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-5-fig1.png

Fig. 1 – Possible reactants for the synthesis of $\mathbf{M}$.

2. (4 pt) $\mathbf{M}$ can be synthesized in two steps from simple reactants (Fig. 1). Choose among the suggested reactants ($\mathbf{N}$ to $\mathbf{Q}$) the ones that can provide $\mathbf{M}$ with very high regioselectivity. Sodium nitrite ($\ce{NaNO2}$) in cold aqueous hydrochloric acid is used as reagent for the first step of the synthesis.

Determination of the association constant $K_\mathrm{t}$

β-cyclodextrin ($\mathbf{C}$, Fig. 2) is a cyclic heptamer of glucose, which can form inclusion complexes with azo compounds. In tasks 3 to 6, we will determine by spectroscopy the association constant $K_\mathrm{t}$, corresponding to the formation of the inclusion complex $\mathbf{CM_{trans}}$ as depicted in Fig. 2.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-5-fig2.png

Fig. 2 – Formation of the $\mathbf{CM_{trans}}$ inclusion complex.

Several solutions are prepared by mixing $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{M_{trans}}$ in different proportions to reach initial concentrations $[\mathbf{C}]_0$ and $[\mathbf{M_{trans}}]_0$. While $[\mathbf{M_{trans}}]_0$ is identical for all solutions, $[\mathbf{C}]_0$ varies. We follow, at a fixed wavelength, the evolution of the difference in absorbance $\Delta A$ between the absorbance of each solution and the pure $\mathbf{M_{trans}}$ solution. We note the molar absorption coefficients of $\mathbf{CM_{trans}}$ and $\mathbf{M_{trans}}$, $\varepsilon_\mathrm{CMtrans}$ and $\varepsilon_\mathrm{Mtrans}$, respectively. $L$ is the path length of the beam through the sample. The absorbance of $\mathbf{C}$ ($\varepsilon_\mathrm{C}$) is negligible.

3. (4 pt) Demonstrate that $\Delta A = \alpha\cdot[\mathbf{CM_{trans}}]$ and express $\alpha$ in terms of known constant(s).

4. (2 pt) Demonstrate that, when $\mathbf{C}$ is in large excess with respect to $\mathbf{M_{trans}}$ (i.e. $[\mathbf{C}]_0 \gg [\mathbf{M_{trans}}]_0$), the concentration of $\mathbf{C}$ may be considered as constant, $[\mathbf{C}] \simeq [\mathbf{C}]_0$.

5. (5 pt) Demonstrate that, when $\mathbf{C}$ is in large excess with respect to $\mathbf{M_{trans}}$ (i.e. $[\mathbf{C}]_0 \gg [\mathbf{M_{trans}}]_0$), $\Delta A = \alpha\cdot\dfrac{\beta\cdot[\mathbf{C}]_0}{1 + K_\mathrm{t}\cdot[\mathbf{C}]_0}$ and express $\beta$ in terms of constant(s) and initial concentration(s).

6. (5 pt) Determine $K_\mathrm{t}$ using the following experimental curve (Fig. 3).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-5-fig3.png

Fig. 3 – Evolution of $1/\Delta A$ as a function of $1/[\mathbf{C}]_0$.

Determination of the association constant $K_\mathrm{c}$

In tasks 7 to 9, we will determine by kinetic studies the association constant $K_\mathrm{c}$, corresponding to the formation of the inclusion complex with $\mathbf{M_{cis}}$, $\mathbf{CM_{cis}}$. A sample containing only $\mathbf{M_{trans}}$ is irradiated, thus producing a known amount of $\mathbf{M_{cis}}$, $[\mathbf{M_{cis}}]_0$. $\mathbf{M_{cis}}$ (free or within the inclusion complex) then thermally isomerizes into $\mathbf{M_{trans}}$. In the absence of $\mathbf{C}$, the isomerization follows a first order kinetics with a rate constant $k_1$. All complexation equilibria are faster than the isomerization processes. The kinetic scheme corresponding to this experiment is provided in Fig. 4.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-5-fig4.png

Fig. 4 – Kinetic scheme for the isomerization of $\mathbf{M_{cis}}$ in the presence of $\mathbf{C}$.

The rate of disappearance $r$ for the total amount of $\mathbf{M_{cis}}$ (free and complexed) is defined as

$$r = k_1[\mathbf{M_{cis}}] + k_2[\mathbf{CM_{cis}}]$$

Experimentally, $r$ follows an apparent first order kinetic law with an apparent rate constant $k_\mathrm{obs}$:

$$r = k_\mathrm{obs}\left([\mathbf{M_{cis}}] + [\mathbf{CM_{cis}}]\right)$$

7. (4 pt) Demonstrate that $k_\mathrm{obs} = \dfrac{\gamma + \delta\cdot k_2[\mathbf{C}]}{1 + K_\mathrm{c}[\mathbf{C}]}$ and express $\gamma$ and $\delta$ in terms of known constant(s).

8. (3 pt) Choose in which condition(s) the half-life $t_{1/2}$ corresponding to $k_\mathrm{obs}$ can be expressed as $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\gamma}\left(1 + K_\mathrm{c}[\mathbf{C}]_0\right)$ given that $[\mathbf{C}]_0 \gg [\mathbf{M_{cis}}]_0$. Mathematically justify your answer.
☐ Very slow isomerization of $\mathbf{M_{cis}}$ within cyclodextrin
☐ Very slow isomerization of free $\mathbf{M_{cis}}$
☐ $\mathbf{CM_{cis}}$ very stable
☐ $\mathbf{CM_{trans}}$ very stable

9. (5 pt) Assuming the condition(s) in task 8 satisfied, determine $K_\mathrm{c}$ by a linear regression using the data below. You may use a calculator or plot a graph.

$$\begin{array}{c|c||c|c} [\mathbf{C}]_0\ (\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}) & t_{1/2}\ (\mathrm{s}) & [\mathbf{C}]_0\ (\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}) & t_{1/2}\ (\mathrm{s}) \\ \hline 0 & 3.0 & 3.0\cdot10^{-3} & 5.9 \\ 1.0\cdot10^{-4} & 3.2 & 5.0\cdot10^{-3} & 7.7 \\ 5.0\cdot10^{-4} & 3.6 & 7.5\cdot10^{-3} & 9.9 \\ 1.0\cdot10^{-3} & 4.1 & 1.0\cdot10^{-2} & 12.6 \end{array}$$

Formation of nanomachines

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-5-fig5.png

Fig. 5 – Cleavage of an azobenzene–cyclodextrin inclusion complex induced by a light-triggered isomerization, which allows delivery of a dye (grey circles).

Another azobenzene compound (for which $K_\mathrm{c} \ll K_\mathrm{t}$), initially in the trans form, is covalently grafted on silica (Fig. 5). The silica pores are filled with a dye (rhodamine B, grey circles in Fig. 5). Upon addition of $\mathbf{C}$, an inclusion complex is formed, which blocks the pores and prevents the release of the dye.

10. (2 pt) Choose the most appropriate condition (one choice only) so that the pores are initially blocked in the presence of $\mathbf{C}$, and the dye can be released upon irradiation.
☐ $K_\mathrm{t} \gg 1$
☐ $K_\mathrm{t} \gg 1$ and $K_\mathrm{c} \ll 1$
☐ $K_\mathrm{t}/K_\mathrm{c} \ll 1$
☐ $K_\mathrm{t} \gg 1$ and $K_\mathrm{c} \gg 1$
☐ $K_\mathrm{c} \ll 1$

This azobenzene-silica powder loaded with a dye is placed in the corner of a cuvette (Fig. 6) so that the powder cannot move into solution. The powder is irradiated at a wavelength $\lambda_1$ to trigger the release of the dye from the pores (Fig. 5). To monitor this release by absorbance spectroscopy we measure the absorbance of the solution at wavelength $\lambda_2$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-5-fig6.png

Fig. 6 – Left: experimental setup used to monitor the release of the dye; right: absorption spectra of trans-azobenzene (full line), cis-azobenzene (dotted line) and rhodamine B (dashed line).

11. (2 pt) Determine $\lambda_1$.

12. (2 pt) Determine $\lambda_2$.

problems.title: Characterization of a block-copolymer
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (48 points, 8% of the total). Characterization of a block-copolymer

Block-copolymers, obtained by linking different polymers (blocks), have unique properties, such as the ability to self-assemble. In this problem, the synthesis and characterization of such a macromolecule are studied.

Study of the first block

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-6-fig1.png

In this first part, we will study the water soluble homopolymer $\mathbf{1}$ (α-methoxy-ω-aminopolyethyleneglycol).
The $^1$H NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{1}$ ($\ce{DMSO}$-$d_6$, $60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $500\,\mathrm{MHz}$) includes the following signals:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Index} & \delta\ (\mathrm{ppm}) & \text{Peak Area} \\ \hline \text{a} & 2.7^{*} & 0.6 \\ \text{b} & 3.3 & 0.9 \\ \text{c} & 3.4 & 0.6 \\ \text{d} & \sim 3.5 & 133.7 \end{array}$$

Table 1, *in the presence of $\ce{D2O}$, the signal at $2.7\,\mathrm{ppm}$ disappears.

1. (4 pt) Match the $^1$H NMR signals (a, b, c, d) from Table 1 with each of the corresponding protons.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-6-fig2.png

2. (4 pt) Express the average degree of polymerization $n$ as a function of the area $A_\mathrm{OC_2H_4}$ of the NMR peak of the repeating unit and the area $A_\mathrm{OCH_3}$ of the NMR peak of the methyl end group. Calculate $n$.

If you could not calculate $n$, the value $n = 100$ can be used in the rest of the problem.

Study of a diblock-copolymer

The synthesis of the second block of the copolymer is performed through the reaction of $\mathbf{1}$ with $\mathbf{2}$ (ε-(benzyloxycarbonyl)-lysine $N$-carboxyanhydride). This yields the block-copolymer $\mathbf{3}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-6-fig3.png

3. (5 pt) Draw the reaction intermediate that is formed in the first step of the addition of $\mathbf{1}$ to $\mathbf{2}$. The second step of the mechanism leads to the formation of a gas molecule, $\mathbf{G}$. Draw its structure.

Problem 7 (54 points, 6% of the total). Ring motion in a [2]catenane

In 2016, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to J.-P. Sauvage, Sir J. F. Stoddart and B. L. Feringa "for the design and synthesis of molecular machines". An example of these is [2]catenane, a molecule consisting of two interlocked rings. In this system, one macrocycle contains a single phenanthroline (bidentate) ligand and the second contains two ligands: a phenanthroline and a terpyridine (tridentate) ligand. A copper ion is coordinated by one ligand from each macrocycle. Depending on the oxidation state of the copper (+I or +II), two configurations are obtained (Fig. 1).

Problem 9 (44 points, 7% of the total). Synthesis of levobupivacaine

Part I.

The local anesthetic bupivacaine (marketed as Marcaine) is on the World Health Organization List of Essential Medicines. Although the drug is currently used as a racemic mixture, it was demonstrated that one enantiomer of bupivacaine, levobupivacaine, is less cardiotoxic and, therefore, safer than the racemate. Levobupivacaine can be synthesized from the natural amino acid L-lysine.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2019-9-fig1.png

problems.title: Two Beauties of Turkey: the Van Cat and the Ankara Cat
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (24 points, 8% of the total). Two Beauties of Turkey: the Van Cat and the Ankara Cat

The most beautiful of cats, the Van cat is a pure breed living only in Lake Van basin. Another endemic cat breed is the Ankara cat. They are called Angora cats. Their most important feature is their two different eye colors.

Just like people, cats can sometimes be stressed and angry. Just as people are made happy by melatonin, the stress of cats can be reduced and they can be made happy thanks to a natural product. Nepetalactone is an organic compound isolated from the plant catnip (Nepeta cataria), which acts as a cat attractant. Nepetalactone is a ten-carbon bicyclic monoterpenoid compound derived from isoprene with two fused rings: a cyclopentane and a lactone.

Problem 2 (77 points, 10% of the total). A Tale of a Reactive Intermediate

Arynes constitute a special class of reactive intermediates. The first experimental evidence for the structure of an aryne (benzyne) was demonstrated in 1953 via the elegant labeling experiments by John D. Roberts and coworkers.

In one such experiment, chlorobenzene, whose carbon at position 1 was labeled with radioactive $^{14}$C, was reacted with $\ce{KNH2}$ in liquid $\ce{NH3}$ to give nearly equal amounts of isotopic isomers $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ along with the inorganic salt $\mathbf{C}$. This reaction proceeds via the formation of aryne intermediate $\mathbf{D}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2020-2-fig1.png

Analysis of the $^{14}$C-labeled product(s) was achieved via degradation experiments (the $^{14}$C-labeled carbons are not shown on the structures). Radioactivities of the intermediates and final products were examined.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2020-2-fig2.png

□ $\ce{BaCO3}$ (Batch 1)

Considering only $\mathbf{B}$:

□ $\ce{BaCO3}$ (Batch 1)
□ Compound $\mathbf{2}$
□ $\ce{BaCO3}$ (Batch 2)

With the aim of facilitating aryne formation, Kobayashi and co-workers developed a fluoride-induced aryne generation protocol. Using this method, benzene derivative $\mathbf{3}$ is reacted with furan ($\mathbf{4}$) in the presence of CsF, resulting in the formation of $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{F}$, and $\mathbf{G}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2020-2-fig3.png

• Combustion analysis of $\mathbf{E}$ revealed the following atom content: 75.8% carbon, 5.8% hydrogen, and 18.4% oxygen.
• $\mathbf{E}$ does not have a proton that is exchangeable with $\ce{D2O}$ in $^1$H-NMR spectroscopy.
• $\mathbf{F}$ is an ionic compound.

2.3 (8.0 pt) Determine the structures of $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{F}$, and $\mathbf{G}$ (without stereochemical details).

In the absence of a nucleophile or a trapping agent, arynes can undergo [2+2]-type cyclodimerization or [2+2+2]-type cyclotrimerization reactions under suitable conditions. The aryne derivative that is obtained when $\mathbf{3}$ is treated with one equivalent of CsF in MeCN can give, in principle, four different dimerization and trimerization products ($\mathbf{H}$–$\mathbf{K}$).

• $\mathbf{H}$ has two planes of symmetry.
• $\mathbf{I}$ is expected to exhibit 21 signals in its $^{13}$C-NMR spectrum.
• $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{J}$ both exhibit an $m/z$ value of 318.1 in their mass spectra.

2.4 (16 pt) Determine the structures of $\mathbf{H}$–$\mathbf{K}$.

When $\mathbf{5}$ is reacted with $\beta$-ketoester $\mathbf{6}$ in the presence of 2 equivalents of CsF at $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $\mathbf{L}$ is obtained as the major product. The $^1$H-NMR and $^{13}$C-NMR data for $\mathbf{L}$, recorded in $\ce{CDCl3}$, are as follows:

• $^1$H-NMR: $\delta$ 7.79 (dd, $J$ = 7.6, 1.5 Hz, 1H), 7.47–7.33 (m, 2H), 7.25–7.20 (m, 1H), 3.91 (s, 2H), 3.66 (s, 3H), 2.56 (s, 3H) ppm.
• $^{13}$C-NMR: $\delta$ 201.3, 172.0, 137.1, 134.4, 132.8, 132.1, 130.1, 127.5, 51.9, 40.2, 28.8 ppm.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2020-2-fig4.png

2.5 (5.0 pt) Determine the structure of $\mathbf{L}$.

2.6 (4.0 pt) In the reaction shown in task 2.5, which of the statement(s) in the answer sheet describe(s) the function of CsF?

• The $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ values of HF and $\beta$-ketoester $\mathbf{6}$ in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) are about 15 and 14, respectively.

□ $\ce{F-}$ hydrolyzes the trifluoromethanesulfonate ($\ce{O3SCF3}$) group of $\mathbf{5}$.

□ $\ce{F-}$ acts as a base to deprotonate of $\mathbf{6}$.
□ $\ce{F-}$ acts as a nucleophile and attacks the ester group of $\mathbf{6}$.

Diazapyrone derivative $\mathbf{8}$ was shown to be a useful reactant for the construction of a variety of cyclic frameworks. Its preparation from phenylglyoxylic acid ($\mathbf{7}$) and its use in two different reactions are described below.

• $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{T}$ are gases under ambient conditions.
• $\mathbf{O}$ and $\mathbf{P}$ are constitutional isomers.
• $\mathbf{Q}$ does not have any signals in its IR spectrum.

Problem 4 (66 points, 10% of the total). Symmetry Does Matter!

There are numerous reactions in organic chemistry that proceed through cyclic transition states and these are classified as pericyclic reactions. Woodward–Hoffmann rules, developed by Robert B. Woodward and Roald Hoffmann, are used to rationalize stereochemical aspects and the activation energy of pericyclic reactions.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2020-4-fig1.png

Woodward–Hoffmann rules

problems.title: Konya, Carrot, Beta-Carotene, Vitamin-A, Immune System, Vision
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (100 points, 14% of the total). Konya, Carrot, Beta-Carotene, Vitamin-A, Immune System, Vision

Mevlana (Rumi) was a great mystic and Sufi poet who lived out his days in Konya in the 13th century. The indirect relevance of Konya to chemistry is that the city provides 65% of the country's carrot production, from which one of the essential vitamins (vitamin A) is obtained.

Carrot is an important source of β-carotene, which gives the vegetable its orange color. This molecule is a red-orange pigment naturally found in plants and fruits and is a provitamin A carotenoid. It is converted to vitamin A, which is essential for normal growth and development, the immune system, and vision function.

β-Carotene has an extended polyene chain of 22 carbon atoms. It is a conjugated π-system, having alternating single and double bonds. Its experimental maximum absorption wavelength ($\lambda_{max}$) is 455 nm. We assume that all the bonds between $\mathrm{C_1}$ and $\mathrm{C_{22}}$ are conjugated bonds. There are 22 π-electrons in the molecule (Figure 1).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2020-5-fig1.png

Figure 1. Ball and stick representation of the structure of β-carotene. The gray and white spheres represent the carbon and hydrogen atoms, respectively. The numbered carbon atoms belong to the linear conjugated π-segment of the molecule.

To a crude approximation, the electrons in the C-2Pz orbitals, which are perpendicular to the molecular plane, are assumed to move along the entire molecule, without interacting with each other. They are like independent particles confined in a molecule moving along the x-axis in one dimension. These characteristics of π-electrons make them eligible for being treated by the simplest model called the particle in one-dimensional box model.

The wave function and the energies of the quantized levels for an electron moving in a one-dimensional box with infinite potential walls are given as follows:

$$\Psi_n(x) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{L}}\,\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L} \qquad \text{(Eq.1)}$$

where n is the quantum number, $n = 1, 2, 3, 4, \ldots\ \infty$, and L is the box length.

$$E_n = \frac{n^2 h^2}{8 m_e L^2} \qquad \text{(Eq.2)}$$

In two dimension, within the framework of independent particle approximation, the wavefunction is expressed as a product of one-dimensional wavefunctions, and the energy is expressed as a sum of one-dimensional energies. The energy levels of the two dimensional rectangular box is given as follows:

$$E_{n_x,n_y} = \left[\frac{n_x^2}{L_x^2} + \frac{n_y^2}{L_y^2}\right]\left\{\frac{h^2}{8 m_e}\right\} \qquad \text{(Eq.3)}$$

where $n_x$, $n_y$ are the quantum numbers and they are positive integers. $L_x$, $L_y$ are the dimensions of the box in the 2D model. They are positive numbers.

5.1 (13.0 pt) Which two of the sentences given below are correct? Tick only one answer which includes correct sentences in your answer sheet.

The β-carotene molecule is orange in color because:

i) it absorbs in the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum.

ii) HOMO → LUMO transition occurs by absorption of IR photon.

iii) the spacing between the 22nd and the 23rd energy levels is equal to the energy of the IR photon at the orange wavelength.

iv) it absorbs green/blue light and it transmits red/yellow color.

v) it absorbs in the UV-Vis region since the molecule has no net dipole moment.

□ a) i and ii □ b) i and iii □ c) i and iv □ d) i and v
□ e) ii and iii □ f) ii and iv □ g) ii and v □ h) iii and iv
□ j) iii and v □ k) iv and v

Although it is highly unrealistic, let us assume that the conjugated segment of the molecule is linear and treated with the particle in a one-dimensional box model as shown in figure 2. In this case, the length of the box can be approximated as $L = 1.40 \times n_C$ (in Å), where $n_C$ is the number of carbon atoms in the conjugated segment.

Use this information to answer the questions 5.2–5.6.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2020-5-fig2.png

Figure 2. Schematic representation of the conjugated line segment made up carbon atoms of β-carotene in a one-dimensional box of length L.

5.2 (13.0 pt) Calculate the energies (in J) of the lowest two energy levels

5.3 (15.0 pt) Draw the wavefunctions of the lowest two energy levels with proper labelling the x-axis.

5.4 (8.0 pt) Sketch the energy level diagram up to n = 4 showing the relative spacing.

5.5 (12.0 pt) What is the total π-energy (in J) of the molecule?

5.6 (10.0 pt) Calculate the wavelength (in nm) at which the transition between the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied energy levels occurs.

Use the particle in a two-dimensional box model to answer questions 5.7–5.8.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2020-5-fig3.png

Figure 3. Schematic representation of the conjugated carbon atoms of β-carotene in a two-dimensional box.

Assume that the conjugated segment is made up of carbon atoms that are all-trans to each other. The motion of the π-electrons is studied in the two-dimensional rectangular box with the dimensions $L_x = 26.0$ Å, $L_y = 3.0$ Å (Figure 3).

5.8 (12.0 pt) What should be the $L_x$ value (in Å) in order for the molecule to absorb light at the experimental $\lambda_{max}$ = 455 nm if $L_y$ is kept constant at 3.0 Å. (Assume that the quantum numbers for homo and lumo are the same as in the question 5.7.)

problems.title: Thermodynamics through an Interstellar Journey
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (80 points, 12% of the total). Thermodynamics through an Interstellar Journey

Part 1

In a hypothetical universe, an unknown amount of diborane participates in the following reaction:

$$\ce{B2H6(g) + 6 H2O(l) -> 2 H3BO3(s) + 6 H2(g)}$$

Assume that in this hypothetical universe, $\ce{H3BO3(s)}$ obtained from this reaction was completely sublimed at 300 K. The necessary energy for sublimation was obtained through work released by one cycle of an ideal heat engine in which one mole of monoatomic perfect gas flows through the cycle described in the pressure (p) – volume (V) diagram below:

• A → B; isothermal reversible expansion receiving 250 J by heat transfer ($q_H$) at a temperature of 1000 K ($T_H$) from a hot source.
• B → D; reversible adiabatic expansion.
• D → C; isothermal reversible compression at a temperature of 300 K ($T_C$) releasing some amount of heat ($q_C$) to a cold sink.
• C → A; reversible adiabatic compression.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2020-6-fig1.png

After heat transfers, the remaining energy is released as work (w). Also, $q_H$ and $q_C$ are related to $T_C$ and $T_H$ as follows:

$$\frac{|q_H|}{|q_C|} = \frac{T_H}{T_C}$$

The efficiency of the cycle can be found by work released by cycle (w) divided by heat absorbed by cycle ($q_H$).

You are provided with the change in enthalpies of the following reactions at 300 K.

$$\begin{array}{ll} (1)\ \ce{B2H6(g) + 6 Cl2(g) -> 2 BCl3(g) + 6 HCl(g)} & \Delta_r H(1) = -1326\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ (2)\ \ce{BCl3(g) + 3 H2O(l) -> H3BO3(g) + 3 HCl(g)} & \Delta_r H(2) = -112.5\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ (3)\ \ce{B2H6(g) + 6 H2O(l) -> 2 H3BO3(s) + 6 H2(g)} & \Delta_r H(3) = -493.4\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ (4)\ \tfrac{1}{2}\,\ce{H2(g)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\ce{Cl2(g) -> HCl(g)} & \Delta_r H(4) = -92.3\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \end{array}$$

6.1 (5.0 pt) Calculate the molar enthalpy of sublimation (in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) for $\ce{H3BO3}$ at 300 K.

6.2 (12.0 pt) Calculate the $\Delta_r U$ (internal energy) in terms of $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ at 300 K for the reactions (2) and (4) given above (assume ideal gas behavior for each gaseous species in each reaction).

6.3 (6.0 pt) Calculate the amount of overall work produced by a heat engine ($|w|$) in terms of J and the amount of overall heat released to the cold sink ($|q_C|$) in terms of J.

6.4 (3.0 pt) Calculate the efficiency of the heat engine described above.

6.5 (6.0 pt) Calculate the entropy change ($\Delta S$) for A → B and D → C processes in the heat engine in terms of $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$.

6.6 (6.0 pt) Calculate the Gibbs energy change ($\Delta G$) in terms of J for A → B and D → C processes in the heat engine.

6.7 (5.0 pt) Calculate the ratio of pressure at point A to the pressure at point B in the cycle cycle (standard pressure: 1 bar).

6.8 (3.0 pt) Calculate the amount of $\ce{H2(g)}$ (in moles) produced according to the reaction given at the beginning of the task for one cycle of the engine.

Part 2

Interstellar journeys can be done by using diborane as rocket fuel. Combustion of diborane is shown below:

$$\ce{B2H6(g) + 3 O2(g) -> B2O3(s) + 3 H2O(g)}$$

Combustion of diborane is experimented in a 100 L closed container at different temperatures and the equilibrium conditions were recorded.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} & 8930\,\mathrm{K} & 9005\,\mathrm{K} \\ \hline \ce{B2H6(g)} & 0.38\,\mathrm{mol} & 0.49\,\mathrm{mol} \\ \hline \ce{H2O(g)} & 0.20\,\mathrm{mol} & 0.20\,\mathrm{mol} \end{array}$$

Partial pressure of $\ce{O2(g)}$ was stabilized to 1 bar and kept constant at all conditions. Assume that in this hypothetical universe; $\Delta_r S^\circ$ and $\Delta_r H^\circ$ are independent of temperature, the standard molar entropy ($S^\circ$) of $\ce{B2O3(s)}$ does not change with pressure, all the gas species behave as an ideal gas, and all species remain in the same phase, without any further decomposition before or after reaction, at all temperatures then:

6.9 (8.0 pt) Calculate $K_p$ (pressure based equilibrium constant) at 8930 K and 9005 K.

6.10 (6.0 pt) Calculate $\Delta_r G^\circ$ of the reaction in terms of $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ at 8930 K and 9005 K. (If you failed to find $K_p$, please use $K_p$ (8930 K) = 2, $K_p$ (9005 K) = 0.5)

6.11 (6.0 pt) Calculate $\Delta_r G^\circ$ (in terms of $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$), $\Delta_r H^\circ$ (in terms of $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$), and $\Delta_r S^\circ$ ((in terms of $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$) of the combustion reaction at 298 K. (If you failed to find $K_p$, please use $K_p$ (8930 K) = 2, $K_p$ (9005 K) = 0.5)

6.12 (8.0 pt) Tick the correct answer in the table by determining whether combustion reactions are favored or not at given T below under standard pressure (1 bar).

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} & \text{favored} & \text{Unfavored} \\ \hline 298\,\mathrm{K} & \square & \square \\ 8930\,\mathrm{K} & \square & \square \\ 9005\,\mathrm{K} & \square & \square \\ 9100\,\mathrm{K} & \square & \square \end{array}$$

6.13 (6.0 pt) Calculate the $\Delta_f H$ ($\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) and $S^\circ$ ($\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$) of $\ce{H2O(g)}$ using the values given in the table below. ($\Delta_f H$ = enthalpy of formation, $S^\circ$ = standard entropy) (If you fail to find $\Delta_r H^\circ$ and $\Delta_r S^\circ$ of the combustion, please use $\Delta H^\circ = 1000\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, $\Delta S^\circ = 150\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$)

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} & \Delta_f H\ (298\,\mathrm{K}) & S^\circ\ (298\,\mathrm{K}) \\ \hline \ce{B2H6(g)} & 36.40\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & 0.23\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \\ \hline \ce{O2(g)} & 0.00\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & 0.16\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \\ \hline \ce{B2O3(s)} & -1273\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & 0.05\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \end{array}$$

problems.title: Boron Compounds and Hydrogen Storage
problems.problem:
Problem 8 (58 points, 14% of the total). Boron Compounds and Hydrogen Storage

Sodium borohydride ($\ce{NaBH4}$) and ammonia borane ($\ce{BNH6}$) are the most studied chemical hydrogen storage materials. In this question, you will explore the chemistry of boron and the use of boron compounds as hydrogen storage materials.

Borax ($\ce{Na2B4O7.nH2O}$) is a boron mineral that is produced by ETI Mining Company in Turkey. $\ce{NaBH4}$ can be synthesized by the reduction of anhydrous borax with metallic sodium under high-pressure hydrogen gas in the presence of silicon dioxide (silica) at 700 °C, namely the Bayer process. In this process, all hydrogen is stored in $\ce{NaBH4}$. On the other hand, it has been shown that ammonia borane ($\ce{BNH6}$) can be synthesized by the reaction of $\ce{NaBH4}$ and ammonium sulfate in dry tetrahydrofuran (THF) at 40 °C (Hint: $\ce{BNH6}$ synthesis must be conducted in a well-ventilated fume-hood because flammable gas is generated as one of the by-products). While $\ce{NaBH4}$ is an ionic compound, ammonia borane is a Lewis acid–base adduct.

8.1 (3.0 pt) Write a balanced chemical equation for the synthesis of $\ce{NaBH4}$ from anhydrous borax.

8.2 (3.0 pt) Write a balanced chemical equation for the synthesis of ammonia borane from $\ce{NaBH4}$.

8.3 (4.0 pt) Draw the molecular geometries of the $\ce{BH4-}$ ion and $\ce{BNH6}$ molecule.

8.4 (4.0 pt) Calculate the hydrogen content of $\ce{NaBH4}$ and $\ce{BNH6}$ as a percentage by mass (wt%).

The hydrogen stored in both compounds can be released via hydrolysis reactions in the presence of a suitable catalyst at room temperature. Upon the hydrolysis reactions, 4 and 3 moles of $\ce{H2}$ gas are released from the hydrolysis of 1 mole of $\ce{NaBH4}$ and $\ce{BNH6}$, respectively, along with metaborate anion including B-O bonds.

8.5 (4.0 pt) Write the balanced chemical equations for the hydrolysis of $\ce{NaBH4}$ and $\ce{BNH6}$.

One of the simplest stable borates is diboron trioxide ($\ce{B2O3}$). Higher borates such as $\ce{B3O6^{3-}}$ having cyclic structures containing B-O-bonds can be formed. Since $\ce{B2O3}$ is an acidic compound, it is easily reacted with water to produce boric acid ($\ce{H3BO3}$). On the other hand, the high temperature and high-pressure reaction of $\ce{B2O3}$ with ammonia yields two-dimensional boron nitride, which consists of planar graphite-like sheets of alternating B and N atoms.

8.6 (4.0 pt) Write the balanced chemical equations for the synthesis of boric acid and boron nitride.

8.7 (6.0 pt) Draw the molecular structures of the $\ce{B3O6^{3-}}$ ion, boric acid, and a single two-dimensional boron nitride sheet. Hint: show at least 10 B atoms in the boron nitride structure.

Furthermore, B-H compounds, called boranes, are an important class of boron compounds. The simplest stable borane is diborane ($\ce{B2H6}$) and many of the higher boranes can be prepared by the pyrolysis of diborane. Diborane can be synthesized via metathesis of a boron halide and a hydride source.

8.8 (3.0 pt) Write a balanced chemical equation for the synthesis of diborane from the reaction of $\ce{BF3}$ and $\ce{LiBH4}$. Hint: both products are boron compounds.

8.9 (2.0 pt) Draw the molecular geometry of the diborane molecule. Hint: there is no B-B bond in the molecule.

$\ce{BH3}$ (borane) is an unstable and highly reactive molecule. Therefore, it is not possible to isolate it as $\ce{BH3}$ under ordinary conditions. However, it can be stabilized via its reaction with carbon monoxide to yield borane carbonyl ($\ce{BH3CO}$) compound, which is an adduct of borane. The preparation of $\ce{BH3CO}$ plays an important role in exploring the chemistry of boranes as it indicates the likely existence of the borane molecule.

8.10 (3.0 pt) Sketch the Lewis dot structure of $\ce{BH3CO}$ molecule by showing the formal charges.

8.11 (2.0 pt) Which of the statements given in the answer sheet is observed in the C−O bond of a CO molecule upon the bond formation between $\ce{BH3}$ and CO ? Tick the correct box.

□ It gets longer because there will be $\pi$-back donation from $\ce{BH3}$ to CO.
□ It gets longer because CO donates $\pi$-bonding electrons to $\ce{BH3}$
□ No or slight change on it because CO donates its mainly non-bonding electrons to $\ce{BH3}$
□ It gets shorter because CO donates $\pi^*$ anti-bonding electrons to $\ce{BH3}$.

Borazine consists of single and double bonded cyclic B−N units and hydrogen atoms attached to these atoms with the molecular formula $\ce{B3N3H6}$ and is isostructural to benzene. Borazine can be synthesized by using a two-step procedure including the synthesis of symmetrically trisubstituted chlorine derivatives of borazine ($\ce{B3N3H3Cl3}$) from the reaction of ammonium chloride and boron trichloride, and then reduction of $\ce{B3N3H3Cl3}$ with $\ce{LiBH4}$ in THF.

8.12 (4.0 pt) Write the balanced chemical equations for the two-step synthesis of borazine starting from ammonium chloride in THF (tetrahydrofuran). Hint: THF stabilizes one of the products by forming a lewis acid-base adduct.

8.13 (4.0 pt) Draw the molecular structures of borazine and its symmetrically trisubstituted chlorine derivative.

Catalysts are substances that accelerate the rate of reactions by allowing them to proceed in a lower energy pathway. The catalytic activity of the catalysts is generally determined by the turnover frequency (TOF), which is calculated by dividing the molar amount of the product to the mole of active catalyst and the time (TOF = mole product/(mole catalyst x time)). A typical hydrolysis of $\ce{BNH6}$ was carried out in 10.0 mL of water by using 100.0 mM $\ce{BNH6}$ and 5.0 mg of CuPt/C catalyst (CuPt alloy nanoparticles supported on carbon black containing 8.2 wt% Pt atom). 67.25 mL of hydrogen gas was generated in 5 minutes.

8.14 (4.0 pt) Assuming the catalytic reaction is performed in standard conditions (1 atm and 273.15 K), calculate the TOF ($\mathrm{min^{-1}}$) of the CuPt/C catalyst in terms of only Pt atoms in the hydrolysis of $\ce{BNH6}$ by considering the volume of the hydrogen gas generated.

As a result of detailed crystal analysis of a synthesized $\mathrm{Cu}_x\mathrm{Pt}_y$ alloy nanoparticle (the subscripts indicate molar percentages of the atoms in the alloy structure), it was determined that the face centered cubic (fcc) unit cell was formed by Pt atoms and the Pt atoms on the face of the fcc unit cell are supposed to be replaced with Cu atoms to form $\mathrm{Cu}_x\mathrm{Pt}_y$ displacement alloy nanoparticles. According to this information, answer the following questions.

8.15 (2.0 pt) Determine the composition of the alloy nanoparticles by finding x and y in the $\mathrm{Cu}_x\mathrm{Pt}_y$ alloy composition.

8.16 (2.0 pt) Sketch the shape of the described crystal unit cell of $\mathrm{Cu}_x\mathrm{Pt}_y$ alloy nanoparticles by showing the placement of atoms on the unit cell.

8.17 (4.0 pt) Another alloy has a $\ce{Cu2Pt1}$ composition. Assume that this alloy also has an fcc unit cell with an edge length of 380 pm, but the Cu and Pt atoms are randomly distributed in the atomic positions. Calculate the density of this alloy in $\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.
