Problem 9 (100 points, 12% of the total). Quantification of Heavy Metal Ions

For the quantitative analysis of heavy metal ions in a factory's wastewater pool, the following steps have been applied by an analyzer at 298 K:

Step 1) 10-mL samples of each were obtained from five different regions in a wastewater pool, mixed in a 100-mL beaker, and then stirred for 5 minutes using a magnetic stirrer.

Step 2) 10-mL of sample solution was taken from the 100-mL beaker and 142 mg of $\ce{Na2SO4}$ was added while stirring, followed by transfer to a three-electrode cell as seen in Figure 1a. In this electrochemical cell, Pt wire, Ag/AgCl (3 M KCl), and Pt foil served as the working, reference, and counter electrodes, respectively.

Step 3) These electrodes were connected to a potentiostat and a constant potential of –0.50 V vs. Ag/AgCl for 14 minutes was applied as seen in Figure 1b (horizontal line). It is assumed that 14 min. is sufficient to complete the expected electrochemical reactions.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2020-9-fig1.png

Figure 1. a) Electrochemical cell design; 1) Working electrode (Pt wire), 2) reference electrode (Ag/AgCl, 3M KCl), 3) counter electrode (Pt foil), 4) cell tap, 5) electrochemical cell, 6) 10-mL of sample solution. b) Potential change of working electrode as a function of time. y-axis: potential/V vs Ag/AgCl, x-axis: time/min.

Step 4) The electrodes were rinsed with distilled water, placed into another electrochemical cell including 10-mL of 0.1 M $\ce{H2SO4}$ solution, and potential was scanned between –0.50 and +0.50 V as seen in Figure 1b (downward sloping line in 2 min.). problems.title: Hydrogen at a Metal Surface
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (24 points, 11% of the total). Hydrogen at a Metal Surface

Hydrogen is expected to be a future energy source that does not depend on fossil fuels. Here, we will consider the hydrogen-storage process in a metal, which is related to hydrogen-transport and -storage technology.

Part A

As hydrogen is absorbed into the bulk of a metal via its surface, let us first consider the adsorption process of hydrogen at the metal surface, $\ce{H2(g) -> 2H(ad)}$, where the gaseous and adsorbed states of hydrogen are represented as (g) and (ad), respectively. Hydrogen molecules ($\ce{H2}$) that reach the metal surface (M) dissociate at the surface and are adsorbed as H atoms (Fig. 1). Here, the potential energy of $\ce{H2}$ is represented by two variables: the interatomic distance, $d$, and the height relative to the surface metal atom, $z$. It is assumed that the axis along the two H atoms is parallel to the surface and that the center of gravity is always on the vertical dotted line in Fig. 1. Fig. 2 shows the potential energy contour plot for the dissociation at the surface. The numerical values represent the potential energy in units of kJ per mole of $\ce{H2}$. The solid line spacing is $20\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, the dashed line spacing is $100\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, and the spacing between solid and dashed lines is $80\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. The zero-point vibration energy is ignored.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1 Definition of variables. Drawing is not in scale.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-1-fig2.png

Fig. 2

A.1 (6 pt) For each of the following items (i)–(iii), select the closest value from A–G.
(i) The interatomic distance for a gaseous $\ce{H2}$ molecule
(ii) The interatomic distance between metal atoms ($d_\mathrm{M}$ in Fig. 1)
(iii) The distance of adsorbed H atoms from the surface ($h_\mathrm{ad}$ in Fig. 1)

A. $0.03\,\mathrm{nm}$ B. $0.07\,\mathrm{nm}$ C. $0.11\,\mathrm{nm}$ D. $0.15\,\mathrm{nm}$ E. $0.19\,\mathrm{nm}$ F. $0.23\,\mathrm{nm}$ G. $0.27\,\mathrm{nm}$

A.2 (4 pt) For each of the following items (i)–(ii), select the closest value from A–H.
(i) the energy required for the dissociation of gaseous $\ce{H2}$ to gaseous H [$\ce{H2(g) -> 2H(g)}$]
(ii) the energy released during the adsorption of a gaseous $\ce{H2}$ [$\ce{H2(g) -> 2H(ad)}$]

A. $20\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ B. $40\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ C. $60\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ D. $100\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ E. $150\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ F. $200\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ G. $300\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ H. $400\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

Part B

The adsorbed hydrogen atoms are then either absorbed into the bulk, or recombine and desorb back into the gas phase, as shown in the reactions (1a) and (1b). H(ab) represents a hydrogen atom absorbed in the bulk.

$$\ce{H2(g) <=>[$k_1$][$k_2$] 2H(ad)} \tag{1a}$$

$$\ce{H(ad) ->[$k_3$] H(ab)} \tag{1b}$$

The reaction rates per surface site for adsorption, desorption, and absorption are $r_1\,[\mathrm{s^{-1}}]$, $r_2\,[\mathrm{s^{-1}}]$ and $r_3\,[\mathrm{s^{-1}}]$, respectively. They are expressed as:

$$r_1 = k_1 P_{\mathrm{H_2}} (1-\theta)^2 \tag{2}$$

$$r_2 = k_2 \theta^2 \tag{3}$$

$$r_3 = k_3 \theta \tag{4}$$

where $k_1\,[\mathrm{s^{-1}\,Pa^{-1}}]$, $k_2\,[\mathrm{s^{-1}}]$ and $k_3\,[\mathrm{s^{-1}}]$ are the reaction rate constants and $P_{\mathrm{H_2}}$ is the pressure of $\ce{H2}$. Among the sites available on the surface, $\theta$ ($0 \le \theta \le 1$) is the fraction occupied by H atoms. It is assumed that adsorption and desorption are fast compared to absorption ($r_1, r_2 \gg r_3$) and that $\theta$ remains constant.

B.1 (5 pt) $r_3$ can be expressed as:

$$r_3 = \frac{k_3}{1 + \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{P_{\mathrm{H_2}} C}}} \tag{5}$$

Express $C$ using $k_1$ and $k_2$.

A metal sample with a surface area of $S = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2}$ was placed in a container ($1\,\mathrm{L} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3}$) with $\ce{H2}$ ($P_{\mathrm{H_2}} = 1.0 \times 10^{2}\,\mathrm{Pa}$). The density of hydrogen-atom adsorption sites on the surface was $N = 1.3 \times 10^{18}\,\mathrm{m^{-2}}$. The surface temperature was kept at $T = 400\,\mathrm{K}$. As the reaction (1) proceeded, $P_{\mathrm{H_2}}$ decreased at a constant rate of $v = 4.0 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Pa\,s^{-1}}$. Assume that $\ce{H2}$ is an ideal gas and that the volume of the metal sample is negligible.

B.2 (3 pt) Calculate the amount of H atoms in moles absorbed per unit area of the surface per unit time, $A\,[\mathrm{mol\,s^{-1}\,m^{-2}}]$.

B.3 (3 pt) At $T = 400\,\mathrm{K}$, $C$ equals $1.0 \times 10^{2}\,\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$. Calculate the value of $k_3$ at $400\,\mathrm{K}$. If you did not obtain the answer to B.2, use $A = 3.6 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{mol\,s^{-1}\,m^{-2}}$.

B.4 (3 pt) At a different $T$, $C = 2.5 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$ and $k_3 = 4.8 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ are given. For $r_3$ as a function of $P_{\mathrm{H_2}}$ at this temperature, select the correct plot from (a)–(h).

problems.title: Isotope Time Capsule
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (35 points, 11% of the total). Isotope Time Capsule

Molecular entities that differ only in isotopic composition, such as $\ce{CH4}$ and $\ce{CH3D}$, are called isotopologues. Isotopologues are considered to have the same chemical characteristics. In nature, however, there exists a slight difference.

Assume that all of the substances shown in this Question are in a gas phase.

Let us consider the following equilibrium:

$$\ce{^{12}C^{16}O2 + ^{12}C^{18}O2 <=> 2 ^{12}C^{16}O^{18}O} \qquad K = \frac{[\ce{^{12}C^{16}O^{18}O}]^2}{[\ce{^{12}C^{16}O2}][\ce{^{12}C^{18}O2}]} \tag{1}$$

The entropy, $S$, increases with increasing the number of possible microscopic states of a system, $W$:

$$S = k_\mathrm{B} \ln W \tag{2}$$

$W = 1$ for $\ce{^{12}C^{16}O2}$ and $\ce{^{12}C^{18}O2}$. In contrast, $W = 2$ for a $\ce{^{12}C^{16}O^{18}O}$ molecule because the oxygen atoms are distinguishable in this molecule. As the right-hand side of the equilibrium shown in eq. 1 has two $\ce{^{12}C^{16}O^{18}O}$ molecules, $W = 2^2 = 4$.

A.1 (8 pt) The enthalpy change, $\Delta H$, of eq. 3 is positive regardless of the temperature.

$$\ce{H2 + DI <=> HD + HI} \tag{3}$$

Calculate the equilibrium constants, $K$, for eq. 3 at very low (think of $T \to 0$) and very high (think of $T \to +\infty$) temperatures. Assume that the reaction remains unchanged at these temperatures and that $\Delta H$ converges to a constant value for high temperatures.

The $\Delta H$ of the following process can be explained by molecular vibrations.

$$\ce{2HD <=> H2 + D2} \qquad K = \frac{[\ce{H2}][\ce{D2}]}{[\ce{HD}]^2} \tag{4}$$

At $T = 0\,\mathrm{K}$, the vibrational energy of a diatomic molecule whose vibration frequency is $\nu\,[\mathrm{s^{-1}}]$ is expressed as:

$$E = \frac{1}{2} h\nu \tag{5}$$

$$\nu = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}} \tag{6}$$

Wherein $k$ is the force constant and $\mu$ the reduced mass, which is expressed in terms of the mass of the two atoms in the diatomic molecule, $m_1$ and $m_2$, according to:

$$\mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2} \tag{7}$$

A.2 (8 pt) The vibration of $\ce{H2}$ is at $4161.0\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ when reported as a wavenumber. Calculate the $\Delta H$ of the following equation at $T = 0\,\mathrm{K}$ in units of $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$.

$$\ce{2HD -> H2 + D2} \tag{8}$$

Assume that:
• only the vibrational energy contributes to the $\Delta H$.
• the $k$ values for $\ce{H2}$, $\ce{HD}$, and $\ce{D2}$ are identical.
• the mass of H to be $1\,\mathrm{Da}$ and the mass of D to be $2\,\mathrm{Da}$.

The molar ratio of $\ce{H2}$, $\ce{HD}$, and $\ce{D2}$ depends on the temperature in a system in equilibrium. Here, $\Delta_{\mathrm{D_2}}$ is defined as the change of the molar ratio of $\ce{D2}$.

$$\Delta_{\mathrm{D_2}} = \frac{R_{\mathrm{D_2}}}{R^*_{\mathrm{D_2}}} - 1 \tag{9}$$

Here, $R_{\mathrm{D_2}}$ refers to $\dfrac{[\ce{D2}]}{[\ce{H2}]}$ in the sample and $R^*_{\mathrm{D_2}}$ to $\dfrac{[\ce{D2}]}{[\ce{H2}]}$ at $T \to +\infty$. It should be noted here that the distribution of isotopes becomes random at $T \to +\infty$.

A.3 (10 pt) Calculate $\Delta_{\mathrm{D_2}}$ with natural D abundance when the isotopic exchange is in equilibrium at the temperature where $K$ in eq. 4 is 0.300. Assume that the natural abundance ratios of D and H are $1.5576 \times 10^{-4}$ and $1 - 1.5576 \times 10^{-4}$, respectively.

In general, the molar ratio of the doubly substituted isotopologue, which contains two heavy isotope atoms in one molecule, increases with decreasing temperature. Let us consider the molar ratio of $\ce{CO2}$ molecules with molecular weights of 44 and 47, which are described as $\ce{CO2}[44]$ and $\ce{CO2}[47]$ below. The quantity $\Delta_{47}$ is defined as:

$$\Delta_{47} = \frac{R_{47}}{R^*_{47}} - 1 \tag{10}$$

$R_{47}$ refers to $\dfrac{[\ce{CO2}[47]]}{[\ce{CO2}[44]]}$ in the sample and $R^*_{47}$ to $\dfrac{[\ce{CO2}[47]]}{[\ce{CO2}[44]]}$ at $T \to +\infty$. The natural abundances of carbon and oxygen atoms are shown below; ignore isotopes that are not shown here.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} & \ce{^{12}C} & \ce{^{13}C} \\ \hline \text{natural abundance} & 0.988888 & 0.011112 \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \ce{^{16}O} & \ce{^{17}O} & \ce{^{18}O} \\ \hline \text{natural abundance} & 0.997621 & 0.0003790 & 0.0020000 \end{array}$$

The temperature dependence of $\Delta_{47}$ is determined as follows, where $T$ is given as the absolute temperature in units of K:

$$\Delta_{47} = \frac{36.2}{T^2} + 2.920 \times 10^{-4} \tag{11}$$

A.4 (9 pt) The $R_{47}$ of fossil plankton obtained from the Antarctic seabed was $4.50865 \times 10^{-5}$. Estimate the temperature using this $R_{47}$. This temperature is interpreted as the air temperature during the era in which the plankton lived. Consider only the most common isotopologue of $\ce{CO2}[47]$ for the calculation.

problems.title: Lambert–Beer Law?
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (22 points, 8% of the total). Lambert–Beer Law?

In this problem, ignore the absorption of the cell and the solvent. The temperatures of all solutions and gases are kept constant at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Part A

An aqueous solution $\mathbf{X}$ was prepared using HA and NaA. The concentrations $[\ce{A-}]$, $[\ce{HA}]$, and $[\ce{H+}]$ in solution $\mathbf{X}$ are $1.00 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$, $1.00 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$, and $1.00 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$, respectively, which are correlated via the following acid-base equilibrium:

$$\ce{HA <=> A- + H+} \qquad K = \frac{[\ce{A-}][\ce{H+}]}{[\ce{HA}]} \tag{1}$$

The optical path length is $l$ in Part A. Ignore the density change upon dilution. Assume that no chemical reactions other than eq 1 occur.

A.1 (10 pt) The absorbance of $\mathbf{X}$ was $A_1$ at a wavelength of $\lambda_1$. Then, solution $\mathbf{X}$ was diluted to twice its initial volume using hydrochloric acid with pH = 2.500. After the dilution, the absorbance was still $A_1$ at $\lambda_1$. Determine the ratio $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HA}}/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{A^-}}$, where $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HA}}$ and $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{A^-}}$ represent the absorption coefficients of HA and of $\ce{A-}$, respectively, at $\lambda_1$.

Part B

Let us consider the following equilibrium in the gas phase.

$$\ce{D <=> 2M} \tag{2}$$

Pure gas D is filled into a cuboid container that has a transparent movable wall with a cross-section of $S$ (see the figure below) at a pressure $P$, and equilibrium is established while the total pressure is kept at $P$. The absorbance of the gas is $A = \varepsilon (n/V) l$, where $\varepsilon$, $n$, $V$, and $l$ are the absorption coefficient, amount of the gas in moles, volume of the gas, and optical path length, respectively. Assume that all components of the gas mixture behave as ideal gases.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-3-fig1.png

Use the following definitions if necessary.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c} & \text{Initial state: D} & \text{Initial state: M} & \text{After equilibrium: D} & \text{After equilibrium: M} \\ \hline \text{Partial pressure} & P & 0 & p_\mathrm{D} & p_\mathrm{M} \\ \hline \text{Amount in moles} & n_0 & 0 & n_\mathrm{D} & n_\mathrm{M} \\ \hline \text{Volume} & V_0 & V_0 & V & V \end{array}$$

B.1 (6 pt) The absorbance of the gas at $\lambda_{\mathrm{B1}}$ measured from direction $x$ ($l = l_x$) was $A_{\mathrm{B1}}$ both at the initial state and after the equilibrium. Determine the ratio $\varepsilon_\mathrm{D}/\varepsilon_\mathrm{M}$ at $\lambda_{\mathrm{B1}}$, where $\varepsilon_\mathrm{D}$ and $\varepsilon_\mathrm{M}$ represent the absorption coefficients of D and of M, respectively.

B.2 (6 pt) The absorbance of the gas at $\lambda_{\mathrm{B2}}$ measured from direction $y$ was $A_{\mathrm{B2}}$ both at the initial state ($l = l_{y0}$) and after the equilibrium ($l = l_y$). Determine the ratio $\varepsilon_\mathrm{D}/\varepsilon_\mathrm{M}$ at $\lambda_{\mathrm{B2}}$.

problems.title: The Redox Chemistry of Zinc
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (32 points, 11% of the total). The Redox Chemistry of Zinc

Zinc has long been used as alloys for brass and steel materials. The zinc contained in industrial wastewater is separated by precipitation to detoxify the water, and the obtained precipitate is reduced to recover and reuse it as metallic zinc.

Part A

The dissolution equilibrium of zinc hydroxide $\ce{Zn(OH)2(s)}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and the relevant equilibrium constants are given in eq. 1–4.

$$\ce{Zn(OH)2(s) <=> Zn^{2+}(aq) + 2OH^-(aq)} \qquad K_\mathrm{sp} = 1.74 \times 10^{-17} \tag{1}$$

$$\ce{Zn(OH)2(s) <=> Zn(OH)2(aq)} \qquad K_1 = 2.62 \times 10^{-6} \tag{2}$$

$$\ce{Zn(OH)2(s) + 2OH^-(aq) <=> Zn(OH)4^{2-}(aq)} \qquad K_2 = 6.47 \times 10^{-2} \tag{3}$$

$$\ce{H2O(l) <=> H+(aq) + OH^-(aq)} \qquad K_\mathrm{w} = 1.00 \times 10^{-14} \tag{4}$$

The solubility, $S$, of zinc (concentration of zinc in a saturated aqueous solution) is given in eq. 5.

$$S = [\ce{Zn^{2+}(aq)}] + [\ce{Zn(OH)2(aq)}] + [\ce{Zn(OH)4^{2-}(aq)}] \tag{5}$$

A.1 (6 pt) When the equilibria in eq. 1–4 are established, calculate the pH range in which $[\ce{Zn(OH)2(aq)}]$ is the greatest among $[\ce{Zn^{2+}(aq)}]$, $[\ce{Zn(OH)2(aq)}]$ and $[\ce{Zn(OH)4^{2-}(aq)}]$.

A.2 (5 pt) A saturated aqueous solution of $\ce{Zn(OH)2(s)}$ with pH = 7.00 was prepared and filtered. NaOH was added to this filtrate to increase its pH to 12.00. Calculate the molar percentage of zinc that precipitates when increasing the pH from 7.00 to 12.00. Ignore the volume and temperature changes.

Part B

Next, the recovered zinc hydroxide is heated to obtain zinc oxide according to the reaction below:

$$\ce{Zn(OH)2(s) -> ZnO(s) + H2O(l)} \tag{6}$$

The zinc oxide is then reduced to metallic zinc by reaction with hydrogen:

$$\ce{ZnO(s) + H2(g) -> Zn(s) + H2O(g)} \tag{7}$$

B.1 (4 pt) In order for reaction (7) to proceed at a hydrogen pressure kept at 1 bar, it is necessary to reduce the partial pressure of the generated water vapor. Calculate the upper limit for the partial pressure of water vapor to allow reaction (7) to proceed at $300\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Here, the Gibbs formation energies of zinc oxide and water vapor at $300\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and 1 bar for all gaseous species are $\Delta G_{\mathrm{ZnO}}(300\,^\circ\mathrm{C}) = -2.90 \times 10^{2}\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\Delta G_{\mathrm{H_2O}}(300\,^\circ\mathrm{C}) = -2.20 \times 10^{2}\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively.

Metallic zinc is used as a negative electrode (anode) material for metal-air batteries. The electrode consists of Zn and ZnO. It uses the following redox reaction to generate electricity with the electromotive force (e.m.f.) at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and pressure of 1 bar, $E^\circ$.

$$\ce{Zn(s) + 1/2 O2(g) -> ZnO(s)} \qquad E^\circ = 1.65\,\mathrm{V} \tag{8}$$

B.2 (3 pt) A zinc–air battery was discharged at $20\,\mathrm{mA}$ for 24 hours. Calculate the change in mass of the negative electrode (anode) of the battery.

B.3 (5 pt) Consider the change of e.m.f. of a zinc–air battery depending on the environment. Calculate the e.m.f. at the summit of Mt. Fuji, where the temperature and altitude are $-38\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (February) and $3776\,\mathrm{m}$, respectively. The atmospheric pressure is represented by

$$P\,[\mathrm{bar}] = 1.013 \times \left(1 - \frac{0.0065h}{T + 0.0065h + 273.15}\right)^{5.257} \tag{9}$$

at altitude $h\,[\mathrm{m}]$ and temperature $T\,[^\circ\mathrm{C}]$. The molar ratio of oxygen in the atmosphere is 21%. The Gibbs energy change of reaction (8) is $\Delta G_{\mathrm{ZnO}}(-38\,^\circ\mathrm{C}) = -3.26 \times 10^{2}\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ at $-38\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and 1 bar.

B.4 (9 pt) Calculate the Gibbs energy change for reaction (6) at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Note that the standard reduction potentials, $E^\circ(\ce{Zn^{2+}/Zn})$ and $E^\circ(\ce{O2/H2O})$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and 1 bar are given as (10) and (11), respectively.

$$\ce{Zn^{2+} + 2e^- -> Zn} \qquad E^\circ(\ce{Zn^{2+}/Zn}) = -0.77\,\mathrm{V} \tag{10}$$

$$\ce{O2 + 4H+ + 4e^- -> 2H2O} \qquad E^\circ(\ce{O2/H2O}) = 1.23\,\mathrm{V} \tag{11}$$

problems.title: Mysterious Silicon
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (60 points, 12% of the total). Mysterious Silicon

Although silicon is also a group 14 element like carbon, their properties differ significantly.

Part A

Unlike the carbon–carbon triple bond, the silicon–silicon triple bond in a compound formulated as $\ce{R^{1}-Si#Si-R^{1}}$ (R: organic substituent) is extremely reactive. For example, it reacts with ethylene to form a cyclic product that contains a four-membered ring.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-5-fig1.png

When $\ce{R^{1}-Si#Si-R^{1}}$ is treated with an alkyne ($\ce{R^{2}-C#C-R^{2}}$), the four-membered-ring compound $\mathbf{A}$ is formed as an initial intermediate. Further reaction of another molecule of $\ce{R^{2}-C#C-R^{2}}$ with $\mathbf{A}$ affords isomers $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$, both of which have benzene-like cyclic conjugated structures, so-called ‘disilabenzenes’ that contain a six-membered ring and can be formulated as $\ce{(R^{1}-Si)2(R^{2}-C)4}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-5-fig2.png

The $\ce{^{13}C}$ NMR analysis of the corresponding six-membered ring skeletons $\ce{Si2C4}$ shows two signals for $\mathbf{B}$ and one signal for $\mathbf{C}$.

A.1 (9 pt) Draw the structural formulae of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$ using $\mathrm{R^1}$, $\mathrm{R^2}$, Si, and C, with one of the possible resonance structures.

A.2 (7 pt) Calculate the aromatic stabilization energy (ASE) for benzene and $\mathbf{C}$ (in the case of $\mathrm{R^1} = \mathrm{R^2} = \mathrm{H}$) as positive values, considering the enthalpy change in some hydrogenation reactions of unsaturated systems shown below (Fig. 1).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-5-fig3.png

Fig. 1

When a xylene solution of $\mathbf{C}$ is heated, it undergoes isomerization to give an equilibrium mixture of compounds $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$. The molar ratio is $\mathbf{D} : \mathbf{E} = 1 : 40.0$ at $50.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $\mathbf{D} : \mathbf{E} = 1 : 20.0$ at $120.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

A.3 (6 pt) Calculate $\Delta H$ for the transformation of $\mathbf{D}$ to $\mathbf{E}$. Assume that $\Delta H$ does not depend on temperature.

The isomerization from $\mathbf{C}$ to $\mathbf{D}$ and to $\mathbf{E}$ proceeds via transformations of $\pi$-bonds into $\sigma$-bonds without breaking any $\sigma$-bonds. A $\ce{^{13}C}$ NMR analysis revealed one signal for the $\ce{Si2C4}$ skeleton of $\mathbf{D}$ and two signals for that of $\mathbf{E}$. The skeleton of $\mathbf{D}$ does not contain any three-membered rings, while $\mathbf{E}$ has two three-membered rings that share an edge.

A.4 (10 pt) Draw the structural formulae of $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ using $\mathrm{R^1}$, $\mathrm{R^2}$, Si, and C.

Part B

Silicon is able to form highly coordinated compounds (> four substituents) with electronegative elements such as fluorine. As metal fluorides are often used as fluorination reagents, highly coordinated silicon fluorides also act as fluorination reagents.

The fluorination reaction of $\ce{CCl4}$ using $\ce{Na2SiF6}$ was carried out as follows.

• Standardization of $\ce{Na2SiF6}$ solution:

· Preparation

Aqueous solution $\mathbf{F}$: 0.855 g of $\ce{Na2SiF6}$ ($188.053\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$) dissolved in water (total volume: 200 mL).

Aqueous solution $\mathbf{G}$: 6.86 g of $\ce{Ce2(SO4)3}$ ($568.424\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$) dissolved in water (total volume: 200 mL).

· Procedure

Precipitation titration of a solution $\mathbf{F}$ (50.0 mL) by dropwise adding solution $\mathbf{G}$ in the presence of xylenol orange, which coordinates to $\ce{Ce^{3+}}$, as an indicator. After adding 18.8 mL of solution $\mathbf{G}$, the color of the solution changes from yellow to magenta. The generated precipitate is a binary compound that contains $\ce{Ce^{3+}}$, and the only resulting silicon compound is $\ce{Si(OH)4}$.

B.1 (5 pt) Write the balanced equation for the reaction of $\ce{Na2SiF6}$ with $\ce{Ce2(SO4)3}$.

• Reaction of $\ce{CCl4}$ with $\ce{Na2SiF6}$:

(Substance losses by e.g. evaporation are negligible during the following operations.)

$\ce{Na2SiF6}$ ($x$ [g]) was added to $\ce{CCl4}$ (500.0 g) and heated to $300\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in a sealed pressure-resistant reaction vessel. $\underline{\text{The unreacted }\ce{Na2SiF6}\text{ and generated NaCl were removed by filtration.}}$ The filtrate was diluted to a total volume of 1.00 L with $\ce{CCl4}$ (solution $\mathbf{H}$). The $\ce{^{29}Si}$ and $\ce{^{19}F}$ NMR spectra of solution $\mathbf{H}$ showed $\ce{SiF4}$ as the only silicon compound. In the $\ce{^{19}F}$ NMR spectrum, in addition to $\ce{SiF4}$, signals corresponding to $\ce{CFCl3}$, $\ce{CF2Cl2}$, $\ce{CF3Cl}$, and $\ce{CF4}$ were observed (cf. Table 1). The integration ratios in the $\ce{^{19}F}$ NMR spectrum are proportional to the number of fluorine nuclei.

Table 1

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c} \ce{^{19}F}\text{ NMR data} & \ce{CFCl3} & \ce{CF2Cl2} & \ce{CF3Cl} & \ce{CF4} \\ \hline \text{Integration ratio} & 45.0 & 65.0 & 18.0 & 2.0 \end{array}$$

$\ce{SiF4}$ is hydrolyzed to form $\ce{H2SiF6}$ according to the following eq. 8:

$$\ce{3SiF4 + 2H2O -> SiO2 + 2H2SiF6} \tag{8}$$

Solution $\mathbf{H}$ (10 mL) was added to an excess amount of water, which resulted in the complete hydrolysis of $\ce{SiF4}$. After separation, the $\ce{H2SiF6}$ generated from the hydrolysis in the aqueous solution was neutralized and completely converted to $\ce{Na2SiF6}$ (aqueous solution $\mathbf{J}$).

The precipitate of unreacted $\ce{Na2SiF6}$ and NaCl, which was removed by filtration in the initial step (underlined), was completely dissolved in water to give an aqueous solution (solution $\mathbf{K}$; 10.0 L).

Then, additional precipitation titrations using solution $\mathbf{G}$ were carried out, and the endpoints of the titrations with $\mathbf{G}$ were as follows:

·For solution $\mathbf{J}$ (entire amount): 61.6 mL.

·For 100 mL of solution $\mathbf{K}$: 44.4 mL.

It should be noted here that the coexistence of NaCl or $\ce{SiO2}$ has no effect on the precipitation titration.

B.2 (15 pt) Calculate the mass of the NaCl produced in the reaction vessel (information underlined), and calculate the mass ($x$ [g]) of the $\ce{Na2SiF6}$ used as a starting material.

B.3 (8 pt) 77.8% of the $\ce{CCl4}$ used as a starting material was unreacted. Calculate the mass of $\ce{CF3Cl}$ generated.

problems.title: The Solid-State Chemistry of Transition Metals
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (45 points, 13% of the total). The Solid-State Chemistry of Transition Metals

Part A

Japan is one of the countries with the highest numbers of volcanos worldwide. When silicate minerals crystallize from magma, a part of the transition-metal ions ($\ce{M^{n+}}$) in the magma is incorporated into the silicate minerals. The $\ce{M^{n+}}$ studied in the problem are coordinated by oxide ions ($\ce{O^{2-}}$) and adopt a four-coordinate tetrahedral ($T_\mathrm{d}$) geometry in the magma and six-coordinate octahedral ($O_\mathrm{h}$) geometry in the silicate minerals, both of which exhibit a high-spin electron configuration. The distribution coefficient of $\ce{M^{n+}}$ between the silicate minerals and magma, $D$, can be expressed by:

$$D = \frac{[\mathrm{M}]_\mathrm{s}}{[\mathrm{M}]_\mathrm{l}}$$

where $[\mathrm{M}]_\mathrm{s}$ and $[\mathrm{M}]_\mathrm{l}$ are the concentrations of $\ce{M^{n+}}$ in the silicate minerals and the magma, respectively. The table below shows the $D$ values of $\ce{Cr^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Mn^{2+}}$ as examples.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} & \ce{Cr^{2+}} & \ce{Mn^{2+}} \\ \hline D & 7.2 & 1.1 \end{array}$$

Let $\Delta_\mathrm{O}$ and $\mathrm{CFSE^O}$ be the energy separation of the d-orbitals of $\ce{M^{n+}}$ and the crystal-field stabilization energy in a $O_\mathrm{h}$ field, respectively. Let $\Delta_\mathrm{T}$ and $\mathrm{CFSE^T}$ be those in a $T_\mathrm{d}$ field.

A.1 (6 pt) Calculate $|\mathrm{CFSE^O} - \mathrm{CFSE^T}| = \Delta\mathrm{CFSE}$ in terms of $\Delta_\mathrm{O}$ for $\ce{Cr^{2+}}$, $\ce{Mn^{2+}}$, and $\ce{Co^{2+}}$; assume $\Delta_\mathrm{T} = 4/9\,\Delta_\mathrm{O}$.

A.2 (3 pt) A linear relationship is observed by plotting $\ln D$ against $\Delta\mathrm{CFSE}/\Delta_\mathrm{O}$ in the Cartesian coordinate system shown below. Estimate $D$ for $\ce{Co^{2+}}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-6-fig1.png

Metal oxides MO (M: Ca, Ti, V, Mn, or Co) crystallize in a rock-salt structure wherein the $\ce{M^{n+}}$ adopts an $O_\mathrm{h}$ geometry with a high-spin electron configuration. The lattice enthalpy of these oxides is mainly governed by the Coulomb interactions based on the radius and charge of the ions and some contributions from the CFSE of $\ce{M^{n+}}$ in the $O_\mathrm{h}$ field.

A.3 (3 pt) Choose the appropriate set of lattice enthalpies [$\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$] from one of the options (a) to (f).

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} & \ce{CaO} & \ce{TiO} & \ce{VO} & \ce{MnO} & \ce{CoO} \\ \hline \text{(a)} & 3460 & 3878 & 3913 & 3810 & 3916 \\ \text{(b)} & 3460 & 3916 & 3878 & 3810 & 3913 \\ \text{(c)} & 3460 & 3913 & 3916 & 3810 & 3878 \\ \text{(d)} & 3810 & 3878 & 3913 & 3460 & 3916 \\ \text{(e)} & 3810 & 3916 & 3878 & 3460 & 3913 \\ \text{(f)} & 3810 & 3913 & 3916 & 3460 & 3878 \end{array}$$

Part B

A mixed oxide $\mathbf{A}$, which contains $\ce{La^{3+}}$ and $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$, crystallizes in a tetragonal unit cell shown in Fig. 1. In the $[\ce{CuO6}]$ octahedron, the Cu–O length along the z-axis ($l_z$) is longer than that of the x-axis ($l_x$), and $[\ce{CuO6}]$ is distorted from the regular $O_\mathrm{h}$ geometry. This distortion removes the degeneracy of the $\mathrm{e_g}$ orbitals ($\mathrm{d}_{x^2-y^2}$ and $\mathrm{d}_{z^2}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-6-fig2.png

Fig. 1

$\mathbf{A}$ can be synthesized by thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of complex $\mathbf{B}$, which is formed by mixing metal chlorides in dilute aqueous ammonia solution containing squaric acid $\ce{C4H2O4}$, i.e., a diacid. The pyrolysis behavior of $\mathbf{B}$ in dry air shows a weight loss of 29.1% up to $200\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ due to the loss of crystallization water, followed by another weight loss up to $700\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ due to the release of $\ce{CO2}$. The total weight loss during the formation of $\mathbf{A}$ from $\mathbf{B}$ is 63.6%. It should be noted that only water and $\ce{CO2}$ are released in the pyrolysis reaction.

B.1 (6 pt) Write the chemical formulae for $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

B.2 (4 pt) Calculate $l_x$ and $l_z$ using Fig. 1.

B.3 (4 pt) For $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ in the distorted $[\ce{CuO6}]$ octahedron in $\mathbf{A}$ of Fig. 1, write the names of the split $\mathrm{e_g}$ orbitals ($\mathrm{d}_{x^2-y^2}$ and $\mathrm{d}_{z^2}$) in (i) and (ii), and draw the electron configuration in the dotted box in your answer sheet.

$\mathbf{A}$ is an insulator. When one $\ce{La^{3+}}$ is substituted with one $\ce{Sr^{2+}}$, one hole is generated in the crystal lattice that can conduct electricity. As a result, the $\ce{Sr^{2+}}$-doped $\mathbf{A}$ shows superconductivity below 38 K. When a substitution reaction took place for $\mathbf{A}$, $2.05 \times 10^{27}$ holes $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$ were generated.

B.4 (4 pt) Calculate the percentage of $\ce{Sr^{2+}}$ substituted for $\ce{La^{3+}}$ based on the mole ratio in the substitution reaction. Note that the valences of the constituent ions and the crystal structure are not altered by the substitution reaction.

Part C

$\ce{Cu2(CH3CO2)4}$ is composed of four $\ce{CH3CO2^-}$ coordinated to two $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ (Fig. 2A). $\ce{Cu2(CH3CO2)4}$ exhibits high levels of structural symmetry, with two axes passing through the carbon atoms of the four $\ce{CH3CO2^-}$ and an axis passing through the two $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$, all of which are oriented orthogonal relative to each other. When a dicarboxylate ligand is used instead of $\ce{CH3CO2^-}$, a “cage complex” is formed. The cage complex $\mathrm{Cu_4}(\mathbf{L1})_4$ is composed of planar dicarboxylate $\mathbf{L1}$ (Fig. 2B) and $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ (Fig. 2C). The angle $\theta$ between the coordination directions of the two carboxylates, indicated by the arrows in Fig. 2B, determines the structure of the cage complex. The $\theta$ is $0^\circ$ for $\mathbf{L1}$. Note that hydrogen atoms are not shown in Fig. 2.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-6-fig3.png

Fig. 2

C.1 (5 pt) The $\theta$ of the planar dicarboxylate $\mathbf{L2}$ below is fixed to $90^\circ$. If the composition of the cage complex formed from $\mathbf{L2}$ and $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ is $\mathrm{Cu}_n(\mathbf{L2})_m$, give the smallest integer combination of $n$ and $m$. Assume that only the $\ce{CO2^-}$ groups of $\mathbf{L2}$ form a coordination bond to $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ ions.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-6-fig4.png

A zinc complex, $\ce{Zn4O(CH3CO2)6}$, contains four tetrahedral $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$, six $\ce{CH3CO2^-}$, and one $\ce{O^{2-}}$ (Fig. 3A). In $\ce{Zn4O(CH3CO2)6}$, the $\ce{O^{2-}}$ is located at the origin, and the three axes passing through the carbon atoms of $\ce{CH3CO2^-}$ are oriented orthogonal relative to each other. When p-benzenedicarboxylate (Fig. 3B, $\mathbf{L3}$, $\theta = 180^\circ$) is used instead of $\ce{CH3CO2^-}$, the $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$ clusters are linked to each other to form a crystalline solid ($\mathbf{X}$) that is called a “porous coordination polymer” (Fig. 3C). The composition of $\mathbf{X}$ is $[\mathrm{Zn_4O}(\mathbf{L3})_3]_n$, and it has a cubic crystal structure with nano-sized pores. One pore is represented as a sphere in Fig. 3D, and each tetrahedral $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$ cluster is represented as a dark gray polyhedron in Fig. 3C and 3D. Note that hydrogen atoms are not shown in Fig. 3.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-6-fig5.png

Fig. 3

C.2 (5 pt) $\mathbf{X}$ has a cubic unit cell with a side length of $a$ (Fig. 3C) and a density of $0.592\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. Calculate $a$ in [cm].

C.3 (5 pt) $\mathbf{X}$ contains a considerable number of pores, and 1 g of $\mathbf{X}$ can accommodate $3.0 \times 10^{2}\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $\ce{CO2}$ gas in the pores at 1 bar and $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Calculate the average number of $\ce{CO2}$ molecules per pore.

problems.title: Playing with Non-benzenoid Aromaticity
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (36 points, 13% of the total). Playing with Non-benzenoid Aromaticity

Prof. Nozoe (1902–1996) opened the research field of non-benzenoid aromatic compounds, which are now ubiquitous in organic chemistry.

Part A

Lineariifolianone is a natural product with a unique structure, which was isolated from Inula linariifolia. From valencene ($\mathbf{1}$), a one-step conversion yields $\mathbf{2}$, before a three-step conversion via $\mathbf{3}$ yields ketone $\mathbf{4}$. Eremophilene ($\mathbf{5}$) is converted into $\mathbf{6}$ by performing the same four-step conversion.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-7-fig1.png

A.1 (5 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{2}$ and $\mathbf{6}$ and clearly identify the stereochemistry where necessary.

Then, ketone $\mathbf{4}$ is converted into ester $\mathbf{15}$. Compound $\mathbf{8}$ (molecular weight: 188) retains all the stereocenters in $\mathbf{7}$. Compounds $\mathbf{9}$ and $\mathbf{10}$ have five stereocenters and no carbon-carbon double bonds. Assume that $\ce{H2{}^{18}O}$ is used instead of $\ce{H2{}^{16}O}$ for the synthesis of $\ce{^{18}O}$-labelled-lineariifolianones $\mathbf{13}$ and $\mathbf{14}$ from $\mathbf{11}$ and $\mathbf{12}$, respectively. Compounds $\mathbf{13}$ and $\mathbf{14}$ are $\ce{^{18}O}$-labelled isotopomers. Ignoring isotopic labelling, both $\mathbf{13}$ and $\mathbf{14}$ provide the same product $\mathbf{15}$ with identical stereochemistry.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-7-fig2.png

A.2 (2 pt) Choose the appropriate structure for $\mathbf{A}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-7-fig3.png

A.3 (19 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{8}$–$\mathbf{14}$ and clearly identify the stereochemistry where necessary. Also, indicate the introduced $\ce{^{18}O}$ atoms for $\mathbf{13}$ and $\mathbf{14}$ as shown in the example below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-7-fig4.png

Part B

Compound $\mathbf{19}$ is synthesized as shown below. In relation to non-benzenoid aromaticity, $\mathbf{19}$ can be used as an activator for alcohols, and $\mathbf{20}$ was converted to $\mathbf{22}$ via ion-pair intermediate $\mathbf{21}$. Although the formation of $\mathbf{21}$ was observed by NMR, $\mathbf{21}$ gradually decomposes to give $\mathbf{18}$ and $\mathbf{22}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-7-fig5.png

$\ce{^1H}$ NMR ($\ce{CD3CN}$, ppm) $\mathbf{20}$: $\delta$ 7.4–7.2 (5H), 3.7 (2H), 2.8 (2H), 2.2 (1H)

$\ce{^1H}$ NMR ($\ce{CD3CN}$, ppm) $\mathbf{21}$: $\delta$ 8.5–7.3 (15H), 5.5 (2H), 3.4 (2H)

B.1 (10 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{17}$–$\mathbf{19}$ and $\mathbf{21}$. Identifying the stereochemistry is not necessary.

problems.title: Dynamic Organic Molecules and Their Chirality
problems.problem:
Problem 8 (26 points, 11% of the total). Dynamic Organic Molecules and Their Chirality

Part A

Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons with successive ortho-connections are called [n]carbohelicenes (here, n represents the number of six-membered rings) (see below). [4]Carbohelicene ($\mathbf{[4]C}$) is efficiently prepared by a route using a photoreaction as shown below, via an intermediate ($\mathbf{Int.}$) that is readily oxidized by iodine.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-8-fig1.png

The photoreaction proceeds in a manner similar to the following example.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-8-fig2.png

Note: For all of Question 8, please draw alternating single and double bonds in your answers to the problems as depicted in the examples of carbohelicene. Do not use circles for conjugated $\pi$ systems.

A.1 (9 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{C}$. Stereoisomers should be distinguished.

A.2 (3 pt) Attempts to synthesize [5]carbohelicene from the same phosphonium salt and an appropriate starting compound resulted in the formation of only a trace amount of [5]carbohelicene, instead affording product $\mathbf{D}$ whose molecular weight was 2 Da lower than that of [5]carbohelicene. The $\ce{^1H}$ NMR chemical shifts of $\mathbf{D}$ are listed below. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{D}$.
[$\mathbf{D}$ ($\delta$, ppm in $\ce{CS2}$, r.t.), 8.85 (2H), 8.23 (2H), 8.07 (2H), 8.01 (2H), 7.97 (2H), 7.91 (2H)]

[5]- and larger [n]carbohelicenes have helical chirality and interconversion between enantiomers of these helicenes is significantly slow at room temperature. The chirality of [n]carbohelicenes is defined as $(M)$ or $(P)$ as shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-8-fig3.png

[n]Carbohelicenes with n larger than 4 can be enantiomerically separated by a chiral column chromatography, which was developed by Prof. Yoshio Okamoto.

Multiple helicenes are molecules that contain two or more helicene-like structures. If its helical chirality is considered, several stereoisomers exist in a multiple helicene. For example, compound $\mathbf{E}$ contains three [5]carbohelicene-like moieties in one molecule. One of the stereoisomers is described as $(P, P, P)$ as shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-8-fig4.png

A.3 (7 pt) The nickel-mediated trimerization of 1,2-dibromobenzene generates triphenylene. When the same reaction is applied to an enantiomer of $\mathbf{F}$, $(P)$-$\mathbf{F}$, multiple helicene $\mathbf{G}$ ($\ce{C66H36}$) is obtained. Given that interconversion between stereoisomers does not occur during the reaction, identify all the possible stereoisomers of $\mathbf{G}$ formed in this process, without duplication. As a reference, one isomer should be drawn completely with the chirality defined as in the example above, with numerical labels; the other stereoisomers should be listed with location numbers and $M$ and $P$ labels according to the same numbering. problems.title: Likes and Dislikes of Capsule
problems.problem:
Problem 9 (23 points, 10% of the total). Likes and Dislikes of Capsule

Good kids don’t do this, but if you unseam a tennis ball, you can disassemble it into two U-shaped pieces.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-9-fig1.png

Based on this idea, compounds $\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{2}$ were synthesized as U-shaped molecules with different sizes. Compound $\mathbf{3}$ was prepared as a comparison of $\mathbf{1}$ and the encapsulation behavior of these compounds was investigated.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-9-fig2.png

The synthetic route to $\mathbf{2}$ is shown below. The elemental composition of compound $\mathbf{9}$: C; 40.49%, H; 1.70%, and O; 17.98% by mass.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-9-fig3.png

A.1 (13 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{4}$–$\mathbf{9}$; the stereochemistry can be neglected. Use "PMB" as a substituent instead of drawing the whole structure of p-methoxybenzyl group shown in the scheme above.

In the mass spectrum of $\mathbf{1}$, the ion peak corresponding to its dimer ($\mathbf{1}_2$) was clearly observed, whereas an ion peak for $\mathbf{3}_2$ was not observed in the spectrum of $\mathbf{3}$. In the $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectra of a solution of $\mathbf{1}_2$, all the NH protons derived from $\mathbf{1}$ were observed to be chemically equivalent, and their chemical shift was significantly different from that of the NH protons of $\mathbf{3}$. These data indicate that hydrogen bonds are formed between the NH moieties of $\mathbf{1}$ and atoms $\mathbf{X}$ of another molecule of $\mathbf{1}$ to form the dimeric capsule.

A.2 (2 pt) Circle all the appropriate atom(s) $\mathbf{X}$ in $\mathbf{1}$.

A.3 (2 pt) Give the number of the hydrogen bonds in the dimeric capsule ($\mathbf{1}_2$).

The dimeric capsule of $\mathbf{1}$ ($\mathbf{1}_2$) has an internal space wherein an appropriate small molecule Z can be encapsulated. This phenomenon is expressed by the following equation:

$$\mathrm{Z} + \mathbf{1}_2 \to \mathrm{Z@}\mathbf{1}_2 \tag{1}$$

The equilibrium constant of the encapsulation of Z into $\mathbf{1}_2$ is given as below:

$$K_\mathrm{a} = \frac{[\mathrm{Z@}\mathbf{1}_2]}{[\mathrm{Z}][\mathbf{1}_2]} \tag{2}$$

Encapsulation of a molecule into a capsule could be monitored by NMR spectroscopy. For example, $\mathbf{1}_2$ in $\ce{C6D6}$ gave different signals in the $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectra before and after addition of $\ce{CH4}$.

Compound $\mathbf{2}$ also forms a rigid and larger dimeric capsule ($\mathbf{2}_2$). The $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{2}_2$ was measured in $\ce{C6D6}$, $\ce{C6D5F}$, and a $\ce{C6D6}/\ce{C6D5F}$ solvent mixture, with all other conditions being kept constant. The chemical shifts for the $\mathrm{H^a}$ proton of $\mathbf{2}$ in the above solvents are summarized below, and no other signals from the $\mathrm{H^a}$ in $\mathbf{2}$, except for the listed, were observed. Assume that the interior of the capsule is always filled with the largest possible number of solvent molecules and that each signal corresponds to one species of the filled capsule.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-9-fig4.png

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \text{solvent} & \delta\ (\mathrm{ppm})\text{ of }\mathrm{H^a} \\ \hline \ce{C6D6} & 4.60 \\ \hline \ce{C6D5F} & 4.71 \\ \hline \ce{C6D6}/\ce{C6D5F} & 4.60,\ 4.71,\ 4.82 \end{array}$$

A.4 (3 pt) Determine the number of $\ce{C6D6}$ and $\ce{C6D5F}$ molecules encapsulated in $\mathbf{2}_2$ giving each $\mathrm{H^a}$ signal.

$\ce{^1H}$ NMR measurements in $\ce{C6D6}$ revealed that $\mathbf{2}_2$ can incorporate one molecule of 1-adamantanecarboxylic acid (AdA), and the association constants ($K_\mathrm{a}$) which are expressed below were determined for various temperatures. [solvent@$\mathbf{2}_2$] denotes a species containing one or more solvent molecules.

$$K_\mathrm{a} = \frac{[\mathrm{Z@}\mathbf{2}_2]}{[\mathrm{Z}][\text{solvent@}\mathbf{2}_2]} \tag{3}$$

Similarly, the $K_\mathrm{a}$ values of $\ce{CH4}$ and $\mathbf{1}_2$ given as eq (2) at various temperatures in $\ce{C6D6}$ were also determined by $\ce{^1H}$ NMR measurements. The plots of the two association constants (as $\ln K_\mathrm{a}$ vs $1/T$) are shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2021-9-fig5.png

No $\ce{C6D6}$ molecule is encapsulated in $\mathbf{1}_2$. In line $\mathbf{II}$, the entropy change ($\Delta S$) is ( 1 ) and enthalpy change ($\Delta H$) is ( 2 ), indicating that the driving force for the encapsulation in line $\mathbf{II}$ is ( 3 ). Therefore, line $\mathbf{I}$ corresponds to ( 4 ), and line $\mathbf{II}$ corresponds to ( 5 ).

A.5 (3 pt) Choose the correct options in gaps (1)–(5) in the following paragraph from A and B.

$$\begin{array}{c|l|l} & \text{A} & \text{B} \\ \hline (1) & \text{positive} & \text{negative} \\ \hline (2) & \text{positive} & \text{negative} \\ \hline (3) & \Delta S & \Delta H \\ \hline (4) & \mathbf{1}_2\text{ and }\ce{CH4} & \mathbf{2}_2\text{ and AdA} \\ \hline (5) & \mathbf{1}_2\text{ and }\ce{CH4} & \mathbf{2}_2\text{ and AdA} \end{array}$$

problems.title: Rapid and Visual Nucleic Acid Testing for COVID-19
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (14 points, 9% of the total). Rapid and Visual Nucleic Acid Testing for COVID-19

Fast and simple methods for early detection of COVID-19 are urgently needed. Gold nanoparticles-aided detection is one of the promising methods. Gold nanoparticles are widely used as a visible readout for test strips due to their high molar extinction coefficients (molar absorptivity). The color appearance of gold nanoparticles is closely associated with their sizes and dispersity. Generally, the larger the gold nanoparticles, the more reddish the color is. Once the nanoparticles are aggregated, the color shifts from red to blue.

When the surface of gold nanoparticles is modified with two kinds of single-stranded nucleic acid fragments $a$ and $b$, the gold nanoparticles would aggregate in the presence of the target nucleic acid ($a'b'$), causing the color change of the solution from red to blue in several minutes (as indicated below). Based on this principle, the target nucleic acids collected from the coronavirus in a sample can be detected.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-1-fig2.png

1.1 (1.0 pt) Indicate the absorption band region of the dispersed gold nanoparticles with an appropriate letter (a-f in the color wheel of Figure 0.1 in General Instructions)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-1-fig1.png

Figure 0.1 (General Instructions). The Color Wheel. a: red, b: orange, c: yellow, d: green, e: blue, f: violet. 1: If a substance absorbs here; 2: it appears as this color.

1.2 (1.0 pt) Indicate the change in the absorption spectrum of the gold nanoparticles once they are aggregated. Compared to the absorption wavelength of the dispersed gold nanoparticles, the wavelength of the aggregated nanoparticles

(a) becomes longer
(b) becomes shorter
(c) does not change

Gold nanoparticles are composed of gold atoms that are closely packed as solid gold (density $\rho = 19.3\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$).

1.3 (4.0 pt) Calculate how many gold atoms ($N$) are there in a spherical gold nanoparticle with a diameter of $30.0\,\mathrm{nm}$.

The synthesis of gold nanoparticles depends on the redox reaction between hydrogen tetrachloroaurate(III) ($\ce{HAuCl4*3H2O}$, $M_\mathrm{W} = 394$) and reducing substances (such as sodium citrate). $5.2\,\mathrm{mg}$ of $\ce{HAuCl4*3H2O}$ was completely converted into uniform spherical gold nanoparticles with a diameter of $30.0\,\mathrm{nm}$ in a $100.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ reaction solution. The absorbance of the resulting red solution was $0.800$ measured at $530\,\mathrm{nm}$ by a UV-Vis spectrometer.

1.4 (4.0 pt) Calculate the molar extinction coefficient (molar absorptivity) of the resulting gold nanoparticles solution at $530\,\mathrm{nm}$ per mol of gold nanoparticles. The optical path of the cuvette used is $1\,\mathrm{cm}$. If you failed to get the number of gold atoms ($N$) in 1.3, use $N = 1.00\times10^{5}$.

The standard addition method was used for colorimetric detection of the target nucleic acid. The original throat swab sample was collected and divided equally into two portions. After addition of the probe solutions and water (as indicated below), the absorbance of the two resulting solutions was measured at $600\,\mathrm{nm}$ separately.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{No.} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Volume of}\\ \text{throat swab}\\ \text{sample (mL)}\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Volume of solution of}\\ \text{gold nanoparticles}\\ \text{modified with nucleic}\\ \text{acid fragments (mL)}\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Volume of standard}\\ \text{solution containing}\\ 2.0\,\mathrm{\mu g\,mL^{-1}}\text{ target}\\ \text{nucleic acid (mL)}\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Volume of}\\ \text{water}\\ \text{(mL)}\end{array} & \text{Absorbance} \\ \hline 1 & 0.10 & 0.80 & 0.00 & 0.10 & 0.400 \\ 2 & 0.10 & 0.80 & 0.10 & 0.00 & 0.900 \end{array}$$

1.5 (4.0 pt) Calculate the concentration of the viral nucleic acids in the original throat swab sample.

problems.title: Chromium in Ancient and Modern Times
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (21 points, 11% of the total). Chromium in Ancient and Modern Times

Black glazed porcelain is a special Chinese porcelain and was popular in the Tang and Song dynasties (ca. 1000 years ago). The ceramic ware contained iron oxides as the main color rendering agent, which was mixed with other transition metal oxides to exhibit different color appearance such as auburn, dark brown or black. Currently, the black glazed porcelain is still popular in China.

The typical black glaze is composed of Fe-containing oxides with a spinel structure. Spinel oxides have the general formula $\ce{AB2O4}$ and the structure consists of a cubic close packing array of $\ce{O^{2-}}$ ions in which the $\mathbf{A}$ cations occupy one-eighth of the tetrahedral vacancies and the $\mathbf{B}$ cations occupy half of the octahedral vacancies, as shown in Figure 2.1(a) for a unit cell.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-2-fig1.png

Figure 2.1 Illustration of spinel structure

The cubic unit cell of a spinel structure can be divided into 8 cubic subunits, and the dashed lines represent the internal edges of the subunits. 4 of the subunits belong to type I, and the other 4 subunits are type II (Figure 2.1(b)). The details of adjacent subunits of type I and type II are shown in Figure 2.1(c).

2.1 (2.0 pt) How many cations of type $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are there in a unit cell?

The black ceramic glaze with spinel structure can be produced by roasting $\ce{Fe2O3}$ and $\ce{Cr2O3}$ in a certain proportion in a reducing atmosphere (reaction (I)). When $\ce{Fe2O3}$ and $\ce{Cr2O3}$ are reacted with the mass ratio of $63.6 : 36.4$, they completely transform into a pure stoichiometric compound. The product has a spinel structure, in which the tetrahedral $\mathbf{A}$ sites are occupied by iron cations only.

2.2 (1.0 pt) In reaction (I), which element is reduced?

2.3 (6.0 pt) Calculate the numbers of $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ and $\ce{Cr^{3+}}$ in the $\mathbf{B}$ sites of one unit cell.

Besides doping in black ceramic glaze, chromium-containing pigments are used in painting and printing due to the abundant color originating from chromium with different oxidation states, such as $+2$, $+3$ and $+6$. The pigment, chrome green ($\ce{Cr2O3}$) can be converted into a series of other compounds ($\mathbf{D}$–$\mathbf{G}$) in the following process, where $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{F}$, $\mathbf{G}$ are yellow, orange and red respectively.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-2-fig2.png

2.4 (1.0 pt) Write the chemical formula of $\mathbf{E}$.

2.5 (2.0 pt) Write the reaction equation of $\mathbf{F} \longrightarrow \mathbf{G}$.

2.6 (1.0 pt) Choose the agent which could be $\mathbf{H}$.

(A) $\ce{FeSO4}$
(B) $\ce{FeCl3}$
(C) $\ce{ZnSO4}$
(D) $\ce{CuSO4}$

The variable valence of chromium is not only important for the production of pigments, but also useful for catalysis. For example, a typical Phillips catalyst for the polymerization of ethylene consists of chromium oxide species grafted onto a porous support material such as amorphous silica. The tetra-coordinated $\mathrm{Cr(VI)}$ specie is the core in the pre-catalyst ($\mathbf{1}$), which is proposed to be reduced quickly into a six-coordinated $\mathrm{Cr(II)}$ specie ($\mathbf{2}$) by the ethylene molecules at the beginning. $\mathbf{2}$ is proposed to further catalyze polymerization of ethylene molecules.

2.7 (1.0 pt) The reaction of $\mathbf{1}$ with ethylene can be traced by UV–vis spectra, which show the light absorption of $\mathbf{1}$ at $21500\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and the light absorption of $\mathbf{2}$ at $16700\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ in the visible region, respectively. Choose the appropriate combination of colors of $\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{2}$.

(A) orange and white, respectively
(B) orange and blue, respectively
(C) blue and orange, respectively
(D) blue and white, respectively

2.8 (5.0 pt) Assuming that the $\mathrm{Cr(II)}$ ion in $\mathbf{2}$ is located in a regular octahedral crystal field with a splitting energy $\Delta_\mathrm{o}$ of $16000\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, draw the configurations of d electrons of the $\mathrm{Cr(II)}$ ion in $\mathbf{2}$, and calculate the crystal field stabilization energy (CFSE) for the $\mathrm{Cr(II)}$ ion in $\mathbf{2}$. (Note: The pairing energy $P$ for $\mathrm{Cr(II)}$ in $\mathbf{2}$ is $23500\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$)

2.9 (2.0 pt) Coordination compounds/ions exhibit paramagnetism when containing unpaired electrons, and the corresponding magnetic moment ($\mu$) of transition metal cations is calculated by the function $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\mu_\mathrm{B}$ where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons. Calculate the magnetic moment in term of $\mu_\mathrm{B}$ for the $\mathrm{Cr(II)}$ ion in $\mathbf{2}$.

problems.title: Capture and Transformation of Carbon Dioxide
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (42 points, 14% of the total). Capture and Transformation of Carbon Dioxide

Climate change is one of the most critical global challenges nowadays. The increase of $\ce{CO2}$ concentration in the atmosphere has been recognized as the primary driver of global warming. The study of the capture and transformation of $\ce{CO2}$ has attracted considerable attention.

Direct air capture (DAC) technology which aims to extract $\ce{CO2}$ directly from ambient air is promising. The conventional method of DAC is wet scrubbing with alkaline hydroxide solutions (typically NaOH), where $\ce{CO2}$ in air is absorbed till pH ≈ 10 (step 1). The spent sorbent is regenerated by dosing calcium hydroxide into the system (step 2). The white precipitate $\mathbf{A}$ received in step 2 decomposes at $700\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, giving rise to $\ce{CO2}$ and another white compound $\mathbf{B}$ (step 3). Finally, calcium hydroxide can be generated by the hydration of $\mathbf{B}$. This process is highly energy-demanding. ($\ce{H2CO3}$: $K_\mathrm{a1} = 4.5\times10^{-7}$, $K_\mathrm{a2} = 4.7\times10^{-11}$)

3.1 (2.0 pt) Write the formulas for $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ respectively.

3.2 (5.0 pt) Write the balanced equations of all possible reactions in steps 1-3. NaOH solution is used as sorbent.

Recently, an electrochemical process was developed for regenerating the alkaline solution in the wet scrubbing process for DAC application, and pure $\ce{CO2}$ gas could be recovered that is suitable for storage or utilization. The process is based on a $\ce{H2}$-recycling electrochemical system (HRES), as shown in Figure 3.1.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-3-fig1.png

Figure 3.1 Schematic drawing of the experimental setup

The electrochemical cell contains three compartments: an anode region (A), an acidifying region (B), and a cathode region (C). They are separated by ion-selective permeable membranes M1 and M2. During the operation, protons produced from $\ce{H2}$ oxidation at the anode are transported to the acidifying compartment where the spent solution ($\ce{Na2CO3}$-$\ce{NaHCO3}$) coming from the air contactor is fed. The decreasing pH of the solution leads to the conversions of carbonate to hydrocarbonate (reaction 1) and hydrocarbonate to carbonic acid (reaction 2). When the solution is saturated by dissolved $\ce{CO2}$ (solubility: $0.033\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$), a further pH decrease leads to the release of $\ce{CO2}$ gas (reaction 3). $\ce{H2}$ generated in the cathode is introduced to the anode and the solution from the cathode can be reused as a DAC absorbent.

3.3 (2.0 pt) Write the electrode reactions in the anode (A) and the cathode (C) respectively.

3.4 (3.0 pt) Write the balanced equations for the reactions 1–3 in the acidifying region (B).

3.5 (2.0 pt) Check all that correctly describe the movement of cations during the system operation.

(a) $\ce{H+}$ ions permeate through M1 from A to B.
(b) $\ce{H+}$ ions permeate through M2 from B to C.
(c) $\ce{Na+}$ ions permeate through M1 from B to A.
(d) $\ce{Na+}$ ions permeate through M2 from B to C.
(e) Both $\ce{H+}$ and $\ce{Na+}$ ions can permeate through M1and M2.

The cell works at a steady state when the current passing through the cell is $2.00\,\mathrm{A}$ and the flow rate of the solution ($0.050\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ $\ce{Na2CO3}$ - $0.10\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ $\ce{NaHCO3}$) into the region B is $10.0\,\mathrm{mL\,min^{-1}}$. The pH in the anode compartment is maintained at 1 in the steady state.

3.6 (8.0 pt) Calculate the generation rate of $\ce{CO2}$ gas (in $\mathrm{mmol\,min^{-1}}$).

Zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (ZIFs), a sub-class of metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising materials for the capture and utilization of $\ce{CO2}$. The structures of ZIFs resemble zeolites. They form 3D frameworks with tetrahedrally coordinated metal ions (e.g. $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$, $\ce{Co^{2+}}$) bridged by imidazolate ($\mathrm{Im^{-}}$) and its derivatives. As the conjugated base of imidazole (HIm), imidazolate anion binds to metal cations (M) by its two N atoms. The fact that the M-Im-M angle is similar to the Si-O-Si angle ($145^\circ$) preferred in zeolites (as shown below) has led to the synthesis of a large number of ZIFs with zeolite-type tetrahedral topologies.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-3-fig2.png

ZIF-8 is one of the representative ZIFs, which adopts a sodalite framework (SOD), as shown in Figure 3.2. ZIF-8 was firstly synthesized by Chinese scientists Xiao-Ming Chen et al. (they named it as MAF-4) by the reaction of $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$ with 2-methylimidazole ($\ce{CH3(C3N2H3)}$, HmIm). It crystalizes in the cubic system with the cell parameter $a = 1.632\,\mathrm{nm}$ for a solvent-free phase with the effective pore diameter (shown by the inside virtual sphere in Figure 3.2d) of $1.16\,\mathrm{nm}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-3-fig3.png

Figure 3.2 Topology of SOD and structure of ZIF-8. (a) Topology of SOD cage; (b) SOD cage in ZIF-8 formed by $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$ (at the centers of the tetrahedra) and imidazolate (H atoms are omitted for clarity); (c) Framework of SOD with the unit cell shown by the square box; (d) Some of the pores are highlighted by virtual spheres in ZIF-8.

Note: If you wish, you may use the symbol "HmIm" and "mIm" representing 2-methylimidazole and 2-methylimidazolate respectively in solving the following questions.

3.7 (2.0 pt) Write the formula of the single sodalite cage.

3.8 (2.0 pt) Write the composition of the unit cell of ZIF-8.

3.9 (5.0 pt) Calculate the inner surface area ($S$) of the pores (modeled by the virtual spheres) of 1 g ZIF-8 (in $\mathrm{m^2}$). If you failed to get the composition of the unit cell, use 3500 as the formula weight of the unit cell.

3.10 (7.0 pt) Calculate the porosity $R$ of ZIF-8 ($R$ is the ratio of pore volume to the actual volume of the material) and the pore volume of 1 g ZIF-8 ($V_p$, in $\mathrm{cm^3}$).

ZIF-8 can also act as a catalyst to promote the conversion of $\ce{CO2}$ to high value-added chemicals. One of the most promising routes for $\ce{CO2}$ fixation is the preparation of cyclic carbonates via $\ce{CO2}$ cycloaddition. An example is shown as below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-3-fig4.png

A mechanism of catalytic conversion of $\ce{CO2}$ to cyclic carbonate over ZIF-8 catalyst is proposed:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-3-fig5.png

3.11 (2.0 pt) If ZIF-8 provides acid sites in the above catalytic process, complete the mechanism by choosing the reasonable intermediates from the following species:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-3-fig6.png

Choose the intermediates corresponding to I and II respectively.

ZIF-8 shows a relatively high thermal stability. However, a recent study revealed that its structure would be destroyed if applied in a wet acidic environment. The co-existence of $\ce{CO2}$ and $\ce{H2O}$ with ZIF-8 resulted in the formation of $\ce{ZnCO3}$.

3.12 (2.0 pt) Write the balanced equation of ZIF-8 with $\ce{CO2}$ and $\ce{H2O}$.

problems.title: A New Journey for Ancient Sulfur
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (45 points, 16% of the total). A New Journey for Ancient Sulfur

Sulfur has been known and used since the ancient times. Nowadays, sulfur is widely used in chemical production and pharmaceutical industry as an inexpensive chemical raw material.

Pyrite ($\ce{FeS2}$) is commonly used as a raw material in the industrial production of elemental sulfur. By heating pyrite in the presence of limited air supply, the theoretical yield of elemental sulfur is 100% and a black magnetic oxide ($\ce{Fe3O4}$) is the other product.

4.1 (2.0 pt) Write the balanced reaction equation that describes the above conversion.

In addition to sulfur, a small amount of $\ce{SO2}$ is generated as a by-product during the actual process. This reaction can be monitored by measuring the amount of $\ce{SO2}$. The following recipe is used for the monitoring:

Raw ore powder is heated in a temperature-controlled tube furnace. The generated $\ce{SO2}$ is absorbed by $2\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ NaOH solution. When the reaction is completed, the solution is transferred to a $500\,\mathrm{mL}$ volumetric flask and diluted by distilled water to the mark. $25.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of this diluted solution is then added into an iodine flask containing $50.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ $0.05122\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ $\ce{I2}$ standard solution and $5\,\mathrm{mL}$ 20% $\ce{H2SO4}$ solution. After maintaining the iodine flask in dark for 5 min, the solution is titrated with $0.1012\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ standard solution. When the color of the solution turns light brown, $3\,\mathrm{mL}$ 0.5% starch indicator is added. Continue the titration until the blue color disappears.

4.2 (4.0 pt) Write the balanced reaction equations involving $\ce{I2}$ in the above measurement.

4.3 (4.0 pt) In such a test experiment starting from pyrite, $17.6\,\mathrm{g}$ of elemental sulfur was collected. The analysis of the by-product gases according to the above procedure resulted in the consumption of $18.47\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ standard solution. Assuming that no other sulfur containing species were produced, calculate what percentage of the sulfur in pyrite was lost as the by-product?

The lithium-sulfur battery is a compelling energy storage system because its high theoretical energy density exceeds conventional Li-ion batteries. The net reaction of a lithium-sulfur battery can be simplified as: $\ce{16 Li + S8 -> 8 Li2S}$. Sulfur is the cathode and metallic lithium is the anode active material during discharge.

4.4 (3.0 pt) Write the balanced equations for reactions that take place at cathode (a) and anode (b) during discharge.

4.5 (1.0 pt) Calculate the mass ratio of the cathode active material to the anode active material, according to the net battery reaction.

A lithium-ion battery (LIB) that possesses an average operating voltage of $3.8\,\mathrm{V}$ and a deliverable capacity of $3110\,\mathrm{mAh}$ can provide energy for a mobile phone to play videos continuously for 22 hours upon a full charge.

4.6 (5.0 pt) If the LIB is replaced by an ideal lithium-sulfur battery pack, which has an average operating voltage of $4.2\,\mathrm{V}$ and contains $23\,\mathrm{g}$ sulfur as the active electrode material that can react stoichiometrically during discharge, calculate how many hours the new battery pack will provide energy for the phone to play videos continuously after a full charge.

Elemental sulfur generally exist as $\ce{S8}$ molecules. In real lithium-sulfur batteries, $\ce{S8}$ is not directly reduced to $\ce{Li2S}$ during discharge, but it undergoes stepwise reactions generating different soluble lithium polysulfides ($\ce{Li2S_{n}}$, $n = 3-8$). These lithium polysulfides could diffuse to the anode and corrode it, which results in the loss of active electrode materials. This phenomenon is called "shuttle effect".

4.7 (2.0 pt) Write the balanced reaction equation for the corrosion of anode by soluble lithium polysulfides ($\ce{Li2S_{n}}$) that produces $\ce{Li2S}$.

In order to suppress the "shuttle effect", the forms of polysulfides in an electrolyte have been extensively studied. $\ce{Li2S6}$ is one of the most representative intermediate products:

problems.title: Interconversion among Nitrogen Oxides
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (45 points, 15% of the total). Interconversion among Nitrogen Oxides

Nitrogen oxides (including $\ce{N2O}$, $\ce{NO}$, $\ce{NO2}$, $\ce{N2O4}$ and etc., usually written as $\ce{NO_{x}}$) are one of the main air pollutants that can cause a series of problems such as ozone depletion, acid rain, photochemical smog, and greenhouse effect. Therefore, the emission and conversion of $\ce{NO_{x}}$ must be controlled to improve air quality. Here let us investigate the oxidation of NO to $\ce{NO2}$ via the reaction of $\ce{2NO + O2 -> 2NO2}$.

Part A

It is generally accepted that this reaction proceeds through the following mechanism in the atmosphere:

$$\ce{2NO <=> N2O2} \qquad (1)$$

$$\ce{N2O2 + O2 -> 2NO2} \qquad (2)$$

Reaction (1) and (2) and the reverse of reaction (1) are elementary reactions. Reaction (1) is a pre-equilibrium reaction, and its equilibrium constant in terms of concentrations is denoted as $K_{c1}$. Reaction (2) is the rate-determining step of the overall reaction, and its rate constant is $k_2$.

5.1 (4.0 pt) Deduce the rate expression for the overall reaction of $\ce{2NO + O2 -> 2NO2}$ as a function of $[\ce{NO}]$, $[\ce{O2}]$, $K_{c1}$ and $k_2$.

The temperature dependence of $K_{c1}$ could be approximately described as $\ln K_{c1} = M - (N/T)$ ($M$ and $N$ are constants). The change of $k_2$ with temperature follows the Arrhenius equation with the pre-exponential factor of $A_2$ and apparent activation energy of $E_{a,2}$. Assume that $E_{a,2}$ and $A_2$ are independent of the temperature.

5.2 (4.0 pt) Deduce the expressions for the pre-exponential factor ($A_+$) and apparent activation energy ($E_{a^+}$) of the reaction of $\ce{2NO + O2 -> 2NO2}$ as functions of $M$, $N$, $A_2$ and $E_{a,2}$.

The apparent rate constant ($k_+$) of the overall reaction is $6.63\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{L^2\,mol^{-2}\,min^{-1}}$ at $600\,\mathrm{K}$, and its apparent activation energy is $1.20\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

5.3 (2.0 pt) Calculate the rate constant (in $\mathrm{L^2\,mol^{-2}\,min^{-1}}$) of this reaction at $700\,\mathrm{K}$.

The standard enthalpies of formation ($\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\ominus_\mathrm{m}$) and standard entropies ($S^\ominus_\mathrm{m}$) at $298.15\,\mathrm{K}$ are as follows:

$$\begin{array}{l|ccc} & \ce{NO(g)} & \ce{O2(g)} & \ce{NO2(g)} \\ \hline \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\ominus_\mathrm{m}\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) & 91.3 & & 33.1 \\ S^\ominus_\mathrm{m}\ (\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}) & 210.8 & 205.2 & 240.1 \end{array}$$

The standard reaction enthalpy and entropy changes of $\ce{2NO + O2 -> 2NO2}$ can be regarded as temperature independent. All the gases are taken to be ideal for the following questions.

5.4 (4.0 pt) Calculate the thermodynamic equilibrium constant ($K_p^\ominus$) of this reaction at $600\,\mathrm{K}$.

5.5 (3.0 pt) Calculate the standard internal energy change $\Delta_\mathrm{r}U^\ominus_\mathrm{m}$ (in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) of this reaction at $600\,\mathrm{K}$.

Experimental observation shows that the rate of the reaction of $\ce{2NO2 -> 2NO + O2}$ is independent on the concentration of NO and $\ce{O2}$.

5.6 (8.0 pt) Deduce the expression of the rate for this reaction (the apparent rate constant could be directly used as $k_-$) and calculate the value of $k_-$ apparent at $600\,\mathrm{K}$. (If you failed to find the $K_p^\ominus(600\,\mathrm{K})$ in question 5.4, use $K_p^\ominus(600\,\mathrm{K}) = 350.0$)

$\ce{NO2}$ gas is introduced to a container with a fixed volume which is held at $600\,\mathrm{K}$ and allowed to reach equilibrium. 20 percent of the reactant is converted to NO and $\ce{O2}$. All the gases are taken to be ideal.

5.7 (4.0 pt) Calculate the total pressure of this reaction system at equilibrium. (If you failed to find the $K_p^\ominus(600\,\mathrm{K})$ in question 5.4, use $K_p^\ominus(600\,\mathrm{K}) = 350.0$)

Part B

Industrial exhaust is a main source of $\ce{NO_{x}}$. One of the approaches to reduce the emission of $\ce{NO_{x}}$ is through the oxidation of NO to $\ce{NO2}$ and the subsequent absorption of the formed $\ce{NO2}$ by absorbents. However, because of the low concentration of NO in exhaust, its spontaneous oxidation in the atmosphere is too slow to meet the demand of industry. Generally, solid catalysts are used to accelerate this reaction. The NO oxidation proceeds on the surface of a specific catalyst (CatX) through the following mechanism (adsorption site is denoted as Site):

$$\ce{O2(g)} + 2\,\text{Site} \underset{k_{\mathrm{S}-1}}{\overset{k_{\mathrm{S}+1}}{\rightleftharpoons}} 2\,\text{O-Site} \qquad \text{(S1)}$$

$$r_{\mathrm{S}+1} = k_{\mathrm{S}+1}\,[\ce{O2}]\,\theta_v^2 \qquad r_{\mathrm{S}-1} = k_{\mathrm{S}-1}\,\theta_\mathrm{O}^2$$

$$\ce{NO(g)} + \text{Site} \underset{k_{\mathrm{S}-2}}{\overset{k_{\mathrm{S}+2}}{\rightleftharpoons}} \text{NO-Site} \qquad \text{(S2)}$$

$$r_{\mathrm{S}+2} = k_{\mathrm{S}+2}[\ce{NO}]\,\theta_v \qquad r_{\mathrm{S}-2} = k_{\mathrm{S}-2}\,\theta_\mathrm{NO}$$

$$\ce{NO(g)} + \text{O-Site} \xrightarrow{k_{\mathrm{S}+3}} \ce{NO2}\text{-Site} \qquad \text{(S3)}$$

$$r_{\mathrm{S}+3} = k_{\mathrm{S}+3}[\ce{NO}]\,\theta_\mathrm{O}$$

$$\ce{NO2}\text{-Site} \underset{k_{\mathrm{S}-4}}{\overset{k_{\mathrm{S}+4}}{\rightleftharpoons}} \ce{NO2(g)} + \text{Site} \qquad \text{(S4)}$$

$$r_{\mathrm{S}+4} = k_{\mathrm{S}+4}\,\theta_{\mathrm{NO_2}} \qquad r_{\mathrm{S}-4} = k_{\mathrm{S}-4}\,[\ce{NO2}]\,\theta_v$$

Assume that the adsorptions of NO, $\ce{NO2}$ and O (from the dissociation of $\ce{O2}$) cannot proceed beyond a monolayer coverage, and these species are adsorbed by the same kind of surface sites. Their fractional coverages ($\theta$, defined as the ratio of the number of adsorption sites occupied to the number of total adsorption sites) are denoted as $\theta_\mathrm{NO}$, $\theta_{\mathrm{NO_2}}$ and $\theta_\mathrm{O}$, respectively. Thus, the fraction of unoccupied adsorption sites ($\theta_\mathrm{v}$) is $\theta_\mathrm{v} = 1 - \theta_\mathrm{NO} - \theta_{\mathrm{NO_2}} - \theta_\mathrm{O}$. Assume that all the adsorption and desorption processes are much faster than reaction (S3).

5.8 (6.0 pt) Deduce the expression for $\theta_\mathrm{v}$ as a function of $[\ce{NO}]$, $[\ce{O2}]$, $[\ce{NO2}]$ and the rate constants involved in reactions (S1)–(S4).

5.9 (4.0 pt) Choose the correct expression for the rate of $\ce{2NO(g) + O2(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$ at the beginning of the reaction. Assume that the concentration and adsorption of $\ce{NO2}$ are both negligible.

(A) $r_{\mathrm{S}+} = \dfrac{k_{\mathrm{S}+3}(k_{\mathrm{S}+1}/k_{\mathrm{S}-1})^{0.5}[\ce{NO}][\ce{O2}]^{0.5}}{1 + (k_{\mathrm{S}+1}[\ce{O2}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-1})^{0.5} + k_{\mathrm{S}+2}[\ce{NO}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-2}}$
(B) $r_{\mathrm{S}+} = \dfrac{0.5k_{\mathrm{S}+3}(k_{\mathrm{S}+1}/k_{\mathrm{S}-1})^{0.5}[\ce{NO}][\ce{O2}]^{0.5}}{1 + (k_{\mathrm{S}+1}[\ce{O2}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-1})^{0.5} + k_{\mathrm{S}+2}[\ce{NO}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-2}}$
(C) $r_{\mathrm{S}+} = \dfrac{k_{\mathrm{S}+3}(k_{\mathrm{S}+1}/k_{\mathrm{S}-1})[\ce{NO}][\ce{O2}]^{0.5}}{1 + k_{\mathrm{S}+1}[\ce{O2}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-1} + k_{\mathrm{S}+2}[\ce{NO}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-2}}$
(D) $r_{\mathrm{S}+} = \dfrac{k_{\mathrm{S}+4}k_{\mathrm{S}+3}(k_{\mathrm{S}+1}/k_{\mathrm{S}-1})^{0.5}[\ce{NO}][\ce{O2}]^{0.5}/k_{\mathrm{S}-4}}{1 + k_{\mathrm{S}+1}([\ce{O2}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-1})^{0.5} + k_{\mathrm{S}+2}[\ce{NO}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-2}}$

For some catalysts, the surface reaction proceeds via an alternative way instead of reaction (S3):

$$\text{NO-Site} + \text{O-Site} \xrightarrow{k_{\mathrm{S}+5}} \text{Site} + \ce{NO2}\text{-Site} \qquad \text{(S5)}$$

$$r_{\mathrm{S}+5} = k_{\mathrm{S}+5}\,\theta_\mathrm{NO}\,\theta_\mathrm{O}$$

This step is also rate-determining for the overall reaction.

A catalyst (CatY) is used to promote the reaction of $\ce{2NO + O2 -> 2NO2}$. When the temperature and NO concentration are constant, the initial reaction rate changes with the concentration of $\ce{O2}$ as follows:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-5-fig1.png

5.10 (6.0 pt) Choose a mechanism that is consistent with this curve.

(A) S3
(B) S5
(C) cannot be determined

problems.title: Enabling Phosphines
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (36 points, 7% of the total). Enabling Phosphines

Phosphines are phosphorus analogues of amines. They also carry a lone pair of electrons at the phosphorus atom and thus exhibit Lewis basicity or nucleophilicity. But in contrast with tertiary amines, chiral phosphines like $\mathbf{P1}$ with three different substituents can be isolated as single enantiomers. Chiral phosphines are often used as chiral ligands in transition metal catalysis.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig1.png

6.1 (3.0 pt) Using $R/S$ symbol, assign the absolute configuration of $\mathbf{P1}$.

In the past two decades, as organocatalysis grew rapidly, a large number of nucleophilic phosphine-catalyzed synthetic reactions have emerged. Among them, one of the most famous phosphine-catalyzed reactions is the Lu (3+2) cycloaddition reaction, which was first developed by Chinese scientist Xiyan Lu. For instance, under the catalysis of triphenylphosphine, ethyl allenoate $\mathbf{1}$ and methyl acrylate $\mathbf{2}$ smoothly produce two cyclopentene derivatives $\mathbf{3}$ (major) and $\mathbf{4}$ (minor).

Lu (3+2) cycloaddition:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig2.png

In a generally accepted mechanism, the Lu (3+2) reaction is a formal cycloaddition reaction. Initially, the catalyst triphenylphosphine engages in a nucleophilic addition to ethyl allenoate $\mathbf{1}$ to generate a zwitterionic intermediate $\mathbf{A}$, which subsequently cyclizes with methyl acrylate $\mathbf{2}$ by two paths. In the path leading to compound $\mathbf{3}$, an in situ generated phosphorus ylide intermediate $\mathbf{B}$ reversibly converts into intermediate $\mathbf{C}$ via proton transfer; $\mathbf{C}$ undergoes an elimination to deliver the major product $\mathbf{3}$ and release the phosphine catalyst. In the path leading to compound $\mathbf{4}$, a phosphorus ylide intermediate $\mathbf{B'}$ is formed, which also reversibly converts into intermediate $\mathbf{C'}$ via proton transfer; $\mathbf{C'}$ undergoes an elimination to give the minor product $\mathbf{4}$ and regenerate the phosphine catalyst.

Mechanism:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig3.png

6.2 (6.0 pt) Draw the two major resonance structures that make up the shown resonance hybrid $\mathbf{A}$ (the involvement of ester group is not considered, and stereochemistry is not required).

6.3 (8.0 pt) Draw the structures of intermediates $\mathbf{B'}$ and $\mathbf{C'}$ (stereochemistry is not required).

Under similar conditions, ethyl allenoate $\mathbf{1}$ and diethyl fumarate $\mathbf{5}$ readily deliver the corresponding cycloaddition product $\mathbf{6}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig4.png

6.4 (5.0 pt) Draw the structure of compound $\mathbf{6}$ (stereochemistry is not required).

Asymmetric Lu (3+2) cycloaddition reaction can be readily realized by utilizing chiral phosphine catalysts. For example, under the catalysis of a chiral bicyclic phosphine $\mathbf{P2}$, ethyl allenoate $\mathbf{1}$ and methyl acrylate $\mathbf{2}$ smoothly delivered an enantio-enriched cycloaddition product $\mathbf{3}$ in 80% ee (enantiomeric excess).

Asymmetric Lu (3+2) cycloaddition:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig5.png

Calculation equation of ee:

$$\mathrm{ee} = \frac{n_\mathrm{major} - n_\mathrm{minor}}{n_\mathrm{major} + n_\mathrm{minor}} \times 100\%$$

$n_\mathrm{major}$ = the amount of major enantiomer

$n_\mathrm{minor}$ = the amount of minor enantiomer

6.5 (6.0 pt) Mark the chirality centers in the chiral phosphine $\mathbf{P2}$ by using asterisks. (Note: points will be deducted for every wrong asterisk until 0 points)

6.6 (3.0 pt) Give the ratio of $n_\mathrm{major}/n_\mathrm{minor}$ of product $\mathbf{3}$.

Lu (3+2) cycloaddition reaction is a versatile tool in organic synthesis. For example, it was successfully used to synthesize (–)-hinesol, an important component of the Chinese medicinal herb Chang Zhu (Atractylodes lancea var Chinensis). Under the catalysis of $\ce{PPh3}$, a chiral cyclohexanone $\mathbf{7}$ cyclized with tert-butyl allenoate $\mathbf{8}$, affording a major product $\mathbf{9}$ and three minor products $\mathbf{10}$, $\mathbf{11}$ and $\mathbf{12}$. Minor products $\mathbf{10}$–$\mathbf{12}$ are all the isomers of $\mathbf{9}$. Compound $\mathbf{9}$ could be readily transformed into (–)-hinesol by a multistep process.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig6.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig7.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig8.png
