https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig9.png

problems.title: Organic Molecules in Life
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (32 points, 9% of the total). Organic Molecules in Life

The synthesis of complex peptides and proteins is a challenging task. On September 17, 1965, Chinese scientists synthesized crystalline bovine insulin artificially for the first time, marking a crucial step in the journey of exploring the secret of life and opening the era of protein synthesis.

Coupling of carboxylic acid groups with amine groups to forge an amide bond is the most elementary reaction in the synthesis of peptides and proteins. Allenone $\mathbf{2}$ was reported to be able to activate the carboxylic acid $\mathbf{1}$ under mild reaction conditions forming the intermediate $\mathbf{3}$. Intermediate $\mathbf{3}$ then reacts with amine $\mathbf{4}$ to give amide $\mathbf{5}$ with high yield, along with the byproduct $\mathbf{6}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-7-fig1.png

Similarly, N-ethynyl-N-methyl-p-toluenesulfonamide (MYTsA) with its major resonance structure $\mathbf{7}$ (involvement of Ts group is not considered) can activate carboxylic acid in the same way as allenone $\mathbf{2}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-7-fig2.png

7.1 (12.0 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{7}$, intermediate $\mathbf{9}$ and compound $\mathbf{12}$. Show the stereochemistry of any stereocenters.

As the length of peptide chain grows, formation of amide bonds becomes more difficult, and conventional condensation methods are not applicable in the synthesis of proteins. In the first synthesis of crystalline bovine insulin, a method based on the chemistry of acylhydrazine $\mathbf{13}$ was developed to achieve the challenging amide coupling between two peptides. As the following equations, compound $\mathbf{15}$ reacts with $\mathbf{16}$ smoothly in the presence of triethylamine.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-7-fig3.png

Note: P1, P2 = peptides

7.2 (8.0 pt) Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{15}$ and $\mathbf{16}$.

In addition to de novo synthesis, scientists can modify existing proteins. Although there are multiple reactive sites on the surface of protein, such as amino groups, thiol groups, and carboxyl groups, the most nucleophilic thiol groups are the preferred site when the protein is treated with electrophilic reagents such as N-phenyl maleimide $\mathbf{18}$ via Michael addition.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-7-fig4.png

Under mild basic conditions (pH = 7.5), reagent $\mathbf{19}$ was proposed to react with the thiol group of protein $\mathbf{20}$ to give a neutral intermediate $\mathbf{21}$ which is attacked by hydroxide to give compound $\mathbf{22}$. Compound $\mathbf{22}$ can equilibrate with an acyclic form $\mathbf{23}$, and subsequently react with another protein $\mathbf{20}$. The resulting major product can exist either in the acyclic form $\mathbf{24}$ or in the cyclic form $\mathbf{25}$ in a similar way as the equilibration between $\mathbf{22}$ and $\mathbf{23}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-7-fig5.png

7.3 (12.0 pt) Draw the structures of intermediate $\mathbf{21}$, compounds $\mathbf{24}$ and $\mathbf{25}$. Stereochemistry is not required.

Chiral compounds are important for human health, for example, more than 50% of the medicines currently in clinical use are single enantiomers of chiral molecules. However, synthesizing chiral molecules in enantio-enriched form is a great challenge. Professor Qilin Zhou's team in Nankai University in China developed a series of chiral spiro catalysts with high activity, raising the efficiency of asymmetric synthesis to a new height, and being widely used in the pharmaceutical industry. Problem 1 (22 points, 5% of the total). Molecular Imaging

Molecular imaging is a powerful tool in medical diagnostics. The nuclear isomer $\ce{^{99m}Tc}$ (m = metastable) of the isotope $\ce{^{99g}Tc}$ (g = ground state) has excellent radiation properties ($\gamma$-emitter, $t_{1/2} = 6.015\,\mathrm{h}$) for radioimaging. $\ce{^{99m}Tc}$ is obtained by $\beta^-$ decay of a mother nuclide in a so-called technetium generator as $\ce{^{99m}Tc}$-pertechnetate $\ce{[^{99m}TcO4]^-}$.

1.1 (1.0 pt) Identify the mother nuclide ($\mathbf{A}$) of $\ce{^{99m}Tc}$ and and the emitted particle ($\mathbf{B}$).

$$\mathbf{A} \longrightarrow \ce{^{99m}Tc} + \mathbf{B}$$

• $\ce{[TcO4]^-}$
• $\ce{[ReO4]^-}$

Tc and Re complexes at the oxidation state +V ($\mathrm{d}^2$ systems) which contain a terminal oxo- (O=) or nitrido-ligand (N≡) are diamagnetic. The scheme below shows three possible molecular orbital energy diagrams.

$\ce{((C4H9)4N)[^{99g}TcO4]}$ is a colorless powder. By the addition of conc. $\ce{HCl}$ this common starting compound for $\ce{^{99g}Tc}$ chemistry is converted into the green complex $\ce{((C4H9)4N)[^{99g}TcOCl4]}$.

problems.title: Electrochemical CO2 Reduction
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (33 points, 5% of the total). Electrochemical $\ce{CO2}$ Reduction

In recent years, the electrochemical conversion of $\ce{CO2}$ into higher value products has been considered a promising and technologically feasible approach to mitigate the negative climatic effects caused by its increasing levels in the atmosphere. Several technologies have been developed to achieve this goal. Among these, $\ce{CO2}$ reduction through electrochemical means ($\ce{CO2}$RR) warrants particular attention due to its ability to be powered by renewable energy to transform environmentally harmful $\ce{CO2}$ into platform chemicals.

Electrocatalysts are essential not only to accelerate the intrinsically slow $\ce{CO2}$RR but also to direct the electrolysis reaction towards the desired reaction products (product selectivity). In this context, it is not only the chemical nature of the catalyst itself which governs the resulting $\ce{CO2}$RR product distribution but also its morphological characteristics on various length scales. A new concept of $\ce{CO2}$RR catalyst design relies on the electrodeposition of foam-type materials, which offer a large surface area that is accessible to reactants (e.g. $\ce{H2O}$, $\ce{H2}$, and $\ce{CO2}$). Copper-based materials are the only known metallic $\ce{CO2}$RR catalysts that can produce hydrocarbons and alcohols in significant amounts from $\ce{CO2}$ electrolysis.

Given below are thermodynamic data of selected substances:

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} & \Delta_f H^\ominus\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) & S^\ominus\ (\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}) \\ \hline \ce{H2O (l)} & -285.83 & 69.95 \\ \hline \ce{O2 (g)} & 0 & 205.15 \\ \hline \ce{H2 (g)} & 0 & 130.68 \\ \hline \ce{CO2 (g)} & -393.52 & 213.79 \\ \hline \text{ethanol (l)} & -276.00 & 159.86 \\ \hline n\text{-propanol (l)} & -302.54 & 192.80 \end{array}$$

Table 1. Standard formation enthalpy $\Delta_f H^\ominus$ and standard entropy $S^\ominus$ for some substances under standard conditions ($T = 298.15\,\mathrm{K}$, $p = 1\,\mathrm{bar}$).

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \text{Cell reaction} & E,\ \mathrm{V}\ \text{vs. SHE} \\ \hline \ce{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- <-> Cu} & +0.34 \\ \hline \ce{2H^+ + 2e^- <-> H2} & 0.00 \end{array}$$

Table 2. Selected half-cell reactions and corresponding standard potentials under the standard conditions.

2.1 (2 pt) Write and balance the chemical equation of the half-cell reactions for the following electrochemical reduction processes in acidic environment (i) $\ce{CO2}$ to ethanol; (ii) $\ce{CO2}$ to $n$-propanol.

2.2 (8 pt) Combine the half-cell of the reduction process with an $\ce{H2}/\ce{2H^+}$ half-cell where the latter acts as anode. Calculate the value of the standard cell potential of the $\ce{CO2}$ to ethanol reduction.

Cu foam electrodeposition processes (see Figure 1) were carried out in an aqueous $1.5\,\mathrm{M}$ sulfuric acid solution containing $0.2\,\mathrm{M}$ copper sulfate ($\ce{CuSO4*5H2O}$) as the copper source. A Cu disk ($1\,\mathrm{cm^2}$) and a Pt foil served as the cathode and the anode, respectively.

2.3 (3 pt) Write all the reduction and oxidation half-cell reactions taking place at the cathode and the anode, respectively.

Figure 1 shows the principle of dynamic hydrogen bubble-templated metal deposition.

Figure 2 displays top-down scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of three different Cu foams obtained upon interruption of the metal deposition at different times: $5\,\mathrm{s}$, $20\,\mathrm{s}$, and $80\,\mathrm{s}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-2-fig1.png

Figure 1. Depiction of the electrodeposition of foam-type materials. In the course of electrochemical metal deposition (black arrows) at high current densities in aqueous media, the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction (HER) takes place on the metallic (Cu) support (1). The surface becomes thus partially covered by $\ce{H2}$ bubbles (2). The $\ce{H2}$ bubbles act as a template for metal deposition (3). As a result a highly porous metal foam emerges (4).

2.4 (3 pt) Considering this mechanism, assign the correct deposition time to the Cu foams shown in Figure 2 (white boxes upper left corner).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-2-fig2.png

Figure 2. Cu foams obtained by galvanostatic Cu electrodeposition at a current density of $j = -3\,\mathrm{A\,cm^{-2}}$. The deposition was, in each case, interrupted at distinct elapsed duration: $5\,\mathrm{s}$, $20\,\mathrm{s}$, and $80\,\mathrm{s}$. The scale bar is the same in all panels.

Bimetallic CuAg systems are excellent catalysts for the electrosynthesis of alcohols from $\ce{CO2}$. $5.4\,\mathrm{mg}$ of a bimetallic Cu-Ag foam catalyst ($90\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$ Cu, $M_{Cu} = 63.546\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$; $10\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$ Ag, $M_{Ag} = 107.868\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$) was galvanostatically deposited onto a Cu foil ($1\,\mathrm{cm^2}$) at a current density of $j = -3\,\mathrm{A\,cm^{-2}}$ applied for $20\,\mathrm{s}$ (the minus sign accounts for a reductive/cathodic process).

2.5 (5 pt) Calculate the Faradaic efficiency (FE in %) of this metal deposition process. FE is defined as $Q_\text{product}/Q_\text{total}\cdot 100\%$. $Q$ denotes the charge.

We consider a $\ce{CO2}$ electrolysis experiment carried out in $35\,\mathrm{mL}$ $\ce{CO2}$-saturated $0.5\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{KHCO3}$ electrolyte solution over the bimetallic Cu-Ag foam catalyst ($90\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$ Cu; $10\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$ Ag). The $\ce{CO2}$ electrolysis was carried out at a constant (total) current density of $j(tot) = -30\,\mathrm{mA\,cm^{-2}}$ for $3600\,\mathrm{s}$ (note the current density is normalized to the geometric surface area of $1\,\mathrm{cm^2}$; the minus sign accounts for a reductive/cathodic process). A product analysis, carried out after the electrolysis, revealed mass concentrations of $41.3\,\mathrm{mg\,L^{-1}}$ and $7.4\,\mathrm{mg\,L^{-1}}$ for ethanol and $n$-propanol, respectively. Both alcohols are liquid reaction products and accumulate in the electrolyte in the course of the electrolysis reaction. We assume that gaseous hydrogen ($\ce{H2}$) is formed as the only by-product of the process.

2.6 (8 pt) Calculate the current densities required for the formation of (a) ethanol ($MW_\text{ethanol} = 46.08\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$) and (b) $n$-propanol ($MW_{n\text{-propanol}} = 60.10\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$) assuming that the current densities do not change with electrolysis time.

2.7 (4 pt) Calculate the volume of the formed hydrogen on the $1\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ catalyst area at $298.15\,\mathrm{K}$ and $1\,\mathrm{bar}$, assuming ideal behavior of the formed hydrogen, and its complete release into the gas phase. If you did not get a result in Task 2.5, continue with $FE_{(EtOH)} = 45.1\%$ and $FE_{(PrOH)} = 4.8\%$.

problems.title: Artificial Photosynthesis
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (29 points, 6% of the total). Artificial Photosynthesis

The field of artificial photosynthesis research aims at storing solar energy in chemical bonds. Photons are absorbed by exciting sensitizers, thereby producing a charge-separated state. The excited electron is transferred to a catalyst (hydrogen evolving catalyst, HER), which is reduced twice and then produces $\ce{H2}$. The photosensitizer or light absorber is often $\ce{[Ru(bpy)3]^{2+}}$ (bpy=2,2'-bipyridine), and the HERs are often cobalt complexes.

Energetics of Water Splitting

3.1 (3 pt) Calculate the enthalpy of the reaction $\ce{H2(g) -> 2H^+(aq) + 2e^-}$.

Solvation enthalpy of proton: $\Delta H_{aq}(\ce{H^+}) = -1190\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

Ionization energy of hydrogen: $\mathrm{IE}_1 = 13.6\,\mathrm{eV}$

Dissociation enthalpy of $\ce{H2}$: $\Delta H_\mathrm{diss}(\ce{H2}) = 432\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

Ideally, electrochemical water splitting into $\ce{O2}$ and $\ce{H2}$ runs at $1.23\,\mathrm{V}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Since $T\Delta S$ for this process is $> 0$, heat from the environment is needed. If additional voltage produces the heat required to compensate the decrease in temperature the process is called thermoneutral.

The enthalpy of $\ce{H2O(l)}$ formation at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $\Delta H^\circ_{\ce{H2O}}$, is $-285\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

3.2 (4 pt) Calculate (a) the water splitting reaction entropy $\Delta S^\circ_\mathrm{R}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ of 1 mol of $\ce{H2O}$ and (b) the voltage at which water splitting is thermoneutral.

Catalysts

Cobalt-salen (salcomin) type complexes are potential catalysts for $\ce{H2}$ formation from protons and electrons. The structure of salcomin is given below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-3-fig1.png

Figure 1. The structure of salcomin.

3.3 (3 pt)

• Determine the oxidation state of the cobalt atom in salcomin.
• Determine the geometric structure around the cobalt center of salcomin, choosing from these three possibilities: tetrahedral, square planar or octahedral.

In solution, salcomin can bind $\ce{O2}$; that links two salcomin moieties by coordinating to the two Co centres. The oxidation state of both Co centres is then +III.

3.4 (2 pt) Draw the resulting structure.

The $\ce{H2}$ formation takes place exclusively at the cobalt center. The reaction is described by a 4-step catalytic cycle starting with $\ce{Co^{2+}}$ using 2 $\ce{H^+}$ and 2 electrons. During one step a hydride is formed by an intramolecular electron transfer.

3.5 (6 pt) Write down two possible variations of the catalytic cycle with charges of the complex and oxidations states of the Co center. The oxidation state on the Co center should not be larger than +III. Mark the hydride formation step with an asterisk and label $\ce{H^+}$ uptake with C (chemical reaction), and electron uptake with E (electrochemical reaction), see example cycle in Figure 2 below. $[\mathrm{Co^{II}}]$ stands for the Cobalt-salen complex.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-3-fig2.png

Figure 2. An example cycle for task 3.5.

Redox Potentials

• Write down the corresponding overall reaction for both processes (only for the complexes, capable of performing it) and calculate the cell potentials at neutral pH.
• The half-cell potential for the proton reduction at pH = 7, $T = 298\,\mathrm{K}$ is $-0.41\,\mathrm{V}$.

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \text{Co(III/II) redox couple} & E^\circ\ \text{vs normal hydrogen electrode} \\ \hline \ce{[Co(H2O)6]}^{3+/2+} & +1.92\,\mathrm{V} \\ \hline \ce{[Co(C2O4)3]}^{3-/4-} & +0.55\,\mathrm{V} \\ \hline \ce{[Co(EDTA)]}^{1-/2-} & +0.38\,\mathrm{V} \\ \hline \ce{[Co(NH3)6]}^{3+/2+} & +0.06\,\mathrm{V} \\ \hline \ce{[Co(en)3]}^{3+/2+} & -0.18\,\mathrm{V} \\ \hline \ce{[Co(CN)5]}^{2-/3-} & -0.6\,\mathrm{V} \end{array}$$

Table 1. Possible redox couples for task 3.6. $\ce{[C2O4]^{2-}}$ = oxalate, en = 1,2-ethylendiamine.

A Glimpse at the Natural Process

The natural storage of biological $\ce{H2}$ equivalents is NADPH, which is produced from $\ce{NADP^+}$ through the addition of a hydride ion. The structure of NADPH is shown in Figure 3.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-3-fig3.png

Figure 3. The structure of NADPH.

3.7 (1 pt) Draw the structure of $\ce{NADP^+}$.

Chlorophyll has an extinction coefficient of about $\varepsilon = 8\cdot 10^4\,\mathrm{M^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$ at $680\,\mathrm{nm}$.

3.8 (4 pt) Assuming an efficiency (photon to hydrogen H atom) of $\phi = 20\%$ at $680\,\mathrm{nm}$ and at a photon flux of $100\,\mathrm{nE\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$ ($1\,\mathrm{E} = 1\,\mathrm{mol}$ of photons), calculate a) the number of photons per second and b) the concentration of chlorophyll in a 1x1x1 cm cell needed to get a turnover frequency of $1\,\mathrm{nmol}\ \ce{H2}$ per second.

The synthesis of fluorinated organic compounds is nowadays heavily based on the availability of specifically designed reagents, compound $\mathbf{4}$ below being an example.

problems.title: Hydrodesulfurization
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (34.5 points, 7% of the total). Hydrodesulfurization

The production of sulfur-free fuels is the general trend towards lowering the emission of sulfur-containing compounds that are toxic to the environment. To remove sulfur, the hydrogen-assisted hydrodesulfurization process is used at the refineries.

5.1 (2.5 pt) Draw the structure of products $\mathbf{A}$ to $\mathbf{E}$ of thiophene hydrodesulfurization, knowing that $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are cyclic regioisomers and $\mathbf{C}$ is cyclic.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-5-fig1.png

Figure 1. Thiophene hydrodesulfurization process.

Sulfur has two most common natural stable isotopes, $\ce{^{32}S}$ and $\ce{^{34}S}$, with a relative molar abundance of $\chi(\ce{^{32}S}) = 94.8\%$ and $\chi(\ce{^{34}S}) = 4.37\%$, respectively. For hydrogen, the stable natural isotopes are $\ce{^1H}$ and $\ce{^2H}$(D), with a relative molar abundance of $\chi(\ce{^1H}) = 99.986\%$ and $\chi(\ce{^2H}) = 0.014\%$, respectively.

5.2 (3 pt) Considering only the isotopes listed above, list all isotopologues of $\ce{H2S}$.

5.3 (3.5 pt) Considering only the isotopes listed above, list all isotopologue of $\ce{H2S}$ containing simultaneously D and $\ce{^{34}S}$ nuclei and for each calculate the respective relative molar abundance in %.

The desulfurization is a catalytic process typically carried out over $\ce{MoS2}$ supported on $\ce{SiO2}$ ($\ce{MoS2}/\ce{SiO2}$) catalyst. To study the surface of the catalyst, isotope exchange methods can be employed. The isotope exchange reaction takes place at the gas-solid interface, resulting in the exchange of the surface atoms exclusively. In a first approximation, the bulk atoms do not participate in the exchange (Figure 2).

In the experiment, the isotope exchange between the $\ce{MoS2}/\ce{SiO2}$ catalyst (Mo mass fraction $w_\mathrm{Mo} = 4.280\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$, initially containing only $\ce{^{32}S}$) and gaseous isotopically-labeled $\ce{H2^{34}S}$ was studied in a flow reactor (Figure 2). The $\ce{MoS2}/\ce{SiO2}$ catalyst ($m_\mathrm{cat} = 1.2350\,\mathrm{g}$) was kept in a flow ($\mathrm{p} = 1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$, $v = 20.0\,\mathrm{mL\,min^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{T} = 23.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) of gas mixture containing $\ce{H2^{34}S}$ balanced with Ar (volume fraction $\phi_{\ce{H2^{34}S}} = 1.00\,\mathrm{vol.\%}$ $\ce{H2^{34}S}$, $\ce{^{34}S}$ isotopic purity $\alpha = 99.95\,mol.\%$).

The experiment duration was $t = 10.0\,\mathrm{min}$ and gas from the outlet was collected during the entire experiment. The measured fraction of $\ce{^{34}S}$ isotope among the sulfur atoms ($\gamma$) in the collected gas phase was $\gamma = 87.3\,\mathrm{mol.\%}$. Assume ideal gas behavior, and that the elemental (not isotopic!) composition of $\ce{MoS2}$ on the surface and in the bulk are identical, and by the end of the experiment all sulfur atoms from the surface are exchanged with the gas phase.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-5-fig2.png

Figure 2. Schematic representation of the experiment in the course ($\mathbf{A}$) and at the final stage ($\mathbf{B}$). Sulfur atoms on the surface are shown in red, sulfur atoms in the bulk are shown in blue. Molybdenum atoms are not shown.

5.4 (5 pt) Calculate the number of exchanged sulfur atoms $n(S)_\mathrm{surface}$, give your answer in mol.

If you have been unable to calculate the number of total exchanged sulfur atoms, use the value $1.53\cdot 10^{-5}\,mol$ in all the following calculations.

Assume that the $\ce{MoS2}$ phase consists of uniform spherical particles, and at the end of the experiment all sulfur atoms located on the surface are exchanged, while the bulk atoms did not participate in the exchange reaction. The density $\rho$ of $\ce{MoS2}$ is $\rho = 5.06\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, the average area occupied by S and Mo atoms on the surface is equal to $A_\mathrm{S} = 3.00\cdot 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{m^2}$ and $A_\mathrm{Mo} = 5.00\cdot 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{m^2}$, respectively. The area of a sphere with radius $R$ can be calculated as $S = 4\pi R^2$, and its volume as $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3$. Assume that isotopic composition does not affect the density of $\ce{MoS2}$.

5.5 (8 pt) Calculate the particle radius $R$ of the $\ce{MoS2}$ particles, give your answer in nm.

In reality, the isotopically-labeled atoms from the surface diffuse into the bulk and the non-labeled atoms from the bulk travel to the surface, undergoing a gradual exchange (Figure 3A). Therefore, for a given moment, the fraction of the labeled atoms inside the particle decreases from the surface of the particle to its center. Simultaneously, with an increase in time of exchange, the involvement of bulk atoms to the exchange reaction increases, as sketched in Figure 3B.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-5-fig3.png

Figure 3. $\mathbf{A}$) Schematic representation of the diffusion of sulfur isotopes from the surface to the bulk in $\ce{MoS2}$ particle. Sulfur atoms on the surface are shown in red, sulfur atoms in the bulk are shown in blue. Molybdenum atoms are not shown. $\mathbf{B}$) The fraction of $\ce{^{34}S}$ atoms in the bulk as function of time and distance from center of the particle. $r_\mathrm{edge}$ corresponds to the radius of $\ce{MoS2}$ particle.

At the end of the experiment, the surface atoms are completely exchanged, and additionally a fraction of the bulk is exchanged due to the diffusion. The fraction $F$ of the exchanged bulk atoms ($n(S)^{ex}_{bulk}$) and the total bulk atoms of sulfur ($n(S)^{total}_{bulk}$) can be calculated as follows: $F = n(S)^{ex}_{bulk}/n(S)^{total}_{bulk} = 1 - e^{-\frac{D\cdot t}{R^2}}$, where $t$ is the time of exchange experiment (described above), $R$ is the particle size (radius for a spherical shape particle) and $D$ is the diffusion coefficient. The catalyst described above was independently studied by means of electron microscopy, which showed that the $\ce{MoS2}$ particles are uniformly distributed spheres with a radius of $35.0\,\mathrm{nm}$.

5.6 (12.5 pt) Using $R = 35.0\,\mathrm{nm}$ as the radius and the data of the exchange experiment described above, calculate the diffusion coefficient $D$ for the diffusion of sulfur atoms in $\ce{MoS2}$, give your answer in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. In your calculations, use the following approximation: $e^x \approx 1 + x$ for $x \ll 1$.

problems.title: Direct conversion of methane to methanol
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (32 points, 7% of the total). Direct conversion of methane to methanol

Methane is widely available as natural gas making it an attractive feedstock for the chemical industry, such as for the production of methanol. However, control of this process is challenging as methanol is more easily oxidized than methane.

Overoxidation is avoided in a chemical looping process, where active sites of copper-exchanged zeolite catalysts provide only the single oxygen atom required for oxidation to methanol and are consumed. In a second step, the catalyst is regenerated with oxygen in the absence of methane. The scheme below shows two potential catalytic copper sites.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-6-fig1.png

During the reaction, $\mathrm{Cu^{II}}$ is reduced to $\mathrm{Cu^{I}}$.

6.1 (2 pt) Give the number of $\mathbf{S1}$ sites and the number of $\mathbf{S2}$ sites required to oxidize one methane molecule to methanol.

In the absence of oxygen, the formed methanol does not desorb from zeolite. If the reaction is performed in a container with constant volume and temperature (an autoclave), a pressure drop results only from the consumption of methane, which can be considered as an ideal gas. In a $1\,\mathrm{L}$ autoclave containing $200\,\mathrm{mg}$ of zeolite loaded with $4.3\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$ copper, the initial methane pressure $p_0 = 933\,\mathrm{Pa}$ dropped to $p_\infty = 925\,\mathrm{Pa}$ after completion of the reaction at $528\,\mathrm{K}$.

6.2 (4 pt) Compute the percentage of copper that reacted.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-6-fig2.png

Figure 1: Semi-logarithmic graph of normalized methane pressure $p$ versus time for the reaction with copper-loaded zeolite containing sites $\mathbf{S1}$ and $\mathbf{S2}$ in an autoclave at various temperatures. The symbols denote experimental data points. The solid lines are linear fits to appropriate time ranges. The dotted lines are guides to the eyes.

6.3 (1 pt) Experimental data is plotted in Figure 1. Based on this, decide on the (pseudo) order of the oxidation of $\ce{CH4}$. Tick the box with the correct statement:

• The reaction is of (pseudo) zeroth order.
• The reaction is of (pseudo) first order.
• The reaction is of (pseudo) second order.

6.4 (2 pt) Write down the (pseudo) rate law for the oxidation of $\ce{CH4}$ that is consistent with the experimental data under the given conditions. Note that it may depend on the concentrations of $\ce{CH4}$ as well as of sites $\mathbf{S1}$ and $\mathbf{S2}$ and on the rate constants.

6.5 (4 pt) Tick the boxes with correct statements:

• At least two types of copper sites react, each with a different rate constant.
• The overall methane oxidation by copper-loaded zeolite is faster at higher temperature.
• At higher temperature, a larger fraction of the copper sites will have reacted with methane after completion of the reaction.
• One of the reactions becomes slower at higher temperature.

Paramagnetic sites $\mathbf{S1}$ can be observed by electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy, whereas diamagnetic sites $\mathbf{S2}$ do not give an EPR signal. EPR spectroscopy measures the number of electron spins. Thus, the number of $\mathbf{S1}$ sites is proportional to the double integral $I_2$ of the EPR spectrum, i.e. $[\mathbf{S1}] \propto I_2$. Spectra were measured at different temperatures $T$ and at each temperature at different times $t$ after initiating the reaction.

6.6 (3 pt) Derive the equation linear in time that relates $I_2(t)$ to the rate constant for the loss of $\mathbf{S1}$ sites.

6.7 (3 pt) Tick the boxes for each measurement that needs to be calibrated with a known Cu(II) standard:

• Total number of paramagnetic Cu(II) sites in the sample
• Concentration of paramagnetic Cu(II) sites in the sample
• Rate constant
• Types of different paramagnetic Cu(II) species in the sample

From EPR measurements, it is known that the rate constant for the reaction with $\mathbf{S1}$ sites at $528\,\mathrm{K}$ is $2.604\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

6.8 (3 pt) Considering Figure 1 and based on a calculation, decide if methane reacts faster or slower with $\mathbf{S2}$ sites than with $\mathbf{S1}$ sites:

• Methane reacts faster with $\mathbf{S1}$.
• Both reaction rates are the same.
• Methane reacts faster with $\mathbf{S2}$.

Methanol can be further converted into valuable olefins with different zeolite catalysts. In this process, one observes an intermediate product with molar mass $86.09\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$, elemental analysis ($55.8\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$ C, $7.0\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$ H) and an $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectrum consisting of signals at four different chemical shifts ($\mathbf{a}$: $12.2\,\mathrm{ppm}$ (1H, s), broad, disappears when $\ce{D2O}$ is added; $\mathbf{b}$: $6.3\,\mathrm{ppm}$ (1H, d); $\mathbf{c}$: $5.7\,\mathrm{ppm}$ (1H, d); $\mathbf{d}$: $2.0\,\mathrm{ppm}$ (3H, s)).

6.9 (4 pt) Draw the structure of the intermediate product and assign protons $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{d}$.

The United States Department of Energy assigned 12 chemical compounds only containing C, H and O as platform chemicals. These are the most promising candidates, easy to prepare from renewable resources and with multiple target derivatives to be prepared from them.

One of them is compound $\mathbf{A}$, that can either be further derivatized or used for example in medicinal applications or in detergents.

• $\ce{^1H}$ NMR in DMSO: $7.81\,\mathrm{ppm}$ ($\mathbf{a}$, s), $13.0\,\mathrm{ppm}$ ($\mathbf{b}$, s, broad, disappears when $\ce{D2O}$ is added), both signals have the same integral.
• $\ce{^{13}C}$ NMR: $165.1\,\mathrm{ppm}$ ($\mathbf{1}$), $150.6\,\mathrm{ppm}$ ($\mathbf{2}$) and $120.6\,\mathrm{ppm}$ ($\mathbf{3}$).
• MW: $156.03\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$. Elemental analysis (EA): $46.15\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$ C, $2.56\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$ H.

6.10 (6 pt) Give a possible structure of $\mathbf{A}$ and assign all protons and carbon $\mathbf{1}$.

problems.title: Enzyme Kinetics
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (34 points, 7% of the total). Enzyme Kinetics

The Michaelis–Menten (MM) mechanism was introduced in 1913 to describe the kinetics of enzyme catalysis. In this mechanism, enzyme $\mathbf{E}$ catalyzes the conversion of substrate $\mathbf{S}$ to the product $\mathbf{P}$:

$$\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{S} \underset{k_2}{\overset{k_1}{\rightleftarrows}} \mathbf{ES} \overset{k_3}{\rightarrow} \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{P}$$

The initial rate for an enzymatic reaction following the MM mechanism is usually given as:

$$v_0 = \frac{v_\mathrm{max}[\mathbf{S}]_0}{[\mathbf{S}]_0 + K_M} \qquad (1)$$

when the initial concentration of $\mathbf{E}$ is much lower than the initial concentration of $\mathbf{S}$ ($[\mathbf{E}]_0 \ll [\mathbf{S}]_0$). The Michaelis constant is defined as $K_M = \frac{k_2 + k_3}{k_1}$. The initial rate can also be expressed as the product of the relative flow $j$ and $[\mathbf{E}]_0$:

$$v_0 = j[\mathbf{E}]_0 \qquad (2)$$

Note: Questions 7.1 and 7.2 can have one, multiple, or no correct answer(s).

7.1 (3 pt) Choose the correct alternative form(s) of the initial rate ($v_0$) expressions (1) and (2). $[\mathbf{ES}]_\mathrm{max}$ is the maximum concentration of the $\mathbf{ES}$ complex.

• $v_0 = \dfrac{k_3[\mathbf{E}]_0[\mathbf{S}]_0}{[\mathbf{S}]_0 + K_M}$
• $v_0 = \dfrac{k_3[\mathbf{E}]}{1 + K_M/[\mathbf{S}]_0}$
• $v_0 = j[\mathbf{ES}]_\mathrm{max}$
• $v_0 = \dfrac{k_3[\mathbf{E}]_0[\mathbf{ES}]_\mathrm{max}}{[\mathbf{S}]_0 + K_M}$
• $v_0 = \dfrac{k_3[\mathbf{E}]_0}{1 + K_M/[\mathbf{S}]_0}$
• $v_0 = \dfrac{j[\mathbf{E}]_0}{K_M + [\mathbf{S}]_0}$

7.2 (4 pt) Choose the pair(s) of axes ($y$ vs. $x$) that are expected to give a linear plot:

• $v_0$ vs. $1/[\mathbf{S}]_0$
• $v_0$ vs. $v_0/K_M$
• $v_0$ vs. $K_M/v_0$
• $1/v_0$ vs. $v_0/[\mathbf{S}]_0$
• $1/v_0$ vs. $v_0/K_M$
• $[\mathbf{S}]_0/v_0$ vs. $[\mathbf{S}]_0$

Many enzymes catalyze multi- rather than single-substrate transformations. However, if the concentration of one of the substrates is much higher than that of the other substrate or it is kept constant, the MM kinetics is also valid. Here we will look at two independent enzymatic systems that follow the MM kinetics.

Enzymatic System I

Enzyme $\mathbf{E}$ converts substrates $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ to products $\mathbf{P_A}$ and $\mathbf{P_B}$. At rapid pre-equilibrium between the free enzyme and all enzyme-substrate complexes, the following $v_0$ equation applies:

$$v_0 = \frac{k[\mathbf{E}]_0[\mathbf{A}]_0[\mathbf{B}]_0}{(K + [\mathbf{A}]_0)(K + [\mathbf{B}]_0)} \qquad (3)$$

$k$ is the rate constant of one of the reactions. The same equilibrium constant $K$ characterizes the dissociation of either substrate from the corresponding active site of $\mathbf{E}$.

7.3 (2 pt) Show that equation (3) takes the MM form (1) if the concentration of substrate $\mathbf{B}$ is maintained at a constant value $c_0$. Give the expression for $v_\mathrm{max}$ in this case.

7.4 (8 pt) Propose a kinetic scheme for the Enzymatic System I consistent with equation (3), showing all the intermediates and products. Indicate the reaction with a rate constant $k$.

Enzymatic System II

Enzyme $\mathbf{E}$ has five active sites, each of which is specific to one of the substrates $\mathbf{S_A}$, $\mathbf{S_B}$, or $\mathbf{S_C}$ that are selectively transformed to products $\mathbf{P_A}$, $\mathbf{P_B}$, or $\mathbf{P_C}$, respectively. There is at least one active site for each substrate. Each active site is independent of the others.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-7-fig1.png

For $\mathbf{E}$, it is known that:

1. The affinity for $\mathbf{S_C}$ is higher than for $\mathbf{S_B}$.

2. The plot of $v_{0i}$ vs $v_{0i}/[\mathbf{S}_i]_0$, known as Eadie–Hofstee plot, for $\mathbf{S_A}$, $\mathbf{S_B}$, $\mathbf{S_C}$, with rate given per active site ($v_{0i}$), is shown below, but the scale and the legend are omitted.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-7-fig2.png

3. When $\mathbf{E}$ is saturated with $\mathbf{S_A}$, $\mathbf{S_B}$, $\mathbf{S_C}$, the catalytic turnover number (TON) for $\mathbf{S_C}$ per site is $10200\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$, and $2023$ $\mathbf{P_A}$, $\mathbf{P_B}$, $\mathbf{P_C}$, product molecules in total are synthesized per second. At the same time, no more than $5.94\cdot 10^6$ molecules of $\mathbf{P_A}$ and $\mathbf{P_B}$ are detected to form per hour.

4. At equimolar concentrations of $\mathbf{S_A}$, $\mathbf{S_B}$, $\mathbf{S_C}$, which are at least $1000$ times lower than corresponding $K_M$ values, the $\mathbf{P_A}$, $\mathbf{P_B}$, $\mathbf{P_C}$, concentrations become proportional to the catalytic efficiency ($\varepsilon_i = \frac{k_{i3}}{K_{M,i}}$), and their ratio is $3:2:5$, respectively.

5. Two $\mathbf{ES}_i$ complexes have equal rate constants for dissociation to $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{S}_i$. The activation barrier for the reaction of $\mathbf{ES_C}$ into the initial compounds is $1266\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$ higher than for the reaction into the final products. Assume that the pre-exponential factors are equal for both reactions and $T = 25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

6. For $\mathbf{E}$ + $\mathbf{S}_i$ reaction: $k_{c1} = 1.57\cdot 10^7\,\mathrm{M^{-1}s^{-1}}$ and $k_{a1} = k_{b1}$.

7.5 (17 pt) Fill in the following table and provide your calculations.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} & \text{Number of active sites} & k_1 & k_2 & k_3 & K_M \\ \hline \mathbf{S_A} & & & & & \\ \hline \mathbf{S_B} & & & & & \\ \hline \mathbf{S_C} & & 1.57\cdot 10^7\,\mathrm{M^{-1}s^{-1}} & & & \end{array}$$

Hints:

• Use information from 1. and 2. to find the relation between $K_{M,A}$, $K_{M,B}$ and $K_{M,C}$ ($<, >, =$).
• Information from 3. and 5. allows you to complete the first column (number of active sites for each substrate) and the last row (all the constants for substrate $\mathbf{S_C}$) of the table. Check that the sum of active sites is equal to 5.

problems.title: Ammonia
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (24 points, 7.5% of the total). Ammonia

The Haber–Bosch process to produce ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen is one of the most impactful industrial processes in history and estimated to sustain around half of today’s population. The process typically occurs at constant temperature and pressure, $400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $100\,\mathrm{bar}$, respectively. Equilibrium between the reactants and the product is established over Fe-based catalysts in the reactor.

The standard gas phase thermochemistry data of $\ce{N2}$, $\ce{H2}$, and $\ce{NH3}$ are shown below. Assume the enthalpy and entropy of the reaction are temperature independent.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} & \ce{N2(g)} & \ce{H2(g)} & \ce{NH3(g)} \\ \hline \Delta_f H^\circ/(\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) & 0 & 0 & -45.9 \\ \hline S^\circ/(\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}) & 191.6 & 130.7 & 192.8 \end{array}$$

1.1 (7 pt) Find the molar nitrogen conversion (in percent) to ammonia under the production conditions from a stoichiometric mixture of nitrogen and hydrogen. Show your calculations for partial credit. If you cannot find a result, use 66% in subsequent calculations.

One of the reactants in the Haber–Bosch process is hydrogen, mainly produced by steam reforming of methane. The two-step process starts with $\ce{CH4}$ reacting with water to produce $\ce{H2}$ and $\ce{CO}$. In a subsequent step, $\ce{CO}$ reacts with water to form $\ce{CO2}$ and additional hydrogen.

1.2 (2 pt) Write the overall reaction equation for the combined process. Give the mass of $\ce{CO2}$ produced in the reaction per $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ of $\ce{H2}$ ($m_{\ce{CO2}}$).

In reality, $7.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ of carbon dioxide is produced for each $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ of hydrogen in steam reforming. The generated ammonia is classified based on $\ce{CO2}$ management. For "gray" ammonia, the $\ce{CO2}$ is released in the atmosphere; for "blue" ammonia, it is captured and stored. "Green" ammonia is made from hydrogen produced without carbon emissions.

1.3 (3 pt) Calculate the mass of the carbon dioxide ($m_{\ce{CO2},\,\text{blue}}$) that needs to be captured to produce 40,000 kg of “blue” ammonia. Assume that carbon dioxide only comes from a real steam reforming process. Assume further that the ammonia is produced at equilibrium from a stoichiometric mixture of nitrogen and hydrogen.

Using cheap renewable hydrogen, the prospect of converting it with captured $\ce{CO2}$ into methanol appears promising. However, in this procedure, there is a competing reaction that produces $\ce{CO}$:

$$\ce{CO2(g) + 3 H2(g) <=> CH3OH(g) + H2O(g)}$$

$$\ce{CO2(g) + H2(g) <=> CO(g) + H2O(g)}$$

Into a reactor maintained at $250\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $50\,\mathrm{bar}$, a mixture containing $\ce{CO2}:\ce{H2}$ in a molar ratio of $1:4$ is fed. It has been found that the $\ce{CO2}$ conversion is 30% and the $\ce{H2}$ conversion is 18.5% when these two reactions are at equilibrium. No other processes need to be considered.

1.4 (5 pt) Calculate the thermodynamic equilibrium constants (at $250\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) of the two reactions.

Heterogeneous copper-containing catalysts are commonly used for $\ce{CO2}$ hydrogenation. Two specific, Cu-containing catalysts ($A$ and $B$) showed promise for converting $\ce{CO2}$ to methanol. These catalysts differ not only in their catalytic rates, but also in surface area, Cu content, and Cu dispersion (the ratio of surface Cu to the total Cu in the catalyst).

Cu dispersion is important, because only Cu species at the surface are active in $\ce{CO2}$ hydrogenation. Under this assumption, 1 mole of active sites corresponds to 1 mole of surface Cu. The efficiency of these active sites is shown by their turnover frequencies ($TOF$, moles of product formed per moles of active site in a given time).

The table below reports the performance (reported as mass of produced methanol per total catalyst mass in a given time) and the specific surface areas of the two catalysts. The Cu content and dispersion of the catalysts was also measured and reported as follows:

1. At the start, all the copper in the catalysts (oxidized beforehand) is present as Cu(II); that was fully reduced to Cu(0) with hydrogen. No other species in the catalysts reacted with hydrogen besides copper oxides.
2. $\ce{N2O}$ was introduced to the reduced samples at room temperature. At this temperature, $\ce{N2O}$ only oxidizes active surface sites to Cu(I).
3. The Cu(I) active surface sites were reduced again to Cu(0) with hydrogen.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-1-fig1.png

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Catalyst performance} \\ (\mathrm{g_{MeOH}\,g_{cat}^{-1}\,h^{-1}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Specific surface area} \\ (\mathrm{m^2\,g_{cat}^{-1}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\ce{H2}\text{ consumed in} \\ \text{step 1 }(\mathrm{mmol\,g_{cat}^{-1}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\ce{H2}\text{ consumed in} \\ \text{step 3 }(\mathrm{mmol\,g_{cat}^{-1}})\end{array} \\ \hline \text{Catalyst } A & 0.80 & 100 & 5.0 & 0.30 \\ \hline \text{Catalyst } B & 0.90 & 120 & 4.0 & 0.70 \end{array}$$

1.5 (3 pt) Find the methanol production rate per total mass of Cu (in $\mathrm{g_{MeOH}\,g_{Cu}^{-1}\,h^{-1}}$) for catalysts $A$ and $B$.

1.6 (3 pt) Find the $TOF$ (in $\mathrm{h^{-1}}$) for catalysts $A$ and $B$. If you cannot find results, use $TOF_\text{Catalyst A} = 100\,\mathrm{h^{-1}}$ and $TOF_\text{Catalyst B} = 1\,\mathrm{h^{-1}}$ in subsequent calculations.

1.7 (1 pt) Indicate the correct statement on the answer sheet.
a. Catalyst $A$ has more efficient active sites.
b. Catalyst $B$ has more efficient active sites.
c. The two catalysts have active sites with the same efficiency.

problems.title: Electronic nose
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (12 points, 6% of the total). Electronic nose

Resistive gas sensors, especially those using semiconducting metal oxides (SMOX), are becoming increasingly popular. They can detect tiny amounts of impurities, are small and stable, and are easy to make and use. These features make SMOX sensors stand out among the many types of gas sensors that work on different physical and chemical principles.

The mixed oxide $\mathbf{X}$ that has the normal spinel crystal structure, $\mathrm{A^{2+}B^{3+}{}_2O^{2-}{}_4}$, is an example of one of these SMOX materials. $\mathbf{X}$ can be obtained by decomposition of the crystalline hydrated metal oxalate $\mathbf{Z}\ce{C2O4}\cdot k\ce{H2O}$ of metal $\mathbf{Z}$ on air. When heated to $140\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the crystalline hydrate loses 19.7% of its mass. Further heating in air leads to the formation of $2.407\,\mathrm{g}$ of black colored $\mathbf{X}$ at $500\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $3.8\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ of carbon dioxide at $101325\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

2.1 (4 pt) Determine the formula of $\mathbf{X}$ and the value of $\boldsymbol{k}$ in $\mathbf{Z}\ce{C2O4}\cdot k\ce{H2O}$.

In the spinel structures oxygen atoms form a face centered cubic (FCC) lattice. In normal spinels the $\mathrm{A^{2+}}$ cations occupy part of the tetrahedral, and the $\mathrm{B^{3+}}$ cations occupy part of the octahedral lattice sites.

2.2 (2 pt) Calculate the percentage of the tetrahedral sites that is occupied in the case of a normal spinel $\mathrm{A^{2+}B^{3+}{}_2O^{2-}{}_4}$.

In addition to the normal spinels, the $\mathrm{MM'_2O_4}$ general formula also describes the inverse and the mixed spinel structures. Here M are the tetrahedrally coordinated, M′ the octahedrally coordinated cations, but contrary to normal spinels, particular cations are not restricted to a single lattice site. A characteristic of the inverse spinel structures is that the electron configuration of the M′ site cations is $\mathrm{d^0}$, $\mathrm{d^5}$ or $\mathrm{d^{10}}$.

2.3 (1 pt) Select on the answer sheet two of the given formulas, which correspond to the structure of inverse spinel: $\ce{Fe3O4}$, $\ce{NiFe2O4}$, $\ce{Mn3O4}$, $\ce{FeCr2O4}$.

Semiconductors are materials whose orbitals contain a small excess or deficit of electrons, leading to negative or positive charges (holes), respectively. These charges can move through the semiconductor and allow it to conduct electricity. Chemical reactions can increase or decrease the charge on a semiconductor, altering its conductivity.

$\mathbf{X}$ is an example of a semiconductor where electricity is carried by positive charges (holes). For a resistive gas sensor based on $\mathbf{X}$, the resistance $R$ is measured over time $t$, while passing a gas over the sensor. This allows redox reactions to occur between the gas and the semiconductor surface, which will change the resistance of the sensor depending on the donor/acceptor properties of the gas. Figure 1 shows the two different types of signal obtained this way.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-2-fig1.png

Figure 1: plot of resistance against time for two possible signal types, (a) and (b). Grey bars = air, white bars = air + analyte gas.

2.4 (2 pt) Correlate the signal type (a or b) obtained from the $\mathbf{X}$ based sensor with the analyte gases ($\ce{H2S}$, $\ce{O3}$, $\ce{NO2}$, $\ce{NH3}$) during their detection at low concentrations.

The dependence of the specific conductivity ($\sigma$) of $\mathbf{X}$ on temperature is described by the Arrhenius law: $\sigma(T) = \sigma_0 \exp(-E_a/(RT))$, where $E_a$ is the activation energy of conductivity. Three types of conductivity can be distinguished in different temperature ranges:

Ionization (I): 444–570 K, Impurity (II): 585–765 K, and Intrinsic (III): 800–905 K.

The sketch below illustrates the conductivity-temperature relation for the three temperature ranges.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-2-fig2.png

2.5 (3 pt) Based on the sketch above, order the activation energies associated with the different conductivity types, $E_a(I)$, $E_a(II)$, and $E_a(III)$, from largest to smallest.

problems.title: Tyrosinase
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (31 points, 7.5% of the total). Tyrosinase

The enzyme tyrosine 3-monooxygenase has an important biological role because it catalyzes the initial and rate-limiting step in the biosynthesis of the neurotransmitter dopamine. In this first step, L-DOPA is produced from the amino acid L-tyrosine (Tyr) in the presence of dissolved oxygen, tetrahydrofolic acid and ferrous ions. In a subsequent step, another enzyme transforms L-DOPA into dopamine.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-3-fig1.png

The activity of the tyrosine 3-monooxygenase enzyme is described well by the simplest model of enzyme action, the Michaelis-Menten equation. This gives the rate of the formation ($r$) of L-DOPA as a function of the enzyme (E) and substrate Tyr (S) concentrations as follows:

$$r = \frac{k[\mathrm{E}][\mathrm{S}]}{K_\mathrm{M} + [\mathrm{S}]}$$

The following values of enzymatic turnover frequency ($k = 250\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$) and Michaelis constant ($K_\mathrm{M} = 0.49\,\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}}$) can be used in this task when needed.

Catechol (1,2-dihydroxybenzene) inactivates the enzyme tyrosine 3-monooxygenase irreversibly by turning it into an inactive form. When a carefully purified sample of catechol is mixed with the enzyme with the exclusion of dissolved oxygen, no change is seen at all. So the reaction of catechol with dissolved oxygen, which produces o-quinone, must be important.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-3-fig2.png

This process can be studied in the absence of the enzyme. A test experiment in a reactor not in contact with ambient air at $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and at pH 7.5 gave the following kinetic data:

$$\begin{array}{l|l|l|l} \begin{array}{l}\text{time} \\ (\mathrm{min})\end{array} & \begin{array}{l}\text{catechol concentration} \\ (\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{l}\text{oxygen concentration} \\ (\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{l}o\text{-quinone concentration} \\ (\mathrm{\mu mol\,dm^{-3}})\end{array} \\ \hline 0 & 2.00 & 0.200 & 0 \\ \hline 20.0 & 1.97 & 0.170 & 30 \\ \hline 40.0 & 1.94 & 0.140 & 60 \\ \hline 60.0 & 1.91 & 0.111 & 89 \\ \hline 80.0 & 1.88 & 0.083 & 117 \\ \hline 100.0 & 1.85 & 0.054 & 146 \end{array}$$

3.1 (5.0 pt) Identify the only by-product (which is not one of the molecules shown in the table above) and write the balanced equation of the process with molecular formulas based on the kinetic data.

3.2 (2.0 pt) Calculate the initial rate ($r_0$) of o-quinone formation in this experiment with an appropriate unit.

The rate law of the process was determined by varying the initial concentrations of the reactants. Changing the oxygen concentration did not influence the initial rate of the process. Using different catechol concentrations gave the following initial rates for o-quinone formation:

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \begin{array}{l}\text{catechol concentration} \\ (\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{l}\text{initial rate of } o\text{-quinone formation} \\ (\mathrm{\mu mol\,dm^{-3}\,min^{-1}})\end{array} \\ \hline 1.0 & 0.75 \\ \hline 4.0 & 3.0 \\ \hline 6.0 & 4.5 \\ \hline 8.0 & 6.0 \\ \hline 10.0 & 7.5 \end{array}$$

3.3 (5.0 pt) Determine the rate law of the reaction between catechol and oxygen producing o-quinone. Calculate the rate constant of this process ($k_\text{catechol}$) with an appropriate unit.

In separate experiments, it was confirmed that neither o-quinone, nor the by-product inactivates the enzyme alone, nor even in combination.

An experiment in which the enzyme is reacted with catechol in the presence of dissolved oxygen did show inactivation, though.

The experiment was done in an open vessel so that any oxygen consumed in the process could be continuously replenished from air. The initial concentration of the enzyme was $4.2\,\mathrm{nmol\,dm^{-3}}$, the initial concentration of catechol was $2.00\,\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}}$ at $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and at pH 7.5.

Samples were taken regularly from the enzyme-catechol reaction mixture, and the activity of the enzyme was assayed by adding L-tyrosine, tetrahydrofolic acid and ferrous ion. During the enzyme activity measurements, the concentration of added L-tyrosine was $10.0\,\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}}$ and the concentration of L-DOPA in each assay sample was measured after 2.0 minutes. The following results were obtained:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-3-fig3.png

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \begin{array}{l}\text{inactivation reaction time} \\ t\ (\mathrm{min})\end{array} & \begin{array}{l}\text{L-DOPA concentration after 2.0 minutes from the start of the assay} \\ {[\text{DOPA}]}\ (\mathrm{\mu mol\,dm^{-3}})\end{array} \\ \hline 0 & 2.0 \\ \hline 20.0 & 1.9 \\ \hline 40.0 & 1.7 \\ \hline 60.0 & 1.3 \\ \hline 70.0 & 1.00 \\ \hline 80.0 & 0.72 \\ \hline 90.0 & 0.38 \end{array}$$

3.4 (4.0 pt) Derive a formula that allows you to calculate the actual concentration of active enzyme ([E]) from the data of these experiments in terms of $k$ ($= 250\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$), $K_\mathrm{M}$ ($= 0.49\,\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}}$), and/or reagent concentrations.

The change in the active enzyme concentration as a function of time is well described by a parabola ($[\mathrm{E}] = [\mathrm{E}]_0 - k_\text{obs} t^2$), where $k_\text{obs}$ is an observed rate constant (i.e. one that can be written later as a combination of elementary rate constants and initial concentrations), and $[\mathrm{E}]_0$ is the initial concentration of the enzyme.

3.5 (3.0 pt) Give the value of $k_\text{obs}$ with an appropriate unit.

3.6 (3.0 pt) Determine the first half-life of the enzyme inactivation reaction. Derive a formula that gives the first half-life as a function of the initial enzyme concentration and of $k_\text{obs}$.

The first half-lives for enzyme inactivation were determined using other initial catechol concentrations. The dependences of active enzyme concentrations on time were very well described by parabolas in these cases as well.

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \begin{array}{l}\text{catechol concentration} \\ (\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{l}\text{first half-life} \\ (\mathrm{min})\end{array} \\ \hline 1.0 & 140 \\ \hline 4.0 & 35 \\ \hline 6.0 & 23 \\ \hline 8.0 & 17.5 \\ \hline 10.0 & 14 \end{array}$$

3.7 (6.0 pt) Derive a rate equation of the enzyme inactivation process consistent with all the experimental observations.

3.8 (3.0 pt) What are the reactants of the rate determining step for the enzyme inactivation process? Select the ONLY correct option on the answer sheet.
A) catechol + $\ce{O2}$ → ...
B) catechol + o-quinone → ...
C) o-quinone + $\ce{O2}$ → ...
D) enzyme + 2 catechol → ...
E) enzyme + $\ce{O2}$ → ...
F) 2 catechol + $\ce{O2}$ → ...
G) enzyme + catechol → ...
H) enzyme + by-product → ...

problems.title: Potassium
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (21 points, 6% of the total). Potassium

Elementary potassium was the first metal synthesized by electrolysis (1807). Humphry Davy used voltaic cells and electrodes immersed into molten $\ce{KOH}$.

4.1 (2 pt) Give balanced equations for the processes taking place on the cathode (1) and the anode (2).

It is little known that only a year after Davy, French chemists have produced potassium in a chemical reduction. One of the methods involved a mixture of potassium carbonate and finely powdered carbon. This mixture was heated to very high temperatures in a gun barrel. Carbon monoxide and potassium vapors were leaving the end of the barrel, where the metal could be condensed to a solid.

4.2 (1 pt) Write down the balanced equation for the reaction giving only these two products.

The chemical production of potassium had a low yield. Depending on the circumstances, a considerable amount of reddish paste was left behind in the gun barrel. Gmelin isolated an interesting compound ($\mathbf{X}$) from this residue in 1825 by recrystallization in water. The exact structure of the byproduct $\mathbf{X}$ was determined more than one and a half century later.

$\mathbf{X}$ is a hydrated salt (2 mol water : 1 mol of salt) forming golden yellow crystals. Its anion has an exceptionally symmetric (shown by vibrational spectra) and stable planar cyclic structure.

The diprotic acid ($\mathbf{Y}$) that can be formed from the salt $\mathbf{X}$ has surprisingly (at least to the superficial observer) low $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ values: 0.8 and 2.2.

4.3 (3 pt) Give the pH where 95% of all dissolved acid $\mathbf{Y}$ is in the neutral acid form.

4.4 (4 pt) Calculate the pH of a $0.01\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ solution of the salt $\mathbf{X}$ in pure water.

The key step in the structure identification of $\mathbf{X}$ was the treatment of the anhydrous salt with methyl iodide. The salt reacted with two equivalents of methyl iodide. The somewhat volatile compound that was obtained had a molar mass of $170.12\,\mathrm{g/mol}$ (measured in a mass spectrometer).

A number of analogous salts were also identified in the mixture in smaller quantities. The appropriate potassium salts when treated with two equivalent of MeI gave derivatives with molar masses of: $142.11\,\mathrm{g/mol}$, $114.10\,\mathrm{g/mol}$, $198.13\,\mathrm{g/mol}$.

4.5 (4 pt) Give the empirical formula of Gmelin’s compound $\mathbf{X}$.

4.6 (3 pt) Draw the structure of the free acid $\mathbf{Y}$.

The extraordinary stability of the series of anions in the salts analogous to X can be attributed to electron delocalization.

4.7 (4 pt) Draw one resonance structure with a significant contribution for the anion in each of the four salts.

problems.title: Unknown
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (44 points, 6% of the total). Unknown

Metal containing salt $\mathbf{A}$ can be prepared in a simple exchange reaction when the cold, saturated aqueous solutions of the two distinctly colored compounds, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are mixed in stoichiometric ratio. $10.00\,\mathrm{g}$ $\mathbf{B}$ in solution mixed with the solution of $12.86\,\mathrm{g}$ $\mathbf{C}$, and immediately cooled to $2\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ will give $4.90\,\mathrm{g}$ solid $\mathbf{A}$. The yield of $\mathbf{A}$ is 32.6 %.

To determine the composition of $\mathbf{A}$, first iodometry is performed. A known mass of $\mathbf{A}$ is added to a titration flask, acidified with sulfuric acid, then KI is added in excess and there is a precipitate formation. After a few minutes, sodium citrate solution is added until the solution is free of precipitate. The citrate ions form a strong complex with a metal ion present in the mixture, reversing completely the reaction leading to the precipitate. The resulting mixture is titrated with sodium thiosulfate solution (Titration I via reaction 1). To the blue titrated solution another portion of sulfuric acid (significantly more than the initial amount) is added to protonate the citrate. The previous solid precipitate is formed once again [reaction 2]. The mixture is titrated with the same thiosulfate solution (titration II via reaction 1).

The average volumes for $100.0\,\mathrm{mg}$ $\mathbf{A}$ with $5.000\cdot10^{-2}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ thiosulfate are $54.12\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ in Titration I and $5.41\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ in Titration II.

When the aqueous solution of $\mathbf{A}$ is heated, the blue precipitate $\mathbf{D}$ can be observed [reaction 3]. Compound $\mathbf{E}$ can be crystallized from the liquid above $\mathbf{D}$. The low temperature during the synthesis of $\mathbf{A}$ is important to avoid contamination by $\mathbf{E}$.

5.1 (4.0 pt) Write balanced equations for reactions [1] and [2].

The thermal decomposition of $\mathbf{A}$ was studied in detail. When pure $\mathbf{A}$ is slowly heated, already at around $75\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ it explodes. When the compound is dispersed in aluminium oxide and the mixture is heated, then the matrix absorbs the excess heat, and the explosion can be avoided. Two decomposition steps can be observed. In the first step (at $65\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) in addition to the 14.1 % mass decrease, a two-component solid residue forms [reaction 4]. The components of this residue can be easily separated, as $\mathbf{F}$ is well soluble in water, while $\mathbf{G}$ does not dissolve at all. The $\mathbf{F}$:$\mathbf{G}$ mass ratio is $1.00:2.97$. On further heating, $\mathbf{F}$ decomposes without a solid residue [reaction 5]. That means pure $\mathbf{G}$ is the final solid decomposition product of $\mathbf{A}$. $\mathbf{G}$ contains two other elements in addition to 27.0 wt% oxygen. One of the two components of the gas mixture forming in the first decomposition step can be easily quantitated if it is absorbed in acid solution.

Some hints

• Compound $\mathbf{A}$ decomposes without releasing oxygen.
• Compound $\mathbf{A}$ contains two different metals.
• Compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ both contain a complex ion.
• $\mathbf{C}$ is a well-known compound for any chemistry student.
• Compound $\mathbf{F}$ does not contain any metal.

5.2 (28.0 pt) Give chemical formulae of $\mathbf{A}$—$\mathbf{G}$. You don’t have to show your calculations, but if your compounds are incorrect you may gain partial marks from correct calculations.

5.3 (12.0 pt) Write balanced equations for reactions [3]—[5].

problems.title: Penicillin
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (38 points, 6% of the total). Penicillin

Penicillins are a group of antibiotics that have played a crucial role in medicine since their discovery.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-6-fig1.png

6.1 (6 pt) Mark the stereogenic carbon centers on the structure of Penicillin VK on the answer sheet. Write the corresponding R/S stereodescriptors next to the centers on the answer sheet.

6.2 (2 pt) Give the total number of possible stereoisomers of Penicillin VK.

One of the many synthetic methods to obtain Penicillin VK starts from the amino acid valine, as shown in the scheme on the next page of this problem.

Hints:

• Among other signals, the $^1$H NMR spectrum of compound $\mathbf{A}$ contains two signals that each integrate to 3H. Both of these signals are doublets.
• Compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ are open-chain compounds, while $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ each have a five membered ring (in addition to any rings in the PhthN-group).
• Brucine is used for chiral resolution.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-6-fig2.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-6-fig3.png

*Please note that in the formation of (+)-$\mathbf{C}$, the word "Separation" means separation.

**Conc. HCl means concentrated HCl.

6.3 (8 pt) Choose the suitable reagent for the numbered steps (1–4) on the answer sheet.
a) $2\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HCl}_{(\mathrm{aq})}$
b) $\ce{SO3}$, $\ce{H2SO4}$
c) $\ce{NaOH}_{(\mathrm{aq})}$
d) $\ce{HCO2H}$, $\ce{Ac2O}$
e) i) $\ce{N2H4}$  ii) $\ce{HCl}_{(\mathrm{aq})}$, AcOH

problems.title: SABIC
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (23 points, 7.5% of the total). SABIC

The Saudi Basic Industries Corporation (SABIC) was established in the mid-1970s as part of Saudi Arabia's plan to diversify its economy. Today, SABIC is a global chemical giant, producing 69 million tons of products annually.

Part A

SABIC's own unique ethene oligomerization technology (oligomers are polymers with few monomer units) produces linear alpha olefins (1-alkenes), which are used in numerous industrial applications.

Linear alpha olefins are produced by catalytic oligomerization of ethene, resulting in a range of chain lengths with a distribution. Different catalysts can yield various distributions of products.

In the geometric or Schulz–Flory distribution, each oligomer fraction is related to the previous fraction by the equation, $T_{n+1} = \alpha T_n$, where $T_n$ represents the molar amount of the oligomer with $n$ ethene units, and $\alpha$ is a constant called the probability of chain propagation. Ethene, the monomer is not a member of the series ($n \geq 2$).

One catalytic oligomerization process can be described by a relatively simple mechanism:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-7-fig1.png

Although this mechanism is not a classical chain reaction because the final product is not produced within the cycle, the usual kinetic treatment of chain reactions can be applied to it. The three processes shown (1–3) are all chain propagation steps. R is lengthened by each cycle.

All three reactions are first order with respect to the chain carriers. For ethene, use an unknown order $\rho$, to be determined later.

7.1 (1 pt) Write the rate equations for reactions 1–3 using $k_1$, $k_2$, and $k_3$ as the corresponding rate constants, which are independent of the carbon chain length.

Chain termination step, producing the oligomers, is a first order reaction competing with reaction 1.

7.2 (2 pt) Write i) the chemical equation and ii) rate equation of termination. Use $k_t$ as the corresponding rate constant.

7.3 (4 pt) Find the value of $\rho$ which ensures that the product mixture of olefins shows the required ratio of products in accordance with the Schulz–Flory distribution when the reaction is run in a closed system. Derive a formula for this case that gives $\alpha$ as the function of rate constants.

Aluminum alkyls are used as co-catalysts in the ethene oligomerization process. It was found that they also catalyzed the Friedel–Crafts alkylation of the aromatic solvents used for the oligomerization.

In a typical oligomerization reaction, an alkylated aromatic compound $\mathbf{Q}$ was isolated from the complex reaction mixture of ethene oligomerization in toluene as solvent. The alkylated aromatic compound $\mathbf{Q}$ has the molecular formula $\ce{C11H16}$ and its $^1$H NMR spectrum contains the following peaks.

$^1$H NMR of $\mathbf{Q}$: $\delta$ 0.9 ($t$, 3H); 1.35 ($m$, 2H); 1.59 ($m$, 2H); 2.34 ($s$, 3H), 2.60 ($t$, 2H); 7.18 ($d$, 2H); 7.22 ($d$, 2H).

7.4 (3 pt) Draw the structure of $\mathbf{Q}$.

Part B

Vitrimers are adaptive polymers with "reversible" covalent bonds, allowing shape-changing and self-healing under specific conditions. This subtask explores the principles of vitrimer chemistry, an important topic in SABIC's polymer research.

A recently elucidated fast and reversible reaction involving dioxaborolanes can serve as the chemical background for such an adaptable polymer network. The two dioxaborolanes below were prepared by the reaction of phenylboronic acid with 1,2-butanediol and 3,5-dimethylphenylboronic acid with 1,2-propanediol, respectively.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-7-fig2.png

They participate in a model metathesis (exchange) reaction. The two carefully purified compounds were mixed in the absence of solvent and the mixture was kept at $60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for two hours. Interestingly, the gas chromatograms of the mixture at the start and at the end of the incubation period showed only the peaks below, with equimolar quantities of the components. The peaks in this system separate in a way that correlates with molar mass: compounds with lower mass appear at earlier elution times.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-7-fig3.png

No catalyst, water, diol or acid was detectable in the mixture.

7.5 (2 pt) Draw the compounds associated with peaks I–IV in the chromatogram.

Linking functional units to a polymer chain is known as grafting, and the functional units are referred to as grafting agents. In this case, the dioxaborolane units are linked to the polymer chains by maleimide groups via a radical process, in which one maleimide group is coupling to the polymer chain at a random carbon atom. The scheme below introduces a flexible synthesis route towards the dioxaborolane maleimide grafting agent used in the vitrimers.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-7-fig4.png

7.6 (3 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{C}$.

7.7 (1 pt) Select on the answer sheet which reagent(s) and/or condition is/are appropriate for linking the dioxaborolane maleimide units to polyethylene.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-7-fig5.png

The vitrimer was prepared as follows:

• Polyethylene is grafted with dioxaborolane maleimide. Assume no side reactions between the dioxaborolane maleimide compounds.
• The reagents are removed from the macromolecules.
• Propanediol functionalized bis-dioxaborolane is added to enable crosslinking.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-7-fig6.png

• The mixture is carefully heated for metathesis (exchange) reaction to take place.

To determine the extent of grafting and crosslinking in the vitrimer, infrared (IR) spectroscopy was used at room temperature where the metathesis reaction is extremely slow. Assume a homogeneous vitrimer.

• All of the small molecules are removed from the polymer.
• The IR spectrum of a thin polymer film is measured.
• IR spectrum contains absorption peaks that correspond to specific functional groups.
• The Beer–Lambert law can be used to quantify the concentration of these functional groups.

The provided data table gives the wavelengths, corresponding molar (related to the specified functional groups) absorption coefficients for relevant characteristic peaks together with the absorbances of the vitrimer sample.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} \begin{array}{l}\text{Vibration wavenumber, with} \\ \text{the functional group indicated}\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Molar absorption coefficient, } \epsilon \\ (\mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,\mu m^{-1}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Sample absorbance at this} \\ \text{wave number, } A\end{array} \\ \hline \begin{array}{l}\text{Imide group band at} \\ 1710\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\end{array} & 2.67 & 0.451 \\ \hline \begin{array}{l}\text{Monosubstituted benzene ring} \\ \text{band at } 1600\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\end{array} & 0.28 & 0.022 \\ \hline \begin{array}{l}\text{Disubstituted benzene ring} \\ \text{band at } 1520\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\end{array} & 0.68 & 0.042 \\ \hline \begin{array}{l}\ce{CH2}\text{ groups of polyethylene,} \\ \text{band at } 1470\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\end{array} & 0.021 & 0.904 \end{array}$$

7.8 (3 pt) Calculate the grafting density ($X_g$) of polyethylene based on the measurements. That is the ratio of the grafted groups over the ethylene units.

7.9 (4 pt) Calculate the percentage of the grafted groups that are not part of a crosslink ($p_{nc}$).

problems.title: Porphyrin complexes
problems.problem:
Problem 9 (35 points, 7.5% of the total). Porphyrin complexes

Part A. Metals in petroleum

Saudi Arabian petroleum, primarily hydrocarbons, contains elements like vanadium in porphyrin complexes, hinting at its biological origins.

Vanadium complex $\mathbf{B}$ is presumably formed in petroleum from chlorophyll according to the following scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-9-fig1.png

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{Step} & \textbf{Name} \\ \hline 1) & \text{Demetallization} \\ \hline 2) & \text{Hydrolysis} \\ \hline 3) & \text{Decarbomethoxylation} \\ \hline 4) & \text{Reduction} \\ \hline 5) & \text{Aromatization} \\ \hline 6) & \text{Decarboxylation} \\ \hline 7) & \text{Metal chelation} \end{array}$$

9.1 (4.0 pt) Assign the molecular formulae a–e (given in the answer sheet) to the intermediates I–V.

Formulae given in the answer sheet: a) $\ce{C32H34N4}$; b) $\ce{C55H74N4O5}$; c) $\ce{C33H34N4O3}$; d) $\ce{C33H34N4O2}$; e) $\ce{C35H36N4O5}$.

9.2 (7.0 pt) Draw the structures of intermediate $\mathbf{A}$ and vanadium complex $\mathbf{B}$ using the pre-drawn framework of porphyrin. (If you need a new template to redraw your structure(s), please ask the supervisor.)

9.3 (1.0 pt) Indicate the oxidation state of vanadium in $\mathbf{B}$.

Part B. Porphyrin non-metal complexes

Porphyrins are known to form chelate-type complexes not only with metals but also with some non-metals, for example, with boron and phosphorus. Octaethylporphyrin ($\ce{H2}$OEP) is often used to model natural porphyrins and to study porphyrin complexes. It has the following structure and can be represented as:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-9-fig2.png

To produce dicationic planar boron porphyrin complex $[\mathbf{X3}]^{2+}$, either $\ce{BCl3}$ or another binary compound $\mathbf{X1}$ can be used as a precursor:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-9-fig3.png

9.4 (3.0 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{X1}$, intermediate complex $\mathbf{X2}$ and the product $[\mathbf{X3}]^{2+}$.

Phosphorus forms porphyrin cationic complexes $[\mathbf{Y1}]^{n+}$, $[\mathbf{Y2}]^{n+}$, and $[\mathbf{Y3}]^{n+}$. The complex $[\mathbf{Y3}]^{n+}$ has one less plane of symmetry compared to $[\mathbf{Y1}]^{n+}$ and $[\mathbf{Y2}]^{n+}$ (ignore ethyl substituents in OEP ligand when considering symmetry). Pyridine (Py) is used here as a basic solvent, “Hal” is one of the halogens: F, Cl, or Br:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-9-fig4.png

9.5 (2.0 pt) Indicate: a) the charge “$n+$” of phosphorus porphyrin complexes; b) the number of planes of symmetry $N(\sigma)$ that complex $[\mathbf{Y1}]^{n+}$ has.

9.6 (4.0 pt) Draw the structures of $[\mathbf{Y1}]^{n+}$, $[\mathbf{Y2}]^{n+}$, and $[\mathbf{Y3}]^{n+}$.

Part C. Porphyrin sandwiches

Porphyrin sandwich-type complexes form when there are several porphyrin rings aligned relative to each other. Examples are $\mathrm{Zr(OEP)_2}$, $\mathrm{Eu_2(OEP)_3}$, $\mathrm{Bi_2(OEP)_2Cl_2}$ that have at least 3 planes of symmetry each. Note that the hole size in the OEP ligand is ca. 4.0 Å, and the average metal–N distances in these complexes are 2.4, 2.5, 2.3 Å, respectively.

9.7 (3.0 pt) Suggest the structures of $\mathrm{Zr(OEP)_2}$, $\mathrm{Eu_2(OEP)_3}$, and $\mathrm{Bi_2(OEP)_2Cl_2}$. You may use a simplified representation of the OEP ligand.

Another type of porphyrin sandwich-type complex is metal–porphyrin dimers with single or multiple metal–metal bonds. For example, $\mathrm{[Ru(OEP)]_2}$ has a Ru$-$Ru double bond (considering only d-electrons). Below is the molecular orbital diagram for an eclipsed dimer of the type $\mathrm{[M(porphyrin)]_2}$ (interaction between $\mathrm{d}_{x^2-y^2}$ is not considered as these orbitals lie high in energy):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2024-9-fig5.png

9.8 (4.0 pt) Draw the $\sigma\ (\mathrm{d}_{z^2}+\mathrm{d}_{z^2})$, $\pi\ (\mathrm{d}_{xz}+\mathrm{d}_{xz})$, $\pi\ (\mathrm{d}_{yz}+\mathrm{d}_{yz})$, and $\delta\ (\mathrm{d}_{xy}+\mathrm{d}_{xy})$ bonding orbitals according to the specified coordinate system.

9.9 (3.0 pt) Calculate the metal–metal bond order in the following complexes in eclipsed conformation: $\mathrm{[Mo(OEP)]_2}$, $\mathrm{[Ir(OEP)]_2}$, $\mathrm{[Re(OEP)]_2{}^{+}}$.

The eclipsed conformation is generally preferred for metal–porphyrin dimers with 7, 8, and 9 d-electrons. Otherwise, these complexes are more stable in a staggered conformation, where the porphyrin rings are rotated relative to each other by $45^\circ$.

9.10 (4.0 pt) Select how the splitting (i.e., the energy between antibonding and bonding orbitals) changes for each type of orbital interaction during the conversion of eclipsed conformation into staggered:
a) increases;
b) remains unchanged;
c) decreases (not to zero);
d) decreases to zero.

(The answer sheet asks for one choice for each of $\sigma/\sigma^*$, $\pi/\pi^*$ and $\delta/\delta^*$.)

Problem 2 (6.5% of the total). Rapamycin - A molecular glue

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-2-fig1.png

Rapamycin was isolated from the bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus in 1972. It acts as a “molecular glue” and inhibits the activity of the protein mTOR through binding to another protein. It has been used to treat various diseases. The stereochemical complexity of rapamycin makes its total synthesis challenging. The figure shows part of the first total synthesis by the Nicolaou group.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-2-fig2.png

The major stereoisomer ($\mathbf{C}$) is formed from the chromium-mediated coupling reaction of aldehyde $\mathbf{A}$ and vinyl iodide $\mathbf{B}$ and can be predicted using the Felkin-Anh model without chelation.

2.1a Draw a Newman projection showing the best approach of the nucleophile in this reaction. Use the labels =O, –H, –$\mathrm{R}^1$, –OMe, and Nu.

2.1b Draw the full structure of the major diastereomer $\mathbf{C}$ showing all stereochemistry.

After a few transformations, $\mathbf{C}$ can be converted into an aldehyde $\mathbf{D}$ which reacts with $\mathbf{E}$ to form $\mathbf{F}$. $\mathbf{F}$ can be further transformed into rapamycin.

2.2a Using the Zimmerman-Traxler model, predict the arrangement of the reactants as they come together to form the six-membered ring transition state in the reaction to form $\mathbf{F}$. Draw the substituents at positions labelled with numbers. If a position does not have a substituent, put an “X” in the box. Boxes 1 and 2 have been filled in as an example. You may use the abbreviation $\mathrm{R}^2$ as given in the scheme above.

Whilst stereochemical control is challenging synthetically, the biological synthesis controls stereochemistry elegantly through an assembly line of various enzymes.
