problems.title: Lanterns and the Burj Khalifa
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (7.5% of the total). Lanterns and the Burj Khalifa

At $829.8\,\mathrm{m}$, Dubai’s Burj Khalifa is the world's tallest structure. To simplify construction, many floors were made from similar pieces. Some artificial "molecular skyscrapers" can be made through coordination chemistry of just two pieces: metal ions and organic ligands.

In these 3D structures, every vertex contains a square planar Pd(II) ion coordinated to four pyridine ligands. Along each edge is a bent organic ligand consisting of two pyridines linked together.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig1.png

The angle between the two $\mathrm{N}\rightarrow\mathrm{Pd}$ bonds from the same ligand controls which structure forms. Larger angles give larger structures.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig2.png

Where free rotation around a bond is possible, the ligand adopts a conformation to form a structure with the smallest possible angle.

3.1 Tick the smallest angle (approximately) between the $\mathrm{N}\rightarrow\mathrm{Pd}$ bonds which could be achieved by ligands $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig3.png

3.2 Using “<”, rank ligands $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$, and $\mathbf{F}$, from smallest angle to largest angle between the $\mathrm{N}\rightarrow\mathrm{Pd}$ bonds that they could form.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig4.png

One series of structures can be modelled as polyhedra with tetracoordinated Pd(II) ions at the vertices. All structures have eight triangular faces ($F_3$), with various numbers of square faces ($F_4$).

The triangular and square faces can be placed onto a square grid, where the relative position of two nearest triangles is described with integer coordinates $h$ and $k$. $Q$ is then given by the equation:

$$Q = h^2 + k^2$$

Part of the grid for a structure with $h = 2$ and $k = 4$ is shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig5.png

The smallest possible structure in this series is an octahedron, where $Q = 1$, and $(h, k) = (0, 1)$ or $(1, 0)$. It has six vertices, eight triangular faces, and 12 edges. Nearest triangles are a move of one face in one direction apart.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig6.png

The second smallest structure is a cuboctahedron, where $Q = 2$. Nearest triangles are a move of one face in each direction apart.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig7.png

3.3 Complete the column in the table for $Q = 2$, describing the number of vertices, $V$, number of edges $E$, the total number of faces, $F$, and the number of square faces, $F_4$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} Q & 1 & 2 \\ \hline (h, k) & (0, 1)\text{ or }(1, 0) & (1, 1) \\ \hline V & 6 & \\ \hline E & 12 & \\ \hline F & 8 & \\ \hline F_3 & 8 & 8 \\ \hline F_4 & 0 & \end{array}$$

All structures obey the following rules:

$$V - E + F = 2$$

$$V = 6Q$$

$$F - V = 2$$

3.4 Complete the table for the third smallest structure, where $Q = 4$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c} Q & 4 \\ \hline (h, k) & \\ \hline V & \\ \hline E & \\ \hline F & \\ \hline F_3 & 8 \\ \hline F_4 & \end{array}$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig8.png

In contrast to these large structures, the smallest structures contain two metals and four ligands and are called lanterns. They are similar in shape to the traditional lanterns seen at the Dubai light festival. Lanterns are formed by ligands such as $\mathbf{L}$, which make two parallel $\mathrm{N}\rightarrow\mathrm{Pd}$ bonds. Ligand $\mathbf{L}$ has two planes of symmetry and can adopt a planar conformation with the angles shown.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig9.png

Hint:

- The transformation from $\mathbf{H}$ to $\mathbf{I}$ could also be achieved by Lewis acid catalysis.

3.5 Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{H}$, $\mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{J}$, $\mathbf{K}$, and ligand $\mathbf{L}$.

Unlike symmetrical ligand $\mathbf{L}$, chiral ligand $\mathbf{M}$ lacks symmetry and exists as a pair of $R$ and $S$ enantiomers.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig10.png

Multiple lantern isomers can be formed from ligand $\mathbf{M}$. We can group these isomers in two ways. Firstly we categorise by the number of each type of ligand in the lantern: (i) all the same ($RRRR$ or $SSSS$), (ii) one different ($RRRS$ or $SSSR$), (iii) $cis$-$RRSS$, and (iv) $trans$-$RSRS$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig11.png

Secondly, the two ends of ligand $\mathbf{M}$ are not the same; the ligand has a head (H) and a tail (T). There are four categories of structure considering head-to-tail orientation: (1) all up (HHHH), (2) three up (HHHT), (3) $cis$-HHTT, and (4) $trans$-HTHT.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig12.png

The 16 possible combinations of these categories are represented by empty cells in the table. Some combinations have only one possible isomer, whereas others have multiple possible isomers. In any one combination, all possible isomers are either chiral or achiral.

3.6 Complete the table by writing "C" for chiral and "A" for achiral. Note, in this part you will be awarded points for each correct answer but deducted points for each incorrect answer down to a minimum of zero. There is no penalty for empty cells.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig13.png

3.7 Complete the table with the number of possible isomers of each combination.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-3-fig14.png

problems.title: The life of tennis balls
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (6% of the total). The life of tennis balls

This problem honours the incredible Rafael Nadal, a true tennis icon who concluded his remarkable career in 2024.

The Dubai Tennis Championships is a prestigious tournament held annually in UAE. Many of the world's top players, including Rafael Nadal, Roger Federer, Novak Djokovic, and Andy Murray have won titles there.

The composition of tennis balls has evolved over hundreds of years. To ensure a good bounce, the inside of modern tennis balls is pressurised above atmospheric pressure. However, old hollow tennis balls just contained air at atmospheric pressure.

In this problem, assume tennis balls have an inner radius of $R = 3.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ that remains constant throughout the pressurisation process. Assume that the composition of air is 20% $\ce{O2}$ and 80% $\ce{N2}$ by volume. Consider that overpressure does not expand the ball.

4.1 Calculate the mass $m$ (in g) of air inside an old tennis ball at $T_0 = 25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Chemists then discovered how to pressurise a ball above atmospheric pressure using a reaction between compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, which forms gas $\mathbf{C}$ (to create additional inner pressure) plus other non-gaseous products.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-4-fig1.png

A capsule with a quantity $m_\mathrm{mix} = 0.3389\,\mathrm{g}$ of a stoichiometric mixture of two white inorganic compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ was placed inside a ball filled with air at atmospheric pressure. They reacted completely inside the ball upon heating to form gas $\mathbf{C}$ and other products (reaction 1) to produce an overall pressure inside the ball of $p = 1.600\,\mathrm{atm}$ (at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$). Once this ball was opened, all residue inside was collected and dissolved in water. The dropping of silver nitrate in that solution gave a white precipitate (reaction 2). This collected precipitate could be partially dissolved in a concentrated aqueous solution of $\mathbf{B}$. By increasing the pH of this mixture, the precipitate dissolved completely (reaction 3). If the same initial capsule of $\mathbf{A}$+$\mathbf{B}$ is dissolved in water and concentrated solution of silver nitrate added, $m_\mathrm{precipitate} = 0.8224\,\mathrm{g}$ of white precipitate formed which was approximately twice the mass of precipitate formed in reaction 2.

When the capsule of $\mathbf{A}$+$\mathbf{B}$ dissolved in a solution of HI the formation of gas $\mathbf{D}$ started, and the solution turned brown (reaction 4). Upon further addition of sodium thiosulfate this colour disappeared (reaction 5).

The densities of gases $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ differ by no more than 10%.

4.2 Write the chemical formulae of compounds $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{D}$.

4.3 Write equations for reactions 1-5.

The pressure inside modern tennis balls is $p_0 = 1.80\,\mathrm{atm}$. They are sold in a pressurised can, with the same pressure in the can as in the ball to stop gas coming out during storage.

Standard balls contain air and premium balls contain pure $\ce{N2}$. Once the can is opened, depressurisation begins, and the gas diffuses out of the balls until the internal pressure reaches atmospheric pressure. Assume there is no diffusion of gas into the balls at any point. The activation energy for the depressurisation of a premium ball is $E_\mathrm{A} = 50.0\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

The rate of ball depressurisation (pressure/time) could be described by similar equations of those used in chemical kinetics. At $T_0 = 25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, once the can is opened, the premium balls depressurise to $p_1 = 1.40\,\mathrm{atm}$ after $t_1 = 241\,\mathrm{h}$ and to $p_2 = 1.19\,\mathrm{atm}$ after about $t_2 = 21$ days. The initial depressurisation rate of regular balls is 10% faster than premium balls.

4.4a Demonstrate that the depressurisation process follows the first kinetic order by calculating the depressurisation rate constant $k_{\ce{N2}}$ for $\ce{N2}$ in $\mathrm{h^{-1}}$.
Note: If you couldn't calculate the answer, use $k_{\ce{N2}} = 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{h^{-1}}$ in further calculations.

4.4b Calculate the (depressurisation) rate constant $k_{\ce{O2}}$ for $\ce{O2}$ in $\mathrm{h^{-1}}$, assuming the rates for both gases are additive.

As well as today being the IChO 2025 theory paper, it is also (perhaps less importantly) the Semi-Finals day at Wimbledon. Amanda Anisimova will start a match in $t_\mathrm{match} = 12.0\,\mathrm{h}$ from now. The weather today in Wimbledon is predicted to be a constant $T_\mathrm{W} = 30.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assume a new set of premium balls, which were manufactured and placed in the can at $T_0 = 25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, are opened now and quickly change to $T_\mathrm{W} = 30.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

4.4c Calculate the pressure $p_\mathrm{start}$ (in atm) of the balls at the start of the match.

problems.title: Solar-powered multi-stage flash desalination
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (6.5% of the total). Solar-powered multi-stage flash desalination

Freshwater is scarce in the arid climate of the UAE. The country relies on solar-powered desalination plants to produce freshwater. A Dubai desalination plant uses a multi-stage flash (MSF) desalination process. In MSF desalination, seawater is heated by passing through a series of heat exchangers to raise its temperature, reaching its saturation temperature at a high pressure. When pressure is reduced, this superheated seawater gives off pure water vapour to become saturated again, a process known as flashing.

Assume seawater in Dubai is at $T_0 = 25.00\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and is an aqueous solution of 3.45 % mass NaCl. Assume complete ionisation of NaCl in water.

The boiling point of seawater is higher than pure water. The boiling point elevation constant, $K_\mathrm{b} = 0.5120\,\mathrm{K\,kg\,mol^{-1}}$.

5.1 Calculate the boiling point, $T$, (in °C) of Dubai seawater at atmospheric pressure.
If you couldn't calculate the answer, use a temperature of $373.50\,\mathrm{K}$ for further calculations.

5.2 Calculate the percentage mass of NaCl, $w_\mathrm{NaCl}$, in water that has a boiling point, $T_\mathrm{b} = 378.00\,\mathrm{K}$.

5.3 The boiling point of seawater also increases as pressure increases. Calculate the boiling point, $T$, (in °C) of the initial Dubai seawater at a pressure, $p = 2.50\,\mathrm{atm}$. The latent heat of vaporisation of water, $E_\mathrm{vap} = 2260\,\mathrm{kJ\,kg^{-1}}$ ($40.716\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$). Assume this is the same for seawater.

In the plant, a flash chamber (of volume, $V = 100\,\mathrm{L}$) contains a mass of $1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ of seawater (l) at $T_1 = 90.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Another mass of $1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ of seawater is then overheated to $T_2 = 110.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at high pressure before being added to this chamber, where a reduction in pressure causes some water to turn into steam.

After equilibrium was established, the temperature in the chamber was $T_\mathrm{f} = 97.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assume there was no loss of energy, and that the latent heat of vaporisation is independent of temperature.

The specific heat capacity of seawater, $C_\mathrm{p} = 3.85\,\mathrm{kJ\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, assumed to be independent of temperature. The density of seawater, $d = 1025\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

5.4 Calculate the amount, $n$, (in mol) of water that vapourised, assuming that the latent heat of vaporization does not depend on pressure, and that the heat capacity of water vapor in the chamber is negligble.
If you couldn't calculate the answer, use $0.56\,\mathrm{mol}$ for further calculations.

5.5 Assuming the initial vapour pressure before addition of the overheated water in the chamber was $p_\mathrm{i} = 0.690\,\mathrm{atm}$, calculate the final vapour pressure, $p_\mathrm{f}$, (in atm) in the chamber assuming the water vapour behaves as an ideal gas.

5.6 Calculate the thermal energy, $E$, (in kWh) required to heat a mass of $1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ of seawater from $T_1 = 25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $T_2 = 110.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
If you couldn't calculate the answer, use $0.1\,\mathrm{kWh}$ for further calculations.

5.7 A plant produces $50{,}000\,\mathrm{m^3}$ of pure water per day. The plant passes Dubai seawater through 30 flash cycles and overall can extract 85% of the water present. Calculate the mass, $m$, (in kg) of Dubai seawater needed per day.
If you couldn't calculate the answer, use $6.0\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{kg}$ for further calculations.

Plants make efficient use of heat exchangers to save energy. We can assume the total energy required by the plant is the same as the energy needed to heat all the seawater from $T_1 = 25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $T_2 = 110.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

5.8 Assuming a $10\,\mathrm{m^2}$ solar panel has a power of $2.00\,\mathrm{kW}$ averaged during the 12 operational hours every day and the efficiency of using energy is 67%, calculate the number of panels, $N$, required for the plant.

problems.title: Solar energy conversion by CO2 reduction
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (6% of the total). Solar energy conversion by $\ce{CO2}$ reduction

Use the following data to solve this problem. Assume enthalpy and entropy changes of reactions do not depend on temperature.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} & \ce{CO2(g)} & \ce{CO(g)} & \ce{O2(g)} & \ce{Zn(s)} & \ce{Zn(l)} & \ce{Zn(g)} & \ce{ZnO(s)} \\ \hline \Delta_f H^\circ_{298}\ /\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & -393.5 & -110.5 & & & 6.5 & 130.4 & -350.5 \\ \hline S^\circ_{298}\ /\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} & 213.8 & 197.7 & 205.1 & 41.7 & 50.8 & 161.0 & 43.7 \\ \hline \text{Melting Point / K} & & & & 692.7 & & & 2247 \\ \hline \text{Boiling Point / K} & & & & & 1180 & & \end{array}$$

Photochemical reduction of carbon dioxide is a promising approach both for solar energy conversion and for reduction of $\ce{CO2}$ content in the atmosphere. There are several ways to convert $\ce{CO2}$ to CO and other useful substances.

Direct decomposition

Direct decomposition of $\ce{CO2}$ to CO and $\ce{O2}$ is a highly endothermic process which requires a large amount of energy – from heat or from light.

6.1 Estimate the temperature (in K) at which half of $\ce{CO2}$ decomposes at equilibrium at a total pressure of 1 bar.

Catalytic decomposition

The use of metal/metal oxide catalytic systems allows the temperature of $\ce{CO2}$ decomposition to be significantly reduced and eases the separation of the gaseous products by using thermochemical cycles.

Consider a catalytic cycle based on the Zn/ZnO system and containing two reactions. The net reaction is $\ce{CO2}$ decomposition into CO and $\ce{O2}$. Reaction 1 is exothermic, while Reaction 2 is highly endothermic – the reactants should be heated to the required temperature.

6.2 Write equations for Reaction 1 and Reaction 2.

The operating temperature for Reaction 1 is $1073\,\mathrm{K}$.

6.3 Calculate the equilibrium constant, $K$, for Reaction 1 and find the degree of $\ce{CO2}$ conversion, $x$, at this temperature.

Reaction 2 is performed at the much higher temperature of $2000\,\mathrm{K}$.

6.4 Calculate the equilibrium pressure of oxygen, $p(\ce{O2})$, in bar, at this temperature.

Photocatalytic reduction

Photocatalytic reduction of $\ce{CO2}$ with water is akin to natural photosynthesis. Plants convert $\ce{CO2}$ to carbohydrates as an energy source, but human civilisation needs hydrocarbons to produce energy. On the way from $\ce{CO2}$ to $\mathrm{C}_x\mathrm{H}_y$ there are many possible intermediate products of $\ce{CO2}$ reduction.

6.5 Complete the table with the formulae of the one-carbon species from $\ce{CO2}$ reduction, containing only H and/or O atoms in addition to the one C. The oxidation number of the carbon in each species is shown. For the oxidation state +2 give the formulae of both an anion "anion" and a neutral molecule "neutral molecule". Indicate only one species in each box.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} +3 & +2\ \text{(anion)} & +2\ \text{(neutral molecule)} & 0 & -2 & -4 \\ \hline \phantom{X} & & & & & \end{array}$$

Visible light ($400\,\mathrm{nm} < \lambda < 700\,\mathrm{nm}$) makes up >40% of the total solar radiation reaching Earth. Light can be absorbed by semiconductors or dyes, leading to electronic excitation which can promote redox reactions. The band gaps of some common semiconductors are listed.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Semiconductor} & \ce{CdS} & \ce{Ge} & \ce{Si} & \ce{SiC} & \ce{WO3} & \ce{ZrO2} \\ \hline \text{Band gap / eV} & 2.4 & 0.67 & 1.1 & 3.2 & 2.8 & 5.0 \end{array}$$

6.6 Tick which semiconductor(s) can be excited by visible light to serve as a potential photocatalyst(s). Support your answer with calculations.

In an early photocatalysis experiment, SiC semiconductor was suspended in $V = 100\,\mathrm{mL}$ of water, and $\ce{CO2}$ was bubbled through at a rate of $v = 3.0\,\mathrm{L\,min^{-1}}$ ($T = 25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $p = 1\,\mathrm{atm}$). The suspension was irradiated by a $P = 500\,\mathrm{W}$ lamp ($\lambda = 365\,\mathrm{nm}$) for $t = 7\,\mathrm{h}$. After irradiation, the solution contained $c(\ce{HCHO}) = 1.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M}$ and $c(\ce{CH3OH}) = 5.4\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M}$.

The apparent quantum yield $\phi$ is defined as:

$$\phi = \frac{N_e}{N_i},$$

where $N_e$ is the number of electrons transferred and $N_i$ is the number of incident photons.

6.7 Calculate the total degree of $\ce{CO2}$ conversion, $\eta$, and the apparent quantum yield of photocatalytic reduction, $\phi$.

problems.title: Dubai crude oil
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (7% of the total). Dubai crude oil

The petroleum industry plays an important role in the UAE economy. The oil called “Dubai Crude” is a benchmark for global oil prices. Crude oil is a complex mixture of organic compounds, mainly hydrocarbons, along with smaller amounts of S, N, and O-containing compounds.

The hydrocarbon composition of oil is characterised by the PONA number. The abbreviation stands for $P$ – paraffins (alkanes), $O$ – olefins (alkenes), $N$ – naphthenes (cycloalkanes), and $A$ – aromatics (arenes). One method to determine the composition of oil is gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS).

Below are mass spectra (electron impact ionisation, $I$ – relative intensity) of four hydrocarbons 1–4 of Dubai Crude oil. They include linear alkane $\mathbf{P}$, linear alkene $\mathbf{O}$, monosubstituted cycloalkane $\mathbf{N}$, and arene $\mathbf{A}$. Alkene $\mathbf{O}$ does not have $cis$–$trans$ isomers. 1’–4’ are selected fragmentation products.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-7-fig1.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-7-fig2.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-7-fig3.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-7-fig4.png

7.1 Draw the structures of 1–4 and 1’–4’. If you cannot determine the structure(s) of 1–4, write the corresponding letter code ($\mathbf{P}$/$\mathbf{O}$/$\mathbf{N}$/$\mathbf{A}$) and the molecular formula.
Hint: Species 3’ is formed by a rearrangement of the molecular ion by the McLafferty mechanism.

To differentiate isoparaffins (isoalkanes, $I$) from $n$-alkanes, the $PIONA$ number may be used for a more precise description of crude oil composition. Below are two mass spectra of branched alkanes 5 and 6. In the mass spectrum of 6, the $[\mathrm{M}+1]^+$ peak has an intensity of ca. 5.4% relative to the intensity of the $[\mathrm{M}]^+$ peak of the molecular ion.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-7-fig5.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-7-fig6.png

7.2 Draw the structures of compounds 5 and 6.

Crude oil is classified by the sulfur content as either sweet (<0.5 wt%) or sour (>0.5 wt%). A $V = 115\,\mathrm{\mu L}$ sample of Dubai Crude oil ($\rho = 871\,\mathrm{g\,dm^{-3}}$) was completely burnt. The resulting gas mixture was passed through a $\ce{H2O2}$ solution containing an excess of $\ce{Ba(OH)2}$, leading to the formation of $m = 1.395\,\mathrm{g}$ of white precipitate. Upon acidification with $\ce{HNO3}$, the precipitate’s mass decreased by 98.95%.

7.3 Calculate the sulfur content ($w(\mathrm{S})$, wt%) of Dubai Crude oil.

In addition to sulfur, crude oil contains trace amounts of selenium, which transfers into the water used during refining. In aqueous solutions, selenium exists as $\ce{SeO3^{2-}}$ and $\ce{SeO4^{2-}}$.

The concentration of $\ce{SeO3^{2-}}$ can be determined chromatographically by its selective reaction with diamine $\mathbf{X}$ under acidic conditions, forming piazoselenol $\mathbf{Y}$. This reaction is complete only at the right pH range.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-7-fig7.png

$\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ elute at different times ($t$) on the chromatogram shown below. The absorption spectra (1 mAbs corresponds to absorbance $A = 0.001$) of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are also provided.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-7-fig8.png

7.4 Tick the optimal wavelength ($\lambda$) for the absorbance measurements in the chromatogram.

• $270\,\mathrm{nm}$
• $300\,\mathrm{nm}$
• $350\,\mathrm{nm}$
• $510\,\mathrm{nm}$

Acidified water from the refining process, containing $\ce{SeO3^{2-}}$ and $\ce{SeO4^{2-}}$ (solution 1), was analysed as follows. A $9.50\,\mathrm{mL}$ sample was mixed with $0.50\,\mathrm{mL}$ of an aqueous solution of $\mathbf{X}$ ($300\,\mathrm{\mu M}$, excess) to form solution 2.

The area, $S$, under each chromatogram peak was measured. These areas are proportional to the amount of the respective species in the peak. In a blank experiment under the same conditions with Se-free water, the peak area of $\mathbf{X}$, $S(\mathbf{X})$ from the free diamine, was $0.825\,\mathrm{mAbs{\cdot}min}$. Running identical measurements with known amounts of $\ce{SeO3^{2-}}$ showed that the peak area for $\mathbf{Y}$ ($\mathrm{mAbs{\cdot}min}$) depends on Se concentration ($\mathrm{\mu M}$) as follows: $S(\mathbf{Y}) = 1.21\cdot c(\mathrm{Se})$.

The measurements for the Se-containing sample (solution 2) were carried out at different pH values, adjusted by adding four different strong acids. The ratios $S(\mathbf{X})/S(\mathbf{Y})$ of the area under peak $\mathbf{X}$ to the area under peak $\mathbf{Y}$ for these measurements are shown in the table below. Assume all reactions have reached equilibrium.

Table. $S(\mathbf{X})/S(\mathbf{Y})$ measured at different pH values with four strong acids

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{pH} & 3.0 & 2.0 & 1.5 & 1.0 & 0 & -0.50 \\ \hline \ce{HNO3} & 1.523 & 3.334 & 5.454 & 7.783 & 10.232 & 13.450 \\ \hline \ce{HCl} & 0.634 & 0.538 & 0.523 & 0.523 & 0.581 & 0.782 \\ \hline \ce{HBr} & 0.523 & 0.377 & 0.368 & 0.368 & 0.399 & 0.546 \\ \hline \ce{HI} & 1.722 & 2.223 & 5.114 & 8.123 & 11.736 & 15.780 \end{array}$$

Hint: You need only two values from the table to solve this question.

7.5 Calculate the concentrations of selenium species ($c_0(\ce{SeO3^{2-}})$, $c_0(\ce{SeO4^{2-}})$, in $\mathrm{\mu M}$) in solution 1.

problems.title: Carbon monoxide: deadly poison or promising therapeutic agent?
problems.problem:
Problem 8 (7.5% of the total). Carbon monoxide: deadly poison or promising therapeutic agent?

Carbon monoxide is a toxic gas because it binds to haemoglobin and blocks oxygen binding. A major source of CO is incomplete combustion of engine fuel. Therefore, many exhausts are fitted with catalytic converters which remove CO and other hazardous compounds including unburnt hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides ($\ce{NO_{x}}$), forming mainly water vapour, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen.

8.1 Write the equations for the reactions of the following in a converter. Tick the box to indicate whether the carbon or nitrogen atom(s) have been oxidised by oxygen, "Ox", been reduced "Red", or stayed at the same oxidation state "Same". Please ignore any reactions between the exhaust gases.

(a) CO
(b) Unburnt hydrocarbon $\ce{C_{x}H_{y}}$
(c) Nitrogen oxides $\ce{NO_{x}}$

Catalytic converters contain nanoparticles of noble metals which act as catalysts, immobilised on a cheap high surface area material such as $\ce{Al2O3}$.

In one experiment, $m(\text{cat.}) = 0.10\,\mathrm{g}$ of catalyst containing $w(\mathrm{Pd}) = 10\,\mathrm{wt\%}$ was used in a tube reactor. Gases were passed over the catalyst under continuous flow. The flow rate of CO gas was $v(\mathrm{CO}) = 10\,\mathrm{mL\,min^{-1}}$, which was mixed with a second flow of air (assume 20% $\ce{O2}$, 80% $\ce{N2}$), at $T = 273.15\,\mathrm{K}$ and $p = 1.00\,\mathrm{atm}$, before entering the reactor.

8.2 Calculate the flow rate $v$ (in $\mathrm{mL\,min^{-1}}$) of air required for the reactants to be present in a stoichiometric ratio.

Assume 10% of the Pd atoms in the nanoparticles are exposed on the surface. Assume the conversion of CO to $\ce{CO2}$ was $\eta = 70\%$.

8.3 Calculate the number of $\ce{CO2}$ molecules, $N$, formed after $t = 1\,\mathrm{h}$ per surface Pd atom.

Ruthenium nanoparticles are efficient catalysts for CO combustion. The bonding interactions between CO molecules and the surface Ru atoms are of two types:

1. $\sigma$-bonding through a lone pair on the carbon atom;
2. $\pi$-interaction through an overlap between the Ru valence d-orbitals and CO molecular orbitals.

8.4 Complete the MO diagram for CO with electrons and the following table with the type ($\sigma$/$\pi$) of overlap for forming each MO.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-8-fig1.png

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{MO} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 \\ \hline \text{Type of overlap} & \phantom{\sigma} & \phantom{\sigma} & \phantom{\sigma} & \phantom{\sigma} & \phantom{\sigma} & \phantom{\sigma} & \phantom{\sigma} & \phantom{\sigma} \end{array}$$

8.5 What is the effect of the Ru–CO $\pi$-interaction on the Ru–CO and the C–O bond strengths? Tick the correct answer.

(i) Ru–CO bond strength:

• increases "in"
• decreases "dec"
• no change "nc"

(ii) C–O bond strength:

• increases "in"
• decreases "dec"
• no change "nc"

Adsorbed CO molecules have strong IR absorptions due to C–O stretching vibrations. Three binding modes for CO adsorbed on a metal surface are shown, where CO can interact with one or more metal atoms. IR peaks in the spectra of free CO and the three binding modes of adsorbed CO were observed at values of 1850, 1930, 2100, and $2143\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2025-8-fig2.png

8.6 Tick which wavenumber corresponds to each adsorption mode ($\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$) and to free CO.

Dispersion of a metal catalyst refers to the percentage of its atoms exposed on the surface. Dispersion can be determined by pulse chemisorption of CO since it adsorbs selectively onto surface atoms. Equal pulses of known amounts of CO are injected and a certain amount is adsorbed from each pulse. The amount remaining is measured by a detector and a peak, the area under which correlates with the amount of unadsorbed CO from each pulse, is plotted as shown below. Injections continue until no more CO adsorbs.

problems.title: A journey through time: The secrets of Avicenna
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (7% of the total; 25 points). A journey through time: The secrets of Avicenna

A chemist found herself in the 11th Century, where she met the renowned physician Avicenna. In Avicenna's laboratory, she discovered a blue elixir and a yellow mysterious stone. She brought them back to 2026. Determined to uncover their composition, she began her research.

Part 1. The blue elixir

At first, the chemist compiled a table listing the names of the only four plants which she saw in Avicenna's lab that could have been used to prepare the elixir, and the compounds that can be extracted from these plants.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-1-fig1.png

Using chromatography, she determined that the elixir consists of four different substances ($\textbf{X}$, $\textbf{Y}$, $\textbf{Z}$ and $\textbf{W}$).

The chemist then discovered that $\textbf{X}$ can isomerise into $\textbf{Y}$ in an acidic medium and that $\textbf{Y}$ has a plane of symmetry.

1.1 Identify $\textbf{X}$ and $\textbf{Y}$. (3.0 pt)

Chromatography also revealed it was substance $\textbf{Z}$ that gave the elixir its blue colour. $\textbf{Z}$ is a derivative of the well-known substance $\textbf{A}$, which has two perpendicular planes of symmetry. When heated, $\textbf{A}$ isomerises into aromatic compound $\textbf{B}$, which has three mutually perpendicular planes of symmetry. When substance $\textbf{Z}$ is chlorinated, a pair of peaks with an intensity ratio of 3:1 is observed in the mass spectrum at m/z 218 and 220, respectively.

1.2 Identify $\textbf{Z}$ and draw the structures of substances $\textbf{A}$ and $\textbf{B}$. (4.0 pt)

The chemist extracted $\textbf{W}$ from the elixir. When $\textbf{W}$ was added to an aqueous $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ solution, a characteristic colour change was observed. Mass spectrometric analysis of $\textbf{W}$ revealed the intensity ratio of $[\mathrm{M}]^+ : [\mathrm{M}+1]^+ = 9:1$, where M is the molecular ion. Assume carbon consists exclusively of $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ and $^{13}\mathrm{C}$, the natural isotopic abundance of $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ is 98.9%, and all other elements are monoisotopic.

1.3 Determine the number of carbon atoms ($n$) from the mass spec data and identify $\textbf{W}$. Show your calculations. (3.0 pt)

Part 2. The mysterious stone

Avicenna had told her the $\textbf{stone}$ was a stoichiometric compound. She dissolved it in dilute nitric acid. After that, she adjusted the pH of the solution to ~4 and added NaF. This led to the formation of precipitate $\mathbf{C}\cdot x\ce{H2O}$, which contained 39.16% water by mass. Anhydrous $\textbf{C}$ reacts with an excess of NaF to yield compound $\textbf{D}$, which contains 32.85% sodium and 12.85% of metal $\textbf{Q}$ by mass, and is used in the industrial production of $\textbf{Q}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-1-fig2.png

1.4 Identify metal $\textbf{Q}$ and compounds $\mathbf{C}\cdot x\ce{H2O}$ and $\textbf{D}$. (4.0 pt)

Avicenna told her that he found the $\textbf{stone}$ in a coal deposit. The $\textbf{stone}$ contains the anion of a highly symmetrical acid $\textbf{F}$. Reaction of $\textbf{F}$ with $\ce{P2O5}$ gives binary compound $\textbf{G}$, which contains 49.98% of oxygen by mass and has a three-fold symmetry axis. $\textbf{F}$ can be prepared by oxidising compound $\textbf{E}$ with potassium permanganate in an acidic solution. $\textbf{E}$ contains 11.18% of hydrogen by mass and has a six-fold symmetry axis.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-1-fig3.png

1.5 Draw the structures of $\textbf{E}$, $\textbf{F}$, and $\textbf{G}$. (7.0 pt)

Then, she analysed the $\textbf{stone}$ thermogravimetrically in open air. A 10.00 g sample began to lose mass at approximately $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and stopped at 5.75 g at $200\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. A second drop in mass was observed at $400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, with a final mass of 1.50 g of compound $\textbf{H}$ remaining constant at higher temperatures.

1.6 Determine the chemical formulae of the $\textbf{stone}$ and compound $\textbf{H}$ using thermogravimetric data. (4.0 pt)

problems.title: Kinetics of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (6% of the total; 35 points). Kinetics of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction

When the chemicals $\ce{KBrO3}$, $\ce{CH2(COOH)2}$ (malonic acid, – MA), $\ce{Ce(SO4)2}$, and $\ce{H2SO4}$ are mixed, the concentration, $C$, of Ce species and the colour of the solution oscillates between yellow (due to $\ce{Ce^{4+}}$) and colourless (due to $\ce{Ce^{3+}}$). A schematic picture is given below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-2-fig1.png

2.1 Write the overall balanced reaction equation of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction (BZ reaction). Note: in this reaction, MA is oxidised to $\ce{CO2}$, $\ce{BrO3^-}$ is reduced to $\ce{Br^-}$, and Ce(IV) is a catalyst. (2.0 pt)

The mechanism of the BZ reaction is shown below (BMA – $\ce{CHBr(COOH)2}$):

$$\begin{array}{l|l|l} \text{Process A} & (1)\ \ce{HBrO2 + BrO3^- + H+} \xrightarrow{k_1} \ce{2 BrO2^. + H2O} & k_1 = 1.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{M^{-2}\,s^{-1}} \\ & (2)\ \ce{BrO2^. + Ce^{3+} + H+} \xrightarrow{k_2} \ce{HBrO2 + Ce^{4+}} & k_2 = 6.2\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{M^{-2}\,s^{-1}} \\ & (3)\ \ce{2 HBrO2} \xrightarrow{k_3} \ce{BrO3^- + HBrO + H+} & k_3 = 4.0\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{M^{-1}\,s^{-1}} \\ \hline \text{Process B} & (4)\ \ce{HBrO2 + Br^- + H+} \xrightarrow{k_4} \ce{2 HBrO} & k_4 = 2.0\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{M^{-2}\,s^{-1}} \\ & (5)\ \ce{BrO3^- + Br^- + 2 H+} \xrightarrow{k_5} \ce{HBrO + HBrO2} & k_5 = 2.1\ \mathrm{M^{-3}\,s^{-1}} \\ & (6)\ \ce{HBrO + MA} \xrightarrow{k_6} \ce{BMA + H2O} & k_6 = 8.2\ \mathrm{M^{-1}\,s^{-1}} \\ \hline \text{Process C} & (7)\ \ce{Ce^{4+} + BMA} \xrightarrow{k_7} \ce{Ce^{3+} + Br^-} + \text{other products} & k_7 = 1.0\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{M^{-1}\,s^{-1}} \end{array}$$

In the BZ reaction, $\textbf{Process C}$ occurs continuously, while $\textbf{Processes A}$ and $\textbf{B}$ alternate with each other. Assume that:

• when $\textbf{Process A}$ occurs the solution is yellow and $\textbf{Process B}$ practically does not occur;
• when $\textbf{Process B}$ occurs the solution is colourless and $\textbf{Process A}$ practically does not occur;
• $[\ce{BrO3^-}]_0 = 0.06$ M, $[\mathrm{MA}]_0 = 0.1$ M, $[\ce{H+}]_0 = 0.8$ M, $[\ce{Ce^{4+}}]_0 = 0.001$ M;
• the concentrations of the reactants (except $\ce{Ce^{4+}}$) and pH are maintained constant throughout the BZ reaction.

2.2 Using the steady-state approximation, calculate the stationary molar concentrations of $\ce{HBrO2}$ in $\textbf{Processes A}$ and $\textbf{B}$, $[\ce{HBrO2}]_\mathrm{A}$ and $[\ce{HBrO2}]_\mathrm{B}$. (11.0 pt)

If you could not calculate $[\ce{HBrO2}]_\mathrm{A}$ and $[\ce{HBrO2}]_\mathrm{B}$, you can use the values $[\ce{HBrO2}]_\mathrm{A} = 1\times10^{-5}$ M and $[\ce{HBrO2}]_\mathrm{B} = 1\times10^{-10}$ M for the following calculations.

During the BZ reaction, the concentrations of $\ce{HBrO2}$ and $\ce{Br^-}$ oscillate strictly in relation to each other, and this is sketched in the phase portrait of $[\ce{HBrO2}]$ vs $[\ce{Br^-}]$:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-2-fig2.png

Here $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{max}$ is the maximum concentration and $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{critical}$ is the critical concentration of $\ce{Br^-}$ at which there is a switch over in processes from $\textbf{A}$ to $\textbf{B}$ or from $\textbf{B}$ to $\textbf{A}$. To switch $\textbf{Process A}$ to $\textbf{Process B}$, the reaction rate of the elementary step (4) must exceed that of the elementary step (1) and vice versa.

2.3 Calculate $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{critical}$. (4.0 pt)

If you could not calculate $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{critical}$, use $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{critical} = 1\times10^{-7}$ M for the following calculations.

2.4 In which direction in the phase portrait of $[\ce{HBrO2}]$ vs $[\ce{Br^-}]$ will the concentrations of $[\ce{HBrO2}]$ and $[\ce{Br^-}]$ change over time? Tick the correct box. (2.0 pt)

The system does not traverse the phase portrait of $[\ce{HBrO2}]$ vs $[\ce{Br^-}]$ at a constant velocity, that is the concentration of $[\ce{Br^-}]$ slowly decreases from $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{max} = 7.0\times10^{-4}$ M to $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{critical}$, and then almost immediately reaches $[\ce{Br^-}]_\mathrm{max}$ again.

2.5 Calculate based on the data the period of oscillations, $\tau$, of the BZ reaction, in seconds. (9.0 pt)

2.6 What will be the effect if the following actions $\textbf{(1-4)}$ are performed on an open system where a BZ reaction is taking place? Tick only one box $\textbf{(a-e)}$ for each case. (4.0 pt)

• 1. Adding of small amount of $\ce{Ce^{4+}}$ during $\textbf{Process A}$.
• 2. Adding of a small amount of $\ce{Ag+}$ during $\textbf{Process B}$.
• 3. Adding of a small amount of $\ce{Br^-}$ during $\textbf{Process B}$.
• 4. Continuous addition of $\ce{Br^-}$.

• [a] prolongs $\textbf{Process A}$
• [b] prolongs $\textbf{Process B}$
• [c] $\textbf{Process A}$ switches to $\textbf{Process B}$
• [d] $\textbf{Process B}$ switches to $\textbf{Process A}$
• [e] oscillations stop

2.7 Which graph qualitatively illustrates the rate of change of Gibbs energy ($\frac{dG}{dt}$) of a $\textbf{closed}$ system in which an oscillatory reaction occurs? Tick the correct box. (3.0 pt)

Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are a class of polymers that form two- or three-dimensional structures through reactions between organic precursors, resulting in covalent bonds to afford porous, crystalline materials. 3.2 Calculate the internal diameter, $d$, in Å, of the honeycomb for $\textbf{COF-2}$, with the following assumptions: (3.0 pt)

• B–O = 1.38 Å
• Note, the diameter of a circle, $d$, inscribed inside a hexagon, is given by $d = \sqrt{3}a$, where $a$ is the side length of the hexagon.
• Neglect the width of the linkers.

The structures shown below can form 2D and 3D COFs. For this question consider only formation of COFs with boronate esters, imines, and C=C bonds through condensation reactions. $\textbf{A–E}$ represent compound classes with different functional groups.

problems.title: The nuclear past of Uzbekistan
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (6% of the total; 22 points). The nuclear past of Uzbekistan

Natural uranium consists primarily of two isotopes, $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ and $^{238}\mathrm{U}$. $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ is responsible for sustaining nuclear fission reactions.

4.1 Calculate the atomic abundance of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ in natural uranium, assuming it consists only of isotopes $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ (235.04 a.u.) and $^{238}\mathrm{U}$ (238.05 a.u.). (2.0 pt)

The main reaction occurring in nuclear power plants is the reaction where $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ absorbs a neutron and undergoes fission, releasing energy and producing three additional neutrons, thus sustaining a chain reaction.

$$\ce{^{235}_{92}U + ^{1}_{0}n -> } \ldots + 3\,\ce{^{1}_{0}n}$$

Neutrons that induce the chain reaction are produced by several ways:

• a) Reaction of $^{11}\mathrm{B}$ with $\alpha$-particles inside the reactor core
• b) Interaction of $\gamma$ rays with $^{2}\mathrm{D}$ nuclei present in the reactor coolant water
• c) Reaction of $^{9}\mathrm{Be}$ with $\alpha$-particles produced in an externally installed neutron source.

4.2 Write the nuclear reaction equations for $\textbf{(a)}$, $\textbf{(b)}$, and $\textbf{(c)}$. (3.0 pt)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-4-fig1.png

The graph above displays the percentage yield, $P(A)$, of fission products by mass number, $A$, resulting from $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ fission.

4.3 Write the main nuclear fission equation for splitting of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ upon neutron absorption. The pair of elements formed in this reaction are in the same group of Periodic Table. (3.0 pt)

4.4 Calculate the energy released in this reaction ($\Delta E$, MeV), if the binding energy $BE(^{235}\mathrm{U}) = 7.59$ MeV/nucleon and average binding energy for fission products $BE(\mathrm{fis.}) = 8.45$ MeV/nucleon. Neglect the binding energy of free neutrons. (2.0 pt)

Fission neutrons are produced with an average energy of 2 MeV and slow down through many scatterings with nuclei. After several collisions, their speed decreases until their average kinetic energy matches that of the surrounding atoms or molecules.

The $\textbf{logarithmic energy decrement}$, $\xi$, shows the average decrease per collision in the logarithm of the neutron energy:

$$\xi = \ln\left(\frac{E_{initial}}{E_{final}}\right)$$

$E_{initial}$ and $E_{final}$ are the initial and final neutron energies per collision.

$\xi$ is a constant for each type of material and does not depend on the initial neutron energy.

4.5 Determine the average number of collisions required, $n_c$, to slow a neutron from 2 MeV to 0.012 eV, using water as the moderator. $\xi$ (water) = 0.948 (2.0 pt)

In 1963, the $\textit{Urtabulak}$ gas field suffered an uncontrolled natural gas well blowout, releasing enormous volumes of burning methane.

4.6 Calculate $\Delta_r H^\circ_{298}$ ($\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) for one mole of methane combustion reaction at 298 K. Assume all species are gaseous. Use the thermodynamic data below (2.0 pt)

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \Delta_f H^\circ_{298}(\ce{CH4}) & -74.8\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ \hline \Delta_f H^\circ_{298}(\ce{H2O}, \text{gas}) & -241.8\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ \hline \Delta_f H^\circ_{298}(\ce{CO2}) & -393.5\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ \hline C_P(\ce{CH4}) & 35\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \\ \hline C_P(\ce{H2O}, \text{gas}) & 34\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \\ \hline C_P(\ce{O2}) & 29\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \\ \hline C_P(\ce{CO2}) & 37\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \end{array}$$

If you did not get an answer for 4.6, use $\Delta_r H^\circ_{298} = -750\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for further calculations.

4.7 Calculate $\Delta_r H_{2000}$ ($\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) per mole of methane combustion reaction at 2000 K. Assume all species are gaseous. (2.0 pt)

If you did not get an answer for 4.7, use $\Delta_r H_{2000} = -700\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for further calculations.

Assume that methane is flowing out the well at 101.325 kPa and 298 K with volumetric flow $Q = 2.2\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{m^3}$ per day before it catches fire.

4.8 Calculate the total energy released per day, $E$, (in $\mathrm{J\,day^{-1}}$) by complete isothermic combustion of methane at $T$ = 2000 K (2.0 pt)

The $\textit{Urtabulak}$ gas leak was ended by detonating a 30-kiloton in TNT equivalent underground nuclear explosion that collapsed the reservoir and sealed the leak. 1 ton of TNT equivalent is 4.184 GJ of energy.

4.9 Using the value from $\textbf{4.4}$, calculate the total number of fissions, $TN$, during the nuclear explosion. Calculate the mass, $m$, of enriched uranium used in the explosion (in kg), assuming it contained 90% by mass of the $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ isotope, and 33% of the $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ underwent fission. problems.title: Cardiolipins
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (6% of the total; 18 points). Cardiolipins

In this problem you are asked to be creative and build molecules from fragments. For instance, if you are required to draw a chiral phospholipid such as $\textbf{W}$ using fragments $\textit{a-e}$, it can be assembled as shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-5-fig1.png

Cardiolipins are a family of acyclic phospholipids differing in fatty acid residues. They are essential for energy production and membrane stability. Defects can lead to certain diseases. $\textbf{PL1}$ belongs to this family. Using only the structural elements $\textit{a-d}$ in the quantities stated below, it is possible to assemble the non-ionised form of $\textbf{PL1}$. R is a hydrocarbon substituent in the fatty acid structure.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-5-fig2.png

$\textbf{PL1}$ does not contain any peroxide bonds.

5.1 Tick one correct statement regarding the value of $n$ (number of type $\textit{a}$ fragments). (1.0 pt)

• (a) $n$ is an even number,
• (b) $n$ is an odd number,
• (c) $n$ can be either an odd or an even number.

Some cardiolipins are chiral molecules, even if they contain four identical fatty acid residues, as in the case of $\textbf{PL1}$. One enantiomer of $\textbf{PL1}$ is found in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and the other only in archaea. All other diastereomers of $\textbf{PL1}$ are achiral molecules, since they have a plane of symmetry. Do not consider the chirality of phosphorus atoms as stereocentres.

$\textbf{PL1}$ is a diprotic acid with the same acidic groups. Its second deprotonation is less favourable ($pK_{a2} \gg pK_{a1}$) due to the special, stable structure of monoanion $\textbf{Y}$.

5.2 Draw the structure of one enantiomer of $\textbf{PL1}$. Draw the structure of $\textbf{Y}$ in a way that shows the stabilisation that explains the difference between $pK_{a1}$ and $pK_{a2}$. Use the abbreviation R for the fatty acid residues. (6.0 pt)

A series of experiments was conducted to identify the fatty acid (RCOOH) in $\textbf{PL1}$ found predominantly in mammalian hearts. During reductive ozonolysis, RCOOH forms three different organic products in equimolar amounts.

5.3 Determine the molecular formula of the fatty acid (RCOOH), if the non-ionised form of $\textbf{PL1}$ contains 255 $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds between atoms in total. Support your answer with calculations. (4.0 pt)

If you were unable to find the structural formula of $\textbf{PL1}$, you can use $\textit{a-d}$ fragments from $\textbf{5.1}$.

100 g of RCOOH reacts with 181.0 g of iodine. RCOOH also reacts in similar way with $\textbf{X}$ and forms an adduct with an iodine mass fraction of 36.57%.

5.4 Determine the molecular formula of $\textbf{X}$. Support your answer with calculations. (2.0 pt)

The phase behavior of $\textbf{PL1}$ depends on pH. In physiological conditions, $\textbf{PL1}$ is a dianion and it forms a lamellar phase.

5.5 Which lipid phase is formed by $\textbf{PL1}$ when both acid residues in it are protonated? Note that knowledge of $\textbf{PL1}$ structure is not required to solve this question. Tick the correct answer. (2.0 pt)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-5-fig3.png

The following balanced reaction equations show the hydrolysis of phospholipids $\textbf{PL1}$-$\textbf{PL3}$:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-5-fig4.png

• The non-ionised form of $\textbf{PL2}$ contains 254 $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds between atoms in total. It is a chiral and a more symmetrical molecule than $\textbf{PL1}$,
• $\textbf{Z}$ contains C, H, and O only, and it doesn’t react with $\ce{H2}$ in the presence of a catalyst,
• Phospholipid $\textbf{PL3}$ is a charged molecule at physiological pH values, and it exists as pair of enantiomers.

5.6 Draw the structures of $\textbf{PL2}$ and $\textbf{PL3}$ using R to show the fatty acid residues. Show stereochemistry where appropriate. (3.0 pt)

problems.title: Carbon Nanorings
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (7% of the total; 83 points). Carbon Nanorings

In 2019, $\ce{C18}$, the first example of a new class of carbon allotropes called cyclo[n]carbons ($\ce{C}_n$) was detected. Cyclocarbons are monocyclic, all-carbon compounds with high strain energy and low stability. They can be generated and analysed by bond-resolved Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM). Cyclocarbons have interesting aromatic properties based on their π systems. $\ce{C13}$ has triplet ($^{3}\ce{C13}$, spin $S = 1$), and singlet ($^{1}\ce{C13}$, spin $S = 0$) forms.

6.1 Based on Hückel’s rule, fill in the table with the number of distinct aromatic ($\textbf{A}$) and anti-aromatic ($\textbf{AA}$) $\pi$-systems present in each of $\ce{C18}$, $\ce{C16}$, $^{3}\ce{C13}$, and $^{1}\ce{C13}$. $\textbf{Fill in all blanks.}$ (10.0 pt)

Later, cyclo[n]carbons $\ce{C10}$, $\ce{C12}$, $\ce{C14}$, $\ce{C20}$, and $\ce{C26}$ were generated by a combination of dehalogenation and retro-Bergman (1) reactions on a surface. AFM images taken during the synthesis of $\ce{C14}$ are shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-6-fig1.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-6-fig2.png

6.2 Draw structures $\textbf{B-D}$. Note they may contain one or more unpaired electrons. The structure of $\textbf{A}$ is given as an example. (11.0 pt)

6.3 The voltages applied during the AFM-mediated synthesis of $\ce{C}_n$ may vary. Using the given C–X bond energies, choose the possible halogen(s) in the halogenated reagent for $\ce{C18}$ synthesis via a retro-Bergman reaction with a voltage of 2.5 V acting on the electrons. (2.0 pt)

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Bond (C–X)} & \text{Bond Dissociation Energy} / \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ \hline \text{C–F} & 467 \\ \hline \text{C–Cl} & 346 \\ \hline \text{C–Br} & 290 \\ \hline \text{C–I} & 228 \end{array}$$

In 2025, the first relatively stable cyclo[48]carbon was synthesised. The molecule was stabilised by catenation (forming interlocking rings) with macrocycle $\textbf{E}$ and was first characterised by electrospray mass spectrometry in positive mode.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-6-fig3.png

6.4 In the mass spectrum obtained, four intense peaks were observed $m/z$: 591, 783, 879, and 1174. Suggest the identity of these ions. Use integer atomic masses and assume no fragmentation happened. The ion corresponding to $m/z$ = 591 is given as an example. (12.0 pt)

Cycloparaphenylene (CPP) is another cyclic, highly-strained molecule commonly called a carbon nanohoop. The synthesis of the smallest known member, [5]CPP, is shown below, where $\ce{PhI(OAc)2}$ acts as a two electron oxidant.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-6-fig4.png

(equiv. = Equivalent, excess = Excess)

6.5 Draw the structures of $\textbf{F-L}$. (24.0 pt)

Next generation nanobelts were constructed from porphyrin rings and triple bonds using the template synthesis method. $\textit{Hint:}$ $\textbf{M}$ is the thermodynamic product and has four types of protons.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-6-fig5.png

(equiv. = Equivalent)

6.6 Draw the structures of $\textbf{M-R}$. (20.0 pt)

When aromatic rings are joined to form a macrocycle, oxidation or reduction can produce global aromaticity, in which π electrons are delocalised around the entire macrocycle. Only the π system forming the continuous conjugated pathway around the ring participates in this delocalisation. As an example, [n]CPPs can become globally aromatic upon addition or removal of electrons. The number of π electrons is counted only along the bold pathway shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-6-fig6.png

When $\textbf{P6}$ is oxidised, it can exhibit global aromaticity and global anti-aromaticity.

6.7 Based on Hückel’s rule, find the minimum number of electrons, $n(e)$, from $\textbf{P6}$ that should be removed to achieve global aromaticity. Write the total number of π electrons, $n(t)$, in the global aromatic system. (4.0 pt)

problems.title: Nitrogen Fixation

The Haber–Bosch process is the principal industrial method for ammonia production. A simplified diagram of an ammonia synthesis plant is shown below.

7.1 Tick the gases contained in $\textbf{M1}$ and $\textbf{M2}$; and tick the correct relationship between $x$ and $y$. (3.0 pt)

An ammonia production complex with a capacity of 660,000 tons per year was commissioned at the $\textit{Navoiazot}$ plant in Uzbekistan, which operates with a 97.0% of overall yield.

7.2 Calculate the mass of $\ce{CH4}$ (tons) required annually to produce 660,000 tons of ammonia, if the $\textit{Navoiazot}$ operates according to the $\textbf{Fig. 1}$. (8.0 pt)

Consider a model of a real reaction system, which includes recirculation of reagents. An open system operates in a cyclic mode. Each cycle consists of four steps:

Nitrogen fixation can also be achieved via binary nitrides (compounds containing $\ce{N^{3-}}$). Such nitrides $\textbf{7}$, $\textbf{8}$, $\textbf{9}$ were obtained from pure elements. Removing $\ce{CO2}$ gas from the atmosphere is key to combat climate change. One promising solution is the photocatalytic reduction of $\ce{CO2}$ to CO using molecular catalyst $\textbf{1}$.

Problem 9 (7% of the total; 53 points). Cyclodextrin Chemistry

Cyclodextrins (CD) are a family of cyclic oligosaccharides, consisting of glucose subunits joined by α-1,4-glycosidic bonds. The three most common cyclodextrins (α-, β-, γ-cyclodextrin) contain 6, 7, and 8 α-D-glucopyranoside units, respectively.

CDs combine macrocyclic properties with glucose chemistry, which was demonstrated in the synthesis of $\textbf{X}$. Primary and secondary hydroxy groups show different reactivity due to being a part of CDs. Stoddart $\textit{et al.}$ synthesised compound $\textbf{K}$, where only one OH group remained free per glucopyranoside unit.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2026-9-fig2.png

equiv. = equivalent
